descs.en: He has one rule: nothing happens while she’s his student. She has a calendar with 266 squares, and an end date.

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Dr. Miles Wei, 31, lecturer in physics, holds office hours on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Shen Yu Jie, final-year student and the best mind in the department, comes on Wednesdays. Every Wednesday. With problems she has already solved.

He has one rule: nothing happens while she is a student in his department. He draws it on his chalkboard as a flat line. She adds an end date. 20 June, 16:00. Then she makes a calendar, two hundred and sixty-six squares long, and draws a physically inaccurate atom in every one.

Between them stand sticky-note physics jokes, a department that has started a betting pool, a supervisor who smokes on a balcony she isn’t allowed on, a mother who calls her daughter the Perfect Jewel in front of guests, a diplomat with a secret, and a grant nobody applied for.

Proof by Induction is a bright, slow-burn campus romance about waiting, about being taken seriously, and about a man who stopped laughing at seventeen and a woman who makes him start again.

The main story is told across four volumes and is complete. Side stories at the end can be read any time. Miles first appears as a side character in Every Flower in the Shop, but this book stands on its own.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
This is a gentle book, but it has some hard moments:

• Emotional control and coercion by a parent, including being cut off financially and made to leave home (Volume Two and Volume Three)

• Online gossip and sexist rumours about a student (Rumours in the Department Kitchen)

• A character coming out to his family at a dinner table, and a parent walking out (The Perfect Jewel Says No)

• Illness with a high fever (Miles Gets Sick and Nobody Notices)

• A relationship between a lecturer and a student that stays strictly non-romantic until she has graduated, and is declared to the department

• Love scenes between the couple after graduation. They are sensual but not explicit (Yu Jie Gets a Job, The Night She Made Him Dance in the Empty Lab)

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
Miles Wei walked into Every Flower in the Shop for one scene, dropped his clicker, asked Elowen if she was happy, and wouldn’t leave my head. This is his book.

I wanted a love story where the most romantic thing anyone does is take the other person’s mind seriously, and where waiting is not a delay but the point. The physics is real, kept at the level of a story: the harmonic oscillator, entropy as counting, strained graphene, and analogue black holes made in water tanks, which real laboratories build.

The jokes are, regrettably, also real. Thank you for reading.

chapters.title: The Girl Who Was Definitely Not Stuck on Quantum Mechanics
chapters.desc: Shen Yu Jie walks into his office with a problem she solved last year. He solves it anyway. Badly, on purpose, she thinks. She’s wrong.
chapters.epigraph: “I have a question about the harmonic oscillator.” “It’s Wednesday.” “I know.”
chapters.content:
Office 412 on the fourth floor of the Hall of Science had a sign on the door that said:

DR. MILES WEI Office hours: Tuesdays and Thursdays, 3–5 p.m. (Other times: please email. I will reply. Eventually.)

Someone had added, underneath, in green marker, a very small drawing of a cat in a box with a question mark over its head. Miles had not drawn it. He did not know who had. He had looked at it every morning for three years and decided, every morning, that it was funny and also slightly wrong, because the cat in Schrödinger’s thought experiment was never actually in a superposition of confused.

At 3:47 p.m. on the second Wednesday of September, someone knocked.

Miles was at his chalkboard. Not a whiteboard. The department had put whiteboards in every office five years ago, and Miles had gone to a hardware shop the same weekend, bought two tins of chalkboard paint, and painted the whole back wall of 412 himself, badly, in a single afternoon. Professor Zhou, the head of department, had come in on Monday and looked at it for a long time and then left without saying anything. Miles took this as permission.

He was halfway through a line of algebra. He didn’t turn round.

“It’s open,” he said. “Unless you’re from facilities about the radiator, in which case I’m not here.”

The door opened.

“I’m not from facilities,” said a girl’s voice. “Is the radiator broken?”

“It makes a noise like a whale,” said Miles, still writing. “Every forty minutes. I timed it. I think it’s trying to communicate.”

“What does it say?”

He stopped writing.

Nobody had ever asked him that before. He had told the whale joke to four colleagues and the facilities man, and all five had laughed politely and changed the subject.

He turned round.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was standing in the doorway with a notebook against her chest. She was about twenty-two. She wore a yellow sundress, white trainers that had once been very expensive and were now covered in what looked like biro, and an enormous grey cardigan with the sleeves pushed up. Her hair was dark and long and held up on the back of her head in a tortoiseshell claw clip that was losing the battle. There were at least four pens stuck into it.

She was smiling at him as if she had just won something.

“Hello,” she said. “I’m Shen Yu Jie. Final year. Professor Gao’s group.” She held up the notebook. “I have a question about the harmonic oscillator.”

Miles looked at her. Then at the door, where his office hours sign was. Then at the calendar on the wall.

“It’s Wednesday,” he said.

“I know.”

“My office hours are Tuesdays and Thursdays.”

“I know that too.” She came in without being asked and sat down in the chair in front of his desk. The chair creaked. “But on Tuesdays and Thursdays there are about fifteen second-years in here asking about their homework, and I didn’t want to wait in a queue behind a boy who thinks Planck’s constant is a type of sandwich.”

Miles opened his mouth. Then he closed it.

There was a second-year called Bai Tianyu who had, last Thursday, asked whether Planck’s constant was the same everywhere or “like, regional”. It had taken Miles twenty minutes to recover.

“You’re not in my course,” he said.

“No. I took Quantum Two last year with Professor Lin. I got the top mark.” She said it without any pride at all, as a simple fact, like it’s raining. Then she opened her notebook and turned it round so he could see. “But I’m stuck. On this. Look.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He looked.

It was the quantum harmonic oscillator. The most famous problem in quantum mechanics: a particle in a potential shaped like a bowl, like a ball rolling back and forth at the bottom of a valley, except that because it was a quantum particle it couldn’t just sit still at the bottom. It had to have a minimum energy, always. It could never stop moving. Every student in the world learned it in their second year.

Her notebook had three pages on it. Neat handwriting. Clear steps. She had written down the Schrödinger equation, set up the problem, introduced the raising and lowering operators, which was the elegant way of doing it, the way most students only learned at the end of the course.

And then, on the third page, she had stopped. There was a big question mark. And underneath, in smaller writing: ???? help.

Miles looked at the question mark.

Then he looked back at the three pages before it.

“You’re not stuck,” he said.

Shen Yu Jie’s smile didn’t move. But something behind it flickered.

“I am,” she said. “Very stuck. Look. Page three. Question mark.”

“You’ve used the ladder operators.” He tapped the second page. “Most second-years don’t meet them until the end of the course. You’ve normalised the ground state. That’s the hard part. After that it’s one line. You apply the raising operator and you get the next state. You must know that, because you wrote it here.” He turned back to page one, where in the margin, very small, almost hidden, she had written the final answer. The energy levels. Perfectly. (n + ½)ħω. “You solved it before you started.”

The office was quiet. Out in the corridor, someone laughed.

Then the radiator, right on schedule, made a long, low, mournful sound like a whale calling across an ocean.

Shen Yu Jie looked at the radiator. Then back at him.

“It says hello,” she said. “The whale. I think it’s lonely.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He should have sent her away.

He knew that, afterwards. He knew it while it was happening. She was a student. She was in his department. She had come on the wrong day with a problem she had already solved, and there was only one reason a student did that, and it was not the harmonic oscillator.

But she was looking at him with that winning smile, and under it there was something else, something that looked very much like a dare, and he had been in this office by himself with the whale for five years and the cactus for three.

So instead, he picked up a piece of chalk.

“Fine,” said Miles. “You’re stuck. Let me un-stick you.”

He turned to the chalkboard. And he solved the quantum harmonic oscillator for her from the beginning, the long way, the hard way, with the differential equation and the Hermite polynomials and no ladder operators at all, the way they did it in 1926, filling the whole wall with chalk. It took twenty-five minutes. He didn’t look at her once. He explained every step as he went, out loud, the way he did in his lectures: why the particle couldn’t stop, why the energy came in steps like a staircase, why the lowest step wasn’t zero, why nature didn’t allow anything to be perfectly still.

“It’s the uncertainty principle,” he said, writing. “If it stopped at the bottom, you’d know exactly where it was and exactly how fast it was going. Zero and zero. And the universe won’t let you know both. So it has to keep moving. Just a little. Forever. Even at absolute zero.” He drew a small curve at the bottom of the bowl. “It’s called zero-point energy. The universe has a rule that nothing is ever allowed to be completely at rest.”

He stepped back.

The whole back wall of office 412 was covered in white chalk. He had chalk on his sleeve, on his hand, probably on his face. He turned round.

She wasn’t looking at the board.

She was looking at him. Her chin was on her hand. The winning smile had gone. What was left was something softer and much more surprised.

“That,” she said, “was the most boring way anyone has ever solved that problem.”

“Yes,” said Miles. “On purpose. So you’d see that you already know the interesting way.”

She stared at him.

“You did the hard version,” she said slowly, “to prove I didn’t need help.”

“You don’t.” He put the chalk down. “You need a different excuse for coming on a Wednesday.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went very pink.

He had not expected that. She had seemed like someone who didn’t go pink. She stood up quickly, and her chair creaked, and one of the pens fell out of her claw clip and rolled under his desk.

“Thank you, Dr. Wei,” she said. “That was very helpful.”

“I didn’t help.”

“It was very helpful anyway.” She picked up her notebook. She went to the door. Then she stopped, with her hand on the frame, and turned round.

“What do you say back?” she asked. “To the whale?”

Miles looked at the radiator.

“Nothing,” he said. “I don’t speak whale.”

“You should learn.” She smiled. A real one this time, crooked, not winning anything. “It’s been calling for three years. Somebody should answer.”

She left.

✦ ✦ ✦

He stood in the middle of his office for a long time, covered in chalk.

Then he crouched down and found her pen under the desk. It was purple. It had a small plastic cat on the end of it, with a question mark painted on its head.

He looked at the pen. Then at the door, where, under his office hours, a small green cat in a box looked back at him with a question mark over its head.

He had been looking at that drawing every morning for three years.

He put the pen in his top drawer. He did not throw it away.

At twenty to five the radiator called again, long and low and mournful, across an ocean.

Miles looked at it.

“Hello,” he said, very quietly.

Then he looked round the empty office to make sure nobody had heard. That was absurd, because nobody ever came to office 412 on a Wednesday. Nobody, until today.

And on Thursday, at three o’clock, when fifteen second-years crowded into office 412 with their homework, and Bai Tianyu asked whether ħ was pronounced “h-bar” or “h-slash”, Miles answered him patiently and found that he kept looking at the door.

She didn’t come.

She came on Wednesday.

chapters.title: Office Hours Are Tuesdays and Thursdays
chapters.desc: She comes on Wednesdays. Every Wednesday. He starts leaving the door open.
chapters.content:
Shen Yu Jie had a roommate called Tao Tao, who was studying biology and had opinions about everything.

“You went to his office,” said Tao Tao, on Wednesday night, lying upside down on Yu Jie’s bed with her feet on the wall. “On purpose. On the wrong day. With the harmonic oscillator.”

“I needed help.”

“You got a hundred in Quantum Two. Professor Lin cried. He said you were the best student he’d had in twenty years. He cried, Jie Jie.” Tao Tao waved a packet of shrimp crisps. “You don’t need help with the harmonic oscillator. You could teach the harmonic oscillator to the harmonic oscillator.”

Yu Jie was sitting at her desk with her back to the room, drawing on a sticky note. She didn’t turn round.

“He did it the long way,” she said.

“What?”

“He did it the long way. On purpose. The whole wall. Hermite polynomials. Twenty-five minutes.” She put down her pen. “To prove I didn’t need him to do it at all.”

Tao Tao stopped crunching.

“That’s,” she said, “either the most insulting thing a man has ever done to you or the most romantic, and I genuinely can’t tell which.”

Yu Jie stuck the sticky note to the edge of her monitor. It was a very small drawing of a whale with a speech bubble. The speech bubble said: hello?

“Neither can I,” she said. “That’s why I’m going back.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went back the next Wednesday, at 3:45, with perturbation theory.

He was at the chalkboard again. She knocked. He said, “It’s open,” without turning round, and then, when she came in, he did turn round, and looked at her, and looked at the calendar, and looked back at her.

“It’s Wednesday,” he said.

“It is,” she agreed, and sat down.

He didn’t send her away.

He didn’t do it the long way either, this time. He looked at her notebook, at the three neat pages and the question mark at the end, and then he said, “What’s the real question?”

“That is the real question.”

“You’ve done first-order perturbation theory perfectly. You’ve done second order. The question mark is at the bit you’ve already written the answer to.” He pointed. The answer was in the margin again, very small. “You keep doing that. Hiding the answer in the margin.”

She looked at the margin.

“Maybe I want someone to find it,” she said.

He looked at her for a moment. She couldn’t read his face at all. He had the kind of face that seemed to be thinking about four things at once, three of which were probably equations.

“Then here’s a real question,” he said, and turned to the board and wrote one.

It was not perturbation theory. It was something else, something she had never seen before: a particle in a potential that was almost a harmonic oscillator, but not quite, bent slightly to one side, like a bowl someone had sat on. He wrote it out in four lines and stepped back.

“Nobody’s solved that one exactly,” he said. “I don’t know the answer. I think it might be interesting.”

She stared at the board.

Then she stood up, took the chalk out of his hand without asking, and started writing.

✦ ✦ ✦

They were still there at six.

The radiator called eight times. Neither of them noticed after the fourth. The whole chalkboard was covered and then wiped and covered again, her handwriting and his tangled together, arrows and crossings-out and a small drawing of a sat-on bowl that she had added in the corner with a face on it. At some point he had sat down on the edge of his desk and she had taken his chair, and they were arguing, quite loudly, about whether the second term could be ignored.

“It can’t,” she said. “Look. If you throw it away, the energy goes negative. Negative. That’s nonsense.”

“It’s not nonsense if the bend is small enough.”

“It’s not small enough. You made it up. You decided it was small because it was easier.”

He opened his mouth to argue. Then he looked at the board. Then he looked at it for a long time.

“You’re right,” he said.

She stopped.

People did not often say that to her. Her mother never had. Her father didn’t speak to her enough to say it. Her brother said “you’re right” the way you’d say “fine” to a child who wanted a sweet.

He said it like a fact. Like a piece of data. As if she had found a mistake in the universe and he was simply recording it.

“You’re right,” Miles said again, standing up and rubbing out the second term with the side of his hand, getting chalk all down his sleeve. “I was being lazy. It does matter. That changes the whole thing.” He turned round, and there was chalk on his face now, a white smudge across one cheekbone, and he was looking at her with an expression she had never seen on a lecturer before, or on anyone: pure, uncomplicated delight. “That’s really good. You saw that in about four seconds. I’ve been looking at this for a week.”

She didn’t know what to do with her hands. She put them in the pockets of her cardigan.

“You have chalk on your face,” she said.

He touched his face. He made it worse.

“Other side,” she said.

He tried the other side. Now there were two white smudges, one on each cheekbone, perfectly matched, like a very nervous tiger.

“Better?” said Miles.

She looked at him for a long moment, with her hands in her cardigan pockets, very seriously.

“Much better,” said Yu Jie. “It’s symmetrical now.”

She didn’t tell him: not for the next hour, while they argued about the second term, and not when she left. On the way down the stairs she started laughing and couldn’t stop until the second floor. He found out at nine that night, in the bathroom mirror, and stood looking at himself for some time.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came every Wednesday after that.

She never came on Tuesdays or Thursdays. On Tuesdays and Thursdays office 412 was full of second-years, and she would walk past at three-thirty on her way to the lab and hear Bai Tianyu asking whether the wave function “like, physically exists” and Miles saying, with infinite patience, “That’s actually a very old and very good question,” and she would smile and keep walking.

On Wednesdays she brought a notebook with a problem she had already solved, with a question mark at the end and the answer hidden in the margin. And he would find the answer, and say “You’ve already done this,” and she would say “Have I?”, and he would sigh and write something new on the board. Something real. Something nobody knew the answer to yet.

She noticed things.

She noticed he drank tea, not coffee, out of a mug that said WORLD’S OKAYEST SON in faded letters. She noticed he had an egg sandwich for lunch every day, from the same machine on the second floor, and that the machine was always out of everything else by noon and he never seemed to mind. She noticed there was a cactus on his windowsill in a small blue pot, grey-green and rather sad, with a label stuck to the pot in his handwriting: SCHRÖDINGER.

“Is it alive?” she asked, on the second Wednesday.

“I don’t know,” said Miles. “I’ve decided not to check. That way it’s both.”

She laughed so hard she had to put her head down on his desk.

He looked at her laughing, his chalk in his hand, with an expression of mild alarm, as if a beaker had unexpectedly started fizzing.

“That was a joke,” he said slowly. “Wasn’t it. I made a joke.”

“You made a joke, Dr. Wei.”

He looked at the cactus. Then back at her.

“Nobody usually laughs,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the fourth Wednesday, she came at 3:45 and the door was open.

Not unlocked. Open. Propped wide with a heavy physics textbook on the floor.

She stood in the corridor looking at it.

He had never propped it before. Every other week she had knocked, and he had said “It’s open” without turning round. This week there was nothing to knock on. The door stood open to the corridor, and inside, at the chalkboard, he was writing something, and on the desk in front of the chair she always sat in there was a second mug. A plain white one. With a teabag in it, and steam coming off it, already poured.

She walked in.

He didn’t turn round.

“Jasmine,” he said, writing. “The machine downstairs only does jasmine or something that claims to be English Breakfast and isn’t. I guessed.”

She sat down. She picked up the mug. It was the right temperature. She took a sip.

“I like jasmine,” she said.

“Good,” said Miles, and kept writing.

“You guessed,” she said.

“I estimated.” He didn’t turn round. “Last Wednesday a teabag wrapper fell out of your cardigan pocket when you took your pen out. Jasmine. With three White Rabbit wrappers. I put them in the bin after you left.” A pause. The chalk squeaked. “It was an educated guess. Most guesses in physics are.”

She looked at the back of his head, at the piece of hair that stuck up.

“You noticed my rubbish,” she said.

“I notice everything,” said Miles, to the board. “It’s a professional failing.”

He didn’t say anything about the door. She didn’t ask.

But when she left at six, she looked back from the end of the corridor, and the door to office 412 was still standing open, propped with Principles of Quantum Mechanics, and Dr. Miles Wei was still at the chalkboard, looking, she thought, at the place where she had been sitting.

chapters.title: The Harmonic Oscillator Is Not a Metaphor
chapters.desc: She makes it one anyway. He explains zero-point energy to a room full of second-years and accidentally confesses something.
chapters.epigraph: “Nothing is allowed to be completely at rest. Not even at absolute zero.” — Dr. Miles Wei, Quantum Mechanics, Lecture 7
chapters.content:
Miles taught second-year Quantum Mechanics on Tuesdays and Thursdays at ten, in Lecture Theatre C, to a hundred and forty students who mostly wanted to be somewhere else.

He didn’t blame them. It was ten in the morning and quantum mechanics was strange, and most of them had chosen physics because they liked the parts that made sense. He did his best. He drew pictures. He told them about the whale. He tried to make them see that the strangeness was the point: that the universe, at the very bottom, was not a clockwork machine but something much odder and more beautiful, something that refused to be pinned down.

Lecture seven was the harmonic oscillator.

He had given this lecture five times. He knew it by heart. He walked into Lecture Theatre C at 9:58 with his notes under his arm and a piece of chalk in his pocket, put the notes on the lectern without looking at them, turned to face a hundred and forty half-asleep second-years, and saw, in the very back row, in the corner seat by the door, a yellow sundress.

He stopped walking.

She waved. A small wave. Just her fingers, over the top of the desk.

Bai Tianyu, in the front row, turned round to see what Dr. Wei was looking at, and then turned back, and looked at Dr. Wei, and his eyes went very wide.

Miles picked up his chalk.

“Good morning,” he said. “Today: why nothing in the universe is allowed to sit still.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was not his best lecture.

It was not his worst, either. He got through the setup. He drew the bowl. He drew the little ball at the bottom, rolling back and forth. He explained why a classical ball could stop at the bottom and a quantum one couldn’t.

But every time he turned round from the board, his eyes went to the back row. And every time, she was looking at him. Not at the board. At him. With her chin on her hand.

At one point he wrote ħ on the board and realised he had drawn the little line through the h four times.

“So,” he said, turning round, clearing his throat, “the uncertainty principle tells us that the particle can’t have exactly zero position and exactly zero momentum at the same time. Which means it can’t be perfectly still at the bottom of the bowl. Which means the lowest possible energy isn’t zero. It’s this.” He tapped the board. “Half of ħω. Zero-point energy.”

A hand went up in the middle of the theatre. A girl with glasses.

“Dr. Wei. Does that mean it’s, like, always moving? Forever?”

“Yes,” said Miles. “Even at absolute zero. Even if you take away every last bit of heat. It still jiggles. Just a little. The universe has a rule that nothing is ever allowed to be completely at rest.”

The girl wrote it down.

In the back row, Shen Yu Jie raised her hand.

The theatre went quiet. A hundred and thirty-nine heads turned round. Nobody raised their hand in the back row of Lecture Theatre C. The back row was where you went to sleep.

Miles looked at her.

“Yes,” he said. “Back row.”

She stood up. She didn’t have to. Nobody stood up to ask questions. But she stood, in her yellow sundress and her enormous cardigan, with three pens in her hair, and said in a clear, carrying voice:

“Dr. Wei. Is that true of people too?”

✦ ✦ ✦

There was a silence.

A hundred and forty second-years looked at the girl in the back row. Then at their lecturer. Then back at the girl. Bai Tianyu’s mouth was slightly open.

“I’m sorry?” said Miles.

“The zero-point energy,” said Yu Jie. “You said nothing in the universe is ever allowed to be completely at rest. Is that true of people? Or just particles?”

Somebody in the middle rows giggled and was shushed.

Miles stood at the front of Lecture Theatre C with chalk on his fingers and looked at her for a long moment.

He knew what she was doing. She was being funny. She was being bold, the way she was bold every Wednesday, arriving on the wrong day with a problem she had already solved. She was standing up in the back row of his lecture to see what he would do.

He should have made a joke. Something about people being too big for quantum effects. Something that would make the theatre laugh and let him move on.

Instead, he heard himself answer the question.

“I think it is,” said Miles slowly. “I think people are a bit like that. You can try to make yourself completely still. You can take away everything. Every distraction. Every person. You can sit in a room with a cactus for three years and tell yourself you’re perfectly at rest.” He looked down at the chalk in his hand. “But there’s always something left over. A little bit of energy you can’t get rid of. The lowest you can go isn’t zero. It’s never zero.” He looked up. “Something always keeps moving.”

The theatre was completely silent.

In the back row, Shen Yu Jie was no longer smiling. She was standing very still, which, he thought distantly, was ironic.

Then Bai Tianyu, in the front row, said, very loudly and with total sincerity, “Dr. Wei, is that going to be on the exam?”

The theatre exploded.

✦ ✦ ✦

He finished the lecture. He didn’t remember how. He packed up his notes at 11:30 and the students filed out past him, and three different girls looked at him as they went with expressions he didn’t understand, and one boy said, “Deep lecture, Dr. Wei,” and patted him on the shoulder.

The back row was empty. She had gone out of the door by the corner seat before the lights came up.

He went up the steps to the back row, which he had not done once in five years of teaching in Lecture Theatre C, and stood by the corner seat.

From up here the chalkboard looked very small and the lecturer did not. You could see everything from the back row: every time the lecturer turned round, every time he looked up, which way his eyes went.

On the desk was a White Rabbit wrapper, smoothed out flat. On the inside of it, in purple biro, in round handwriting, very small:

½ħω. Never zero.

He stood there for a long time. Then he folded it in half and put it in his wallet, behind his staff card, and told himself it was because someone ought to tidy the theatre.

He went back to office 412 and shut the door and sat at his desk and put his face in his hands.

“A cactus for three years,” he said into his palms. “You said a cactus for three years. In front of a hundred and forty people.”

On the windowsill, Schrödinger said nothing. Schrödinger was either alive or dead and, either way, was not going to help.

Someone knocked.

He looked up. It was Tuesday. It was 11:42. His office hours didn’t start until three.

“It’s open,” he said.

Dr. Fang Hao put his head round the door. Fang Hao was the astrophysicist in office 413 next door: thirty-five, round-faced, cheerful, married to a pastry chef, and the single greatest source of gossip on the fourth floor. He was holding a paper bag that smelled of butter.

“Croissant?” said Fang Hao.

“No, thank you.”

Fang Hao came in anyway and shut the door behind him and sat on the edge of Miles’s desk and took a croissant out of the bag and ate half of it in one bite.

“So,” he said, through crumbs. “I hear you gave a very moving lecture this morning.”

Miles closed his eyes.

“Three different second-years have already posted about it,” said Fang Hao happily. “One of them wrote, and I quote, ‘Dr. Wei just compared himself to a lonely quantum particle in front of the whole class and I think I’m going to cry.’ It has four hundred likes.” He finished the croissant. “Also, apparently a girl stood up in the back row and asked if it applied to people. Final-year. Yellow dress. Gao’s group.” He looked at Miles over the top of the paper bag. “The same yellow dress that comes up to the fourth floor every Wednesday at quarter to four and doesn’t leave until six.”

Miles opened his eyes.

“How do you know that?”

“Miles,” said Fang Hao gently. “My office is next door. The walls are cardboard. I hear the two of you arguing about potential wells every Wednesday for two hours. Last week she called you lazy and you said you’re right.” He took out the second croissant. “I’ve never heard you say you’re right to anyone. Not to me, not to Zhou, not to the facilities man about the radiator.”

“She was right.”

“I know. That’s not the point.” Fang Hao bit the second croissant. “The point is, she’s a student. In this department. And you’re a lecturer. And the walls are cardboard, and I’m not the only one who can hear.”

Miles looked at him.

“Nothing is happening,” he said.

“I know nothing is happening. You’re you.” Fang Hao stood up and brushed crumbs off his trousers. “I’m just saying. Be careful, Miles. People talk. Gao’s already noticed. She asked me last week why her best student keeps coming back from the fourth floor with chalk on her cardigan.”

He went out. At the door, he turned back.

“For the record,” he said, “I thought it was a lovely lecture.”

He shut the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles sat at his desk.

Then he opened his top drawer. The purple pen with the plastic cat on the end was still there, where he had put it on the first Wednesday.

He took it out and turned it over in his fingers.

Is that true of people too?

He had told a hundred and forty second-years that nothing was allowed to be completely at rest. That there was always something left over. That the lowest you could go was never zero.

He had been talking about physics. Mostly.

He put the pen back in the drawer and closed it, and pulled a pad of paper towards him, and started writing out a rule.

chapters.title: Miles Wei Has One Rule
chapters.desc: He turns her down kindly, with a diagram on the chalkboard. He accidentally gives her a date.
chapters.epigraph: “Not while you’re a student in this department.” “And when I’m not?” “…I didn’t think about that part.”
chapters.content:
On Wednesday, she came at 3:45 and knocked, and he said, “It’s open,” the way he always did.

But the chalkboard was clean.

Completely clean. Every equation from last week wiped off, the black paint shining. And in the middle of it, in neat white chalk, there was a diagram.

Yu Jie stopped in the doorway.

It was a graph. A horizontal line across the bottom, labelled TIME. A vertical line on the left, labelled nothing at all. And across the middle, a single straight line, very carefully drawn, perfectly flat, from one side of the board to the other.

Above the line, he had written: Professional distance.

Below it, smaller: (constant).

She looked at the graph. Then at him. He was sitting behind his desk, not at the board, with his hands folded in front of him like a man about to give bad news to a patient.

“Please sit down,” said Miles.

She sat down. She held her notebook against her chest.

“Is this about the lecture?” she said.

“Partly.”

“I’m sorry. I shouldn’t have stood up. It was—”

“It was a very good question.” He looked at his folded hands. “That isn’t the problem. The problem is that I answered it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He had clearly practised.

She could tell, because he spoke in complete paragraphs, and because every so often he stopped and looked slightly to the left, as if reading from notes written on the inside of his own head.

“You’re a student,” he said. “In this department. I’m a lecturer. I don’t teach you, and I don’t supervise you, and I’m not on any of your committees. But I’m in this department, and you’re in this department, and there are rules about that, and there are also things that aren’t rules but should be.” He paused. “And my colleague next door can hear everything through the wall.”

“Dr. Fang.”

“Dr. Fang.” He looked pained. “Who has told me, quite kindly, that people are talking. And that Professor Gao has noticed. And that a second-year wrote online that I compared myself to a lonely particle.”

“You did, a bit.”

“I know I did.” He took off his glasses and rubbed his eyes and put them back on. “So. I’ve made a rule. For myself. Not for you. You can do what you like. But I’m telling you what it is, because I think you should know, and because I don’t think it would be fair to keep seeing you on Wednesdays without saying it.”

He stood up and went to the chalkboard and tapped the flat line.

“Nothing happens,” said Miles, “while you’re a student in this department.”

Yu Jie looked at the line.

“Nothing,” he repeated. “No—” he made a vague gesture with the chalk “—anything. You can still come on Wednesdays, if you want. I’ll even make tea. We can still argue about bent harmonic oscillators. That’s physics. Physics is allowed.” He tapped the line again. “But it stays flat. Constant. That’s the rule.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She was quiet for a long moment.

She had been turned down before. Not often. She was Shen Yu Jie, and she was pretty, and her family owned half the harbour, and boys usually didn’t turn her down so much as follow her around holding things. But it had happened twice, and both times it had been unpleasant: once with a laugh, once with a lecture about how she was too much.

This was nothing like that.

He had drawn her a graph.

He had stayed up, she thought, probably most of the night, working out how to say it kindly. He had wiped his whole chalkboard, the board he had painted himself, so the graph would be the only thing on it. He had used the word fair.

And he had said anything, with a vague gesture, as if he didn’t trust himself to say what anything was.

She put her notebook down.

“Can I ask a question?” she said.

“Of course.”

“Is it a rule because you don’t want to,” said Yu Jie, “or because you can’t?”

He went still with the chalk in his hand.

She watched him think about it. She was learning his face. He didn’t lie well; she suspected he had never tried. He looked at the flat line on the chalkboard, and then at the floor, and then at the cactus, and then, finally, at her.

“It’s a rule,” he said.

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It’s the only answer I’m allowed to give.” He put the chalk down on the ledge. “That’s rather the point of the rule.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She looked at the graph.

Professional distance. (constant). A flat line, from one edge of the board to the other. TIME along the bottom.

Then she stood up, and walked to the board, and picked up the chalk he had just put down.

“You’ve drawn the axis wrong,” she said.

“I’m sorry?”

“Your time axis.” She tapped it. “It doesn’t go on forever. It can’t. I’m a final-year student. I graduate in June.” She looked at him over her shoulder. “When, exactly, do I stop being a student in this department?”

He blinked.

“I—when you graduate,” he said. “Obviously.”

“Which is when?”

“The ceremony is the twentieth of June. It finishes at four.” He paused. “Technically you’re a student until the end of the ceremony. That’s when you get the certificate. At four o’clock you’re an alumna.”

“Four o’clock on the twentieth of June,” said Yu Jie.

“Yes.”

She turned back to the board.

At the far right-hand end of his perfectly flat line, she drew a short vertical mark, very neat. Beside it she wrote, in small white letters: 20 June, 16:00.

Then, very carefully, she drew what came after.

The flat line stopped at the mark. And on the other side of it, she drew nothing at all. No line. Just empty board, black and shining.

She put the chalk back on the ledge and stepped away.

“There,” she said. “Now it’s a proper graph. A function that’s constant on a finite interval.” She looked at him. “You didn’t say anything about what happens after the interval ends.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles stood in front of his own chalkboard and looked at it for a very long time.

At his flat line. At her mark. 20 June, 16:00. At the empty space after it, where she hadn’t drawn anything at all.

She watched him understand what he had done.

He had made a rule. A careful, kind, responsible rule. He had stayed up all night to make it. And he had defined it, without realising, in terms of a date. A specific date and time, nine months away, written on his own chalkboard in her handwriting.

He hadn’t told her no. He had told her not yet. And he had told her exactly how long not yet would last.

“I didn’t,” he said slowly, “think about that part.”

“I know,” said Yu Jie. She picked up her bag. “You’re very clever, Dr. Wei. But you only ever solve for the bit of the problem you’re looking at.”

She looked at the board one more time.

“Also, your line is very straight.”

“Thank you.”

“Suspiciously straight. Nobody draws a line that straight freehand.” She narrowed her eyes. “Did you use a ruler?”

He looked at the floor. “The metre rule from the second-year teaching lab. I borrowed it at seven this morning.”

“So you stayed up all night working out how to turn me down kindly,” said Yu Jie, “and then you came in at seven and borrowed a metre rule so the line would be perfect.”

“It had to be constant,” said Miles. “That was the whole point.”

She pressed her lips together very hard so as not to smile at him, and failed.

She went to the door. Then she stopped and turned round.

“Same time next Wednesday?” she said. “For physics. Which is allowed.”

He looked at her. Then at the board. Then back at her.

“Yes,” said Miles, a little helplessly. “Physics is allowed.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went down four flights of stairs without touching any of them.

Out in the courtyard of the Hall of Science, in the September sun, she took out her phone and opened her calendar and scrolled forward, past October, past New Year, past spring, all the way to the twentieth of June.

She made a new event. Four o’clock in the afternoon.

She stared at the name box. Then she typed:

The end of the interval.

Up on the fourth floor, in office 412, Miles Wei stood in front of his chalkboard for twenty minutes without moving. Then he picked up the rubber to wipe it clean.

He wiped his flat line off. He wiped off Professional distance and (constant) and the time axis.

He stopped at the little vertical mark at the end. 20 June, 16:00.

He looked at it for a long time.

He didn’t wipe that off. He left it there, in the bottom right-hand corner of his chalkboard, small and neat in her handwriting, where nobody else would notice.

It stayed there all year.

chapters.title: A Countdown Disguised as a Semester
chapters.desc: Yu Jie makes a calendar. Miles finds it. He says nothing. Then he gives her a problem whose answer is a number she knows very well.
chapters.content:
The calendar was Tao Tao’s idea, technically.

“If you’re going to be insane about it,” said Tao Tao, on Saturday, lying on the floor of their room with her feet on Yu Jie’s bed, “at least be organised. Make a chart. Tick off the days. Like a prisoner.”

“I’m not a prisoner.”

“You’re counting down two hundred and seventy days until a man you’ve known for a month is allowed to have coffee with you. That is literally what prisoners do.” Tao Tao threw a shrimp crisp at her. “I’m opening a betting pool. Half the biology department is in already. The odds on ‘she gives up by Christmas’ are terrible, I warned everyone.”

Yu Jie didn’t answer. She had already got out a large sheet of graph paper.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took her all Saturday afternoon.

She drew it in pencil first, then ink. Nine months, from the end of September to the twentieth of June, one small square for every day, arranged in rows like a periodic table. She coloured the weekends pale blue and the exam weeks red and the holidays yellow. In the bottom right-hand corner, the very last square, the twentieth of June, she drew larger than the rest and outlined in gold.

Then she sat back and looked at it and felt slightly ridiculous.

Two hundred and sixty-six squares now. She had started counting on the day of the graph.

“You need a symbol,” said Tao Tao, who had come over to look. “For crossing them off. Something meaningful. Not just an X. An X is very prison.”

Yu Jie thought about it.

Then she picked up a fine purple pen and, in the first square, the day of the graph, she drew a very small atom: a dot in the middle with three tiny elliptical orbits around it, like a cartoon of what nobody had believed atoms looked like for a hundred years.

“Why an atom?” said Tao Tao.

“Because it’s always moving,” said Yu Jie. “Even when it looks still. Zero-point energy.”

Tao Tao looked at her for a long moment.

“You,” she said, “are the most hopeless person I have ever met, and I once dated a boy who wrote me a song about mitochondria.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She folded the calendar into quarters and carried it in the back of her physics notebook, so she could draw the atoms wherever she was. In the lab. In the library. On the bus home on Sunday, to the big white house on the hill above the harbour that her mother called the family residence and Yu Jie called the museum.

Sunday dinner at the museum was at seven. It was always at seven. It had been at seven for twenty-two years.

Her mother sat at the end of the long table. Shen Ruolan was fifty-four and looked forty, with perfect skin and perfect posture and a voice like a very sharp knife wrapped in silk. Her father sat at the other end and read his phone. Her brother Yu Ming, who was thirty-four and ran the company, sat on her mother’s right and said nothing unless he was spoken to.

“You look tired,” her mother said, as the soup came.

“I’ve been in the lab.”

“You’re always in the lab.” Her mother tasted her soup. “Your skin suffers. Your hair suffers. You have ink on your hands, Yu Jie. Ink. Like a schoolgirl.” She put down her spoon. “The Lus are coming to the Foundation gala in December. Their son is back from Geneva.”

Yu Jie’s spoon stopped.

“Lu Zhiyuan,” said her mother. “The diplomat. Twenty-nine. Very good family. Very good prospects. He’s been posted back home for two years. The Foreign Affairs Office. I showed his mother your photograph, the one from your cousin’s wedding, in the blue dress. She was very impressed.”

“Ma.”

“Wear the blue dress. And do something about your hair.”

“Ma, I’m not—”

“You’re twenty-two,” said her mother. Very gently. The knife inside the silk. “You’re a beautiful girl from a very good family, and you have spent four years in a laboratory doing something nobody in this family understands. That’s fine. It’s a hobby. Every girl needs a hobby.” She picked up her spoon again. “But it’s time to think about your real future. You’re the Perfect Jewel, darling. That’s what everyone calls you. Jewels are meant to be worn.”

Yu Jie looked down at her soup.

Under the table, in her lap, her physics notebook was open on her knees, and the calendar was unfolded inside it, and she was holding the purple pen.

Nobody saw her draw the atom in today’s square. Nobody ever looked at what was in her lap.

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles found the calendar on the fifth Wednesday.

It wasn’t on purpose. She had brought a notebook with a problem in it, the way she always did, and put it down on his desk, and gone to get water from the cooler in the corridor. And while she was gone, a sheet of folded graph paper slid out of the back of the notebook and fell open on his desk.

He looked at it.

He didn’t mean to. He was going to fold it back up. But it was a grid, and he was a physicist, and it was impossible for him to look at a grid without understanding it.

Small squares. Nine rows. A periodic table of days. Weekends in blue. Exams in red. The last square, bottom right, larger, outlined in gold. And beside it, in purple ink, in her round handwriting:

20 June. 16:00. The end of the interval.

The first fourteen squares each had a very small purple atom drawn in them. A dot with three orbits. Careful. Neat. One a day.

Two hundred and fifty-five days still to go.

He sat very still at his desk with the calendar in front of him.

He heard her footsteps coming back down the corridor.

He folded the calendar along its creases, exactly as it had been, and slid it into the back of her notebook, and closed the notebook, and put it square on the desk where she had left it. When she came in with her water, he was standing at the chalkboard with his back to the room, writing something.

He didn’t say anything.

She didn’t notice anything.

He wrote the problem slowly, so his hands would stop shaking.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was a counting problem.

Not quantum mechanics. Something simpler, almost a puzzle: a particle that could take one step left or right every day, a probability for each step, a question about how many days it would take, on average, to reach a certain point. A random walk. The kind of thing they set first-years to warm up.

She looked at it, puzzled.

“This is easy,” she said.

“Humour me.”

She sat down and worked it out. It took her four minutes. She wrote the answer at the bottom and turned the notebook round.

255.

She looked at the number. She looked at it. Then she looked up at him, slowly, and her face went through about four things in a row, and the last one was pink.

He was standing at the chalkboard with his hands in his pockets, looking at the cactus.

“That’s a nice number,” said Miles, to Schrödinger.

She stared at him.

“You saw it,” she said.

“It fell out.” He didn’t look at her. “It’s a very well-made calendar. The atoms are a good touch. Physically inaccurate, but a good touch.”

“Physically inaccurate?”

“Electrons don’t orbit like that. It’s the Bohr model. It was abandoned in 1925.” He paused. “But it’s the one everyone draws. It’s the one that looks like an atom. I understand.”

She put her head down on his desk, on top of the notebook, and stayed there.

“I’m going to die,” she said, into the paper.

“Please don’t,” said Miles. “There are two hundred and fifty-five days left. It would be a waste.”

She lifted her head.

He was still looking at the cactus. But the tips of his ears had gone red.

“Dr. Wei,” she said. “Your ears have gone red.”

“Blood flow,” said Miles, to the cactus. “It’s a thermoregulatory response.”

“To what?”

There was a pause in which he could visibly be seen searching the room for a stimulus that was not her, and failing to find one.

“Insufficient data,” he said.

She put her head back down on the notebook and laughed until the radiator joined in.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went home and lay on her bed and stared at the ceiling for an hour while Tao Tao demanded to know what had happened.

“He saw it,” she said finally.

Tao Tao sat up so fast she hit her head on the bookshelf. “He saw it? The prison calendar? With the atoms?”

“He said the atoms were physically inaccurate.”

“Oh no.”

“And then he set me a problem,” said Yu Jie, “where the answer was the number of days left.”

Tao Tao stared at her.

“He what?”

“He worked out how many days were left. From the calendar. In about ten seconds, while I was getting water. And then he wrote a problem on his chalkboard where the answer was two hundred and fifty-five. And then he said it was a nice number.” She put her arm over her eyes. “And then his ears went red.”

Tao Tao was silent.

“Jie Jie,” she said finally, very seriously. “That man is counting too.”

Yu Jie didn’t say anything.

But that night, when Tao Tao was asleep, she got out the calendar and the purple pen and drew the day’s atom. And then, very small, in the corner of the square, almost too small to see, she drew a second one.

For him.

chapters.title: The Coffee Cup Physics Jokes Were Not Flirting
chapters.desc: They were absolutely flirting. A sticky note on a mug. Then another. Then a war. Dr. Fang is keeping score.
chapters.epigraph: “Why can’t you trust atoms? They make up everything.” — sticky note, yellow, Wednesday
chapters.content:
The first sticky note was on the jasmine tea.

It was the sixth Wednesday. She came in at 3:45, and the door was propped open with Principles of Quantum Mechanics, and the white mug was on the desk in front of her chair with steam coming off it. And stuck to the side of the mug, just above the handle, there was a small square yellow sticky note.

On it, in his neat, slightly cramped handwriting:

Why can’t you trust atoms?

(Answer on the bottom of the mug.)

She picked up the mug. She turned it over carefully, so the tea wouldn’t spill. On the bottom, on a second, smaller sticky note:

They make up everything.

She looked up.

He was at the chalkboard with his back to her, writing. He didn’t turn round.

“That’s a terrible joke,” she said.

“It’s a classic,” said Miles, to the board.

“It’s on the side of cereal boxes.”

“Classics are classics for a reason.” He kept writing. “They’re tested. Peer-reviewed. Statistically reliable.”

“Did you test it on Dr. Fang first?”

He paused, chalk on the board.

“…He didn’t laugh,” he admitted.

She laughed so hard she spilled the tea.

✦ ✦ ✦

She took the sticky notes home. Both of them. She stuck them on the wall above her desk, next to the calendar, and Tao Tao looked at them and said nothing at all, which from Tao Tao was the most devastating comment possible.

The next Wednesday, there was another.

What did the photon say when the hotel porter offered to carry its luggage?

(Bottom.)

“No thanks. I’m travelling light.”

The Wednesday after:

A neutron walks into a bar and asks how much for a drink. The barman says: “For you? No charge.”

She groaned so loudly that Dr. Fang knocked on the wall from office 413.

She stuck them all above her desk. A small yellow row, growing.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the ninth Wednesday, she struck back.

She came at 3:45 as usual. The tea was there, with its sticky note. Schrödinger’s cat walks into a bar. And doesn’t. She read it and rolled her eyes and stuck it in her notebook and sat down and they argued about the bent oscillator for two hours, and at six, when she left, she stopped at the door.

On the outside of the door, under his office hours sign, under the little green drawing of the cat in the box that had been there for three years, she stuck a pink sticky note.

It said:

Dr. Wei: Why did the physics lecturer break up with the biology lecturer?

There was no chemistry.

— A student who is definitely not stuck on quantum mechanics

She walked away down the corridor and didn’t look back.

✦ ✦ ✦

He found it at 8:15 the next morning.

He was unlocking his door with his bicycle helmet still on, and an egg sandwich from the machine in his other hand, and he saw the pink square stuck under the sign and stopped.

He read it.

He read it again.

He stood in the corridor of the fourth floor of the Hall of Science at 8:16 on a Thursday morning, in his bicycle helmet, holding an egg sandwich, and made a sound that he had not made, as far as he could remember, since he was seventeen years old.

It was quiet. Short. A sort of snort, through his nose, that he tried to swallow and couldn’t.

Next door, the door of office 413 opened, and Dr. Fang Hao put his head out, holding a croissant.

“Was that you?” said Fang Hao.

“No,” said Miles.

Fang Hao looked at him. At the helmet. At the sandwich. At the pink sticky note on the door. He came out into the corridor and read it, chewing.

Then he looked at Miles with an expression of enormous, delighted horror.

“Oh,” said Fang Hao softly. “Oh, no. Oh, Miles. You’ve started a war.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was a war.

It went on for weeks. Every Wednesday, there was a yellow sticky note on her tea. Every Wednesday evening, there was a pink one on his door. Fang Hao started keeping score on a piece of paper taped to the inside of his own door, out of sight, with two columns headed Y and P, and gave each joke marks out of ten, and showed the paper to anyone who asked, which by the end of the month was most of the fourth floor.

Yellow: “I’d tell you a joke about thermodynamics, but it would go off on a tangent and lose all its energy.” 6/10. Points off for being too long.

Pink: “Dr. Wei, are you made of copper and tellurium? Because you’re Cu-Te.” 9/10. Devastating. Miles went red for an hour.

Yellow: “Never trust a quantum physicist. They’re always uncertain.” 4/10. Weak.

Pink: “Dr. Wei, if you were an angle, you’d be acute one.” 8/10. Fang Hao laughed so hard he choked on a croissant.

“They’re not flirting,” Miles told him, the third time Fang Hao came in to read him the scores.

“Miles.”

“They’re physics jokes. It’s a scientific exchange. A form of peer review.”

“She called you Cu-Te. In public. On your door. Professor Zhou saw it on his way to the lift. He stood there for a full minute. He didn’t say anything.” Fang Hao looked at him with pity. “Then he went into the lift and I heard him laugh. Zhou. Laugh. I didn’t know he could.”

Miles put his face in his hands.

“They’re not flirting,” he said through his fingers.

“Then why,” said Fang Hao gently, “do you keep every single one of the pink ones in your top drawer?”

Miles lifted his head.

Fang Hao pointed his croissant at the desk. “You opened it yesterday to get a pen. It was full of pink paper. And a purple pen with a cat on it.” He took a bite. “Cardboard walls, Miles. And I have very good eyes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the second Wednesday of November, Professor Gao Meiling came up to the fourth floor.

She didn’t knock. Professor Gao never knocked. She was fifty-eight and had run the condensed matter group for twenty years and had won two national prizes and a reputation for terrifying her students into brilliance. She smoked thin cigarettes on the balcony outside her lab, which was forbidden, and nobody had ever had the courage to tell her.

She opened the door of office 412 at 5:15 p.m. and stood in the doorway.

Inside, her best student was sitting in Dr. Wei’s chair, with chalk on her cardigan, arguing loudly about whether a second-order correction was physically meaningful. Dr. Wei was sitting on the edge of his own desk, with chalk on his face, arguing back. Between them, on the desk, was a mug of jasmine tea with a yellow sticky note on it.

Both of them stopped talking.

Professor Gao looked at the chalkboard, which was covered in both of their handwriting. She looked at the mug. She looked at the sticky note.

She walked to the desk and peeled it off the mug and read it.

Why did the physicist break up with the electron? She was too negative. (Not true. She is very positive. This joke does not apply to anyone in this room.)

Professor Gao looked at the note for a long time.

Then she looked at Miles.

Then at Yu Jie.

Then she stuck the note back on the mug, very precisely, exactly where it had been.

“Shen Yu Jie,” she said. “Your thesis draft is due on Monday. I haven’t seen a single page.”

“Yes, Professor.”

“My office. Eight a.m. Tomorrow.”

“Yes, Professor.”

Professor Gao turned to go. In the doorway, she stopped and looked back at Miles. Her face was perfectly unreadable.

“Dr. Wei,” she said.

“Professor Gao.”

“That,” said Professor Gao, “is a very bad joke.”

She shut the door.

They sat in silence. Through the wall, from office 413, they heard Dr. Fang Hao laughing so hard he had to cough.

“She put it back,” said Yu Jie at last. “Exactly where it was.”

“She’s a condensed matter physicist,” said Miles. “They like things on the right lattice site.”

Yu Jie looked at the yellow note on the mug. She is very positive. This joke does not apply to anyone in this room.

“Dr. Wei,” she said. “Who in this room is very positive?”

He looked at the chalkboard with great concentration.

“It’s a general statement,” he said. “About electrons.”

“There aren’t any electrons in this room.”

“There are about ten to the twenty-nine electrons in this room,” said Miles, to the board. “Give or take the books. I was being inclusive.”

She laughed so hard she had to put her forehead down on the desk. Through the wall, Fang Hao, who had only just stopped coughing, started again.

chapters.title: Her Supervisor Is Very Interested
chapters.desc: Eight a.m. with Professor Gao, on a balcony where smoking is forbidden. Then Gao climbs the stairs to the fourth floor.
chapters.epigraph: “A man like Wei will hold to a rule until it kills him. Make sure it isn’t you it kills.” — Professor Gao Meiling
chapters.content:
Professor Gao’s lab was on the second floor of the Hall of Science, at the end of a corridor that smelled of liquid nitrogen and burnt toast. Nobody knew why it smelled of toast. There was a theory that one of the cryostats had a fault. There was another theory that Professor Gao ate toast at her desk at six every morning and refused to open a window.

At 7:58 on Thursday, Yu Jie knocked on the office door.

“Balcony,” said a voice from inside.

She went through the office, past three desks buried in papers and a whiteboard covered in phase diagrams, and out of a glass door onto a narrow balcony overlooking the car park. There was a sign on the glass door that said NO SMOKING ON BALCONIES: UNIVERSITY POLICY 14.2.

Professor Gao was leaning on the railing, smoking.

She didn’t turn round. She was a small woman with short grey hair and a lab coat she had clearly been wearing since the nineties. She held her cigarette between two fingers like a pencil.

“Shen Yu Jie,” she said. “Sit.”

There was a plastic chair. Yu Jie sat.

Professor Gao smoked for a while in silence, looking at the car park.

“I have supervised forty-one final-year students in twenty years,” she said finally. “Six of them were brilliant. You are the seventh. You are also the only one who has spent the autumn of her final year hiding her brilliance under a yellow dress and a pile of bad jokes.”

Yu Jie opened her mouth.

“Don’t,” said Professor Gao. “I’m not finished.” She tapped ash over the railing. “Your thesis is on topological phases in strained graphene. It’s a good problem. I gave it to you because I thought you could do something with it that nobody else in this building could. That was in June. It is now November. You have sent me one email. It said, and I quote, going well!!! will send soon!!! with three exclamation marks.”

“I’ve been working on it.”

“On Wednesdays,” said Professor Gao, “you are on the fourth floor.”

Yu Jie went very still.

✦ ✦ ✦

Professor Gao finally turned round. She looked at her student for a long time with her sharp black eyes.

“I know what’s going on,” she said. “Everybody knows what’s going on. Fang Hao has a scoreboard on his door. Zhou laughed in a lift. Half the second-years think Dr. Wei is a tragic romantic hero because he compared himself to a particle.” She took a drag. “I want to know what you think is going on.”

Yu Jie looked at her hands.

She thought about lying. She was good at lying. She did it every Sunday at seven, at the museum, smiling at her mother over the soup.

She didn’t.

“He has a rule,” she said. “Nothing happens while I’m a student in this department. He drew me a graph.”

Professor Gao’s eyebrows went up a millimetre.

“A graph.”

“A flat line. Professional distance, constant.” Yu Jie felt her face go hot. “I put an end date on it. The twentieth of June. Four o’clock. He didn’t argue.”

Professor Gao looked at her for a long time.

Then, to Yu Jie’s astonishment, she laughed. Short and dry, like a cough.

“Of course he drew a graph,” she said. “Of course he did.” She stubbed out her cigarette on the railing. “And what are you doing until June? Counting?”

“I made a calendar.”

“With what?”

“…Atoms.”

“Bohr atoms?”

“They’re the ones that look like atoms.”

“They’re physically inaccurate.”

“That’s what he said.”

Professor Gao looked at the sky for a moment, as if asking it for patience.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Listen to me,” she said. She sat down on the railing, which was also not allowed. “I’m going to tell you something, and then I’m going to tell you what to do, and you’re going to do it.”

Yu Jie waited.

“I know Miles Wei,” said Professor Gao. “I was on the panel that hired him. I’ve watched him for five years. He is the best physicist in this department under forty, and he is the loneliest man I have ever met, and he doesn’t know either of those things.” She looked at Yu Jie. “He came here at twenty-six and shut himself in that office with a cactus and painted his own wall and never once went to a department dinner. He eats the same sandwich every day. His mother phones the department secretary to ask if he’s eating.”

Yu Jie hadn’t known that. Something in her chest hurt.

“Something happened to him,” said Professor Gao. “When he was young. I don’t know what. But he decided that wanting things was dangerous, and he stopped. He made himself a rule. He’s very good at rules.” She paused. “A man like that will hold to a rule until it kills him. Do you understand? He will not bend it. Not for you. Not for himself. If you push him, he won’t break the rule. He’ll break.”

Yu Jie didn’t say anything.

“So here’s what you’re going to do,” said Professor Gao. “You’re going to stop hiding. You’re going to write that thesis, and you’re going to make it the best thesis this department has seen in ten years, and you’re going to defend it in May in front of a committee and make them weep. You’re going to graduate in June with every prize there is.” She stood up. “And then, at four o’clock on the twentieth, you can do whatever you like. Climb the stairs to the fourth floor in your yellow dress. Throw sticky notes at him. I don’t care.”

“And until then?”

“Until then,” said Professor Gao, “Wednesdays are fine. Physics is allowed. I asked Fang Hao. Apparently the two of you have been doing real work up there. He says the bent oscillator thing might be publishable.” She opened the glass door. “But you send me twenty pages by Monday, or I’ll come up to the fourth floor myself and confiscate the tea.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She did come up to the fourth floor. That afternoon. Not for the tea.

Miles was at his desk marking second-year homework. Bai Tianyu had written, in answer to a question about the hydrogen atom, the electron is basically just vibing. Miles was trying to decide how many marks that was worth.

The door opened without a knock.

Professor Gao came in and shut it behind her and stood in front of his desk with her hands in the pockets of her ancient lab coat.

He stood up.

“Professor Gao.”

“Sit down, Wei. I’m not your mother.” She didn’t sit. She looked at the chalkboard, which today had only a few equations on it, and in the bottom right-hand corner, very small, in round handwriting that wasn’t his: 20 June, 16:00.

She looked at it.

Miles followed her eyes and went red to the ears.

“She told me about the graph,” said Professor Gao.

“I—”

“I’m not here to tell you off. You haven’t done anything wrong. That’s the problem.” She turned from the board and looked at him. “You’ve made a rule. It’s a good rule. It’s the right rule. If you’d done anything else, I’d have had to report you, and I’d have done it, and I’d have been very sorry, because you’re the best young physicist I’ve seen in this building.”

Miles didn’t know what to say. He said nothing.

“But I want to say one thing,” said Professor Gao. “Then I’ll go.”

She came and stood right in front of his desk.

“That girl,” she said, “has spent her whole life being told that what she is, is decoration. Her mother calls her the Perfect Jewel in front of guests. She has a brother who runs a company and a father who doesn’t look up from his phone. Nobody in that family has ever once asked her about a single equation.” Her voice was very level. “She is the best student I have had in twenty years, and until this autumn she was hiding it, because she thought nobody wanted it.”

Miles was very still.

“And then she came up four flights of stairs,” said Professor Gao, “and you did the harmonic oscillator the long way to prove she didn’t need you. And you said you’re right to her. And you gave her a problem nobody knows the answer to.” She leaned on the desk. “Do you know what that is, to a girl like that? It isn’t flirting. It’s the first time in her life anyone has taken her mind seriously.”

He couldn’t speak.

“So keep your rule,” said Professor Gao. “Keep it until June. I’ll hold you to it. But don’t you dare,” and her voice dropped, “make her pay for it. Don’t you dare make her think that because you won’t touch her, you don’t want what she can do. Don’t make her go back to hiding.”

She straightened up.

“Keep giving her the hard problems, Wei,” she said. “That’s allowed. That’s more than allowed. That’s your job.”

She went to the door. She opened it. Then she looked back at the bottom right-hand corner of the chalkboard.

“And for heaven’s sake,” she said, “get a better joke book.”

She shut the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles sat at his desk.

Then he pulled the stack of second-year homework towards him, and found Bai Tianyu’s answer about the electron vibing, and gave it two marks out of five, and wrote in the margin: Not wrong, exactly. Please explain what “vibing” means in terms of a wave function. I would genuinely like to know.

Then he took a fresh sticky note, yellow, and wrote on it, slowly, crossing out twice.

He didn’t write a joke.

On Wednesday, when she came at 3:45, the yellow sticky note on the side of her tea said:

Professor Gao says your thesis is on strained graphene. I’ve read three papers on it this week. I have questions. Real ones. Would you mind explaining it to me?

(No joke today. Sorry. The joke book is being replaced.)

She read it. She read it again.

Then she put her mug down and looked at him, standing at the chalkboard with a clean piece of chalk held out toward her, waiting.

“You read three papers on strained graphene,” she said. “This week.”

“Four. The fourth one was wrong, so I’m not counting it. I read it twice to make sure.”

“For me?”

He looked at the chalk in his hand.

“For the physics,” said Miles. Then, after a moment, very quietly: “Mostly.”

And she stopped hiding.

chapters.title: A Study Group of One
chapters.desc: She drags him to the library café on a Saturday. Her friends are terrible at thermodynamics. He is terrible at leaving.
chapters.epigraph: “It’s a study group. Physics is allowed.” “It’s a café.” “Physics happens in cafés. Ask Einstein.”
chapters.content:
“It’s a study group,” said Yu Jie.

“It’s a café,” said Miles.

“It’s a study group in a café. Physics is allowed. You said so. On your graph.” She was standing in the doorway of office 412 on a Friday, not a Wednesday, which was already against the rules, holding a flyer. LIBRARY CAFÉ: OPEN SATURDAYS 9–9. “My friends are failing thermodynamics. All three of them. It’s a crisis. You’re the only person I know who can explain entropy without making people cry.”

“I made a second-year cry about entropy last term.”

“That was Bai Tianyu. He cries about everything. He cried at a dumpling.” She waved the flyer. “Ten o’clock. Tomorrow. One hour. Purely academic. You don’t even have to sit next to me. Sit next to Tao Tao. She bites, but only people she likes.”

He looked at her. Then at the flyer. Then at the bottom right-hand corner of his chalkboard, where 20 June, 16:00 sat in small round writing.

“One hour,” he said.

She smiled like she had won the national lottery.

✦ ✦ ✦

The library café was on the ground floor of the main library, a long room with big windows and terrible coffee and the best cakes on campus, because Dr. Fang’s wife supplied them. On Saturday mornings it was full of students pretending to work.

Miles arrived at 9:57, on his green bicycle, with a backpack containing two textbooks, a pad of paper, four pencils and an egg sandwich in case the café didn’t have one.

Yu Jie was already there, at a big table by the window, with three other people.

Tao Tao he recognised from the betting pool; Fang Hao had shown him a screenshot. She was small and fierce with a bleached streak in her hair and a T-shirt that said I’M HERE FOR THE MITOCHONDRIA. Beside her was a tall, sleepy boy called Ah Peng, studying chemistry, who appeared to be wearing pyjama trousers. And a quiet girl in glasses called Li Wen, from engineering, who had three highlighters lined up in front of her in colour order and looked at Miles as if he were an exam.

“Dr. Wei,” said Yu Jie, standing up. “This is the study group. Study group, this is Dr. Wei. He’s going to save your lives.”

Tao Tao looked Miles up and down for a long, unblinking moment.

“So you’re the cactus man,” she said.

Yu Jie kicked her under the table.

✦ ✦ ✦

He sat next to Tao Tao.

He had said he would. He sat on the opposite side of the table from Yu Jie, as far away as the table allowed, next to a biology student who had immediately moved her chair two inches closer to his and was watching him like a cat watching a bird.

Then Ah Peng pushed a sheet of homework across the table and said, “Dr. Wei, I don’t understand anything about entropy, I don’t even understand what the word means, I think it’s fake,” and Miles forgot about the table and the distance and the corner of the chalkboard and everything else.

“It’s not fake,” he said. “It’s the most real thing there is. Can I borrow that napkin?”

He drew on the napkin. A box with a wall down the middle. Dots on one side. Then the wall gone, and the dots spread through the whole box.

“Why do the dots spread out?” he asked.

“Because… they want to?” said Ah Peng.

“They don’t want anything. They’re dots. They just move randomly. So why do they always end up spread out, and never all go back to one side?”

Ah Peng stared at the napkin.

“Because,” said Li Wen slowly, from the end of the table, “there are more ways to be spread out than there are to be on one side?”

Miles looked at her with that expression Yu Jie had seen on the second Wednesday: pure, uncomplicated delight.

“Yes,” he said. “Exactly. That’s it. That’s entropy. That’s all it is. Counting the number of ways. Messy is more likely than tidy because there are more ways to be messy.” He tapped the napkin. “That’s why your room gets untidy on its own but never tidies itself. That’s why ice melts. That’s why time only goes forwards.”

“That’s why time goes forwards?” said Ah Peng, waking up.

“That’s one of the best explanations we have.”

Li Wen picked up a highlighter and wrote MESSY = MORE WAYS across the top of her notes in pink, and underlined it twice.

Across the table, Yu Jie sat with her chin on her hand and watched him, and didn’t say anything at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

The hour became two. Then three.

He went through their homework, one problem at a time, on napkins, because he had forgotten to take out his pad of paper and nobody reminded him. He explained the Carnot cycle using a cup of coffee. He explained heat engines using Ah Peng’s pyjama trousers, which nobody, including Ah Peng, ever fully recovered from. He found three mistakes in Li Wen’s textbook and she wrote them down in a special notebook as if they were treasure.

At some point, Tao Tao went quiet and stopped watching him like a cat. She put her chin on her hand too.

At 12:40, Ah Peng said, “Dr. Wei, why aren’t all lecturers like you?” in a voice of genuine anguish.

Miles looked up from his napkin, surprised, as if he had forgotten anyone else was there.

“They are,” he said. “Mostly. You just have to ask the right questions.”

“I never ask questions,” said Ah Peng. “I’m scared they’ll think I’m stupid.”

Miles put down his pencil.

“The stupidest thing I ever did,” he said, “was not ask a question when I was your age. For a year. Because I didn’t want anyone to know I didn’t understand. And then I had to learn the whole thing again, alone, later, much more slowly.” He looked at Ah Peng. “Ask the question. The worst thing that happens is someone explains it.”

There was a small silence at the table.

Across from him, Yu Jie was looking at him with an expression he couldn’t read. Soft and very still.

He looked back at her, for a second too long.

Then the café door opened, and Professor Zhou Lin, head of the department, walked in with his wife to buy a cake.

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles saw him first.

He saw Professor Zhou see the table: four students, napkins everywhere, and Dr. Miles Wei in the middle of them, three hours into a Saturday, looking across the table at a girl in a yellow cardigan with exactly the expression a hundred and forty second-years had posted online about.

Professor Zhou didn’t say anything. He nodded once, politely, and went to the counter.

But Miles was already standing up.

He packed his backpack in about eight seconds. Textbooks, pencils, the uneaten egg sandwich. He didn’t look at anyone.

“I have to go,” he said. “I’m sorry. I forgot. A meeting.”

“On a Saturday?” said Tao Tao.

“Yes. Very important. Thank you. Good luck with the exam. Ask questions.” He was already at the door. “Messy is more likely than tidy.”

He went out. The door swung shut behind him.

At the table, nobody said anything for a long moment.

Then Tao Tao said, very quietly, “Oh, Jie Jie.”

Yu Jie was looking at the door. Her face was perfectly calm. It was her Sunday face, the one she wore at the museum at seven o’clock over the soup.

She picked up one of the napkins he had left behind. The box with the wall. The dots spreading out. Underneath, in his small neat handwriting: There are more ways to be messy.

She folded it carefully and put it in her pocket.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was waiting at the bicycle rack when she came out an hour later.

She stopped. She hadn’t expected him to be there. He was standing next to his old green bicycle, holding the handlebars, not looking at her.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

“You had a meeting.”

“I didn’t have a meeting.” He looked at the ground. “Professor Zhou came in. And I saw his face, and I saw what it looked like. Me, on a Saturday, with you. Three hours.” He pushed his glasses up. “And I panicked. I don’t panic. I’m very bad at it. I didn’t know what to do, so I left.”

“You could have said goodbye.”

“I know. I’m sorry.” He finally looked at her. “Your friends. Are they all right?”

“Ah Peng says he’s going to change to physics.”

Miles looked alarmed. “He mustn’t. He’s very bad at it.”

She laughed, despite herself.

They stood by the bicycle rack in the November sun. Students went past. Somewhere, a dog was barking.

“It was the best three hours I’ve had in a very long time,” said Miles quietly, to his handlebars. “That’s the problem.”

Then he unzipped his backpack, took out the egg sandwich, still in its plastic triangle, and held it out across the bicycle at the full length of his arm.

“You didn’t eat,” he said. “You gave Ah Peng your cake at eleven, because he said entropy made him hungry, and you didn’t order anything else. I noticed. Before.”

“Before you ran away.”

“Before I ran away,” Miles agreed. “It’s egg. It was the only thing the machine had. I’m sorry.”

She took it. It was warm from being in his backpack, which was not hygienic, and she didn’t care.

“How long have you been standing here?” she said.

He looked at his watch, because of course he did.

“Fifty-six minutes.”

“Dr. Wei. It’s November.”

“I’m aware of the date,” said Miles, to his handlebars. “I wasn’t sure which door you’d come out of. There are two.”

She didn’t say anything.

He got on his bicycle. He put on his helmet. He looked at her once more.

“The napkin,” he said. “You took it.”

She put her hand in her pocket. She didn’t take it out.

“You left it,” she said.

He looked at her pocket for a moment. Then he nodded, as if that answered something, and rode away down the long path between the trees, wobbling slightly, the way he always did on the first few metres.

She watched him go.

That night, she drew the atom in the day’s square. And then, beside it, very small, she drew a box with a wall down the middle, and dots spreading out on both sides.

There are more ways to be messy.

Two hundred and ten days left.

chapters.title: Miles Gets Sick and Nobody Notices
chapters.desc: Except one student, with soup, a thermometer, a lecture, and his sister on speakerphone.
chapters.epigraph: “This is not allowed.” “I’m a student delivering soup. It’s community service.”
chapters.content:
On the twelfth Wednesday, the door to office 412 was closed.

Not propped open with Principles of Quantum Mechanics. Closed. And locked. Yu Jie tried the handle twice. She knocked. She stood in the corridor at 3:47 with her notebook against her chest and listened, and there was nothing: no chalk, no radiator whale, no voice saying it’s open, unless you’re from facilities.

The door of office 413 opened.

Dr. Fang Hao looked out. For once he wasn’t eating anything.

“He’s not here,” he said. “He cancelled his lecture yesterday, and tomorrow’s. Emailed at six in the morning. One line. Unwell, apologies, will reschedule.” Fang Hao frowned. “He’s never cancelled anything. Not once in five years. He gave a lecture with a broken wrist once. He wrote on the board with his left hand. It was illegible, but he did it.”

Yu Jie stood very still.

“Has anyone checked on him?”

Fang Hao opened his mouth. Then closed it.

“I sent him a message,” he said. “He didn’t answer. I assumed he was asleep.” He looked at her. “He lives alone. He doesn’t really know anyone. His family is four hours away.”

“Where does he live?”

Fang Hao looked at her for a long moment.

“That,” he said carefully, “is not the kind of information I should give a student.”

“Dr. Fang.”

He sighed. He went back into his office and came out with a sticky note. Yellow. He held it out to her.

“Staff flats,” he said. “The old block behind the sports ground. Number fourteen, third floor. I didn’t give you this. If anyone asks, you found it in the bin.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The staff flats were a tired five-storey building from the 1980s with a broken lift and a noticeboard in the lobby covered in reminders about recycling. She climbed to the third floor with a plastic bag in each hand.

In one bag: a flask of chicken congee from the canteen, ginger tea from the shop by the gate, a bottle of paracetamol, a box of tissues, and a thermometer. In the other: oranges, because Tao Tao had said you always bring oranges, it was the law.
