Number fourteen had a plain brown door. There was no name on it. There was a small cactus on the mat outside, in a blue pot, exactly like Schrödinger.

She knocked.

Nothing. She knocked again, louder.

Footsteps. Slow. A long pause on the other side of the door, as if someone was looking through the peephole and not believing it.

The door opened six inches.

Miles looked terrible.

He was wearing a grey jumper over pyjamas, and a scarf, and socks with holes in them. His hair was standing straight up on one side. His glasses were crooked. His face was flushed red and his eyes were glassy, and his nose was so blocked his voice came out like it was coming through a sock.

“Shen Yu Jie,” he said.

“Dr. Wei.”

“You’re on my doorstep.”

“I am.”

“It’s Wednesday.”

“I know.” She held up the bags. “You’ve got a fever. You cancelled two lectures. Dr. Fang says you once taught with a broken wrist. Therefore you are dying.”

He looked at the bags. Then at her.

“This,” said Miles, very slowly, through his blocked nose, “is not allowed.”

“I’m a student delivering soup,” said Yu Jie. “It’s community service. I’m sure there’s a box I can tick.” She pushed the door gently. “Let me in. You’re swaying.”

He was swaying.

He let her in.

✦ ✦ ✦

The flat was small and very clean and completely empty of anything that wasn’t a book.

Books on shelves. Books on the floor. Books on the kitchen counter, in neat stacks, with sticky notes in them. A sofa, one armchair, a table with one chair. A kettle. A window with a view of the sports ground and, on the sill, three more cacti in blue pots.

There was no food in the kitchen. She checked. There was a jar of instant coffee, which he didn’t drink, a packet of crackers that had gone soft, and an egg.

One egg.

“When did you last eat?” she said.

He had sat down on the sofa very suddenly, as if his legs had made a decision without him. “Monday,” he said. “I think. I had a sandwich.”

“An egg sandwich.”

“…Yes.”

She took out the thermometer and held it out.

He looked at it. Then at her.

“I’m a lecturer,” he said. “You’re a student. You can’t take my temperature.”

“Then take it yourself,” said Yu Jie. “I’ll stand over here. Very professionally. At a distance. With the soup.”

He took it himself.

Thirty-nine point one.

She looked at the little screen and felt something go cold in her stomach.

She did the arithmetic without wanting to. A sandwich on Monday. An email at six on Tuesday morning. Then nothing. That made two days in this flat with a fever climbing, one egg in the fridge and nobody at the door. If she hadn’t come, nobody would have, not until somebody noticed that the lecturer who had once taught with a broken wrist hadn’t turned up to teach at all.

She thought of him on the kitchen floor and couldn’t stop thinking of it: the long thin shape of him on the cold lino, his glasses skidded under the counter, the kettle still on.

Her hands had started to shake. She put the thermometer down on the arm of the sofa so that he wouldn’t see.

“Right,” she said. “Lie down.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She did everything at a distance. Mostly.

She heated the congee in his one saucepan and put it in his one bowl and put it on the table and made him sit at his one chair and eat it while she stood across the room by the window, very professionally, holding the oranges. She made the ginger tea. She found his only blanket in the cupboard and put it on the arm of the sofa and pointed at it until he lay down and pulled it over himself.

She lectured him the whole time.

“You live on egg sandwiches. You don’t have any food. You don’t have a single vegetable in this flat. You have one egg. You have more cacti than plates. When you got sick, you didn’t tell anybody, you just emailed at six in the morning and locked yourself in. What if you’d fallen? What if you’d hit your head? Nobody would have found you until Thursday office hours, when Bai Tianyu came looking for you to ask if gravity is real.”

“Gravity is real,” said Miles, from under the blanket.

“I know gravity is real.”

“He asked me last week. If it was a theory or a fact.” He coughed. “It was quite a good conversation.”

She put the ginger tea down on the floor beside the sofa, as far away from him as her arm would reach, and went back to the window.

“You’re impossible,” she said.

“You’re standing very far away,” said Miles.

“I’m being professional.”

He looked at her over the blanket with glassy, feverish eyes.

“You brought oranges,” he said.

“Tao Tao said it was the law.”

“Nobody,” said Miles, “has ever brought me oranges.”

✦ ✦ ✦

His phone rang.

It was on the floor beside the sofa, next to the tea. He looked at the screen and closed his eyes.

“My sister,” he said. “She calls on Wednesdays. If I don’t answer, she calls my mother, and my mother calls the department secretary.”

“Then answer.”

He answered. He put it on speaker, because his hands were shaking too much to hold it.

“There you are,” said a woman’s voice, very loud and very blunt. “You sound awful. Are you sick? You sound sick. Have you eaten? You haven’t eaten. I can hear it in your voice. You sound like a man who has eaten one sandwich since Monday.”

Yu Jie put her hand over her mouth.

“Lan,” said Miles weakly. “I’m fine.”

“You’re not fine. You never say you’re fine. You say ‘I’m all right’ when you’re fine. ‘Fine’ means you’re dying.” A pause. “Is someone there? I can hear someone breathing. Miles. Is there a person in your flat?”

Miles looked at Yu Jie across the room in total panic.

Yu Jie looked back at him.

Then she walked over and bent down toward the phone on the floor and said, very politely, in her best Sunday-dinner voice: “Hello. I’m a student. From the physics department. I brought congee.”

There was a long silence from the phone.

“A student,” said Wei Lan slowly.

“Yes.”

“In his flat.”

“Delivering soup. It’s community service.”

Another long silence.

“Is she pretty?” said Wei Lan.

“Lan,” said Miles.

“I’m asking a medical question. I’m a nurse. It affects his recovery.” A pause. “Student. What’s his temperature?”

“Thirty-nine point one,” said Yu Jie. “He took it himself. I stood by the window.”

“Good girl. Make him drink water. A litre at least. Paracetamol every six hours, not more. If it goes over thirty-nine and a half or he gets confused or he can’t keep water down, take him to the clinic, I don’t care what he says, he’ll argue, he always argues, ignore him.” Wei Lan’s voice changed slightly. Softened. “And thank you. Nobody ever checks on him. He doesn’t let them.”

“He let me,” said Yu Jie, before she could stop herself.

There was a very long pause.

“Did he,” said Wei Lan. Not a question.

“I’m hanging up now,” said Miles.

“Miles, wait, what’s her—”

He hung up.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stayed until his temperature went down.

It took three hours. She sat at his one chair at his one table at the far side of the room and worked on her thesis on her laptop, very professionally, and every hour she said “Temperature” and he took it himself and read it out. Thirty-nine. Thirty-eight point seven. Thirty-eight point two.

“Shen Yu Jie,” he said, at thirty-eight point two, with his eyes shut.

“Mm.”

“You’ve been typing the same sentence for twenty minutes. I can hear it. Type, type, type. Delete, delete, delete.”

She took her hands off the keyboard. “You’re supposed to be resting.”

“I am resting. I’m resting and listening.” A pause. “What’s the sentence?”

“It’s about edge states.”

It was not about edge states. It was He has more cacti than plates and I would like to buy him some plates, and she had typed it and deleted it nine times.

“Liar,” said Miles, very kindly, from under the blanket.

She didn’t answer. She typed the sentence a tenth time and looked at it for a long moment. Then she deleted it again, put her chin on her hand, and watched the blanket rise and fall across the room.

At some point he fell asleep on the sofa. She heard his breathing change.

She looked up from her laptop.

He was lying on his side with the blanket pulled up to his chin and his glasses still on, crooked, and one hand hanging off the edge of the sofa, the fingers curled. His face, asleep, looked younger. Softer. The frown he wore when he was thinking about four things at once was gone.

She got up. She went across the room. Very quietly.

She took his glasses off. Carefully, so she wouldn’t wake him. She folded them and put them on the floor beside the tea.

She did not touch anything else. Not his hair. Not his hand. She stood beside the sofa for a long moment with her own hands in the pockets of her cardigan, holding them there.

Then she went back to the chair on the other side of the room.

✦ ✦ ✦

When he woke, it was dark outside, and she was gone.

His temperature was thirty-seven point eight. The flat smelled of ginger. There was a bowl of congee on the table under a plate, still faintly warm. The paracetamol was beside it, with a note: Every 6 hours. Next one at 10 p.m. Not before. Your sister will know.

There was a bag of oranges on the kitchen counter.

And in the fridge, which had been empty except for one egg, there were now four more boxes of congee, a bag of green vegetables, a carton of milk, a loaf of bread, and a small plastic tub with a yellow sticky note on the lid.

He took it out.

Inside were peeled orange segments, every single bit of pith picked off.

The sticky note said:

Why did the lecturer catch a cold?

Because he left his door open all autumn.

(Close it at night. Open it on Wednesdays.)

He stood in front of his open fridge in his pyjamas and holey socks, holding a tub of perfectly peeled oranges.

Then he ate every single segment, standing up, at ten o’clock at night, and took his paracetamol at exactly the right time, and texted his sister one word before she could call their mother.

Alive.

The reply came in four seconds.

Marry her.

He put the phone face down on the counter and did not answer, and went to bed, and slept for eleven hours, and dreamed of oranges.

chapters.title: He Laughs in a Seminar
chapters.desc: The first time in fourteen years. The whole room goes quiet. Then an invitation arrives with a family crest on it.
chapters.epigraph: “Dr. Wei laughed.” “Out loud?” “Out loud. Zhou dropped his pen.” — overheard, fourth-floor kitchen
chapters.content:
The department seminar was on Friday afternoons at four, in the small lecture room on the third floor with the broken blind.

It was not, as a rule, exciting. A visiting speaker would come from another university and present their research to thirty physicists, half of whom were checking their email. Professor Zhou would sit in the front row and ask one question, always the same question, in different words: But have you considered the boundary conditions? Dr. Fang would bring cake. Afterwards there would be warm white wine in plastic cups and people would stand around talking about funding.

Miles went every week. He sat in the third row on the left, by the window with the broken blind, and listened properly, and asked one question if he had one and none if he didn’t, and left before the wine.

Final-year students were allowed to come. Almost none of them did.

On the first Friday in December, he walked in at 3:58 and she was in the second row on the right.

✦ ✦ ✦

He had been back at work for a week. His fever had gone. His fridge had stayed full, mysteriously, all week: on Monday a box of dumplings had appeared outside his door with no note, and on Thursday a bag of oranges, and Fang Hao had looked at both and said nothing in a very loud way.

He had not said anything to her about the flat. She had not said anything to him. On Wednesday, she had come at 3:45, and the door had been open, and the tea had been on the desk with a sticky note that said Thank you and nothing else, no joke, and she had read it and put it in her notebook and sat down and they had done physics for two hours and neither of them had mentioned oranges.

Now she was in the second row of the department seminar, in a dark green jumper instead of a yellow dress, with her hair down for once, taking notes.

He sat in the third row on the left, by the broken blind.

She didn’t turn round. But he saw her shoulders change when he sat down.

✦ ✦ ✦

The visiting speaker was a professor from the capital called Professor Huang, who was famous, and knew it.

He was presenting a new model of electrons in a strange material, a sheet of carbon one atom thick, stretched and twisted. Strained graphene. He spoke for forty minutes, very fast, with a great many slides, and at the end of every slide he looked at the audience as if he expected applause.

Miles listened. It was a clever model. It was also, he thought around minute thirty, slightly wrong. There was an assumption on slide nineteen that didn’t hold if the strain was uneven. He was writing a note to himself about it when he looked up and saw that in the second row, Shen Yu Jie had stopped taking notes.

She was sitting very straight. Looking at slide nineteen.

He knew that look. He had seen it on the second Wednesday, when she found the mistake in his bent oscillator in four seconds.

Dr. Huang finished. Polite applause. Professor Zhou raised his hand and asked about the boundary conditions. Dr. Huang answered at length. Two more questions from the audience, safe ones.

Then a hand went up in the second row.

The room shifted. Thirty physicists looked at the final-year student with her hand up. Professor Zhou turned round in his seat. Dr. Huang squinted at her.

“Yes? The young lady?”

Yu Jie stood up.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Slide nineteen,” she said. Her voice was clear and not at all nervous. “You assume the strain is uniform across the sample. But in real devices it isn’t. It’s worse at the edges. If you put an uneven strain into your model, your gap closes. The topological phase you’re describing goes away.” She paused. “I’ve been working on this for my thesis. With non-uniform strain, I think it doesn’t survive. Unless you’re working with very small samples. Which you didn’t say.”

There was a silence in the small lecture room on the third floor.

Dr. Huang looked at her. His smile had become slightly fixed.

“That’s an interesting point,” he said. “For a student. But I think if you look more carefully at the—”

“I have looked,” said Yu Jie politely. “I ran it. Last Wednesday. With help.”

She did not look at the third row on the left. She did not have to. Thirty heads turned to look at it anyway.

Miles sat very still by the broken blind.

Dr. Huang followed their eyes. He looked at Miles. Miles looked back at him.

“Dr. Wei?” said Dr. Huang. “Is this your student?”

“No,” said Miles. “She’s Professor Gao’s.” He paused. “But she’s right. About slide nineteen. I was writing it down myself.” He held up his notebook, where he had written, in small letters: Slide 19. Uneven strain. Gap closes? “She just saw it faster.”

At the back of the room, someone made a small sound. It was Professor Gao, who had come in late and was standing by the door with her arms folded and an expression of fierce, enormous satisfaction.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dr. Huang recovered. He was a professional. He said that it was a very interesting question and he would look into it, and thanked her, and moved on, and Yu Jie sat down, very pink, and wrote something in her notebook so she wouldn’t have to look at anyone.

There was one more question. Then the chair thanked the speaker. Then the applause.

And then Dr. Huang, who was gathering up his laptop and clearly wanted the last word, said into the microphone, with a little laugh, to the room in general:

“Well. I see this department produces very confident students. I’ll have to be careful next time. Maybe I should bring my own lecturer to defend me.”

Polite laughter.

And Shen Yu Jie, in the second row, without looking up from her notebook, said quite clearly in the small silence after it:

“You’d need a very strong one. My gap doesn’t close.”

The room went quiet. Then a few people laughed. Fang Hao, in the back, put his hand over his mouth.

And in the third row on the left, by the broken blind, Miles Wei laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Not a small laugh. Not the snort through the nose in the corridor at the pink sticky note.

A real laugh. Out loud. It came up out of him before he could stop it, from somewhere very deep and very long unused, and it filled the small lecture room: helpless and surprised, his head going back, his notebook sliding off his knee onto the floor.

He hadn’t laughed like that since he was seventeen. Since a library, and two girls fighting, and the day he decided that it was safer to want nothing.

The room went completely silent.

Professor Zhou had turned all the way round in his front-row seat and was staring. He had dropped his pen. Dr. Fang was staring. Professor Gao, by the door, had raised both eyebrows to her hairline. Dr. Huang was standing at the lectern with his laptop half closed, his mouth slightly open. Thirty physicists who had worked in the same building as Dr. Miles Wei for five years, and had never heard him make a sound louder than I have a question about the boundary conditions, sat and looked at him laughing by the broken blind.

He stopped.

He looked around the room. He looked at all the faces.

He went red. Slowly. Starting at his ears and going all the way down to his collar.

“Sorry,” said Miles. “I’m sorry. That was—sorry.” He picked up his notebook from the floor. “It was a good joke.”

In the second row, Shen Yu Jie had turned round in her seat.

She was looking at him. Not smiling. Just looking. With an expression on her face that he couldn’t read at all, soft and stunned, as if she had just watched an experiment do something no theory had predicted.

He looked back at her across two rows of chairs, in front of the whole department.

For one second, he forgot the rule.

Then he remembered it, and looked down at his notebook, and the chair said, “Well! Wine is in the corridor,” and the room broke up into noise, and the second was over.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t stay for the wine. He never stayed for the wine.

But she was on the stairs. She wasn’t waiting, exactly. She was holding a plastic cup of warm white wine she wasn’t drinking and reading a notice about fire drills with tremendous attention, two steps up from the third-floor landing, exactly where anyone going up to the fourth floor would have to pass.

He passed. One step above her, he stopped.

“That was a very good question,” he said. “Slide nineteen.”

“That was a very good laugh,” said Yu Jie, to the fire drill notice. “Four seconds. Nearly five. I counted.”

“You counted.”

“I’m a physicist. I needed a baseline.” She turned her head and looked up at him, and her eyes were very bright. “For next time.”

He opened his mouth. Nothing came out of it. He went on up the stairs, and she heard him walk straight into the fire door at the top, say “Sorry” to it, and go through.

But when he got back to office 412, there was an envelope on his desk.

Not a sticky note. A real envelope, thick, cream-coloured, heavy paper, the kind he associated with weddings and lawyers. His name was written on the front in beautiful black calligraphy: Dr. Miles Wei. On the back, pressed into a circle of dark red wax, there was a crest. An elegant letter S, entwined with what looked like a ship’s anchor.

He opened it.

The Shen Foundation requests the pleasure of your company at its Annual Winter Gala in celebration of its new endowment to the City University Department of Physics Saturday, the twentieth of December The Harbour Hotel, seven o’clock Black tie

And underneath, on a separate card, in handwriting he did not recognise—elegant, sharp, slanting:

Dr. Wei. Professor Gao tells me you are the department’s most promising young lecturer. As the Foundation’s new gift will fund the physics department for the next ten years, my husband and I would be delighted to meet you. — Shen Ruolan

Miles read it twice.

Shen.

He sat down very slowly.

He knew the name, of course. Everyone in the city knew the name. Shen Holdings owned half the harbour. The new wing of the hospital had their name on it. There was a Shen Building downtown that was forty storeys high.

He had never once, in three months of Wednesdays, connected it to a girl in a yellow sundress with four pens in her hair and biro all over her trainers, who peeled every bit of pith off an orange and drew Bohr atoms on a calendar.

Shen Yu Jie.

The Perfect Jewel, Professor Gao had said. Her mother calls her that in front of guests.

He looked at the elegant card. My husband and I would be delighted to meet you.

Then he looked at the bottom right-hand corner of his chalkboard, where in small round handwriting it said 20 June, 16:00.

Next door, through the cardboard wall, Fang Hao was telling someone, at great length and very loudly, that Dr. Wei had laughed, out loud, in a seminar, and that Zhou had dropped his pen.

Miles put the invitation down on his desk. He put it face down.

He sat in office 412 with the radiator calling like a whale and the cactus being both alive and dead on the windowsill, and for the first time since September, he did not know what the rule was for.

chapters.title: Miles in a Rented Suit
chapters.desc: He looks like he’s about to defend a thesis. His sister takes over. Dr. Fang provides croissants and terrible advice.
chapters.epigraph: “Black tie means a bow tie, Miles. Not a black tie.” — Wei Lan, on video call, despairing
chapters.content:
He didn’t own a suit.

He had owned one. He had bought it at twenty-five for his PhD defence, in grey, from a department store, and worn it once more at his cousin’s wedding, and then put it in the back of the wardrobe in the staff flat, where it had stayed for six years. When he took it out on Monday, it was two sizes too big across the shoulders, because he had lost weight, and had a moth hole in the left lapel, and smelled of the wardrobe.

He stood in front of the small mirror on the back of the bathroom door and looked at himself in it.

He looked, he thought, like a man about to be told his thesis had failed.

✦ ✦ ✦

“No,” said Fang Hao.

It was Tuesday lunchtime. Miles had brought the suit to work in a bag, because he didn’t know what else to do, and Fang Hao had come into office 412 with a croissant and seen the bag and demanded to see what was in it.

Miles held it up.

Fang Hao looked at it for a long moment. He put down his croissant.

“Miles,” he said gently. “That is not a suit. That is a cry for help.”

“It’s grey.”

“It’s the colour of a filing cabinet. It has a hole in it. It’s from—what year is this from?”

“It was for my defence.”

“That was six years ago. You were a different shape. You were a different person.” Fang Hao picked up the croissant again, as if he needed strength. “And the invitation says black tie. Do you know what black tie means?”

“A black tie,” said Miles.

Fang Hao closed his eyes.

✦ ✦ ✦

He called his sister on Tuesday night, because Fang Hao had told him to and because he had run out of other ideas.

Wei Lan answered on video. She was in her scrubs, in the staff kitchen of the hospital in their hometown, eating noodles out of a plastic tub. She was twenty-eight and looked like him, if he had been shorter and louder and had never once in his life been uncertain about anything.

“You never video call,” she said immediately. “Something’s happened. Is it the soup girl?”

“There’s a gala,” said Miles.

Wei Lan put down her chopsticks.

“A gala.”

“The Shen Foundation. They’re giving money to the department. I’ve been invited. Professor Gao says I have to go. The dean will be there.” He held up the invitation to the camera. “It says black tie. Fang Hao says I don’t know what black tie means.”

“What do you think it means?”

“A black tie.”

Wei Lan stared at him through the screen.

“Black tie means a bow tie, Miles,” she said. “Not a black tie. A bow tie. And a dinner jacket. A tuxedo. Black, with satin on the lapels.” She picked her chopsticks back up and pointed them at the camera. “You’re going to rent one. Tomorrow. And you’re going to send me photographs from the changing room. Every single one. And I’m going to say no to all of them until you find the right one.”

“I don’t need—”

“Miles.” Wei Lan leaned in. “Is she going to be there?”

He was quiet.

“The soup girl. The one with the oranges. Is she going to be at the gala?”

“Her name is Shen Yu Jie,” said Miles, after a long moment. “And it’s her family’s gala.”

There was a silence on the other end of the line. Wei Lan put down her noodles entirely.

“Shen,” she said. “As in—”

“As in Shen Holdings. As in the Shen Building. As in half the harbour.” He looked at the invitation. “I didn’t know. Until the invitation. She never said. She has biro on her shoes, Lan. She eats White Rabbit sweets out of her cardigan pocket. She peeled every bit of pith off an orange.”

Wei Lan looked at her brother through the screen. Her face had changed.

“Oh, Miles,” she said quietly.

“What?”

“Nothing.” She picked up her chopsticks again. “Tomorrow. The rental place on Harbour Road. Photographs. Every single one. And get a haircut.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He rented a tuxedo on Wednesday morning, before office hours that weren’t office hours.

He sent his sister eleven photographs from the changing room. She said no to ten of them. The eleventh was black, slim, with satin lapels and a white shirt with tiny buttons, and a black silk bow tie that came already tied on a strap, because she said he would strangle himself if he tried to tie a real one.

“That one,” Wei Lan texted. “Buy it, don’t rent it. You’ll need it again.”

“Why would I need it again?” he texted back.

She sent him a single emoji. A ring.

He put his phone in his pocket and did not answer.

The tailor at the rental shop, an elderly man with a tape measure around his neck and pins in his mouth, looked at Miles in the mirror for a long time while he adjusted the trousers.

“Big night?” he said, through the pins.

“A gala.”

“For a girl?”

Miles went red.

The tailor took the pins out of his mouth. He looked at Miles’s reflection, at the tall, thin, hunched man in a beautiful black tuxedo with his glasses slightly crooked and his hair sticking up at the back and an expression of total, helpless terror.

“Stand up straight,” said the tailor. “Shoulders back. Like that. Good.” He stepped back. “You look like a man who knows something nobody else does.”

Miles looked at himself in the mirror.

He stood up straight.

“I do, a bit,” he said. “I’m a physicist.”

“Then look like one,” said the tailor, and went to get his receipt book.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 3:45 that afternoon she came in and sat down and picked up her tea, and looked at him over the top of it for a long time.

“You have a pin in your jumper,” she said.

He looked down. A tailor’s pin was stuck in the left elbow of his grey jumper, right beside the hole. He took it out, put it on the desk and regarded it as if it had betrayed him.

“A tailor,” he said.

“A tailor.”

“For the gala. Professor Gao says I have to go.” He paused. “My sister says I have to send her photographs.”

Yu Jie looked down at her notebook. She was quiet for so long that he began to think he had done something wrong.

“I don’t have to come,” he said. “If it would be easier. I can tell Professor Gao I have a fever. There’s a precedent.”

“No.” It came out much too fast. She put down her pen. “Come. Please. It’s only that I’ve never had anyone there before. Anyone who—” She stopped and started again, more carefully, the way you rebuild a line of working that has a mistake in it. “Anyone who knows I can do the harmonic oscillator.”

He looked at her across the desk.

“Somewhere you can find me, then,” said Miles. “Not in a corner. I’ll ask Fang Hao where people stand.”

She picked the pin up off his desk, put it in her cardigan pocket with the White Rabbit wrappers, and did not give it back.

✦ ✦ ✦

He got a haircut on Thursday. The barber asked how he wanted it and he said “shorter” and the barber looked at the back of his head, where the piece that always stuck up was sticking up, and sighed, and did his best.

On Friday, Fang Hao came into office 412 with two croissants and sat on the desk and said, “Right. Gala rules.”

“There are rules?”

“There are always rules. Rule one: don’t talk about physics for more than five minutes at a time. Rich people get bored.”

“What do I talk about?”

“Their yachts. Their children. The weather. Anything.” Fang Hao bit his croissant. “Rule two: don’t stand in the corner. You always stand in the corner. Stand near the food, people come to the food.”

“I don’t eat at parties.”

“Hold a plate anyway. It gives your hands something to do.” Another bite. “Rule three: when you see her, and she’s with her family, and they’re all dressed in diamonds, and her mother is introducing her to men who own shipping companies—”

He stopped. He looked at Miles.

Miles was very still behind his desk.

“Rule three,” said Fang Hao, more gently, “is don’t leave early. You always leave early. Whatever happens. Stay until the end.”

Miles looked at the corner of his chalkboard. 20 June, 16:00.

“Why?” he said.

“Because,” said Fang Hao, “she’s going to be standing in a ballroom being a Perfect Jewel for her mother. All night. And she’s going to look across that room, at some point, and she’s going to want to see one person there who knows she has biro on her shoes.” He stood up and brushed crumbs off his trousers. “That’s you, Miles. Don’t leave.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday at six-fifteen, Miles stood in front of the small mirror on the back of his bathroom door in a black tuxedo, a white shirt with tiny buttons, and a pre-tied bow tie, with his hair shorter and the piece at the back, against all odds, lying flat.

He looked at himself.

He did not look like a man about to defend a thesis. He looked, he thought, like someone he didn’t recognise. Someone who might, possibly, be going somewhere he wanted to go.

He took a photograph and sent it to his sister.

She replied in four seconds.

Oh. Oh, Miles.

Then, a second later:

Don’t talk about entropy.

Then, a second after that:

Don’t leave early.

He put the phone in his inside pocket. Then he took it out again and looked at the photograph he had sent her for a long moment, at the stranger in the tuxedo.

Then he opened the drawer of his one table at home, the one where he kept nothing important, where he had moved it in November after Fang Hao saw it in his office, and took out a purple pen with a small plastic cat on the end of it, with a question mark painted on its head.

He put it in his inside pocket, next to his phone.

He didn’t know why. He only knew that if he was going to stand in a ballroom full of diamonds tonight, he wanted to have something in his pocket that had been hers before it was a jewel.

chapters.title: The Shen Family Gala
chapters.desc: The Perfect Jewel at the top of the stairs. Two married women who recognise him across the room. And a very large man by the pillar, glaring.
chapters.epigraph: “Miles Wei. As I live and breathe. In a tuxedo.” — Aurelia Chen
chapters.content:
The ballroom of the Harbour Hotel had been decorated in white and silver, and every surface that could hold a candle held one.

Miles stood just inside the doors with a glass of something sparkling he hadn’t asked for and looked at it all. The chandeliers. The ice sculpture of a ship, slowly melting into a silver tray. Four hundred people in black and jewels, talking in the soft, low, expensive murmur of people who did not have to raise their voices to be heard. A string quartet in the corner playing something he recognised from a film. A banner over the stage: THE SHEN FOUNDATION: INVESTING IN TOMORROW.

He had been in a room like this once before. Five years ago, at his old school’s sixtieth anniversary, where he had given a speech about light and dropped his clicker halfway through.

He looked for the nearest corner.

Then he remembered Fang Hao’s rule two, and walked to the food instead, and picked up a plate, and held it.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t see her at first.

He saw Professor Gao, in a black dress that was clearly twenty years old and that she was wearing like armour, standing with the dean and looking furious about it. He saw the head of department, Professor Zhou, who nodded to him across the room with the expression of a man who has heard that his youngest lecturer laughed in a seminar and is still trying to process it. He saw three men he recognised from the newspaper and a woman he recognised from a television drama.

Then the quartet stopped playing.

A man at the microphone said, “Ladies and gentlemen, the Shen family,” and the room turned toward the grand staircase at the far end, and there they were.

Shen Guoqiang, the father, tall and silver-haired and expressionless, in a tuxedo that fitted him like he had been born in it. Beside him, his wife, Shen Ruolan, in pale grey silk, with diamonds at her throat, smiling a smile so perfect it looked painted on. Behind them, the son, Shen Yu Ming, thirty-four, handsome and cold.

And on her mother’s other side, one step behind, coming down the white marble staircase in a long dress the colour of the sky just before dawn, with her hair up in a smooth, perfect coil and diamonds in her ears and not a single pen anywhere: the Perfect Jewel.

Miles forgot he was holding a plate.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was beautiful. Of course she was. He had known that. He had known it on the first Wednesday, with the claw clip and the biro trainers. He was a physicist, not a fool.

But she had never been beautiful like this.

Like a photograph. Like something behind glass. She came down the stairs with her chin up and her back straight and one hand on the banister, and she was smiling, a small, polite, perfect smile that he had never once seen on her in three months of Wednesdays. It went nowhere near her eyes. Her eyes were looking straight ahead, at nothing, at a point just over the heads of the four hundred people watching her.

Her mother put a hand on her arm at the bottom of the stairs and turned her, gently, toward the room. The way you would turn a vase to show its best side.

People applauded.

He thought about the girl lying with her head on his desk, laughing so hard at a cactus joke she couldn’t breathe. He thought about her standing up in the back row of Lecture Theatre C in a yellow sundress to ask if zero-point energy applied to people. He thought about her pink sticky note on his door. Cu-Te.

He looked at the girl at the bottom of the white marble staircase with diamonds in her ears and her mother’s hand on her arm, smiling her perfect, empty smile.

He understood, for the first time, what Professor Gao had meant.

She was hiding it. Because she thought nobody wanted it.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Miles Wei,” said a voice behind him. “As I live and breathe. In a tuxedo.”

He turned round.

He hadn’t heard that voice in five years, and for nine years before that he had heard it in his nightmares.

Aurelia Song—Aurelia Chen now, he remembered, she had married someone frightening—stood in front of him in a gold dress that shimmered when she moved, with a necklace of sapphires the size of quail’s eggs and an expression of wicked, enormous delight. She looked exactly the same as she had at seventeen. That was the worst part. She looked exactly as she had on the day she had stood in the school library and told Elowen Lin, in front of everyone, that Miles was hers.

Behind her, very calm, in grey, stood a man with watchful eyes who could only be her husband.

“Aurelia,” said Miles.

“You remember.” She looked him up and down. “Your bow tie is crooked. Of course it is. Some things never change.” She reached out and fixed it in three sharp movements before he could stop her, the way she had done at the reunion five years ago. “There. Now you look like a man who could have murdered someone in a nicer suit. That’s a compliment. Ask my husband. Chen Si, say hello to Miles. He’s the boy I didn’t get.”

“Good evening,” said Chen Si mildly. He offered his hand. “I’ve heard a great deal about you. Mostly unprintable.”

Miles shook it. His own hand was cold.

“And of course,” said Aurelia, looking past his shoulder with a gleam in her eye, “you remember Elowen.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He turned round again.

Elowen Lin—Elowen Zhao—was standing two metres away, in dark green silk, with a glass of water in her hand. She was smiling at him: a small, quiet, amused smile, much warmer than he remembered. She looked older than at the reunion. Softer. Her hand, holding the glass of water, had a heavy gold ring on it with a square green stone, and there was a faint green stain on her thumb that no amount of washing had got out: stems, cut that morning.

And behind her, a step back and slightly to the left, by a marble pillar, stood the largest and most frightening man Miles had ever seen.

He remembered him. Of course he did. He had walked up to him at the reunion five years ago, out of breath, and said something about Elowen not looking like she wanted to run. He had thought about it many times since, with embarrassment.

Zhao Zhendong was wearing a black suit and no expression at all. He was standing with his hands at his sides. And he was looking at Miles across the two metres between them with the steady, flat, unblinking focus of a very large dog that has decided someone is standing too close to its owner.

He was glaring.

“Miles,” said Elowen. “It’s good to see you.” She turned her head slightly. “Zhendong. You remember Miles. From the reunion.”

“Yes,” said Zhao.

That was all. Yes. He did not move. He did not blink. He did not stop glaring.

Aurelia, beside Miles, made a small sound of pure joy.

“He’s still jealous,” she whispered, delighted, to her husband. “Five years. A wedding. He’s still jealous of the physics boy. Look at his face.”

“I can see his face, my queen,” said Chen Si.

Miles stood between the two women who had once torn a school apart fighting over him, holding an empty plate, with an arms dealer glaring at him from beside a pillar, and felt a very strong desire to go and stand in a corner.

He didn’t. He thought of Fang Hao. Don’t leave early.

“You look well,” he said to Elowen, because it was true and because he couldn’t think of anything else.

Aurelia looked pointedly at the glass of water in Elowen’s hand. Then at the arms dealer by the pillar, who had moved half a step closer to his wife the moment a man with a tray of champagne came within two metres of her.

“She’s very well,” said Aurelia, with enormous meaning. “She has three hundred white roses to do for a wedding tomorrow, so she’s on water, and he’s driving her to the flower market at half past three in the morning to carry the buckets. And he has glared at every man who has come within two metres of her since the door opened. Five years married. I’m not saying anything. I’m just standing here.”

Elowen closed her eyes briefly.

“Aurelia.”

“I said nothing.”

And behind her, by the pillar, for just a second, the glaring arms dealer’s mouth moved at one corner, very slightly, in something that on another man might have been a smile.

Then he looked back at Miles. And glared.

✦ ✦ ✦

He survived ten minutes of Aurelia. She told him he looked thin. She told him she had read about his laugh in the seminar online, and that she had laughed so hard she had to sit down, because she hadn’t heard him laugh since the library. She told him he was the only man she had ever failed to get, and that she was very glad, now, because look what she got instead, and put her hand on her husband’s arm in a way that made Chen Si’s calm face go briefly, completely soft.

Elowen said very little. She watched him with her quiet, amused, much-too-perceptive eyes.

At some point, Aurelia followed his gaze across the ballroom.

To the far side of the room, by the stage, where the Shen family stood in a little island of light. Where the father was talking to the dean. Where the mother was introducing the daughter to a line of men in tuxedos, one after another, her hand on her daughter’s elbow. Where the Perfect Jewel was smiling her perfect, empty smile at each of them in turn, and saying something polite, and not once looking at anything.

He had been counting. He hadn’t meant to. That one was the sixth. The fifth had been a man he estimated at forty-five, with very clean fingernails. Working it out from the floor tiles, Miles put him forty centimetres from her. He had looked at her earrings the whole time he talked, and at one point had put a hand on her arm to make a point and left it there two seconds longer than the point needed.

Miles had disliked him with a precision that surprised him. He had never in his life had an opinion about a stranger’s fingernails. He had one now. He found he was holding the empty plate so tightly that the rim had printed a line across his palm.

Aurelia went very quiet. For Aurelia.

Then she turned and looked at Miles. Really looked at him. At his face. At where his eyes had been.

“Oh,” said Aurelia Chen softly. “Oh, Miles.”

“What?”

She looked back across the ballroom. At the girl in the dawn-coloured dress.

“That’s the Shen girl,” she said. “The Perfect Jewel. Ruolan’s daughter.” She looked at him again. “She’s a physics student. At your university.”

Miles said nothing.

Elowen, beside him, said nothing either. But she put her glass of water down very gently on a passing tray, and looked at him with an expression he remembered from a library, a long time ago, when she had been fifteen and tired and he had been the only person who didn’t want anything from her.

It was the look of someone who recognised something.

And across the ballroom, at that exact moment, as if she had felt it, Shen Yu Jie stopped smiling at the man in front of her, and turned her head, and looked straight across four hundred people, past the ice ship and the chandeliers and the string quartet, to where he was standing.

Their eyes met.

For one second, the perfect smile went away. Something else came onto her face instead. Something startled, and unguarded, and very much like relief.

Then her mother’s hand tightened on her elbow, and she turned back to the man in front of her, and the Perfect Jewel was back.

But Miles had seen it. And so, standing beside him, had Aurelia, and Elowen, and Chen Si.

And so, from beside the marble pillar, had Zhao Zhendong.

Who, for the first time all evening, stopped glaring at Miles, and looked across the ballroom at the girl in the dawn-coloured dress, and then back at Miles, with an expression of slow, dawning, deeply suspicious interest.

chapters.title: Yu Jie Is Not Jealous of Women Married to Dangerous Men
chapters.desc: She is a little jealous. She would like that noted privately. Then Aurelia Chen corners her in the powder room.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m not jealous.” “You’ve folded that napkin into a swan, unfolded it, and folded it into a smaller swan.”
chapters.content:
There were nine men.

Yu Jie counted them, because counting was the only thing keeping her face still. Nine men in an hour and a quarter, one after another, each brought to her by her mother’s hand on her elbow and her mother’s voice saying, “Ruolan’s daughter, Yu Jie. She’s at the university. Physics, can you imagine? She’ll grow out of it.”

The son of a shipping company. The son of a bank. A man who owned eleven restaurants and told her about each one. A man who had just come back from Switzerland and wanted her to know it. A widower of forty-four with very clean fingernails who looked at her the way her mother looked at a vase in an antique shop. Every one of them smiled at her. Every one of them looked at the diamonds in her ears before they looked at her face.

She smiled back. She said thank you. She said how interesting. She said, when the restaurant man asked what she was studying, “Oh, just physics,” and laughed a little, the way her mother had taught her, so that it sounded like a hobby.

Just physics.

She thought of the chalkboard in office 412 and felt sick.

✦ ✦ ✦

And then she had looked across the ballroom, between the sixth man and the seventh, and seen him.

He was by the food. He was by the food. Holding an empty plate. In a black tuxedo, a real one, with satin lapels, and a bow tie, and his hair cut shorter so the piece at the back almost lay flat. He was standing very straight, straighter than she had ever seen him stand, and he looked like—

She didn’t have a word for what he looked like. She had a great many words for many things, in three languages and the language of mathematics, and none of them were good enough.

He looked like someone she would have crossed a ballroom for, if her mother’s hand hadn’t been on her elbow.

And standing in front of him, fixing his bow tie with three sharp, intimate little movements as if she had every right in the world to touch his collar, was the most beautiful woman Yu Jie had ever seen.

✦ ✦ ✦

She knew who Aurelia Chen was. Everyone did. She was in the society pages twice a month: at the opera, at the races, at the opening of something. The gold dress was probably worth more than Tao Tao’s family home. The man standing calmly behind her, in grey, was Chen Si. Yu Jie’s father did not do business with Chen Si. Her father, who did business with everyone, had once said at dinner, in a very quiet voice, that the Shen family would never do business with Chen Si, and then changed the subject, and nobody had ever brought it up again.

And beside Aurelia, in green, with a glass of water, was Elowen Zhao.

Yu Jie knew about her too. Everyone knew about Elowen Zhao now: the florist from the Walled City who had married the most frightening man in the city. Her mother had a great deal to say about it, always at dinner, always in the tone she used for things that were not done. A shopgirl. With that man. They say he bought her shop on the first night.

The most frightening man in the city was standing by a pillar, staring at Miles as if he would like to fold him in half.

And Miles was standing between Aurelia Chen and Elowen Zhao, the two most talked-about women in the room, and they were both talking to him. Smiling at him. Aurelia had her hand on his arm. Elowen was looking at him with a quiet, warm expression, as if they shared something old.

They did share something old. Yu Jie knew it suddenly, the way she knew when an equation was going to come out. You did not look at someone like that unless you had known them for a long time.

Two women who fought over him.

Fang Hao had said that. Once, in September, through the cardboard wall, not knowing she could hear. He hasn’t laughed since high school. Something happened. Two girls. Big drama.

She looked at the two most beautiful women in the room, one in gold and one in green, both married to dangerous men, both laughing with Miles Wei by the dessert table as if he were theirs.

The seventh man was talking to her about golf.

“How interesting,” said Yu Jie, and folded her napkin into a swan.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was not jealous.

She wanted that clear. She was a scientist, and she had looked at the evidence, and the evidence was that both of those women were married, very publicly, to men who could buy and sell the harbour and possibly had. Aurelia Chen had a hand on her husband’s arm that was not the hand of a woman thinking about anyone else. Elowen Zhao kept looking back at the man by the pillar every few seconds, as if checking he was still there.

There was nothing to be jealous of.

She unfolded the napkin swan and folded it into a smaller swan.

It was just that they had known him. When he was seventeen. Before the rule. Before the cactus and the egg sandwiches and the one egg in the fridge. They had known a boy who laughed, and they had fought over him, and he had walked away from both of them and never laughed again.

And Yu Jie, who had made him laugh for the first time in fourteen years in a seminar room in front of the whole department, had to stand on the other side of a ballroom in her mother’s diamonds and smile at a man who was talking about his handicap.

And then Miles looked up and saw her.

Across four hundred people. Their eyes met.

She forgot to smile. For one second she forgot everything: her mother, the golf, the diamonds, the swan. She just looked at him, and he looked at her, and she felt something come onto her face that she couldn’t stop.

Then her mother’s hand tightened on her elbow.

“Yu Jie,” said Shen Ruolan softly, without moving her lips. “You’re staring. Who is that?”

“Nobody,” said Yu Jie. “A lecturer. From the department.”

Her mother followed her gaze across the ballroom. To the tall thin man in the new tuxedo by the dessert table, standing between Aurelia Chen and Elowen Zhao.

Her mother’s eyes narrowed. Very slightly.

“Ah,” said Shen Ruolan. “The young one. Professor Gao’s favourite. I wrote to him.” She turned her daughter firmly back toward the eighth man. “He’s very thin. Smile, darling. This is Mr. Huo. His family owns the airport.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She escaped at nine-fifteen, during the speeches.

Her father was on the stage, talking about investing in tomorrow, in his flat, expressionless voice. Her mother was standing beside him, smiling. Her brother was by the bar, on his phone. Nobody was watching the Perfect Jewel. For the first time all evening, nobody had a hand on her elbow.

She went down a corridor lined with mirrors to the ladies’ powder room, which was the size of her apartment and had velvet sofas and gold taps and an attendant who handed out towels, and sat down on a velvet sofa, and put her face in her hands.

She didn’t cry. She didn’t cry at galas. She had made that rule at fourteen, at her first one, after her mother told her in the car on the way home that she had laughed too loudly at the dinner table and embarrassed the family.

She took out her phone. She had one message, from Tao Tao: how’s the zoo? any rich boys worth eating?

She typed: nine. all inedible. he’s here.

WHO

you know who.

IN A TUX???

yes.

SEND PHOTO

no.

JIE JIE SEND A PHOTO OR I WILL DIE

he’s talking to aurelia chen and elowen zhao, Yu Jie typed. they both know him from school. they’re both married to men who look like they kill people for a living. they’re both gorgeous. i’m not jealous.

Three dots. Then:

you’re a little jealous

i would like that noted privately

NOTED. PRIVATELY. now go back out there and

The door of the powder room opened.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia Chen came in, in a shimmer of gold, and stopped.

She looked at the velvet sofa. At the girl sitting on it, in a dress the colour of dawn, with her diamonds and her perfect hair and her phone clutched in both hands.

“Oh, good,” said Aurelia. “I was hoping it was you.”

She sat down on the other end of the sofa without asking. She crossed her legs. She looked Yu Jie up and down with frank, total, unembarrassed interest, the way Tao Tao looked at a new species of fungus.

“You’re Ruolan’s girl,” she said. “The Perfect Jewel.”

“Yu Jie,” said Yu Jie.

“Yu Jie,” repeated Aurelia. “Physics.”

“Yes.”

“At City University.”

“…Yes.”

“With Miles.”

Yu Jie said nothing at all. She put her phone face down on her knee.

Aurelia smiled. It was a slow, wicked, delighted smile, like a cat finding an open door.

“Sweetheart,” she said. “You looked at him across that ballroom like he was the last lifeboat on the Titanic. And he looked back at you like he’d been hit with one. I’ve known Miles Wei since he was sixteen years old and I have never, ever seen his face do that.” She leaned in. “So. How long?”

“There’s nothing,” said Yu Jie. Her voice came out very steady. “He’s a lecturer. I’m a student. He has a rule.”

“Of course he has a rule.” Aurelia rolled her eyes to the gold ceiling. “He had a rule at sixteen. No girlfriends until university. He wrote it in the front of his physics notebook. I know because I stole it and read it. Then Elowen and I had a fight in the library about him that the school still talks about, and he went white as a sheet, and walked out, and chose a textbook over both of us.” She shrugged one bare gold shoulder. “Honestly, it was the right choice. I was a nightmare. Elowen was asleep on her feet. We didn’t want him. We wanted to win.”

Yu Jie looked at her.

“Did you love him?” she said, before she could stop herself.

Aurelia looked at her. The wicked smile changed into something else.

“No,” she said. “Not really. I loved that he didn’t want me. Nobody ever didn’t want me.” She tilted her head. “Do you?”

Yu Jie didn’t answer.

She didn’t have to. Aurelia Chen, who had grown up in rooms like this one and could read a face across a ballroom, looked at hers and saw everything.

“Oh, sweetheart,” she said softly.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Here’s a thing about Miles,” said Aurelia, after a while. She was fixing her lipstick in the gold mirror opposite, talking to Yu Jie’s reflection. “He thinks wanting things gets people hurt. He watched two girls tear each other apart over him in a library when he was seventeen, and he decided it was his fault, because he was the thing we were fighting about. So he stopped being a thing anyone could want. He made himself boring on purpose. Did you know that? He used to be funny. He used to do impressions of the physics teacher.”

Yu Jie’s throat felt tight.

“He laughed,” she said. “Two weeks ago. In a seminar. Out loud.”

Aurelia’s hand stopped with the lipstick an inch from her mouth.

“That was you?” She turned round on the sofa. “The seminar? Someone put it online. Some second-year. Dr. Wei LAUGHS, the department is shaking. I watched it six times.” She stared at Yu Jie. “What did you say?”

“I told a professor from the capital my gap doesn’t close.”

Aurelia looked at her.

Then she threw her head back and laughed so loudly the powder-room attendant dropped a towel.

“Oh, I like you,” said Aurelia Chen. “Oh, Ruolan is going to hate this.” She stood up in a shimmer of gold and held out her hand to pull Yu Jie up from the sofa. “Come on. Speeches are nearly over. Your mother will be looking for you, and if she finds you in here with me, she’ll have a stroke, and I’m not ready to be blamed for that yet.”

Yu Jie took the hand. She stood up.

At the door, Aurelia stopped and looked back at her.

“For what it’s worth,” she said. “I’m married to a man the newspapers call a gangster. Elowen’s married to a man who sells guns. Neither of us is jealous of anything you’ve got, except one thing.” She smiled, not wickedly this time. “He laughed for you. He never once laughed for us.”

She opened the door and went out in a blaze of gold, and left Yu Jie standing in the doorway of the powder room with her phone in her hand and her heart beating very fast.

She looked down at the phone.

Tao Tao had sent eleven more messages, all of them in capitals.

Yu Jie typed one word back.

Noted.

Then she put the phone in her small silver bag, and lifted her chin, and walked back down the corridor of mirrors toward the ballroom, past her own reflection twenty times over: a girl in a dawn-coloured dress, diamonds, hair perfect, not a single pen.

In the last mirror, just before the ballroom door, she stopped.

She reached up and took one of the long silver pins out of the smooth, perfect coil of her hair, and pulled out one strand at the side, so it fell loose against her cheek. Just one. Very small. The kind of thing nobody would notice.

Nobody except a physicist who noticed everything.

Then she went back in.

chapters.title: Elowen Asks Him One Question
chapters.desc: Five years ago he asked her on a balcony. Tonight, on a terrace over the harbour, she asks him back.
chapters.epigraph: “Are you happy, Miles?” He had never once, in thirty-one years, thought about it.
chapters.content:
He went out onto the terrace at nine-twenty, because the speeches were very long and Shen Guoqiang had started talking about quarterly growth, and Fang Hao’s rules hadn’t said anything about speeches.

The terrace ran the length of the ballroom, above the harbour. It was cold, December cold, and nobody else was out there except a waiter smoking by the far railing who put his cigarette out guiltily when he saw a guest and went inside. The harbour was black and silver. The lights of the ships moved slowly across it. On the far side of the water, the Shen Building stood forty storeys high with its name lit up in white at the top, so that you could see it from everywhere in the city.

He leaned on the cold stone balustrade and looked at it.

Shen.

He thought of the girl at the bottom of the white staircase with her mother’s hand on her elbow. He thought of her looking across the ballroom at him. That one second, when the perfect smile had gone, and something else had come into her face instead.

Relief. That was what it had been. As if he were a door she had been looking for in a room with no doors.

He thought of the nine men. He had counted them too.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You never stay for speeches,” said a voice beside him. “You didn’t stay for them at the reunion either.”

Elowen Zhao had come out onto the terrace with a pashmina around her shoulders and her glass of water. She came and leaned on the balustrade beside him, a comfortable distance away, and looked out at the harbour too.

Behind them, through the glass doors, Miles could see a very large shape standing just inside. Not coming out. Just standing there, with his back to the speeches, watching the terrace.

“Your husband,” said Miles.

“He’ll stay inside,” said Elowen. “I asked him to. He’s very good at doing what I ask, as long as he can see me while he does it.” She smiled slightly at the harbour. “He’s been jealous of you for five years. He knows it’s ridiculous. He told me so. He said, I know it’s ridiculous, Elowen, he’s a physicist, he would lose a fight to a coat stand. And then he glared at you anyway.”

“I would lose a fight to a coat stand,” Miles agreed.

“I know. I told him.”

They stood in silence for a while. It was a good silence. It always had been, with Elowen. In the school library, years ago, when they had both stayed late—her because she didn’t want to go home, him because he didn’t have anywhere else to be—they had sat at opposite ends of the same table for hours without speaking, and it had been the most restful thing in either of their lives.

He hadn’t understood, then, that she didn’t want to go home because home was a house full of guns. He had only understood that she was tired, and that she didn’t want anything from him, and that it was nice.

“Three hundred white roses,” he said. “Aurelia said. At half past three in the morning.”

Elowen laughed softly.

“He’ll carry every bucket,” she said. “He always does. He stands in the flower market at four in the morning in a suit that costs more than the market, holding buckets of eucalyptus, and the old women who sell peonies have stopped being afraid of him and started giving him tea.” She shook her head. “Last month he closed the shop for a week without telling me and took me to the mountains. He’d had someone learn the whole order book. He’d booked a cabin with a hot spring. He said, You haven’t had a day off in ten years.” She looked down at the harbour. “I hadn’t. I didn’t know you were allowed.”

“Were you?”

“I am now.” She smiled. “We’re going to Iceland in February. To see the lights. He’s read eleven books about them. He keeps telling me facts at dinner.” She was quiet for a moment. “I love him so much I can hardly breathe some days.”

Miles looked at her.

He had known Elowen Lin at sixteen. Grey, exhausted, guarded, holding up the whole world with her two thin arms. He had never once seen her face look the way it did now, talking about a man and a hot spring and the northern lights.

“You’re happy,” he said. It wasn’t a question.

“Yes,” said Elowen simply.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Five years ago,” she said, after a while, “at the reunion. You came and found me on a balcony like this one, and you asked me a question. Do you remember?”

He remembered. He had thought about it many times. He had walked out onto the balcony and found her alone, looking at the city, in a red dress, with that huge dangerous man by the wall inside, and he had asked her the only thing he could think of to ask. Because she had looked, under all the elegance, so exactly like the tired girl in the library.

“I asked if you were happy,” he said.

“You did.” Elowen turned and looked at him. “And I didn’t know. Nobody had ever asked me. I had to stand there and think about it. It was the first time in my whole life I had thought about it.” She held his eyes. “It was one of the most important things anyone ever did for me, Miles. I don’t think you knew that.”

He hadn’t.

“So I’ve been waiting five years,” said Elowen, “to give it back.”

She was quiet for a moment.

“Are you happy, Miles?”

✦ ✦ ✦

He opened his mouth to answer.

Then he closed it.

He stood on the cold terrace above the harbour and thought about it. Properly. The way he thought about a problem nobody knew the answer to.

He thought about the staff flat behind the sports ground. Books on every surface. One chair at one table. Three cacti on the windowsill and one on the mat. A fridge with one egg in it, until a girl had filled it with congee and oranges.

He thought about the egg sandwich he ate every day at 12:30 at his desk, because it took no decisions. About going to every department seminar and sitting in the same seat and leaving before the wine. About five years in office 412, writing papers on light bending around galaxies, with his door shut, until September.

He thought about the chalkboard. 20 June, 16:00, in small round writing in the bottom right-hand corner.

He thought about the second Wednesday of September, at 3:47, when the door had opened and a girl in a yellow sundress had come in with the harmonic oscillator and the answer hidden in the margin.

He thought about laughing in the seminar.

“I don’t know,” he said finally. His voice came out strange. “I’ve never thought about it.”

Elowen waited.

“I thought,” said Miles slowly, “that I was all right. That’s what I tell my sister. I’m all right. I have my work. I have the cactus. I don’t bother anyone, and nobody bothers me, and nobody gets hurt.” He looked at the harbour. “I thought that was the same thing as happy. I thought it was close enough.”

“And now?”

He was silent for a long time.

“Since September,” he said, “I’ve been happy on Wednesdays.”

He heard himself say it and went red, even in the cold.

“Between 3:45 and six,” he said. “On Wednesdays. And on the Saturday at the library café, for three hours. And when she brought oranges.” He pushed his glasses up his nose. “And then the rest of the week, I’m all right. Like before. Except it doesn’t feel close enough any more.”

Elowen didn’t say anything.

“She’s twenty-two,” said Miles. “She’s a student in my department. Her family owns that building.” He nodded across the harbour at the forty white storeys. “Her mother introduced her to nine men tonight. I counted. She’s going to graduate in June and do something extraordinary and some man from a shipping company is going to—” He stopped. “And I’m a lecturer who lives in a staff flat and eats the same sandwich every day. I have a rule. It’s a good rule.”

“It is a good rule,” said Elowen.

“Then why,” said Miles, “does it feel like I’m standing on the wrong side of it?”

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen looked at him for a long time in the cold.

Then she looked through the glass doors, to where the very large shape of her husband stood watching her, motionless, through the glass.

“I had a rule too,” she said. “For a long time. Don’t want anything you can’t afford to lose. I made it when I was seven, the night my mother died. I kept it until I was twenty-four.” She pulled the pashmina tighter. “Then a man walked into my shop in the rain and bought every flower I had, and I spent a year trying to keep my rule, and it nearly killed both of us.”

Miles listened.

“I’m not going to tell you to break your rule,” said Elowen. “You’re right to keep it. Keep it until June. You’d never forgive yourself if you didn’t.” She turned back to him. “But Miles. A rule is for not doing things. It isn’t for not wanting them. You’ve been mixing the two up since you were seventeen.”

He stood very still.

“You can keep your distance,” said Elowen, “and still want her. You can wait for her, and still be happy that she exists. You’re allowed to stand on the right side of a rule and still look at what’s on the other side.” She smiled slightly. “You’re a physicist. You know about light. It bends around heavy things. It doesn’t stop going where it was going.”

He stared at her.

“Did you just make a gravitational lensing metaphor?”

“I read your paper,” said Elowen. “The one from the reunion. I read all of them. I didn’t understand most of it, but I liked the pictures.”

Miles looked at her. Then, unexpectedly, he laughed. Quietly. Out on the cold terrace, above the black and silver harbour.

The second time in fourteen years.

Through the glass doors, the very large shape of Zhao Zhendong went perfectly still.

✦ ✦ ✦

The terrace door opened behind them.

Not Zhao. He hadn’t moved. It was someone else: a girl in a dawn-coloured dress, with diamonds in her ears and one strand of hair fallen loose against her cheek, standing in the doorway with the warm gold light of the ballroom behind her. She had clearly come out to be alone, and found the terrace occupied, and stopped.

She looked at Miles. Then at Elowen beside him. Then at Miles again, still half-laughing.

Something went across her face, very fast, and was gone.

“Sorry,” said Shen Yu Jie, in her polite gala voice. “I didn’t know anyone was—”

“I was just going in,” said Elowen.

She pushed herself off the balustrade. She went past Yu Jie in the doorway. And as she passed, she stopped, and leaned close, and said something very quietly that Miles couldn’t hear.

Yu Jie went pink. All the way to the loose strand of hair.

Then Elowen went inside, into the warm light, straight to the very large man waiting by the glass, who put one hand at the small of her back without looking away from the terrace, and steered her gently back toward the ballroom, and glared over his shoulder at Miles one last time as they went.

And the terrace door swung shut behind them.

And Miles and Yu Jie were alone on the cold stone terrace above the harbour, three metres apart, with the Shen Building lit up white across the water.

“What did she say to you?” said Miles.

Yu Jie looked at him in the cold. At the tuxedo and the bow tie and the hair cut short. At his face, which was still a little red from laughing.

“She said,” said Yu Jie, “he just told me he’s happy on Wednesdays.”

Miles closed his eyes.

“That woman,” he said, “has been dangerous since she was sixteen.”

And Yu Jie, in her mother’s diamonds, on her father’s terrace, stopped being the Perfect Jewel and started to laugh.

chapters.title: The Diplomat Her Mother Chose
chapters.desc: Lu Zhiyuan is a perfect match on paper: twenty-nine, five languages, a beautiful waltz. Yu Jie hates paper. Then he offers her a deal.
chapters.epigraph: “On paper, we’re perfect.” “I hate paper.” “Good. So do I. Shall we dance anyway?”
chapters.content:
They had four minutes on the terrace.

Afterwards, Yu Jie would count them. Four minutes, from the door swinging shut behind Elowen Zhao to the door opening again. She would count them the way she counted the squares on her calendar: carefully, one by one, so she could keep them.

For the first minute, they laughed. Both of them. She couldn’t stop, and then he couldn’t either, and the waiter who had come back out for his cigarette took one look at the two of them, the Shen heiress and the man in the new tuxedo, three metres apart and laughing helplessly at nothing, and went back inside again.

For the second minute, they didn’t say anything at all. They just stood at the cold balustrade with three metres between them and looked at the harbour, and it was the same silence as office 412 on a Wednesday at five o’clock, when the problem was finished and neither of them wanted to leave.

The wind came up off the harbour, cold and wet and smelling of salt. She was in silk with bare arms and she did not shiver, because the Perfect Jewel did not shiver in public. She had been trained out of it at fourteen.

He noticed anyway. He walked round behind her, a long way behind, and came back to the balustrade on her other side, between her and the open end of the terrace where the wind was coming from. He stayed three metres away, exactly three; he checked it against the paving stones.

On her side, the wind dropped. Not much. Enough.

She knew what he had done. She didn’t say so. Neither of them said anything. It was the second minute, and the second minute was for not saying things.

In the third minute, he said, without looking at her:

“Your hair.”

She put her hand up to the loose strand by her cheek.

“It came down,” she said.

“No, it didn’t,” said Miles. “You took a pin out. There’s a space in the coil on the left side where the pin was. It’s about two centimetres.” He paused. “I’m sorry. I notice things. I can’t stop.”

She didn’t say anything. Her heart was going very fast.

In the fourth minute, he turned his head and looked at her, finally, properly, in the cold light from the ballroom, at the diamonds and the dawn-coloured dress and the one loose strand of hair, and said very quietly:

“You don’t look like yourself tonight.”

“Who do I look like?”

“Like a photograph of you,” said Miles. “Taken by someone who’s never met you.”

She opened her mouth.

And the terrace door opened behind them, and her brother said, “Yu Jie. Mother wants you. Now. Lu Zhiyuan has arrived.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Shen Yu Ming was thirty-four, and handsome, and ran the logistics arm of Shen Holdings, and had never once in his life asked his little sister a question about anything she was studying.

He stood in the terrace doorway with his phone in his hand and looked at Miles with total, polite indifference, as if he were a pillar.

“Dr. Wei, isn’t it?” he said. “From the university. My mother says thank you for coming.” Then, to Yu Jie: “Now, please. She’s waiting.”

Yu Jie looked at Miles.

He had straightened up from the balustrade. He was standing very straight, in the tuxedo, with his face perfectly calm and his hands at his sides. He gave her a small nod. Professional. Three metres.

Go, said the nod. It’s all right. I know.

She went.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lu Zhiyuan was waiting with her mother by the dance floor, and he was perfect.

She saw that at once, the way you see that a proof is elegant before you have checked it line by line. He was twenty-nine, tall, in a midnight-blue dinner jacket that fitted him perfectly. He had a calm, intelligent, handsome face and very good manners and the slight weariness at the corners of the eyes of a man who has spent too many nights at too many receptions in too many countries. His father was a former ambassador. He worked at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. He spoke five languages. Her mother had told her all of this in the car on the way, three times, in a list.

“Zhiyuan,” said Shen Ruolan, glowing. “This is Yu Jie. My daughter.”

He bowed slightly over her hand. He did not look at her diamonds. He looked at her face.

“Miss Shen,” he said. “I’ve heard a great deal about you.”

“From my mother.”

“From your mother,” he agreed, with a straight face. “At length. In a list.”

Yu Jie looked at him in surprise.

Behind him, the string quartet started to play a waltz.

“Zhiyuan dances beautifully,” said her mother. “He learned in Vienna. Go on, both of you. Everyone’s watching.”

Everyone was. Four hundred people. Her mother had made sure of it.

Lu Zhiyuan held out his hand.

“On paper,” he said, very quietly, so only she could hear, “we’re perfect. You know that.”

“I hate paper,” said Yu Jie.

He looked at her for a moment. Something changed in his calm, tired eyes. Something that looked almost like relief.

“Good,” said Lu Zhiyuan. “So do I.” He smiled, very slightly. “Shall we dance anyway? It will make your mother very happy, and it will make mine very happy, and then they’ll both leave us alone for at least an hour.”

She took his hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

He did dance beautifully. He had learned in Vienna. He held her correctly, at exactly the right distance, his hand light on her back, and steered her round the floor in long, smooth turns as if she weighed nothing, and the four hundred people watched them, and somewhere at the edge of the floor her mother was glowing like a lamp.

“So,” said Lu Zhiyuan, in the middle of the second turn. “Physics.”

She looked at him warily. “Yes.”

“What kind?”

Nobody had ever asked her that at a gala. Not once. Nine men tonight, and twenty or thirty at every gala before, and not one of them had ever asked her what kind.

“Condensed matter,” she said. “Topological phases in strained graphene. It’s a sheet of carbon one atom thick. If you stretch it in the right way, the electrons inside start behaving as if there’s a magnetic field, even when there isn’t one. And at the edges, strange things happen. Things that might be useful for computers one day. Or might not. That’s what I’m trying to find out.”

She stopped. She had forgotten to laugh, the way her mother had taught her, so it sounded like a hobby.

Lu Zhiyuan was looking at her with real interest.

“That,” he said, “is the most interesting thing anyone has said to me at a party in three years. Last week a man in Brussels talked to me about his boat for forty minutes.”

She laughed. She didn’t mean to.

“So you see,” said Lu Zhiyuan, turning her again, “we already have something in common. We both find these parties unbearable, and we’re both very good at hiding it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the third turn, she saw Miles.

He had come back in from the terrace. He was standing at the edge of the dance floor. Not in a corner. Not by the door. By the food, with an empty plate in his hand, exactly where Fang Hao had told him to stand. Very straight. Watching.

Watching her dance with the perfect man her mother had chosen.

His face was completely calm. He looked like he was listening to a seminar. Only someone who had spent fourteen Wednesdays in office 412 would have known that he was holding the plate so hard his knuckles had gone white.

She missed a step.

Lu Zhiyuan caught her. Smoothly. Nobody noticed. He brought her round in a long, easy turn so her back was to the edge of the floor and she couldn’t see the food table any more, and then he looked over her shoulder, at the place where she had been looking.

He looked for a long moment.

“Ah,” said Lu Zhiyuan softly.

She went cold.

“The lecturer,” he said. “The thin one in the new tuxedo. He’s been standing in that exact spot for ten minutes with an empty plate, and he hasn’t taken his eyes off you once.” He brought her round again. “And you’ve looked at him four times since we started dancing. I counted. I’m a diplomat. Counting things is half the job.”

“It isn’t what you think.”

“I don’t think anything,” said Lu Zhiyuan. “I’m very good at not thinking things. It’s the other half of the job.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They danced for a while in silence.

Then, at the end of the waltz, as the music slowed, he said very quietly, close to her ear, in a voice that was not his reception voice at all:

“Miss Shen. May I make you an offer?”

She looked up at him.

“My parents have been trying to marry me off for four years,” said Lu Zhiyuan. “Your mother has been trying for two. They’ve decided that we’re perfect. They’re going to keep trying until something happens.” His hand on her back was very steady. “I would like to propose an arrangement. Not a marriage. An arrangement.”

“What kind of arrangement?”

“We let them think it’s working,” said Lu Zhiyuan. “We have dinner when they ask us to. We dance at galas. We’re seen together, very correctly, at a distance. You tell your mother I’m charming. I tell mine you’re brilliant, which is true. And while they’re busy planning a wedding that will never happen, they stop introducing us both to other people.” He smiled slightly. “It buys us time. Both of us.”

She stared at him.

“Why would you want that?” she said. “You’re perfect. You could marry anyone.”

Something flickered behind his calm, tired eyes. Just for a second.

“I could marry anyone my parents want,” said Lu Zhiyuan. “That isn’t the same thing.” The music was ending. “Let’s just say there is someone I’m not allowed to be seen with, Miss Shen. Not in rooms like this one. And I’ve become very tired of rooms like this one.”

The waltz ended.

He stepped back, exactly the right distance. He bowed. Four hundred people applauded. Her mother, at the edge of the floor, put a hand to her diamonds as if she might faint with happiness.

“Think about it,” said Lu Zhiyuan, smiling his reception smile again. “I’m in no hurry. I’m very good at waiting. It’s the third half of the job.”

“That’s three halves.”

“Diplomacy,” said Lu Zhiyuan gravely, “is not an exact science.”

And for the second time that night, Shen Yu Jie forgot to laugh like a hobby and laughed like herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the edge of the dance floor, by the food table, Miles Wei put down his empty plate.

He had watched the whole waltz. Every turn. He had seen the perfect man in midnight blue hold her at exactly the right distance and steer her round the floor as if she weighed nothing. He had seen him lean close and say something in her ear. He had seen her look up at him in surprise. And at the end, he had seen her laugh, a real laugh, her own, not the gala one.

He had seen Shen Ruolan watching it, glowing.

He stood very straight and thought about Fang Hao’s rule three. Don’t leave early. Whatever happens.

He thought about the rule on the chalkboard. Nothing happens while you’re a student in this department.

He thought about Elowen on the terrace. A rule is for not doing things. It isn’t for not wanting them.

He had never in his life wanted anything as much as he wanted, right now, to walk across that dance floor.

He didn’t. He picked his plate back up. He stood by the food. He stayed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Across the ballroom, as the quartet started something new, Shen Ruolan bent her head to her daughter’s ear and said, glowing, without moving her lips:

“The Lus are coming to New Year dinner. Both families. I’ve already spoken to his mother.” Her hand closed on Yu Jie’s elbow. “Nothing official, of course. Not until you graduate. But I thought July. July is a lovely month for an engagement.”

Yu Jie stood very still in her mother’s diamonds.

“July,” she said.

“After the twentieth of June,” said her mother, “there’s really nothing to wait for, is there, darling? The degree will be finished. You’ll have had your little hobby.” She patted her daughter’s arm. “And jewels are meant to be worn.”

Across the room, by the food table, a thin man in a new tuxedo was standing very straight, holding an empty plate.

The twentieth of June.

Yu Jie looked at him. He looked back.

He didn’t know. He couldn’t have heard. But he looked at her face across four hundred people, and something in his own face changed, as if he had seen an equation on her that he didn’t like the answer to.

She looked away first.

She smiled at her mother, her perfect smile, and said, “Of course, Mother,” and went to say goodbye to Lu Zhiyuan, very correctly, at exactly the right distance.

And in the small silver bag on her wrist, her phone buzzed with an event she had made in September and set to remind her once a month:

The end of the interval. 20 June, 16:00.

chapters.title: Miles Takes the Long Way Home
