chapters.desc: One in the morning, no coat, silver shoes that hurt. He walks her home through the sleeping city, three metres apart, and stops one block early on purpose.
chapters.epigraph: “You’re walking very slowly.” “I’m calculating the optimal route.” “It’s a straight line, Miles.” “Not if you do it properly.”
chapters.content:
He stayed until the end.

He stayed through the speeches and the dancing and the auction, where a businessman paid a sum he couldn’t imagine for a weekend on a yacht. He stayed through the dessert, which he didn’t eat, and the coffee, which he didn’t drink, and the moment just after midnight when Professor Gao came past him on her way out, in her twenty-year-old black dress, and looked at him standing by the food table, and said “Good,” and nothing else, and left.

He stayed while the Shen family stood at the top of the white staircase and said goodbye to four hundred guests one by one. He stayed while Aurelia Chen kissed him on both cheeks and said “Wednesdays,” in a terrible whisper, and went off on her husband’s arm, laughing. He stayed while Zhao Zhendong walked past him with his wife and stopped, for one second, and looked down at him from a great height and said:

“She’s a good girl. The Shen one.”

Miles looked up at him.

“Yes,” he said.

Zhao looked at him for a long moment with his flat, dark, unreadable eyes.

“Don’t be stupid about it,” he said, and walked on.

Elowen, on his arm, looked back over her shoulder and smiled.

Miles stood by the empty food table in the emptying ballroom and wondered whether he had just been threatened or blessed by an arms dealer, and decided that with that man it was probably the same thing.

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten to one, he went down the hotel steps into the cold.

There was a line of black cars at the bottom, waiting with their engines running. The doormen were whistling for taxis. Rich people in furs stood about in groups, laughing, their breath white in the air. He had his phone out to call a taxi of his own when he saw her.

She was standing at the side of the steps, a little way from the cars, in the shadow of a stone pillar. Alone. No coat. Her bare arms wrapped around herself. Her silver bag on her wrist. And she was holding her shoes, high silver heels, one in each hand, and standing on the cold stone in her stockings.

He put his phone away.

He went down the steps toward her, not quickly, keeping well to the side, away from the light.

“You’re not wearing any shoes,” he said.

She looked round. She didn’t look surprised to see him. She looked as if she had been waiting.

“They’re very beautiful shoes,” said Yu Jie. “Italian. My mother chose them. They were designed by a man who has never once walked anywhere.” She held one up. “I can’t feel my toes. I don’t know if that’s the shoes or the cold.”

“Where’s your coat?”

“In the car. With my mother.” She nodded toward the black cars. One of them, long and dark, had its back door open. A driver stood beside it. “She’s waiting for me. We’re going back to the family house tonight. She wants to talk about July.”

Miles didn’t know what July was. He didn’t ask. He looked at the long dark car and the open door and the bare arms of the girl standing barefoot on the stone.

“You don’t want to get in that car,” he said.

It wasn’t a question.

She looked at him in the shadow of the pillar. Her eyes were very bright.

“No,” said Yu Jie. “I don’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He took off his jacket.

He didn’t think about it. He just did it. He took off the black jacket with the satin lapels, which Wei Lan had made him buy and not rent, and held it out at arm’s length, as far as his arm would go, so that his hand wouldn’t come anywhere near her.

She looked at it.

“That’s not professional distance,” she said.

“It’s a metre and a half,” said Miles. “My arm is very long. And you’re going to get hypothermia, and then I’ll have to explain to Professor Gao why her best student in twenty years died of cold on the steps of the Harbour Hotel in front of me, and she’ll kill me, and then there’ll be two of us, and the department can’t afford it.”

Yu Jie took the jacket.

She put it on. It was much too big. The sleeves came down over her hands. It was still warm, and it smelled of the rental shop and, underneath that, faintly, of chalk dust and jasmine tea.

She stood in it for a moment with her eyes closed.

Then she opened them, and took out her phone, and sent a message, and put the phone away.

“What did you say?” said Miles.

“I told my mother I’m going back to my apartment. With Tao Tao. Because I have to work on my thesis early tomorrow, because my supervisor is a monster.” She looked at him in his shirtsleeves and bow tie in the cold. “It’s true. She is.”

Down at the bottom of the steps, a phone rang in the long dark car. After a moment, the driver closed the back door. The car pulled away.

Yu Jie let out a long, white breath.

Then she opened the tiny silver bag on her wrist, felt about in it, took out a single White Rabbit sweet and held it out to him at the full length of her arm.

“You didn’t eat anything,” she said. “All night. I watched. You held an empty plate for six hours.”

“That’s not professional distance,” said Miles.

“It’s a metre and a half,” said Yu Jie. “My arm’s shorter than yours. But it’s a very small sweet.”

He took it by the very end of the twist of paper, so that their fingers came nowhere near each other. He unwrapped it and ate it on the steps of the Harbour Hotel at one in the morning, in his shirtsleeves and bow tie, and it was, he thought, the best thing he had eaten in his life.

“Now,” she said. “I need to get home. And I don’t have any shoes I can walk in, or any money, because my bag is the size of a biscuit, and I’ve never in my life called a taxi by myself.”

“You’ve never called a taxi?”

“There’s always a driver.”

Miles looked at her. At the tiny silver bag. At the Italian shoes. At his own jacket hanging off her shoulders, the sleeves over her hands.

“How far is your apartment?” he said.

“Two kilometres. Up the hill. By the east gate of the university.”

He thought about it.

“I’ll walk you,” said Miles. “Three metres away. On the other side of the road if you like. It’s one in the morning. I’m not putting you in a taxi with a stranger in my jacket. Professor Gao would kill me twice.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He did not walk on the other side of the road. But he walked three metres away. She had to keep stopping to let him catch up.

They went up through the old harbour streets in the cold, past the closed shutters of the fish market and the all-night noodle stall where three taxi drivers were eating at a plastic table and looked at them with deep interest: a man in a white shirt and bow tie, and a girl in a ball gown and a man’s tuxedo jacket, carrying her shoes. Past the dark windows of the bank, and the little temple on the corner with the incense still burning, and the bakery where someone was already starting the morning bread, so that the whole street smelled warm.

She had put her shoes back on after the first hundred metres, because the pavement was too cold, and now she was limping.

He noticed. He slowed down. He slowed down so much that she turned round and looked at him.

“You’re walking very slowly,” she said.

“I’m calculating the optimal route,” said Miles.

“It’s a straight line, Miles. Up the hill. I can see the university from here.”

“Not if you do it properly.” He pushed his glasses up. “If you go straight up the hill, it’s steep, and you’re in those shoes, and it’ll take twenty-two minutes. If you go round by the park, along the old wall, it’s flatter. It’s longer. Thirty-eight minutes.”

She looked at him for a long moment in the light from the bakery window.

“That’s longer,” she said.

“It’s flatter,” said Miles. “For the shoes.”

He looked at the pavement while he said it.

She didn’t say anything. She turned left toward the park.

Twenty metres later, he said to her back, “I could give you my shoes.”

She stopped. “Then you’d be barefoot.”

“I have thicker skin. Statistically.” He considered it. “They’re a forty-four. You’re a thirty-seven. You’d be walking in two boats. I’ve modelled it. It isn’t better.”

She turned round, very slowly, under the streetlight.

“How do you know my shoe size?”

He looked, abruptly, at a lamppost.

“The label inside your trainers,” he said. “You take them off under my desk when you’re thinking. Every Wednesday, at about half past four.”

There was a short silence on the pavement.

“I didn’t know I did that,” said Yu Jie.

“The left one first,” said Miles, to the lamppost. “Always.”

She turned and walked on toward the park, limping. He couldn’t see her face, which was probably just as well for both of them.

✦ ✦ ✦

The old city wall ran along the edge of the park, low and grey, with lamps every fifty metres. Nobody was there. The trees were bare and the paths were white with frost and the whole city lay below them, the harbour and the ships and the Shen Building lit up white across the water.

They walked along the wall. She went first. He came three metres behind.

For a while, neither of them spoke.

Then she said, without turning round:

“You said I looked like a photograph. Of me. Taken by someone who’d never met me.”

“I’m sorry. It was rude.”

“It was the nicest thing anyone said to me all night.” She stopped under a lamp and turned round. “Nine men told me I looked beautiful. You told me I didn’t look like myself.” Her breath was white in the lamplight. “You’re the only person in that whole room who knows what I actually look like.”

He stopped too. Three metres away.

“Yellow,” he said. “Biro on your trainers. Four pens in your hair. A cardigan with White Rabbit wrappers in the pocket. One shoelace undone, usually the left.” He paused. “Ink on your fingers. Right hand, middle finger, where you hold the pen. You never wash it all off.”

She stood very still under the lamp in his jacket.

“You’re doing it again,” she said, unsteadily. “The noticing.”

“I can’t stop,” said Miles. “I told you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They walked on.

At the end of the wall, they came down a flight of old stone steps, and she took her shoes off again, and he didn’t say anything, and she walked barefoot down the cold steps holding them. At the bottom, the path came out onto the main road by the university. They could see the east gate from there, and the row of apartment buildings opposite it, where the rich students lived.

“Which one?” said Miles.

“The tall one at the end. With the blue door.”

He looked at it. It was about two hundred metres away, at the end of the road, under a streetlamp. There was a security guard in a little lit-up box by the gate. There was also, on the corner opposite, a 24-hour convenience shop, very bright, where two students in pyjamas were buying instant noodles and looking out of the window.

Miles stopped walking.

He stopped one block early, at the corner, in the dark between two streetlamps, where nobody in the shop or the guard box could see him.

She stopped too. She looked at him.

“It’s just there,” she said.

“I know.”

“You’re stopping.”

“I know,” said Miles. “On purpose.” He nodded toward the bright windows of the convenience shop, the students in pyjamas. “There are people. Students. If they see you come home at half past one in the morning in my jacket with me—” He stopped. “I won’t do that to you. Not before June. I won’t give anyone anything to say about you.”

She looked at the bright shop. Then at him, in the dark, in his shirtsleeves and bow tie, his arms crossed against the cold.

“You walked me the long way,” she said. “Thirty-eight minutes.”

“Forty-one,” said Miles. “You stopped under three lamps.”

“And now you’re stopping a block early. So nobody sees.”

“Yes.”

“Because of the rule.”

“Because of you,” said Miles.

He said it quietly, to the pavement. The words came out white in the cold air and hung there between them for a moment, and then they were gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

She took off his jacket.

She held it out to him at arm’s length. Her arm wasn’t as long as his. She had to step forward to make it reach, one step, so there were only two metres between them, and he had to step forward too to take it, and for a second they were both holding the jacket, one sleeve each, in the dark between two streetlamps, a metre apart.

The closest they had ever been.

She was shivering. He could see the white of her breath. He could see the loose strand of hair against her cheek, and the two-centimetre space in the left side of her coil where the pin had been.

He could see her face. Not the photograph. Her.

“Miles,” she said.

He waited.

She didn’t say it. Whatever it was. She stood in the cold, holding one sleeve of his jacket, and looked at him for a long moment with her eyes very bright, and didn’t say it, because it was December and there were a hundred and eighty-two squares left on the calendar and he had a rule and she had promised Professor Gao.

“Thank you,” she said instead. “For staying until the end.”

She let go of the sleeve.

She turned and walked the last block alone, barefoot, carrying her Italian shoes, in a dress the colour of dawn, past the bright windows of the convenience shop and the students in pyjamas, who stared, and the security guard in his box, who stared, and in through the blue door.

She didn’t look back. He knew she wouldn’t. She was being careful for him, the way he was being careful for her.

He stood on the dark corner in his shirtsleeves with his jacket in his hands until a light came on, on the sixth floor of the tall building with the blue door.

Then he put the jacket on. It was still warm. It smelled of rental shop and, now, faintly, of something sweet and light, like orange blossom.

He walked home across the sleeping campus, past the dark sports ground. Nine minutes exactly.

He didn’t feel the cold at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the sixth floor, Tao Tao was sitting up on the sofa in pyjamas with a face mask on, waiting.

She looked at Yu Jie coming in barefoot, carrying her shoes, with her cheeks pink from the cold and her eyes very bright.

“You walked,” said Tao Tao. “From the harbour. In those.”

“He walked me.”

Tao Tao pulled off the face mask.

“Where did he stop?”

“At the corner. One block early. On purpose. So nobody would see.” Yu Jie sat down on the floor with her back against the sofa and put her face in her knees. “He took the long way. Along the wall. He said it was flatter, for the shoes. He said that, Tao Tao. Flatter, for the shoes.”

Tao Tao was silent for a moment.

“That man,” she said finally, “is going to be the death of both of you.”

Yu Jie didn’t answer.

She got up after a while and went to her bedroom, still in the dawn-coloured dress, and turned on the light, and took the graph-paper calendar down from the wall. She found the square for the twentieth of December. She drew the purple atom in it.

Then, beside it, very small, she drew a lamp. Three lamps. A wall. A long curved line along the bottom of the square, the long way round.

Flatter, for the shoes.

A hundred and eighty-two squares left. And in July, an engagement she had not agreed to.

She sat on her bed in her mother’s diamonds and looked at the gold square at the end of the calendar for a very long time.

chapters.title: The Thesis Draft Covered in Red Pen
chapters.desc: He’s not her supervisor. He reads it anyway, all night, and finds the flaw that would have sunk her in May.
chapters.epigraph: “This is beautiful. Now prove it.” — margin note, page 41, red ink
chapters.content:
The thesis arrived in his inbox on the fifth of January, a Monday, at 11:52 p.m.

It did not come from her. It came from Professor Gao, with no message in the body, just a subject line: Read this. Properly. I want your notes by Friday. — G. And an attachment: ShenYJ_thesis_draft1.pdf, 118 pages.

He looked at it for a long time.

He was sitting on his sofa in the staff flat in a jumper and holey socks, with a cup of tea going cold and a paper on lensing in galaxy clusters open on his knee. The heating had broken again. Outside, it was snowing a little, the thin grey city snow that never settled.

He knew what he should do. He should write back to Professor Gao and say: I don’t think it’s appropriate for me to read this. He should say: I am not her supervisor. I am not on her committee. He should say: You know why.

He opened the attachment.

✦ ✦ ✦

Topological Edge States in Non-Uniformly Strained Graphene Shen Yu Jie Supervisor: Professor Gao Meiling

He read the abstract. Then he read it again.

Then he put down the paper on lensing in galaxy clusters, and got up, and made a fresh pot of tea, and found a red pen in the kitchen drawer, and printed all 118 pages on the small printer in the corner that jammed every fifteen sheets, and sat down at his one table on his one chair, and began.

He did not stop until ten past seven in the morning.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was very good.

He had known it would be. He had spent four months of Wednesdays watching her mind work at his chalkboard. But he had not known it would be this good. He had not known that the girl who wrote sticky notes about copper and tellurium could write, on page nine, a paragraph about electrons moving along the edge of a sheet of carbon that was so clear and so precise that he read it three times, and then put down his pen, and sat for a while looking at the snow.

She wrote like she talked: fast, bright, impatient, with sudden jumps that made you run to keep up. But underneath the speed, every step was there. Every assumption named. Every approximation justified. She had taken a problem that Dr. Huang from the capital had got wrong in front of thirty physicists and built, step by step, a model that got it right.

He wrote in the margins as he went. Small, neat, red.

Page 4: Define this term before you use it. The committee will be tired. Be kind to them.

Page 12: Lovely.

Page 17: This approximation is fine, but say WHY it’s fine. Someone will ask.

Page 23: You have used the word “obviously” four times on this page. Nothing in physics is obvious. If it were, we wouldn’t need physicists.

Page 31: This figure is beautiful. The axis labels are too small. Professor Zhou is fifty-nine and refuses to wear his glasses.

Page 38: I had to stop and think here for twenty minutes. That’s a compliment.

Page 39: There is a very small atom drawn in the margin beside Figure 6. Three orbits. I assume it was not meant to be submitted. I have not corrected it. (Physically inaccurate. Please leave it in.)

Page 41: This is beautiful. Now prove it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At about four in the morning, on page 67, he found the problem.

It was in chapter three, in the middle of the long calculation that was the heart of the whole thesis: how the edge states behaved when the strain was uneven. She had made a choice about the boundary conditions at the edge of the sample. It was a natural choice. It was the choice almost anyone would make. It made the mathematics much simpler.

It was also, he realised slowly, with a cold feeling in his stomach, not quite right.

Not wrong, exactly. It worked for the shape of sample she had chosen. But it didn’t work for the general case. And her whole conclusion, the big claim at the end of the thesis, the thing that made it more than a good student project, depended on the general case.

If the committee found it in May, they would not fail her. She was too good for that. But they would take the big claim away. They would say: very promising, but the main result doesn’t hold. She would graduate with a good degree instead of an extraordinary one. And somewhere in a big house on the hill, a woman in pale grey silk would say: You’ve had your little hobby.

And Professor Zhou, who always asked about the boundary conditions, would find it in about four minutes.

Miles sat at his one table with the snow coming down outside and the red pen in his hand.

He could fix it. He could see how. It would take a different choice at the boundary, and about three pages of extra calculation, and a small change to one figure. He could write it in the margin right now in red ink: Here. Do it this way. She would have it by Friday. The thesis would be saved.

It would also, very slightly, stop being hers.

✦ ✦ ✦

He put down the red pen.

He got up and walked round the small flat twice. He stood at the window and looked at the thin grey snow falling on the sports ground. He thought about Professor Gao on his first day, five years ago, telling the new lecturer: The worst thing you can do to a good student is give them the answer.

He thought about Yu Jie at his chalkboard on the second Wednesday, finding the mistake in the bent oscillator in four seconds, and the look on her face. Not pride. Joy. The pure, fierce joy of seeing something that nobody had seen.

He sat back down.

He picked up the red pen.

On page 67, next to the boundary condition, he wrote:

Stop. Look at this line again. It works for your rectangle. Does it work for any shape? What happens at a corner?

On page 68:

If it doesn’t work for any shape, what does that do to your conclusion on page 104?

On page 69:

I think you know how to fix this. I think you know better than I do. I watched you find a mistake in my work in four seconds in September. I’m giving you four months. You have plenty of time.

(Professor Zhou will ask about the boundary conditions. He always asks about the boundary conditions. When he does, I want you to smile.)

✦ ✦ ✦

He finished at ten past seven.

He had written on 103 of the 118 pages. Two hundred and twelve notes. He counted them, because he was a physicist and couldn’t help it. Two hundred and twelve small red notes in his neat handwriting: corrections, questions, the occasional lovely, and on page 67, the three notes that mattered.

On the last page, after the bibliography, he sat for a long time with the pen.

Then he wrote, very small, at the bottom:

Your gap doesn’t close.

He put the pages in a brown envelope. He wrote Professor Gao on the front. He did not write anything else.

He went to work through the thin snow on his green bicycle, without sleeping, and put the envelope in Professor Gao’s pigeonhole at 7:48, and went up to office 412 and sat down at his desk and fell asleep with his head on a stack of second-year homework until Fang Hao knocked on the wall at ten and said, “Are you dead?”

“No,” said Miles into the homework.

“You sound dead.”

“I was reading.”

There was a pause through the cardboard wall.

“Reading what?” said Fang Hao, in the voice of a man who already knew.

✦ ✦ ✦

Professor Gao called Yu Jie into her office on Thursday morning.

Not to the balcony. To her desk. She was not smoking. She had the brown envelope on the desk in front of her, and a cup of black tea, and she did not say anything at all.

Then she pushed the envelope across the desk.

“Your draft,” she said. “I asked someone to read it. Someone who isn’t your supervisor. A second pair of eyes. I do this for all my best students.” She paused. “This is the first time I’ve had it back with two hundred and twelve notes.”

Yu Jie looked at the envelope. Nothing was written on it except Professor Gao. In small, neat letters that she would have known anywhere.

Her hands were not quite steady when she opened it.

She read the first note on page four. Define this term before you use it. The committee will be tired. Be kind to them. She turned the page. Lovely. She turned again.

You have used the word “obviously” four times on this page.

She put her hand over her mouth.

Professor Gao drank her tea and watched her student read, and didn’t say anything, and didn’t hurry her.

She read all of it, right there at Professor Gao’s desk, page by page. It took an hour and twenty minutes. Every note. I had to stop and think here for twenty minutes. That’s a compliment. This is beautiful. Now prove it.

When she got to page 67, she stopped.

She read the three notes. She read the line he was pointing at. She read it again.

Professor Gao watched her face. She watched it go still, and then go white, and then, very slowly, change. The fear went out of it. Something else came in. Fierce and bright and absolutely focused.

“Corners,” said Yu Jie under her breath. “Oh, no. Corners.”

“Can you fix it?”

“I don’t know yet.” She was already reaching for a pen, already turning the page over to the blank back of it, already writing. “I think—if the boundary isn’t fixed, if you let it—no. Wait. If you—” She stopped, and looked up at her supervisor, and her eyes were blazing. “He didn’t tell me how. He could have. He knows. He must know. He didn’t tell me.”

“No,” said Professor Gao. “He didn’t.”

“He gave me four months.”

“He did.”

Yu Jie looked down at the page. At the small neat red handwriting. I think you know better than I do.

Her eyes filled. She blinked hard.

“He thinks I can do it,” she said.

“So do I,” said Professor Gao. She drank the rest of her tea. “Go and do it. And Shen Yu Jie.”

Yu Jie looked up.

“Read the last page,” said Professor Gao, “somewhere private.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She read the last page in a cubicle in the third-floor women’s toilets, with the door locked, sitting on the closed lid, with the brown envelope on her knees.

After the bibliography. At the very bottom. Very small.

Your gap doesn’t close.

She sat there.

Then she took out her phone and texted Tao Tao.

he read my whole thesis. all night. 212 notes. he found a mistake that would have killed me in may. he didn’t fix it. he told me he thinks i can.

Tao Tao replied in six seconds.

jie jie that is the most romantic thing i have ever heard and it is about BOUNDARY CONDITIONS

Yu Jie laughed out loud, alone in a toilet cubicle on the third floor of the Hall of Science, with tears running down her face.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took her nineteen days.

She worked every day, at the lab, at her apartment, on the floor of the library café with napkins. She filled two notebooks. She tried four approaches that didn’t work. On the eleventh day, she tried one that almost worked and cried for an hour out of pure frustration and then ate an entire bag of White Rabbit sweets and started again. On the nineteenth day, at a quarter past two in the morning, sitting on her bedroom floor in pyjamas with the graph-paper calendar on the wall above her, she found it.

It wasn’t the fix he had seen. She found out later that it wasn’t. It was a different one. Better. Cleaner. It worked for any shape. It worked at the corners. And it did something else as well, something neither of them had expected: it made the big claim at the end of her thesis even bigger.

She sat on the floor and looked at the page.

Then she took a sticky note, yellow, and wrote on it, and on Wednesday at 3:45 she stuck it to the side of his tea.

Corners. Fixed. Not your way. Mine.

(Better.)

He read it. He read it twice.

Then he looked up at her, standing at his chalkboard in a red jumper with four pens in her hair and ink on her middle finger, holding out a clean piece of chalk to him with a look of pure, fierce, triumphant joy.

“Show me,” said Miles Wei.

She showed him.

It took forty minutes. When she finished, he stood in front of the chalkboard with his arms folded and looked at it for a long time without saying anything.

Then he said, very quietly:

“That’s better than mine.”

“I know.”

“That’s much better than mine.”

“I know,” said Shen Yu Jie, and her whole face was shining.

“You wrote lovely in my margins,” she said. “Nine times.”

“Eleven.”

“I counted nine.”

“Two of them are on the back of page 88. I ran out of margin.” He pushed his glasses up. “I stopped at eleven. It was becoming unprofessional.”

“Eleven is unprofessional?”

“Ten was the limit,” said Miles. “I calculated it in advance. Then I went over.”

He turned and looked at her, there at his chalkboard, three metres away.

He didn’t say anything else. He didn’t have to. She could see it on his face, every bit of it, every single thing he wasn’t allowed to say: the pride, and the joy, and something else, under both of them, so big and so careful that it frightened her a little.

In the bottom right-hand corner of the board, in small round writing, it still said 20 June, 16:00.

One hundred and forty-three squares left.

chapters.title: Rumours in the Department Kitchen
chapters.desc: A photograph on the student forum. A man’s tuxedo jacket at half past one in the morning. Then Miles hears what the postdocs are saying, and finds out he has a temper after all.
chapters.epigraph: “The Shen girl’s buying her degree, and he’s getting paid in kind.” — Dr. Ren Bo, fourth-floor kitchen, Tuesday, 12:31 p.m.
chapters.content:
The photograph appeared on the university forum on the fifth of February, a Thursday, at 8:14 in the evening.

It was not a good photograph. It had been taken through the window of a 24-hour convenience shop, at night, on a phone, by someone who had been holding instant noodles in the other hand. It was blurry and orange from the streetlights. It showed a girl in a long pale dress walking barefoot along a pavement toward a building with a blue door, carrying a pair of high-heeled shoes. She was wearing a man’s black dinner jacket. It was much too big for her. The sleeves came down over her hands.

You could not see her face. But you could see the shoes, and the dress, and the blue door.

The post was titled: Which rich girl came home at 1:30am in a guy’s tux before christmas?? (Engineering building opposite the east gate)

For the first two days, nobody cared. There were eleven comments. Most of them were about the shoes.

Then, on Saturday morning, someone posted a second photograph underneath.

It was a photograph of a door. Office 412, the Hall of Science. Taken in the autumn, by a second-year on the way to office hours, because they had thought it was funny. A plain wooden door with a nameplate, Dr. M. Wei, and a sign about office hours with a green cat in a box, and, stuck all over it, pink sticky notes. Dozens. In round handwriting.

And underneath, a comment:

the shen heiress is a physics final year. just saying. look at the jacket.

By Monday, there were four hundred and sixty comments.

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles didn’t see it.

He didn’t use the forum. He didn’t know the forum existed. He didn’t know until Tuesday lunchtime, when he went to the fourth-floor kitchen at 12:30 to make his tea and eat his egg sandwich, as he had every working day for five years, and stopped in the doorway.

There were three people in the kitchen. Two of them were postdocs from the theory group, Dr. Ren Bo and a woman called Wu Na. The third was a PhD student he didn’t know well. They had a phone propped against the kettle and were looking at it together.

They didn’t see him. The door had been open. He was quiet. He was always quiet.

“—four hundred comments,” Wu Na was saying. “Someone found the jacket on the hire shop’s website. It’s the same lapels.”

“Of course it is,” said Dr. Ren. He was thirty-three, clever, ambitious, and had applied for a lectureship in the department two years ago and not got it. “Everybody knew. Fang Hao had a scoreboard. And the Shen Foundation just gave this department forty million. Forty million, and their daughter’s hanging round Wei’s office every Wednesday like a cat.” He laughed. “It’s obvious, isn’t it? The Shen girl’s buying her degree. And he’s getting paid in kind.”

The PhD student laughed uncomfortably.

Wu Na said, “Ren, don’t,” but she was smiling.

“What? It’s true. You think a twenty-two-year-old heiress is going to the fourth floor every week for quantum mechanics?” Dr. Ren scrolled on the phone. “She’ll get a first, he’ll get a lab, and Gao will retire on a nice pension. Everybody wins. Except anyone in this department who actually earned—”

He looked up.

He saw Miles in the doorway.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nobody in the Hall of Science had ever seen Miles Wei angry.

They had seen him quiet. They had seen him absent-minded and lost in a calculation and apologising to a chair he had walked into. They had seen him, once, laugh in a seminar. They had never seen him angry, and most of them, if asked, would have said that he didn’t have a temper at all. That he was too gentle for it. Too far away.

He wasn’t far away now.

He walked into the kitchen. He didn’t hurry. He went past Wu Na, who stepped back, and past the PhD student, who looked at the floor, and stopped in front of Dr. Ren Bo, about a metre away.

He was taller than Ren by a head. Ren had never noticed that before. Nobody had. Miles always stood as if he were trying to take up less room.

He was standing up straight now.

“Say it again,” said Miles.

His voice was perfectly level. Perfectly quiet. It was the voice he used in lectures to explain something important. Everyone in the kitchen went very still.

Dr. Ren tried to smile. “Wei, come on. It was a joke. Everyone’s—”

“Say it again,” said Miles, “about her.”

Ren didn’t say anything.

“No,” said Miles. “I didn’t think you would.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He looked at the phone propped against the kettle. At the blurry orange photograph. The barefoot girl with the shoes in her hand and his jacket over her shoulders, walking alone to a blue door.

He looked at it for a long time.

Then he looked back at Ren.

“That photograph,” he said, “is of a student who was cold at one in the morning on the twentieth of December, because her shoes hurt and her coat was in a car she didn’t want to get into. I gave her my jacket. I walked her home. I stopped a block away so that nobody would see me with her. Nobody did. I went home alone.” His voice didn’t rise at all. “That’s all that happened. That’s all that’s happened since September. You can ask anyone. You can ask Fang Hao. You can ask Professor Gao. You can ask the woman herself, if you can find the courage to speak to her, which I doubt.”

Ren’s face had gone red.

“But that isn’t what I want to talk about,” said Miles. “You said she’s buying her degree.”

“I didn’t mean—”

“She is the best student this department has had in twenty years.” Miles said it the way he would say the speed of light is constant. “Professor Gao says so. I say so. Two weeks ago she found a solution to a problem in her thesis, and her solution was better than the one I’d found after a whole night of trying. Hers was better than mine. Much better. In May she is going to defend it in front of a committee, and Professor Zhou is going to ask her about the boundary conditions, and she is going to answer him, and she is going to be extraordinary.”

He stepped a little closer.

“You didn’t get the lectureship two years ago, Dr. Ren,” he said quietly, “because in your interview you were asked a question about boundary conditions by Professor Zhou, and you didn’t know the answer, and you pretended that you did. I know, because I was in the room. I was on the panel as the junior member, to see how it was done. You talked for four minutes. It was all wrong. Everybody knew.”

Ren had gone from red to white.

“Shen Yu Jie,” said Miles, “has never once pretended to know an answer she doesn’t. Not once. Not to me, not to a famous professor from the capital in front of thirty people. She’d rather be wrong in public than pretend.” He looked at Ren with his calm, level, terrible gaze. “That’s why she’s better than you. Not her money. Her.”

He picked up his tea mug from the drying rack. WORLD’S OKAYEST SON.

“If I hear you say anything about her again,” he said, “in this kitchen, or anywhere else, I won’t say anything to you. I’ll go straight to Professor Zhou and the university’s harassment office, and I’ll tell them exactly what you said, word for word. Paid in kind. I have a very good memory. You know I do.”

He walked to the door.

Then he stopped, and turned round, and said, in exactly the same level voice:

“And it’s not forty million. It’s thirty-eight. If you’re going to spread rumours in a physics department, at least get the numbers right.”

He went out.

✦ ✦ ✦

Fang Hao was standing in the corridor outside, holding a croissant. He had heard everything. The cardboard walls went all the way down the fourth floor.

He looked at Miles coming out of the kitchen with his WORLD’S OKAYEST SON mug and his perfectly calm face.

He looked at Miles’s hands. They were shaking so badly he could barely hold the empty mug.

“Office,” said Fang Hao. “Now.”

He took the mug out of Miles’s hands, and steered him down the corridor into 412, and shut the door, and put the mug on the desk, and made Miles sit down.

Then he went to his own door, office 413, and took down the scoreboard. The one with the Y and P columns, all the jokes since October, Cu-Te 9/10. He took it down very carefully, and folded it, and put it in his pocket.

“I’m sorry,” he said, coming back into 412. “That was me. The scoreboard. I thought it was funny. I thought it was—” He stopped. “I didn’t think.”

Miles was sitting at his desk with his hands flat on it, looking at them.

“It wasn’t you,” he said. “It was me. It was the jacket. I should never have given her the jacket.”

“She’d have frozen.”

“I should have called her a taxi. I should have called her driver back. I should have—” He stopped. “I stopped a block away, Hao. I did everything right. I did everything exactly right, and it doesn’t matter, because a boy buying noodles took a photograph, and now there are four hundred and sixty people saying she’s—” He couldn’t finish.

Fang Hao sat down on the corner of the desk.

“Have you seen the comments?” he said quietly.

“No.”

“Don’t.”

Miles looked up at him.

“Some of them are about you,” said Fang Hao. “Most of them are about her. About her family. About what she’s for.” He looked away. “It’s an internet forum. They’re children. They’ll get bored in a week.”

“She’ll have seen it.”

Fang Hao didn’t say anything.

Miles looked at the chalkboard. At the bottom right-hand corner. 20 June, 16:00.

“She’ll have seen it,” he said again. “And her mother will have seen it. And her mother is the kind of woman who calls her daughter a jewel in front of guests.” He put his face in his hands. “What have I done.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past three, there was a knock on the door of office 412.

It wasn’t Wednesday. It was Tuesday. Office hours. Tuesdays and Thursdays, 3–5 p.m.

Miles looked up.

The door opened, and it wasn’t a second-year. It was Professor Zhou Lin, head of department, fifty-nine years old, in his cardigan, with his reading glasses in his hand because he refused to wear them.

He looked at Miles behind his desk. He looked at Fang Hao on the corner of it. He looked at the chalkboard, and the small round writing in the bottom right-hand corner.

“Dr. Fang,” he said mildly. “Would you give us a moment?”

Fang Hao went.

Professor Zhou closed the door. He sat down in the chair where Yu Jie always sat, on Wednesdays, and put his reading glasses on the desk, and folded his hands.

“I’ve had three emails,” he said. “One from a parent of a second-year, about the forum. One from the student newspaper, asking for a comment. And one from Dr. Ren Bo, twenty minutes ago, saying that you threatened him in the kitchen.”

Miles sat very still.

“I didn’t threaten him,” he said. “I told him I would report him for harassment if he said it again. That’s not a threat. That’s a procedure.”

Professor Zhou’s mouth moved, very slightly, at one corner.

“Yes,” he said. “That’s more or less what Wu Na said, when I asked her. She came to my office at one o’clock. She said she was ashamed of herself.” He paused. “She also told me what Dr. Ren said. Word for word. Paid in kind.”

Miles didn’t say anything.

Professor Zhou looked at him.

“I’m not here about Dr. Ren,” he said. “I’ll deal with Dr. Ren. I’m here about you, Miles.” He leaned forward. “There’s no complaint. There’s nothing for the university to investigate. A photograph of a girl in a jacket and a door with sticky notes on it is not misconduct. I want to be very clear about that.”

“But.”

“But,” said Professor Zhou. “In September, before any of this, I assigned the examining panels for this year’s final-year theses. Supervisor, plus two internal examiners from the department.” He took a folded sheet of paper out of his cardigan pocket and put it on the desk. “I put you on Shen Yu Jie’s. As second examiner. Because her thesis uses methods from your field, and because you’re the best person in this building to examine it.”

Miles looked at the paper.

Thesis Examining Panels. Condensed Matter. SHEN Yu Jie. Supervisor: Prof. Gao M. Internal Examiners: Prof. Zhou L.; Dr. Wei M.

His own name. In the second slot. In Professor Zhou’s neat type, from September.

He had forgotten. He had completely, entirely forgotten. September had been a long time ago. Before the second Wednesday.

“I am going to have to answer the student newspaper,” said Professor Zhou quietly, “and that parent, and possibly the dean, and possibly Shen Ruolan, who sits on the university council. And when I answer them, Miles, I need to be able to say that nobody with any personal interest in this student is going to have any part in deciding her grade.” He looked at Miles over his folded hands. “So I have to ask you a question. And I need you to think about it carefully before you answer.”

Miles already knew the question.

He looked at the chalkboard. 20 June, 16:00.

He looked at the paper on the desk with his name on it.

“You don’t have to ask it,” he said.

Professor Zhou raised his eyebrows.

“I’ll write it down,” said Miles. “Tonight. Properly. You’ll have it on your desk in the morning.”

chapters.title: Miles Recuses Himself
chapters.desc: One page, written at his one table between midnight and four. The most honest document in the history of the department. Then the Wednesday rules change, and Fang Hao brings croissants.
chapters.epigraph: “I have a personal interest in this student. I wish to state clearly what it is, so that nobody else has to guess.” — Dr. M. Wei, letter to the Head of Department
chapters.content:
He wrote it at his one table in the staff flat, between midnight and four in the morning.

It took him eleven drafts. He wrote them by hand first, on graph paper, because that was how he thought. The first draft was four lines long and said nothing at all. I wish to withdraw from the examining panel of SHEN Yu Jie due to a potential conflict of interest. He read it back and it looked like a lie. Not because any of it was false, but because it was hiding something, and he had never been able to bear documents that hid things.

The second draft was three pages long and he tore it up.

By the sixth draft, he had stopped trying to sound like a university form and started trying to sound like himself. By the ninth, he had stopped being frightened of it. By the eleventh, at ten to four, it was one page long, and it was true, and he typed it up and printed it and signed it, and sat at his one table looking at it while the sky outside the window went from black to grey.

Then he put it in an envelope and rode to the Hall of Science in the dark and slid it under Professor Zhou’s door at 6:40 in the morning, before anyone else was in the building, so that he couldn’t change his mind.

✦ ✦ ✦

To: Professor Zhou Lin, Head of Department From: Dr. Miles Wei Re: Examining panel, SHEN Yu Jie

Professor Zhou,

I am writing to withdraw from the examining panel for Shen Yu Jie’s final-year thesis, with immediate effect. I should have done this earlier. I am sorry that I did not.

I have a personal interest in this student. I wish to state clearly what it is, so that nobody else has to guess.

Since September, Miss Shen has come to my office on Wednesday afternoons to discuss physics. I have enjoyed these discussions more than any part of my work in five years here. She is the most gifted student I have taught. Over these months, I have come to care for her in a way that is not appropriate for a lecturer to feel for a student in his department, and I have known this since at least October.

I want to be equally clear about what has not happened. There has been no relationship of any kind. I have never touched her. I have never been alone with her outside the Hall of Science, except on one occasion, the night of 20 December, when I walked her home from the Shen Foundation gala because she had no coat and it was one in the morning. I stopped one street away from her building. I did not go in.

I told her in September that nothing would happen while she was a student in this department. I wrote it on the chalkboard in my office, where it still is. I intend to keep to it.

Because of the above, I cannot be a fair examiner of her work, and I should not be seen to be one. I want there to be no question, now or ever, that any mark she receives was earned by anything other than her own work. Her work is extraordinary. It deserves a panel that nobody can doubt.

I have not discussed this letter with Miss Shen. I have also not discussed it with Professor Gao, though in January, at her request, I read a draft of the thesis and gave written comments, which I gave to Professor Gao and not to the student. I attach a copy of those comments. They contain no answers, only questions. Miss Shen solved the main problem I identified herself, by a method better than the one I would have suggested. I would be grateful if this could be noted.

If the department or the university feels that any further action is needed regarding my own conduct, I will cooperate fully. I would only ask that nothing in this letter is used in any way that harms her. None of this is her fault. If there is any fault, it is mine.

Yours sincerely, Miles Wei

✦ ✦ ✦

Professor Zhou read it at 8:15, standing at his desk in his cardigan, with his reading glasses on, which he only wore when nobody was watching.

He read it twice.

Then he sat down, and took off his glasses, and looked out of his window at the car park for a long time.

At 8:40, he picked up his phone and called Professor Gao, and said: “Come to my office. Don’t smoke on the way.”

She came at 8:43, smelling of smoke.

He handed her the letter without a word. She read it standing up, by the window. He watched her face. He had known Gao Meiling for twenty-six years. He had seen her face do many things. He had never, in twenty-six years, seen it do what it did now, reading the line I have come to care for her in a way that is not appropriate.

It went soft. For about two seconds. Then she put it back.

“That idiot,” said Professor Gao.

“Yes.”

“That honest, stupid, beautiful idiot.” She put the letter down on his desk. “He’s put it in writing, Lin. On the record. I have come to care for her. He’s handed you his head on a plate. If anyone wanted to make trouble, if Ruolan Shen wanted to make trouble—”

“I know.”

“He could have just said conflict of interest. Four words. Nobody would have asked.”

“I know,” said Professor Zhou. He picked up the letter again and looked at it. “But read it again, Meiling. Read who he’s protecting.”

She read it again.

I want there to be no question, now or ever, that any mark she receives was earned by anything other than her own work.

I would only ask that nothing in this letter is used in any way that harms her. None of this is her fault.

Professor Gao was quiet.

“He’s made himself the target,” she said finally. “So that there’s nothing left to aim at her.”

“Yes,” said Professor Zhou. “I think that’s exactly what he’s done.” He put the letter in a folder. “And I think, in thirty-four years in this profession, it’s the most honest document anyone has ever given me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He called Miles in at eleven.

Miles came. He had not slept. He sat in the chair in front of Professor Zhou’s desk with his hands on his knees and his face very calm and the look of a man who has prepared for the worst and is waiting to hear how bad it is.

“I’ve read your letter,” said Professor Zhou.

“Yes.”

“I’ve accepted your withdrawal from the panel. Dr. Fang will replace you. He’s qualified, and he has no personal interest, except in croissants.” Professor Zhou folded his hands. “I’ve also spoken to the university’s legal office this morning, without giving any names, and described the situation in general terms. Their view is that there has been no breach of any policy. A lecturer who has feelings for a student and declares them, withdraws from assessment, and has no relationship with that student is not committing misconduct. He’s doing exactly what the policy asks.”

Miles let out a breath he seemed to have been holding since four in the morning.

“However,” said Professor Zhou.

Miles’s shoulders went back up.

“The legal office also said that the Wednesday meetings should continue only if they are clearly academic, clearly supervised, and clearly visible.” Professor Zhou looked at him over his folded hands. “So. From this afternoon, Wednesday afternoons move out of office 412. They will take place in the third-floor seminar room. The one with glass walls. With the door open.”

“Yes,” said Miles.

“Physics only.”

“It’s always been physics only.”

Professor Zhou looked at him.

“Miles,” he said gently. “I was at that seminar, the Friday in December. I heard you laugh. I have seen the corner of your chalkboard. I have read the sticky notes on your door, because they were on your door, and I walk past your door to the lift.” He paused. “Cu-Te was quite good.”

Miles went red to the collar.

“Physics only,” said Professor Zhou, “and a third person present.”

“A third person?”

There was a knock on the door. It opened before anyone answered it.

Dr. Fang Hao stood in the doorway with a paper bag in his hand and an expression of pure, radiant innocence.

“I volunteered,” he said. “I’ll bring croissants.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Jie found out at one o’clock that same day, from Professor Gao, on the balcony.

Not everything. Professor Gao didn’t show her the letter. She told her that Dr. Wei had withdrawn from her examining panel, of his own accord, and that Dr. Fang would take his place. She told her that the forum had been reported to the university and that the two photographs had been removed. She told her that Dr. Ren Bo had been spoken to by the head of department, and would be making a formal apology to Wu Na, who had made a formal complaint about him after the kitchen, and that if Yu Jie wanted to make one too, she could.

And she told her that Wednesday afternoons, from now on, would be in the third-floor seminar room with glass walls, with the door open, with Dr. Fang present.

Yu Jie listened to all of it in silence, sitting on the plastic chair in the cold.

“Why did he withdraw?” she said finally.

Professor Gao smoked for a while without answering.

“Because he wanted there to be no question,” she said, “that your marks are yours.”

“That isn’t all,” said Yu Jie. “Is it.”

Professor Gao looked at her. Her sharp black eyes were very steady.

“No,” she said. “That isn’t all.”

“What did he say? In the letter. There was a letter. There’s always a letter, with him. He writes things down.”

Professor Gao tapped her ash over the railing.

“He said that none of it was your fault,” she said. “He said that if there was any fault, it was his.” She paused. “And he said some other things, which are not mine to tell you, and which you will have to ask him about yourself. On the twentieth of June. At one minute past four.”

Yu Jie sat very still on the plastic chair.

“He put it on the record,” she said slowly. “Didn’t he. Whatever it was. He wrote it down and gave it to Professor Zhou. So that if anyone ever said anything about me, about my degree, about my family’s money, there would already be a piece of paper in a file saying it was him.” Her voice cracked. “He made himself the one they’d blame.”

Professor Gao didn’t say anything.

She didn’t have to.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first Wednesday in the glass seminar room was that afternoon, the eleventh of February.

She came at 3:45. The door was open. The room was cold and bright, with a long white table and a whiteboard instead of a chalkboard, and three glass walls that looked out onto the corridor, where students walked past and looked in.

He was standing at the whiteboard holding a marker pen as if it had personally offended him.

“I don’t like these,” he said, by way of hello. “They squeak. And they run out. And they smell of chemicals. I asked facilities for a chalkboard. They said this is the twenty-first century.”

“It is the twenty-first century.”

“Chalk is still better.”

At the far end of the long white table, Dr. Fang Hao was sitting with his feet up on a chair, a stack of marking in front of him, and a paper bag of croissants open at his elbow. He waved.

“Don’t mind me,” he said. “I’m furniture. I’m a very well-fed piece of furniture. Proceed with the physics.”

She looked at Miles at the whiteboard. Three metres. The glass walls. The open door. The students in the corridor. Fang Hao eating a croissant.

He looked back at her.

She wanted to say: You wrote a letter. She wanted to say: You put your name on a piece of paper so nobody could put mine on one. She wanted to say: What did you write? What did you say? Tell me. Tell me now.

She didn’t.

She sat down at the long white table, and took out her notebook, and took the purple pen with the plastic cat on the end out of her claw clip—he had given it back to her in January, in a sticky note that said I think this is yours. It keeps asking questions.—and said:

“I want to talk about corners again. I think there’s a second paper in it.”

He looked at her for a moment. Something moved in his face, behind the calm.

Then he uncapped the squeaking marker.

“Show me,” said Miles.

At the end of the table, Fang Hao put down his croissant, and pretended to mark, and didn’t turn a single page for two hours.

At twenty-five past five she packed up her printouts. On the way to the door she stopped, put a small cardboard box down on the corner of the long white table at arm’s length from him, and slid it the last few centimetres with one finger.

White chalk. Twelve sticks, the old-fashioned kind, from the second-year teaching lab.

“It won’t work on the whiteboard,” said Miles.

“I know. It isn’t for the whiteboard.” She hitched her bag onto her shoulder. “It’s so you’ve got something in your pocket that doesn’t squeak.”

She went out through the open glass door. He stood looking at the box for so long that Fang Hao had to cough.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 5:30, when she had gone, he was wiping the whiteboard. It took a long time. The marker didn’t come off properly. There was always a grey ghost of everything left behind.

Fang Hao was still sitting at the end of the table.

“She knows,” he said.

“Knows what?”

“About the letter. Gao told her there was one. She didn’t tell her what was in it.” Fang Hao looked at him. “She looked at you for two hours like she wanted to climb over this table.”

Miles kept wiping.

“She didn’t, though,” he said.

“No,” said Fang Hao. “She didn’t. She talked about corners for two hours instead.” He stood up and brushed crumbs off his trousers. “And you know what, Miles? I’ve watched a lot of people fall in love in this building. Postdocs. PhD students. Lecturers. One very embarrassing visiting professor from Hamburg.” He picked up his marking. “I have never, ever seen two people work this hard at not doing it.”

He went to the door.

“The second paper,” he said, “is going to be very good, by the way. I understood about a third of it. It was the most romantic third of anything I’ve ever sat through.”

He left.

Miles stood alone in the glass seminar room, in front of the grey ghost on the whiteboard, where a diagram of a sheet of carbon with sharp corners still showed faintly through.

In the bottom right-hand corner, without thinking, he had written something at some point in the afternoon, very small, in marker pen. He didn’t remember doing it.

20 June, 16:00.

He looked at it for a long time.

He didn’t wipe it off.

chapters.title: She Cries in a Stairwell
chapters.desc: New Year’s Eve dinner at the museum, with the Lus at the table and the forum on her mother’s phone. Not because of him. Because of her mother.
chapters.epigraph: “I let you have your little hobby. I let you have your little man. Now the hobby is over.” — Shen Ruolan
chapters.content:
New Year’s Eve dinner at the Shen house was always at seven, and always in the big dining room, and always eleven courses.

Yu Jie had been to twenty-two of them. She knew every one. The cold plates first, arranged in the shape of a phoenix, because her mother had seen it once in a magazine. Then the soup. Then the fish, whole, which you were not allowed to turn over because it meant a boat would capsize and the business would fail. Then, much later, the dumplings, folded by the cook and not by the family, because her mother said folding dumplings was for people who couldn’t afford a cook.

She had folded dumplings once, at Tao Tao’s family flat, in the first year of university. Tao Tao’s grandmother had shown her how to pleat the edges with her thumbs. She had been so happy she had nearly cried, and Tao Tao’s grandmother had patted her hand and given her a red envelope with twenty yuan in it, and she still had the envelope in her desk drawer.

This year, the Lus came at six-thirty.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lu Zhiyuan’s parents were elegant and quiet and very correct. His father had been an ambassador to three countries and sat at the table as if it were a negotiation. His mother wore jade and smiled at Yu Jie with the anxious hopefulness of a woman who has been trying to marry her son off for four years.

Lu Zhiyuan himself was charming to everyone. He talked to her father about trade. He talked to her brother about shipping routes. He praised her mother’s phoenix. He was seated next to Yu Jie, at exactly the right distance, and turned to her at exactly the right moments, and said exactly the right things, and under the table, during the fish, he slid his phone sideways on his knee so that she could see the screen.

Hang in there. Course 3 of 11. Halfway to the dumplings.

She nearly laughed. She turned it into a cough.

Her mother looked at her sharply across the table.

✦ ✦ ✦

It happened between the eighth course and the ninth.

The servants were clearing the plates. Her father had gone to take a phone call. Her brother was on his own phone. The Lus were admiring the view of the harbour from the window. And her mother got up, and came round the table, and put her hand on Yu Jie’s elbow, and said softly, smiling, “Come and help me with something, darling,” and took her out of the dining room, down the corridor, into the small sitting room with the glass cabinets, and shut the door.

The small sitting room was where her mother kept her collection. Porcelain. Jade. A pair of Ming vases. And on the middle shelf, under its own little light, a single pearl on a silver stand, which her grandmother had given her mother on her wedding day. The Perfect Jewel. That was where the name came from. Yu Jie had been told the story at every New Year since she was four.

Her mother let go of her elbow.

She took her phone out of the pocket of her pale grey silk and unlocked it and held it out.

It was the forum. The first photograph. The orange streetlight, the blurry girl, the shoes in her hand, the jacket with the sleeves over her hands. And below it, the second photograph. Office 412. Dr. M. Wei. The pink sticky notes.

The photographs had been removed from the forum on Tuesday. Her mother had screenshots.

“Somebody sent these to me,” said Shen Ruolan pleasantly. “On Monday. An old friend. She thought I should know.” She looked at her daughter. “Do you know how many people at that gala have seen these, Yu Jie? Do you know how many of my friends? Do you know what they are saying about this family?”

Yu Jie didn’t say anything.

“The lecturer,” said her mother. “The thin one. In the tuxedo. I invited him. I wrote to him personally.” Her smile didn’t move at all. “And he put my daughter in his jacket and walked her home at one o’clock in the morning, and the whole city has seen it.”

“Nothing happened,” said Yu Jie. Her voice was very steady. “He gave me his jacket because I was cold. He walked me home because I didn’t have a coat. He stopped a block away. He didn’t—”

“I don’t care what happened.”

Her mother said it quite gently.

“I don’t care what happened,” said Shen Ruolan, “and I don’t care what didn’t. I care what it looks like. That’s all that matters, Yu Jie. That’s all that has ever mattered. You should know that by now. I have been teaching it to you since you were four years old.” She put the phone away. “I spoke to Professor Zhou on Friday. He told me that the lecturer has withdrawn from your examining panel. He was very polite about it. He said it was a formality.” She smiled. “People don’t withdraw from things as a formality, darling.”

“Mother—”

“I let you have your little hobby,” said her mother. “I let you go to that university instead of the one I chose. I let you live in that apartment with that girl who studies fungus. I let you wear those terrible shoes and spend your Wednesdays on the fourth floor with your little man, because I thought it would pass, and because your father said it would do no harm.” She stepped closer. Her perfume was very expensive and very cold. “It has done harm. So now the hobby is over.”

Yu Jie stood very still in front of the glass cabinet with the single pearl.

Her nails were in her palms. She could feel each one, four small crescents on each hand, pressing harder and harder, because if she pressed hard enough the pain was something she could think about instead. Her heart was going so fast she could hear it in her ears, a thin high rushing like the sea in a shell. The little light above the pearl hummed. In twenty-two years she had never noticed that it hummed.

“The Lus have agreed,” said her mother. “The engagement will be announced at the end of June. The week after your graduation. We’ll have it here. Two hundred guests.” She reached out and tucked the loose strand of Yu Jie’s hair, the one she always let fall now, back behind her ear. Very gently. “You’ll finish your degree, because it would look strange if you didn’t. And then you’ll stop. Zhiyuan’s work will take him abroad. Geneva, possibly. You’ll go with him. It’s a very good life, darling. It’s a beautiful life. It’s the life you were made for.”

“I’m not a pearl,” said Yu Jie.

Her mother looked at her with mild surprise.

“Of course you are,” said Shen Ruolan. “You always have been. I made you one.” She turned toward the door. “Jewels are meant to be worn, Yu Jie. Not left on the fourth floor of a science building to collect chalk dust.”

She opened the door.

“Come back to the table,” she said. “The dumplings are coming. And smile. Zhiyuan’s mother is watching.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She smiled.

She went back to the table and sat next to Lu Zhiyuan and smiled through the dumplings and the whole steamed chicken and the sweet soup with the glutinous rice balls, and when the clock struck midnight and the fireworks went up over the harbour, she stood at the big window with the two families and watched them and smiled, and when Lu Zhiyuan’s mother took her hand and pressed a red envelope into it and said, with tears in her eyes, “We’re so happy,” she smiled.

Under the table, during the sweet soup, Lu Zhiyuan had looked at her face once, and gone very quiet, and texted on his knee:

What did she say to you?

She didn’t answer.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t cry that night. She didn’t cry at the family house, in her old bedroom with the canopy bed and the dolls in glass cases. She didn’t cry the next day, or the one after that, through all the visits and the red envelopes and the endless smiling. She didn’t cry when she got back to her apartment on the fourth day of the New Year, and Tao Tao took one look at her and said, “What happened,” and she said, “Nothing,” and went to her room and shut the door.

She didn’t cry when she looked at the calendar on her wall. One hundred and twenty squares left until the gold one. And then a week. And then two hundred guests. And then Geneva.

She went to the Hall of Science on Monday morning, the twenty-third of February, because the building was open again after the holiday, and because she didn’t know where else to go, and because the lab was the only place in the world where nobody had ever once called her a jewel.

The building was nearly empty. Most people were still away.

She went up the back stairs, the old concrete ones at the north end that nobody used because the lift was faster. She went up past the first floor. Past the second, where Professor Gao’s lab was, still dark. Past the third.

Between the third floor and the fourth, on the little landing where the stairs turned, there was a narrow window that looked out over the bare trees of the campus and the grey February sky.

She stopped there.

She didn’t decide to. Her legs stopped. She stood on the landing and looked out of the narrow window at the grey sky, and the whole of the last five days came up out of her at once, from somewhere very deep, like water coming up through a floor.

She sat down on the cold concrete step.

She put her face in her hands.

And she cried.

It was not pretty crying. It was the kind that hurts. Her throat closed like a fist, a hot ache sat at the hinge of her jaw, and her breath came in pieces that didn’t fit together. She pressed the heels of her hands into her eyes until she saw colours. The concrete was so cold through her jeans that her legs went numb, and she didn’t move. Five days of smiling came off her face all at once, and her face didn’t know what to do without it. She bit the sleeve of her jumper so that no sound would get out into the empty building, and the sound got out anyway, thin and high, like something small caught in a door.

✦ ✦ ✦

He heard her from the fourth-floor corridor.

He had come in early, because the staff flat was cold and the heating had broken again, and because there was nobody to see him at the Hall of Science during the holiday, and he could work in office 412 with the door shut and not be looked at. He was walking from the kitchen back to his office with his WORLD’S OKAYEST SON mug when he heard it, faintly, through the fire door at the end of the corridor.

Someone crying in the back stairwell.

Not loudly. Muffled. The kind of crying where you are trying very hard not to make any sound and failing.

He stopped.

He stood in the empty corridor for a long moment, holding his tea.

Then he put the mug down on the floor, very carefully, against the wall, and went to the fire door and opened it.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was sitting on the third step from the bottom of the flight, on the landing below him, with her back against the wall and her face in her hands. She was in jeans and a big grey jumper he had never seen before, and her hair was down, and there were no pens in it at all. Her shoulders were shaking.

She heard the door. She looked up.

Her face was wet and red and blotchy and absolutely nothing like a photograph.

“Oh,” said Yu Jie. “No. Not you. Please. I don’t want—not you. Go away. I’m fine.”

He didn’t go away.

He came down the stairs. Slowly. Not to her. He stopped on the step four steps above where she was sitting, and sat down there, on the cold concrete, with his long legs folded up and his arms around his knees.

Four steps. About two metres. Above her, not beside her.

He didn’t say anything.

He took a packet of tissues out of the pocket of his cardigan, the kind his sister made him carry, and leaned down as far as he could, and put it on the step just above her head, and sat back again.

She looked at the tissues. Then at him.

Then she took one, and blew her nose very loudly, and started crying again.

✦ ✦ ✦

He waited.

He waited the way he had waited in the glass seminar room, the way he waited at the chalkboard when she was working something out. Patiently. Not hurrying her. As if he had all the time in the world, and was glad to spend it here, on a cold concrete step, in an empty building, on a grey Monday morning.

After a long time, she stopped.

She sat with her back against the wall and a wad of wet tissues in her hand and looked at the narrow window and the grey sky.

“It isn’t you,” she said. Her voice was thick. “I want you to know that. It isn’t you. It isn’t the forum, or the photographs, or the letter. It isn’t anything you did.”

“All right,” said Miles.

“It’s my mother.”

He waited.

“She had the photographs,” said Yu Jie. “On her phone. Someone sent them. She took me into the room where she keeps the pearl, and she showed me, and she said she didn’t care what happened. Only what it looked like. And then she said—” Her voice broke. She stopped. She tried again. “She said the engagement is at the end of June. The week after graduation. Two hundred guests. And then I stop. I just stop. Physics, the lab, Professor Gao, everything. I go to Geneva with a man who’s very kind and doesn’t love me, and I wear dresses, and I go to parties, and I smile.” She looked down at the tissues. “She said I was made for it. She said she made me for it.”

He didn’t say anything.

“And you said?” he asked quietly.

“I said I’m not a pearl.” She laughed, a wet, broken sound. “And she said, Of course you are. As if I’d said I wasn’t a girl. As if it was a fact. And then I went back to the table and ate the dumplings and smiled for five days.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He looked at her, sitting below him on the cold step in a big grey jumper with no pens in her hair.

“My parents,” said Miles, after a while, “are retired schoolteachers. They live in a small flat by the sea, four hours from here. My father taught maths for thirty-eight years. My mother taught literature. When I was nine I told them I wanted to understand why light bends, and my father went to the library that weekend and came home with every book on optics they had, and sat with me at the kitchen table every evening for a year, working through them, even though he didn’t really understand them either.”

She was listening.

“They never once told me what to be,” said Miles. “They never once wanted me to be anything except whatever I was. And I was very lucky. I know that. I’ve always known it.” He looked at his hands. “So I don’t know what it’s like. What you have. I don’t know anything about it. I can’t tell you I understand, because I don’t.”

He paused.

“But I can tell you one thing that’s true. If you want it.”

She looked up at him.

“The thesis,” said Miles, “is the best thing I have read this year. Not the best student thing. The best thing. I read it from midnight until seven in the morning and I didn’t notice the time once. On page nine you wrote a paragraph about electrons moving along an edge, and I put my pen down, and I sat and looked at the snow for ten minutes, because it was so beautiful I didn’t want to read the next line yet.”

Her face crumpled.

“Nobody made you for that,” said Miles. “You made it. You. At two in the morning on your bedroom floor, with your corners. I watched you do it for four months.” His voice was very quiet in the stairwell. “Your mother can call you anything she likes. She can put you in any room, with any pearl. But I’ve seen what you actually are. And it isn’t a jewel.”

“What is it?” she whispered.

He thought about it, the way he thought about everything. Properly.

“A physicist,” he said simply.

✦ ✦ ✦

She cried again. But differently. Not like water coming up through a floor. Like something breaking open that had been shut for a very long time.

He sat four steps above her and didn’t touch her. He didn’t move. He couldn’t. It was February, and she was a student in his department, and there were a hundred and seventeen squares left, and he had written a letter.

It hurt. He had not known that it would hurt physically. His hands ached with it, a real ache in the tendons, the way they ached after a whole night of writing. His whole body leaned toward her on the step, and he held it back the way you hold a door shut in a wind. Every time her shoulders shook, something in his chest pulled tight, as if there were a wire strung between them and someone kept tugging on it.

But he leaned down, slowly, and put his hand on the step just above her head. Flat on the cold concrete. Not touching her. Just there. About twenty centimetres from her hair.

She looked at it.

Then she reached up, slowly, and put her own hand on the step beside his. Flat on the cold concrete. Not touching. A finger’s width apart.

They stayed like that. Two hands on a cold step, a finger’s width apart, in an empty stairwell, in an empty building, on a grey Monday morning in February.

She stopped crying.

“Thank you,” she said finally, very quietly. “For not going away.”

“I nearly did,” said Miles. “I put my tea down on the floor. It’s probably cold.”

She laughed. Wet and shaky, but a real laugh.

“You put your tea on the floor?”

“Against the wall. Very carefully.”

“You’ll kick it over.”

“I will,” Miles agreed. “Almost certainly.”

She wiped her face with the back of her hand. She took her hand off the step. He took his off a second later.

She stood up. He stayed sitting.

She looked up at him, four steps above her, with his long legs folded up and his arms round his knees and his glasses slightly crooked, and said:

“I’m not going to Geneva.”

He looked back at her.

“I don’t know how yet,” said Shen Yu Jie. “But I’m not going.”

She turned, and went down the stairs, past the third floor, past the second, and he listened to her footsteps going down and down the empty concrete stairwell until he heard the fire door at the bottom open and close.

Then he went back up, and opened the fire door at the top, and kicked his tea over.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, she took the calendar off her bedroom wall.

She looked at the gold square at the end. 20 June. Then she looked at the week after it, where her mother’s engagement would be. Those squares weren’t on the calendar. She had never drawn them. The calendar ended at the gold square, because she had made it in September, when the twentieth of June had seemed like the end of everything.

She took a pencil. She drew a line after the gold square. Then another square. Then another.

She didn’t know what would go in them yet.

But she drew them anyway. A whole new row of squares, after the gold one, going on past the edge of the page and onto the wall.

And in the first one, the twenty-first of June, very small, she wrote:

Not a pearl.

chapters.title: The Grant Nobody Applied For
chapters.desc: Five years of funding, a laboratory with a water tank that bends light, and a donor who wants no name. Miles is overjoyed for exactly two days.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody gives four million to a theorist, Miles. Nobody. Theorists are cheap. We need chalk and a chair.” — Dr. Fang Hao
chapters.content:
The email came on the second of March at 9:04 in the morning, and Miles read it four times before he understood it.

Dear Dr. Wei,

I am delighted to inform you that the Department of Physics has received a restricted gift from a private charitable trust, to establish a five-year research programme under your direction. The gift is for the creation of a laboratory for analogue gravity and gravitational optics, including equipment, two postdoctoral positions, one PhD studentship, and your own salary for the full five-year period.

The donor wishes to remain anonymous.

Please come to my office at your earliest convenience to discuss.

Zhou Lin Head of Department

He sat at his desk in office 412 and looked at the screen.

Then he looked at the cactus.

“Schrödinger,” he said. “I think something has happened.”

The cactus, as usual, declined to say whether it had or not.

✦ ✦ ✦

The trust was called the Bending Light Foundation. It had been registered in January. It had one purpose, and the purpose was him.

Professor Zhou explained it in his office with the door closed and the paperwork spread out on his desk. Four million over five years. A real laboratory, in the empty basement rooms under the east wing that had been storage since the nineties. Equipment. People. And his salary, guaranteed, until the end of the programme.

“That last part,” said Professor Zhou, “is unusual.”

Miles was still looking at the figure on the first page. “Why?”

Professor Zhou took his reading glasses off and looked at him.

“Miles,” he said. “When does your contract end?”

Miles blinked. “August.”

“And what happens in April?”

“The review.” He had almost forgotten. He was a lecturer on a five-year fixed-term contract. Every lecturer was, at the start. At the end of the five years there was a review, by the department and then by the university council, and the council decided whether to make the post permanent. It was usually a formality for anyone who published. He published a great deal. He hadn’t thought about it since Christmas. “It’s a formality.”

“It is usually a formality,” said Professor Zhou carefully. “This year, it may not be.”

Miles looked at him.

Professor Zhou put his glasses back on and looked down at the papers, as if he didn’t want to say the next part to anyone’s face.

“There is a member of the university council,” he said, “who has written to the Vice-Chancellor, twice since New Year, to ask whether the department’s recent difficulties will be considered at your review. She has asked whether it is appropriate for a lecturer who has declared a personal interest in a student to be given a permanent post.” He paused. “She has asked very politely. She is a very polite woman. She has also mentioned, in both letters, the size of her family’s gift to this department.”

Miles sat very still.

“Shen Ruolan,” he said.

Professor Zhou said nothing, which was answer enough.

“I see,” said Miles.

He looked at the paperwork. Your own salary for the full five-year period.

“So a gift arrives,” he said slowly, “a few weeks after those letters, from a trust nobody has heard of, that pays my salary for five years. Which means that whatever the council decides in April, the department can keep me. Because the money is restricted. It can only be spent on me.”

“Yes,” said Professor Zhou.

“That’s a very convenient gift.”

“It is a very convenient gift,” agreed Professor Zhou. “I have asked the university’s finance office to check the source. They tell me the trust is properly registered, and the money is clean, and the trustees are a firm of lawyers who will not tell anyone anything. Which is what lawyers are for.” He looked at Miles over his glasses. “I don’t know who gave it, Miles. Officially. I would very much like it to stay that way, until April at least.”

Miles looked at him for a long time.

Then he looked at the figure on the first page again. Four million.

A laboratory.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t think about where it came from.

That was the thing he would remember afterwards, and be ashamed of. He was a physicist. He questioned everything. He asked where the error bars were. He asked what the assumptions were. He asked, always, about the boundary conditions.

But for two whole days, he didn’t ask. Because someone had given him a laboratory.

He had wanted one since he was nine. Since his father brought home every book on optics from the library and they sat at the kitchen table working through them. Since he first read that ripples on a tank of flowing water could be made to behave the way light behaves near a black hole, if you made the water flow in exactly the right way. Analogue gravity. Real experiments. Not just chalk and a chair and the universe a long way away, but light on a table in front of you, doing what he had only ever done on paper.
