He had applied for the money three times in five years. He had been told three times that it was a very interesting proposal and that theorists didn’t need laboratories.

He went down to the basement under the east wing on Tuesday afternoon with a set of keys from facilities and a torch, and stood in the empty storage rooms among broken chairs and old filing cabinets and boxes of exam papers from 1997, and shone the torch around, and saw it.

Where the long tank would go, along the north wall. Where the laser bench would go. The flow pumps. The cameras. The computers. A desk for the postdocs. A whiteboard—no. A chalkboard. A real one.

He stood in the dark basement with the torch and couldn’t stop smiling.

The first thing he thought, before the pumps and the cameras and the postdocs, was: I have to tell her. Wednesday, a quarter to four. He would draw the tank on the board. She would take the marker out of his hand and redraw his flow arrows, tell him the hump was the wrong shape, and be right. He found he had already decided which way round to draw it, so she would be able to see it properly from her chair.

He stood in the basement for a long time and practised how he would tell her. It did not once occur to him that she already knew.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Nobody,” said Fang Hao on Wednesday, “gives four million to a theorist.”

They were in the glass seminar room. It was 3:30. She hadn’t come yet. Fang Hao was eating a croissant and had been listening to Miles describe the laboratory for twenty minutes.

“Somebody did,” said Miles.

“Nobody, Miles. Theorists are cheap. We need chalk and a chair. I’ve been trying to get a new chair for three years.” Fang Hao frowned. “And they paid your salary. Who pays a lecturer’s salary? Donors fund buildings. They want their name on a wall. They don’t want to pay for a man to sit in a room. Unless—”

He stopped.

Miles was drawing the tank on the whiteboard. He didn’t notice.

“Unless,” said Fang Hao slowly, “the point is the man in the room.”

Miles kept drawing.

“Where’s it from?” said Fang Hao.

“A trust. The Bending Light Foundation. Anonymous. Zhou says the money’s clean.”

“Bending Light.” Fang Hao put down his croissant. “Miles. Who in this city knows that you study light bending around heavy things? Who’s heard you talk about it for hours? Who’s sat across a table from you every Wednesday since September and drawn atoms on a calendar?”

Miles stopped drawing.

He stood with his back to Fang Hao and the marker in his hand.

“No,” he said.

“Miles—”

“No. She’s twenty-two. She’s a student. She doesn’t have four million.” He turned round. “She’s never even called a taxi.”

Fang Hao looked at him with enormous pity.

“Her family owns half the harbour,” he said gently. “Do you really think she doesn’t have four million?”

✦ ✦ ✦

She came at 3:45.

She came in through the open glass door in a blue jumper with four pens in her hair and a stack of printouts for the second paper, and she was smiling. She had been smiling more since the stairwell. Not the gala smile. A new one. Quieter and more determined, as if she had decided something.

“I did the corners for hexagons,” she said, dropping the printouts on the long white table. “It works. It actually works. Look at page three—”

“Did you give the department four million,” said Miles.

He said it without thinking. Without any of the careful preparation he would have made, if he had had time to make it. It came out flat and quiet and straight, the way his questions in seminars came out.

She stopped.

She stood there with one hand on the printouts. The smile stayed on her face for one second too long, and then it went.

At the end of the table, Fang Hao very slowly stopped chewing.

“What?” said Yu Jie.

“The Bending Light Foundation,” said Miles. “A trust. Registered in January. Four million. A laboratory for analogue gravity, and my salary for five years.” He looked at her. “I’m asking if it was you.”

She looked at him across the long white table. He watched her face. He had spent six months watching her face at a chalkboard. He knew it better than his own.

He saw her think about lying.

He saw her decide not to.

“It’s not for you,” she said. “It’s for the laboratory. You’ve wanted one since you were nine. You told me. In October. You said you wanted to make light bend in a water tank and nobody would give you the money because you were a theorist—”

“It was you.”

Silence.

“Yes,” said Shen Yu Jie.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say anything.

He stood at the whiteboard, where he had drawn the long tank in squeaking blue marker, with the flow arrows, and the laser, and the beam of light bending, and he looked at it.

Two days. He had been happy for two days. Down in the dark basement with a torch, seeing where everything would go.

“Fang Hao,” he said finally, without turning round. “Would you give us a moment.”

“I’m supposed to be the third person,” said Fang Hao. “Zhou said.”

“Then stand outside the door,” said Miles. “The door is glass. You can see everything. I won’t move from this spot. But I’d like to say something to her that I don’t want anybody else to hear.”

Fang Hao looked at him. Then at her.

He stood up, and picked up his croissant, and went out, and stood in the corridor with his back to the glass, pretending to read the noticeboard.

The door stayed open.

Miles turned round.

“Where did it come from?” he said quietly. “The money.”

“My grandmother.” Her voice was steady, but her hands were holding the printouts very tightly. “She left me a trust when she died. My father’s lawyers manage it, but it’s mine. I could use it when I turned twenty-one. I never touched it. I didn’t want anything of theirs.” She swallowed. “Then I found out what my mother was planning. About your review.”

“How did you find out?”

“Lu Zhiyuan. His mother heard it from my mother, at a tea. He told me in January.” She lifted her chin. “She was going to take your job away, Miles. Because of a photograph. Because of me. Because you gave me your jacket and wrote an honest letter. She was going to end your career and smile about it at the next gala. I couldn’t—I wasn’t going to let—”

“So you bought me.”

The words fell into the glass room like a dropped plate.

She went white.

“That isn’t—”

“It’s what it looks like,” said Miles. His voice was very quiet. “Isn’t it. That’s what your mother taught you. It doesn’t matter what happened. It matters what it looks like.” He looked at her. “And what it looks like is that the Shen girl paid four million to keep her lecturer in a job. That’s what Dr. Ren said in the kitchen. She’s buying her degree, and he’s getting paid in kind. And you’ve just made it true.”

She stood very still.

He saw it hit her. He saw it go all the way in.

He didn’t stop. He couldn’t. Something had come up in him that he didn’t recognise: something hot and hurt and terrible, that had been sleeping since a school library fourteen years ago.

“I wrote that letter,” he said, “so that nobody could ever say your marks were bought. I put my name on it. I told Zhou things I’ve never told anyone. I did it so there would be nothing left for anybody to say about you. And you’ve gone and—” His voice cracked. “You’ve made it so that every single thing I do for the next five years, every paper, every result, every time I walk into that laboratory, people will look at me and think, the Shen girl paid for that.”

“Miles—”

“You didn’t ask me.”

There it was. That was the thing. That was the thing under all the other things.

“You didn’t ask me,” he said again, more quietly. “You decided what I needed. You decided it, and you arranged it, with lawyers, in secret, and you didn’t ask. That’s what they do. Your family. Your mother. They decide what people are for and they arrange it and they don’t ask.” He looked at her across the long white table. “I didn’t think you were like them.”

She made a small sound, like something tearing.

Her hand went to her chest, flat, the heel of it pressed against her breastbone, the way you would hold a cut closed. Her face did not move at all. That was the worst part. He had seen that face laughing with its head down on his desk. He had seen it blotched and wet in a stairwell. Now it went perfectly, terribly smooth: it was the face from the bottom of the white marble staircase. He understood, with a cold drop in his stomach, that he had put it there.

In the corridor, through the glass, Fang Hao had turned round from the noticeboard. His face was horrified.

✦ ✦ ✦

She put the printouts down on the table. Very carefully. Squared the edges.

Then she looked up at him, and her eyes were full, but her voice, when it came, was perfectly steady, and very cold. Colder than he had ever heard it. It was, he realised with a lurch, her mother’s voice.

“You’re right,” she said. “I didn’t ask you. Because if I had asked, you’d have said no. You’d have said it was against the rules. You’d have let them take your job and your career and your whole life, and you’d have gone home to your staff flat with one egg in the fridge and said, It’s all right, I have the cactus.” Her voice wavered for the first time. “You put yourself on the record for me. You made yourself the target. You didn’t ask me either, Miles. You just did it. Because you decided I needed protecting.”

He opened his mouth.

“So don’t you dare,” said Shen Yu Jie, “tell me I’m like my mother. Because I did exactly what you did. The only difference is, I had money, and you had a pen.”

She picked up her bag.

“The laboratory,” she said, “was for the boy who wanted to make light bend in a water tank. I thought you’d be happy.” Her voice broke at last. “I thought just once, somebody I—somebody would be happy, because of something I did. Not because of what I looked like.”

She walked out.

She went past Fang Hao in the corridor without looking at him. She went down the corridor, and through the fire door, and he heard her going down the back stairs, fast, past the landing with the narrow window, until the sound was gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles stood alone in the glass seminar room in front of the whiteboard.

On it, in squeaking blue marker, the long tank. The flow arrows. The laser. The beam of light, bending.

And in the bottom right-hand corner, where he had written it without thinking three weeks ago and never wiped it off: 20 June, 16:00.

Fang Hao came back in. He didn’t say anything. He sat down at the end of the table and looked at the printouts she had left behind, squared at the edges. Corners for hexagons. It works.

“Hao,” said Miles, after a long time.

“Yes.”

“I think I’ve just done something very stupid.”

Fang Hao looked at the empty doorway. Then at the man at the whiteboard, standing very straight, with his hands shaking at his sides.

“Yes,” he said gently. “I think you have.”

chapters.title: He Finds the Name
chapters.desc: A purpose clause in a trust deed, signed with three initials. Then a diplomat in a perfect suit comes to Thursday office hours with no physics question at all.
chapters.epigraph: “To fund research into the bending of light, under the direction of a scientist who takes students’ questions seriously.” — Deed of the Bending Light Foundation, clause 2
chapters.content:
He didn’t sleep on Wednesday night.

He sat at his one table in the staff flat with a cup of tea going cold and the window black, and heard her voice over and over. I did exactly what you did. The only difference is, I had money, and you had a pen.

He tried to argue with it. He was good at arguing. He set it out the way he would set out a proof: the assumptions, the steps, the conclusion. He found the place where her argument was wrong.

He couldn’t find it.

He got up and made tea and didn’t drink it. He sat down. He got up again. There was a dull pain under his breastbone that he couldn’t account for, like the ache after running, though he had not run anywhere. Every time he closed his eyes he saw her hands squaring the edges of the printouts on the long white table, very carefully, so they lined up, the way you tidy a room you are about to leave for good. At two in the morning he realised he had been sitting in the dark for an hour with his coat on, as if some part of him had been about to go somewhere and had not been told where.

At three in the morning he gave up and wrote I am an idiot on a sheet of graph paper, in neat capitals, and sat looking at it. It was the most accurate thing he had written all year.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday morning he went to see Professor Zhou and asked to read the trust deed.

“The whole thing?” said Professor Zhou.

“The whole thing.”

Professor Zhou looked at him for a long moment, at the shadows under his eyes and the jumper he had clearly slept in, if he had slept. Then he unlocked a drawer and took out a thin folder and handed it over without a word.

Miles read it standing up by the window.

It was nine pages. Most of it was lawyers. Definitions. Trustees. Investments. What happened if the university ceased to exist. He read every word, because he always did, and because he was looking for something and didn’t know what.

He found it on page two.

Clause 2. Purpose.

The purpose of the Foundation is to fund research into the bending of light, under the direction of a scientist who takes students’ questions seriously.

He read it three times.

It was not lawyers’ language. It was hers. You could hear her in it: the speed, the plainness, the slight impatience. Somebody had sat in a lawyer’s office in January and been told that the purpose clause should say for the advancement of research in the field of gravitational optics and related disciplines, and had said no. Had insisted. Had made the lawyer write it down the way she wanted.

A scientist who takes students’ questions seriously.

He turned to the last page.

Settlor: And a signature. Small, round, quick, not at all like her mother’s elegant slanting hand. Three letters joined together.

S.Y.J.

And underneath, typed by the lawyer: Funds settled from the estate of the late Madam Shen Lihua, in accordance with the terms of her will.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Who was Shen Lihua?” said Miles.

He said it to Professor Gao, on the second-floor balcony, twenty minutes later. He had gone straight down the stairs with the folder still in his hand, and through the lab that smelled of toast, and out onto the balcony, and she had looked at his face and handed him her cigarette without a word, as if she thought he might need it, and he had handed it back, because he didn’t smoke.

“Her grandmother,” said Professor Gao. “Her father’s mother.” She took a long drag. “She died four years ago. The only person in that family who ever bought the girl a chemistry set.”

Miles looked at her.

“Yu Jie told me once,” said Professor Gao. “In her first year, when she was still frightened of me. I asked her why physics, and she said, My grandmother gave me a chemistry set for my eighth birthday, and my mother threw it away, and my grandmother bought me another one and kept it at her house, and every Sunday I went and set things on fire in her kitchen.” She tapped ash over the railing. “She said her grandmother was the only person who ever asked her what she wanted to be.”

Miles stood very still.

“How much?” he said. “In the trust. Before.”

Professor Gao looked at him.

“I don’t know,” she said. “But I can tell you this. That girl lives on her family’s allowance. Every penny she spends comes from her mother. Her apartment is her father’s. Her clothes are her mother’s choices, except the ones she buys in secret.” She stubbed out the cigarette. “If she had a trust of her own that her mother couldn’t touch, from the only person in that family who loved her for what she was, then it would have been the only thing in her life that was really hers.”

The wind blew across the car park.

“And she gave it to you,” said Professor Gao. “All of it, if I know her. To keep you in a job she thought her mother was going to take away.” She looked at him with her sharp black eyes. “What did you say to her, Wei? Fang Hao came to my office yesterday looking as if somebody had died.”

Miles told her.

All of it. So you bought me. You didn’t ask me. I didn’t think you were like them.

Professor Gao listened without interrupting.

When he had finished, she was silent.

“Well,” she said finally. “I’ve read your letter to Zhou. I know you can be honest. I didn’t know you could be cruel.”

He flinched.

“Neither did I,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Thursday office hours were at three.

He went, because he always went. He sat in office 412 with the door propped open with Principles of Quantum Mechanics, because it was Thursday and there was no rule about Thursdays, and he answered questions from second-years about the hydrogen atom and tried to listen to them properly and failed.

At 3:20, Bai Tianyu came in and asked whether, if he was made of atoms, and atoms were mostly empty space, he was mostly empty space.

“Yes,” said Miles.

Bai Tianyu looked devastated.

“But so is everything else,” said Miles. “So it evens out. When you lean on a wall, you’re mostly empty space leaning on mostly empty space. The electrons push back. That’s why you don’t fall through.” He paused. “It’s a very good question. Most people never ask it. Write it down.”

Bai Tianyu wrote it down and left, comforted.

At 3:40, the doorway darkened.

It wasn’t a student.

It was a man of about thirty in a beautifully cut charcoal suit, with a calm, handsome face and tired eyes and a briefcase, standing in the doorway of office 412 looking at the sign about office hours, and the green cat in its box, and then at the room: the books, the painted chalkboard, the cactus on the windowsill, and the bottom right-hand corner of the board.

He looked at that for a long moment.

Then he looked at Miles.

“Dr. Wei,” he said. “We weren’t introduced at the gala. I’m Lu Zhiyuan.” He smiled slightly. “I’m told these are your office hours. I don’t have a question about quantum mechanics. Is that a problem?”

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles stood up.

He didn’t know what to do with his hands. He put them in his pockets. He took them out. He looked at the man in the doorway: the man in midnight blue who had danced with her in long smooth turns, who had leaned close and said something in her ear and made her laugh her own laugh. The perfect match. The engagement at the end of June.

“It’s not a problem,” he said. “Please. Sit down.”

Lu Zhiyuan came in and sat down in the chair. The Wednesday chair. Her chair. He put his briefcase on his knees and looked around the office with real interest, as if it were a foreign country.

“You painted the board yourself,” he said.

“Yes. How did you—”

“The edges. There’s a line where the roller stopped.” Lu Zhiyuan looked at the cactus. “And that must be Schrödinger.”

Miles stared at him.

“She talks about you,” said Lu Zhiyuan. “We have dinner every two weeks. Our mothers arrange it. We sit in a very expensive restaurant at a very correct distance and our mothers’ friends report back that we looked very happy.” He smiled faintly. “And she talks about you. For two hours. The cactus. The egg sandwich. The harmonic oscillator, which I still don’t understand. The fever and the oranges. The seminar. The long way home, because it was flatter for the shoes.” He looked at Miles. “I have heard about the corner of your chalkboard more times than I’ve heard my own name.”

Miles sat down very slowly.

“Why are you here?” he said.

“Because she hasn’t talked about you since yesterday afternoon,” said Lu Zhiyuan. “We had dinner last night. She didn’t say your name once. She ordered a salad and didn’t eat it and talked about the weather for two hours. The weather, Dr. Wei. I’ve sat through a great many diplomatic dinners. I know what it means when somebody talks about the weather.” He put his hands together on top of the briefcase. “So I asked her what had happened. And she told me. And I thought, since nobody else is going to come and explain this to you, I would.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Explain what?”

Lu Zhiyuan looked at him for a long moment with his calm, tired eyes.

“In January,” he said, “at a tea, my mother heard your Mrs. Shen tell three other women that she was going to make sure, very politely, that a certain young lecturer at City University did not get a permanent post. She said it the way she might say she was going to have a dress altered. My mother told me, because she thought it was charming. Ruolan protects her girl so well.” His voice didn’t change at all. “I told Yu Jie the next day. She went white. She asked me if I knew a lawyer who didn’t work for her father. I did.”

Miles said nothing.

“She went to see him on the fifteenth of January,” said Lu Zhiyuan. “I went with her, because she asked me to, and because I don’t think she’d ever been into a lawyer’s office on her own. She sat in front of him in a yellow jumper with pens in her hair and told him she wanted to give away her grandmother’s trust. All of it.” He paused. “The lawyer asked her if she was sure. She said yes. He asked her if she understood that it was everything she had of her own. She said yes. He asked her three times. Lawyers have to. The third time, she said, My grandmother bought me a chemistry set when nobody else would. She’d want it to go to someone who would have bought me one too.”

Miles put his hand over his eyes.

“Then the lawyer wrote down the purpose clause,” said Lu Zhiyuan, “in proper legal language. And she read it and said no. And made him write it again. Her way.” He was quiet for a moment. “A scientist who takes students’ questions seriously. She said that was the only qualification that mattered. She said she had met a great many scientists, and only one of them had ever done it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The radiator went off like a whale.

Neither of them looked at it.

“You think she bought you,” said Lu Zhiyuan. “I understand why. I know what this city is like. I know what people will say. But in my profession, Dr. Wei, we have a different word for what she did.”

Miles took his hand away from his eyes.

“A guarantee,” said Lu Zhiyuan. “When one country wants to protect another country from a third country it can’t control, it doesn’t buy it. It guarantees it. It puts something of its own on the table, something valuable, so that the third country can’t touch the second without touching the first.” He looked at Miles. “She didn’t buy you. She put the only thing she owned between you and her mother. That’s not a purchase. That’s a shield.”

Miles was very quiet.

“I told her she was like her mother,” he said finally. His voice came out rough. “I said, I didn’t think you were like them.”

Lu Zhiyuan closed his eyes briefly.

“Yes,” he said. “She told me. She didn’t cry when she told me. She talked about the weather afterwards.” He opened his eyes. “I would say that was the worst thing you could possibly have said to her. But you know that already. That’s why you look like you haven’t slept.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He stood up after a while. He picked up his briefcase.

At the door, he stopped, and looked back at the man sitting at the desk in office 412 with his head in his hands.

“Dr. Wei,” he said. “May I tell you something? In confidence. I’ve told almost nobody. I’m not sure why I want to tell you, except that you have a very trustworthy face, and you are about to spend a long time feeling very sorry for yourself, and I think it might help.”

Miles looked up.

“I’m not going to marry her,” said Lu Zhiyuan. “Whatever my mother says, or hers. Not in June, not ever. She knows that. We made an arrangement at the gala. A very civilised one.” He smiled slightly. “Because she’s in love with a physicist who has a rule. And I’m in love with a translator called Kai who lives in a flat above a shoe shop and makes me terrible coffee every Sunday, and whom I’m not allowed to be seen with in any room my mother would set foot in.”

Miles stared at him.

“Oh,” he said.

“Yes,” said Lu Zhiyuan. “Oh.”

“Is that—” Miles didn’t know how to ask it. “Is that a secret?”

“From everyone in the world,” said Lu Zhiyuan, “except Kai, and Yu Jie, and now you.” He looked at Miles with something very like fondness. “I told her at the second dinner. She hugged me across the table in front of forty people and two of her mother’s friends, and then told them she’d dropped her earring.”

Miles laughed. He didn’t mean to. It came out of him in the middle of everything, surprised and shaky.

Lu Zhiyuan smiled.

“So you see,” he said. “I know what it’s like. To stand on the right side of a rule and look at someone on the other side of it. I’ve been doing it for six years.” He opened the door wider. “But I’ve never once told Kai he was like the people who make the rules. Because he isn’t. He’s the reason I can bear them.”

He paused.

“She’s the reason you laugh, Dr. Wei,” he said quietly. “Don’t make her talk about the weather.”

He went out. His footsteps went down the corridor, unhurried, toward the lift.

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles sat in office 412 for a long time after the diplomat had gone.

Then he opened the drawer of his desk.

In it were the things he kept. A spare pair of glasses. A packet of tissues his sister made him carry. A small stack of pink sticky notes, held together with a paper clip. Cu-Te. No chemistry. Acute one. A second napkin from the library café, one of the many he had drawn on that Saturday, which had ended up in his backpack when he fled: a box, dots spreading out. She had the first one. He had never told her he’d kept this. And the yellow note from the tub of peeled oranges in his fridge. Close it at night. Open it on Wednesdays.

He looked at them.

Then he took out a fresh yellow sticky note, and a pen, and wrote on it.

He crossed it out.

He wrote it again. He crossed it out again.

He wrote it eleven times. He threw away ten.

The last one said only:

You were right. I did the same thing. I’m sorry.

He looked at it. Then he put it in his pocket, and got his coat, and went out to find her.

chapters.title: Their First Real Fight
chapters.desc: An intercom by a blue door, in the rain. “You bought me a lab.” “I bought you time.” Both of them are right. That’s the problem.
chapters.epigraph: “You bought me a lab.” “I bought you time. There’s a difference. You’re a physicist. You of all people should know the difference.”
chapters.content:
The security guard at the blue door was called Old Huang, and he had worked there for eleven years, and he had seen a great many young men come to that door at night. Boyfriends. Ex-boyfriends. Drunk boys from the engineering faculty with guitars.

He had never seen one like this.

It was raining. Not hard, but steadily, the cold March rain that came in off the harbour and got into everything. And the young man standing in front of Old Huang’s little lit-up box was soaked through: a tall, thin man of about thirty with no umbrella and glasses spotted with rain and a cardigan that had clearly once been grey and was now dark charcoal with water, holding his hand very carefully over the front pocket of it as if there were something in there that mustn’t get wet.

“Good evening,” said the young man. “I’m sorry to bother you. I’d like to speak to Miss Shen Yu Jie, on the sixth floor. If she’ll see me. My name is Miles Wei.” He paused. “She may not want to see me. That would be very reasonable. If she doesn’t, please tell her that’s all right, and I’ll go.”

Old Huang looked at him for a long moment.

Then he picked up the phone to the sixth floor.

✦ ✦ ✦

It wasn’t Yu Jie who answered. It was the roommate. Old Huang knew the roommate. She was small and fierce and had a bleached streak in her hair and had once threatened to bite a delivery driver.

“Who?” said Tao Tao’s voice down the line, very loud.

“A Dr. Wei,” said Old Huang. “He’s wet.”

There was a pause on the line. Then a muffled conversation, too far from the phone to hear. Then Tao Tao again, louder.

“She says no.”

Old Huang looked at the young man in the rain.

“She says no,” he said.

The young man nodded. He didn’t seem surprised. He stood there for a moment, in the rain, with his hand over his pocket.

“Could I ask you one more thing?” he said. “I’m sorry. Is there an intercom? On the door? Could she—would she just listen? She doesn’t have to say anything. She doesn’t have to come down. I just need to say one thing, and then I’ll go.”

Old Huang looked at him.

Then he picked up the phone again.

✦ ✦ ✦

The intercom on the blue door crackled.

Nobody said anything. But it was on. He could hear it: the faint hiss of an open line, and behind it, very faintly, music, and someone breathing.

He stood in front of the blue door in the rain and looked at the little metal grille.

All the way here, on his bicycle in the rain, he had been preparing what to say. He had it in order. He had the assumptions and the steps and the conclusion. He had I was wrong and You were right and Lu Zhiyuan came to see me.

He opened his mouth, and none of it came out.

“I read the trust deed,” he said instead. “Clause two.”

Silence on the intercom. Just the breathing.

“A scientist who takes students’ questions seriously,” said Miles. “You made the lawyer write it again. Your way. I could hear you in it.” He swallowed. “And I read the signature. And underneath it said Shen Lihua. And I went to Professor Gao, and she told me about the chemistry set.”

Nothing. The rain.

“I said you were like them,” said Miles. “Your family. I said, I didn’t think you were like them. I’ve thought about it every minute since. It’s the worst thing I’ve ever said to anyone. It was wrong, and it was cruel, and I said it because I was hurt and I wanted you to be hurt too, and that’s not a reason, that’s just a fact about me that I didn’t know until yesterday and I’m ashamed of it.”

His voice was going. He kept going anyway.

“You were right,” he said. “I did the same thing. I wrote the letter without asking you. I decided you needed protecting and I did it, and I didn’t ask, and I thought that was noble. And then you did exactly the same thing for me, and I called it buying.” He took his hand off his pocket and took out the sticky note. It was only slightly damp. “I wrote it down. So I’d get it right. It says, You were right. I did the same thing. I’m sorry.” He looked at it. “It took me eleven tries. I’m very bad at this.”

The intercom crackled.

And then her voice came through it, small and tinny and very close:

“You bought me a lab.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He stood very still in the rain.

“What?” he said.

“That’s what you were going to say.” Her voice through the little metal grille was thick, as if she had been crying, or was trying not to. “In the glass room. Before you said the other thing. I watched your face. You were going to say, You bought me a lab. As if it was the same as buying a car. Or a dress. As if I’d gone into a shop and pointed at you.”

“Yu Jie—”

“I didn’t buy you a lab.” The intercom hissed. “I bought you time. There’s a difference. You’re a physicist. You of all people should know the difference.”

He opened his mouth.

“My mother was going to end your career in April,” said Yu Jie. “April, Miles. Before my defence. Before graduation. Before the twentieth of June. She was going to make sure that on the twentieth of June at four o’clock, when I walked up to the fourth floor, you weren’t there. That you’d packed your books and your cactus and gone back to your parents by the sea, and I’d never see you again, and it would be my fault.” Her voice cracked right through. “I didn’t buy you anything. I bought us until June. That’s all. Just until June. I put my grandmother’s money in front of you so my mother couldn’t get to you until June, and then you could do whatever you wanted. You could give it back. You could leave. You could tell me you never wanted to see me again. But at least it would be your choice. Not hers.”

The rain ran down his glasses. He didn’t wipe them.

“And you stood in that glass room,” she said, “and looked at me like I was her.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“I know,” said Miles.

He said it to the metal grille. Very quietly.

“I know I did. I’m sorry. I’ll be sorry.” He took a breath. “But I need to say something else. Not to win. I’m not trying to win. Just because it’s true, and you asked me in September whether the rule was because I didn’t want to or because I couldn’t, and I said it’s a rule, and that wasn’t honest, and I promised myself I’d be honest with you.”

Silence on the intercom.

“I can’t keep it,” said Miles.

The breathing on the other end stopped.

“The money,” said Miles. “The lab. I can’t keep it. Not because it’s yours. Not because of what people will say. I don’t care what people say. I thought I did. Lu Zhiyuan came to see me, and I found out I don’t.” He wiped his face with his wet sleeve, which made it worse. “I can’t keep it because it was the only thing you had that was yours. From the only person in your family who loved you for what you are. And you gave it to me to keep me safe from your mother.” His voice broke. “And that means you’re not safe. You don’t have anything now. If she cuts you off. If she takes the apartment and the allowance. If you say no to Geneva. You don’t have anything of your own left, because you gave it all to me.”

The intercom was silent for a long time.

“That isn’t your decision,” she said finally. Quietly.

“I know.”

“It was my money. My grandmother’s. My choice.”

“I know.”

“So you don’t get to give it back. You don’t get to decide that either. You don’t get to go to Professor Zhou and refuse it and lose your job so that I can feel safe. That’s—” Her voice shook. “That’s the letter again, Miles. That’s you deciding what I need, and doing it, and calling it protecting me.”

He stood in the rain.

She was right. He could see it. She was right, and he was right, and both things were true at once, and there was no way to make them both go away.

“Then what do we do?” he said.

The intercom crackled.

“I don’t know,” said Shen Yu Jie. Her voice was very small. “I don’t know. I’ve never had a fight before. Not a real one. In my family you don’t fight, you just smile until somebody gives up.” A long, shaky breath. “I don’t know how to do this.”

“Neither do I,” said Miles. “I’ve never had anyone to fight with.”

✦ ✦ ✦

For a while, neither of them said anything.

The rain fell. Old Huang, in his little lit-up box, was pretending very hard to read a newspaper and had not turned a page in ten minutes.

“Are you still there?” she said.

“Yes.”

“You’re standing in the rain.”

“Yes.”

“Old Huang says you don’t have an umbrella.”

“I forgot it.”

“You always forget it.” Her voice cracked on something that might have been a laugh. “You’ll get sick again. And I can’t bring you soup this time. Because I’m angry with you. I’m very angry with you. You looked at me like I was my mother.”

“I know.”

“I’m going to be angry with you for a while.”

“That’s all right,” said Miles. “That’s fair. I would be.”

“Don’t come on Wednesday.”

He closed his eyes.

“All right,” he said.

“Not this Wednesday. Not next Wednesday. I need—” Her voice wavered. “I need to think. Without you looking at me. You always look at me like you can see everything, and I need to think about something you can’t see yet.”

“All right,” said Miles again.

He didn’t argue. He wanted to. He wanted to stand at the blue door in the rain until she came down. He wanted to say, I’ll wait. I’m very good at waiting. Come down.

He didn’t. Because she had asked him not to, and he had spent six months learning that the most important thing he could do for her was listen when she asked him for something.

“The sticky note,” said Yu Jie. “Give it to Old Huang.”

He looked down at the damp yellow square in his hand. You were right. I did the same thing. I’m sorry.

He went to the little lit-up box and held it out. Old Huang took it, very carefully, as if it were a document of state.

Then Old Huang reached under his desk, brought out a large black umbrella and held it out through the window of the box.

“From upstairs,” he said. “The first time I rang. The little fierce one said, she says no. And then she said, and she says give him an umbrella, he won’t have one, he never has one.”

Miles took the umbrella. He held it closed in both hands and looked at it as if it were the most complicated object anyone had ever given him.

“Miles,” said the intercom.

He turned back to it.

“Go home,” she said. “Straight home. And have a hot bath and drink something with ginger in it and take paracetamol if you start feeling hot, every six hours, not more.” A pause. “Your sister would know.”

“I will,” said Miles.

“And Miles?”

“Yes?”

The intercom was quiet for so long that he thought she had hung up.

Then, very small and tinny through the little metal grille:

“I’m still angry. But I’m glad you came.”

The line clicked off.

✦ ✦ ✦

He rode home the straight way. Six minutes.

He had a hot bath. He drank ginger tea from a box of it that had appeared in his kitchen in November and which he had not finished, because he was saving it. He did not get a fever. He lay awake until four and listened to the rain.

On the sixth floor of the building with the blue door, Old Huang came up in the lift at eleven, which he had never done in eleven years, and knocked, and handed a slightly damp yellow sticky note to the small fierce roommate, who took it, and said “thank you, Uncle Huang,” in a very different voice from the one on the phone, and shut the door.

She took it to the bedroom.

Yu Jie was sitting on the floor with her back to the bed and her knees up and the calendar on the wall above her. Her face was wet.

She had been there since six, when she came in from the lab and sat down without taking off her coat. Her eyes were swollen almost shut. There was a White Rabbit sweet in her fist that she had unwrapped at some point and never eaten, and it had gone soft and sticky against her palm. Every so often her breath caught, hard, three times in a row, the way it does after crying has gone on far too long, and her whole body jumped with it.

Tao Tao gave her the note and sat down beside her without a word.

Yu Jie read it. You were right. I did the same thing. I’m sorry.

In small, neat letters. Slightly smudged by rain. And at the bottom, very small, which he must have added at the last minute, on the eleventh try:

(Please don’t talk about the weather.)

She put her face on her knees.

“Lu Zhiyuan,” she said, muffled. “He told him. About the weather. That traitor.”

“I love that traitor,” said Tao Tao.

“So do I,” said Yu Jie, and started crying again, and Tao Tao put an arm round her and didn’t say anything, and they sat on the floor under the graph-paper calendar while the rain went on outside.

A hundred and seven squares to the gold one. And then the new row, going on past the edge of the paper, onto the wall, that she had drawn after the stairwell.

Not a pearl.

She looked at it.

Then she wiped her face, and got up, and went to her desk, and took out a pad of paper, and started to write a list. It was a very short list. It had only two things on it.

1. Give the money back. Myself. Not him.

2. Tell them no.

chapters.title: Two Weeks of Not Speaking
chapters.desc: Wednesdays are empty. He keeps the door open anyway. Fang Hao eats for two. Somewhere in the basement, a water tank is waiting.
chapters.epigraph: “It’s 5:30. She’s not coming.” “I know.” “Then why are you still sitting here?” “Because she might.”
chapters.content:
On the first Wednesday, he was in the glass seminar room at 3:30.

He didn’t know why. She had said don’t come. He had said all right. There was no reason for him to be there. Professor Zhou’s rule said Wednesday afternoons with a third person present, physics only, door open. It did not say anything about Wednesday afternoons with nobody.

He went anyway. He sat at the long white table with the door open and a stack of second-year homework in front of him and a cup of jasmine tea that he had made in the fourth-floor kitchen, in a white mug, out of habit. The white mug. Not his.

He realised what he had done when he put it down on the table. He looked at it for a long time.

At 3:44, Fang Hao came in with a paper bag of croissants and stopped in the doorway.

He looked at Miles. At the empty chair across the table. At the white mug of jasmine tea in front of it.

He didn’t say anything. He sat down at the far end, as usual, with his feet up on a chair, and opened the paper bag, and took out a croissant, and ate it very slowly.

At 3:45, the corridor outside the glass walls was empty.

At 4:00, it was still empty.

At 5:30, Fang Hao said, very gently, “It’s half past five. She’s not coming.”

“I know,” said Miles.

“Then why are you still sitting here?”

Miles looked at the open door.

“Because she might,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t.

He went home at six. He poured the cold jasmine tea down the sink in the fourth-floor kitchen and washed the white mug and put it back on the rack. Dr. Ren Bo was in the kitchen, and saw, and said nothing, and left very quickly.

He rode home the straight way.

At his one table, he took out a sheet of graph paper and wrote at the top: Wednesday 11 March.

Then he wrote her a letter.

He didn’t mean to send it. He knew as he wrote it that he wouldn’t. It was the kind of letter you wrote because if you didn’t, the words would sit in your chest all night and you wouldn’t be able to breathe around them.

I went to the glass room today. I know you said not to come. I didn’t go to see you. I went because it’s Wednesday, and since September Wednesdays have been the shape of my week, and I didn’t know what else to do with the shape.

I made you tea. I didn’t mean to. My hands did it.

Bai Tianyu asked yesterday whether, if time only goes forward because of entropy, it would be possible to go back if you tidied everything up perfectly. I said in principle, yes, but you’d have to tidy every single atom in the universe, including the ones in your own brain, and you wouldn’t remember that you’d done it. He said that was the saddest thing he had ever heard. I think he might be right.

I keep thinking about the stairwell. Your hand on the step next to mine. A finger’s width.

I’m sorry. I’ll keep saying it. I don’t know how many times you need to hear it. I don’t mind. I’ll say it as many times as it takes.

He folded it in half. He put it in the drawer of his one table, the drawer where he kept nothing important.

There was nothing else in it. There had been, until January: a purple pen with a plastic cat on the end. He had given it back to her. He wished, now, that he hadn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the basement of the east wing, the water tank arrived on Friday.

He had forgotten it was coming. He had ordered it in the two days before the glass room, when he had been happy, from a firm across the harbour that built tanks for fluid dynamics labs and had one sitting in its warehouse. It was four metres long and made of thick clear acrylic, and it came on a lorry with two men and a forklift and a great deal of shouting, and it took them three hours to get it down the basement ramp.

He stood in the empty storage room among the broken chairs and watched them put it against the north wall, exactly where he had imagined it with the torch.

When they had gone, he stood in front of it alone.

It was beautiful. Clear and empty and very long, catching the light from the bare bulb in the ceiling. When it was filled with water and the pumps were running, you would be able to make the water run faster and faster over a smooth hump on the bottom, until at the top of it the current ran faster than the little waves on the surface could swim against it, and they couldn’t get back upstream. A horizon. An edge past which nothing came back. A black hole, made of water, on a table in front of you.

He had wanted to build one since he was nine.

He put his hand flat on the cold clear side of the tank.

The laboratory was for the boy who wanted to make light bend in a water tank. I thought you’d be happy.

He was happy. That was the worst part. He stood in the basement with his hand on the tank and he was so happy it hurt, and it was hers, and she wasn’t speaking to him, and he didn’t know what to do with any of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Professor Gao summoned him to the balcony on Monday.

She didn’t say hello. She lit a cigarette and looked at the car park and said:

“She’s working in my lab. Fourteen hours a day. She sleeps on the sofa in my office three nights a week. She has finished the corners for hexagons and the corners for triangles and has started on a general theory of corners that may, if she is right, be the most important thing anybody in my group has done in ten years.” She smoked. “She has not laughed once. She has not eaten anything I’ve seen except White Rabbit sweets. Her roommate came to my office on Friday and shouted at me for twenty minutes about her not sleeping, and I let her, because she was right.”

Miles held on to the railing.

“She told me not to come,” he said.

“I know.”

“I’m doing what she asked.”

“I know,” said Professor Gao. “I’m not telling you to go to her. If you go to her when she has asked you not to, I will push you off this balcony myself.” She tapped ash over the edge. “I’m telling you so that you know. Because I think you’ve been sitting in that glass room every Wednesday imagining that she’s fine, and I want you to stop imagining that.”

“I wasn’t imagining she was fine,” said Miles quietly. “I was imagining she was worse.”

Professor Gao turned and looked at him.

At the shadows under his eyes. At the jumper he had slept in again. At the way he was holding the railing.

“You’re not eating either,” she said.

“I eat a sandwich.”

“An egg sandwich. At 12:30. Every day.” Professor Gao’s mouth went thin. “Fang Hao says you’ve started leaving half of it.” She smoked for a while. “You two are the most ridiculous people I have ever met, and I have met physicists who believe the moon landings were filmed in a basement.”

“Which basement?”

“Wei.”

“Sorry.”

She looked out at the car park.

“She asked me something on Friday,” she said. “At two in the morning, in my office, when she thought I’d gone home. I hadn’t. I came back for my glasses. She was sitting at my desk with the light off and she didn’t see me. She was on the phone.” Professor Gao paused. “She asked someone for an appointment. With her father. At his office. Alone.”

Miles went still.

“She said, I need to see him myself. Not my mother. Not my brother. Him. Tell him it’s about his mother’s money.”

Miles said nothing for a long time.

“The sofa in your office,” he said finally. “Is it warm?”

Professor Gao looked at him. “It’s a university sofa, Wei. It was bought in 1994. It is not warm.”

He nodded, as if he were recording a result.

The next morning at 7:40, before anyone else was in the building, there was a carrier bag outside the door of Professor Gao’s lab. Inside it was a grey blanket, folded into a very precise square, and no note. Professor Gao looked at it for a long time. She suspected it was the only blanket he owned. It smelled faintly of chalk.

She put it on the sofa and said nothing to anyone.

That night she stayed late on purpose. At two in the morning she stood in the dark doorway of her own office and saw her best student asleep on the 1994 sofa, the grey blanket pulled up to her chin and her face turned into it, as if she knew exactly whose it was.

In the staff flat, with the heating broken again, Miles slept under his coat.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the second Wednesday, he was in the glass seminar room at 3:30 again.

He did not make her tea. He made himself not do it. He stood in the fourth-floor kitchen holding the white mug for a long moment and then put it back on the rack and made his own, in WORLD’S OKAYEST SON, and carried it downstairs.

Fang Hao came at 3:44 with two paper bags instead of one.

“I’m eating for two,” he said. “Somebody has to.”

He put the second bag down in front of Miles. Inside was an egg sandwich, made with proper bread from Fang Hao’s wife’s bakery, cut into triangles, and a tub of peeled orange segments.

Miles looked at it.

“My wife made it,” said Fang Hao. “She says if you don’t eat it she’ll come here herself, and she’s much more frightening than Gao. She once threw a rolling pin at a health inspector.”

Miles ate the sandwich.

He ate the orange segments. Somebody had picked off every bit of the pith.

“Did your wife do the oranges too?” he said.

Fang Hao looked at him.

“No,” he said. “Those came in a tub on the pastry counter yesterday morning, with a note that said for the fourth floor. No name. My wife said a girl in a yellow raincoat left it at seven a.m. and ran away before anyone could ask.”

Miles put down the last segment.

He sat at the long white table with the glass walls and the open door and the empty chair, and put his face in his hands.

“She’s angry with me,” he said into his hands.

“Yes.”

“And she peeled me an orange.”

“Yes,” said Fang Hao. “Both of those things are true.” He ate a croissant thoughtfully. “I’ve been married nine years, Miles. Let me tell you something. The anger is about what you said. The orange is about who you are. She can be angry with what you said for as long as she likes. She’s still peeling oranges for who you are.”

Miles looked up.

“Is that true?” he said. “Is that how it works?”

“I have no idea,” said Fang Hao. “I’m a theorist. But it sounded good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t come.

At 5:30, Fang Hao packed up and went home to his wife. At six, Miles was still there. At half past six, the cleaners came, and looked at him, and cleaned round him.

At ten to seven, he got up.

He went to the whiteboard. He found a marker pen that still worked. And in the bottom right-hand corner, next to 20 June, 16:00, which had been there for five weeks now, he wrote something very small:

Still here.

Then he went down to the basement.

The tank was waiting against the north wall, clear and empty, four metres long. He had not filled it. He had not ordered the pumps. He had not hired the postdocs or the PhD student or bought the cameras. He had told Professor Zhou to wait.

He stood in front of it in the light of the bare bulb.

“I don’t know if I can keep you,” he said to the tank.

His voice echoed in the empty basement.

“You’re the most beautiful thing anyone has ever given me. And I don’t know if I can keep you.” He put his hand flat on the cold acrylic. “Because it’s not my choice. She was right about that. It’s hers.”

He stood there.

Then he went upstairs, and got his bicycle, and rode home the straight way, and wrote the second letter he would not send:

Wednesday 18 March. I wrote “still here” on the whiteboard. I don’t know if you’ll see it. I don’t know if you’ll go in there. But if you do. I am.

He put it in the drawer with the first.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the third floor of the Hall of Science, at eight o’clock the next morning, Shen Yu Jie walked past the glass seminar room on her way to Professor Gao’s lab, as she had walked past it every day for two weeks, without looking in.

She looked in.

She didn’t mean to. Her eyes went sideways on their own, the way they always went to him across a ballroom.

The room was empty. The long white table. The chairs. The whiteboard, with its grey ghosts of every diagram ever drawn there and wiped away.

And in the bottom right-hand corner, in small neat letters she would have known anywhere:

20 June, 16:00.

Still here.

She stopped in the corridor.

She stood there for a long time, holding her bag against her chest, looking through the glass at those two small words.

Then she took her phone out of her pocket. She opened her calendar. She found an appointment she had made at two o’clock in the morning nearly two weeks ago, in Professor Gao’s dark office.

Friday 20 March. 10:00. Shen Holdings, 40th floor. Father.

She looked at it.

She looked back at the whiteboard.

Still here.

“Okay,” said Shen Yu Jie, under her breath, to nobody. “Okay.”

She went to the lab. She worked for fourteen hours. She did not sleep on Professor Gao’s sofa that night. She went home, and ate a whole bowl of noodles that Tao Tao made her, and slept for nine hours, and on Friday morning she put on a dark blue dress, and took all the pens out of her hair, and put them back in again, all four, and went to see her father.

chapters.title: Yu Jie Gives the Money Back
chapters.desc: The fortieth floor of the Shen Building, alone, with four pens in her hair. Her father has never once asked her about an equation. Today, he asks.
chapters.epigraph: “Your grandmother said you would come here one day and ask me for something. She said I should listen.” — Shen Guoqiang
chapters.content:
The Shen Building had forty floors, and her father’s office was on the fortieth, and she had been there exactly three times in her life.

Once at six, for a photograph for a magazine, in a white dress, sitting on his knee. Once at fourteen, for her grandmother’s eightieth birthday lunch, in the private dining room. Once at eighteen, when she had been accepted to read physics at City University instead of economics at the university her mother had chosen, and her father had called her in, and looked at her across his desk for a long time, and said, “Your mother is very upset,” and nothing else, and sent her home.

She went up in the glass lift at 9:52 on Friday morning, alone.

The lift was on the outside of the building. As it rose, the city fell away beneath her: the harbour, the ships, the old city wall where she had walked the long way in December, the roofs of the university on the hill. She could see the Hall of Science from here. A small grey block among the trees.

She thought about a whiteboard with two words in the corner.

The lift doors opened.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father’s secretary was a woman called Madam Kong, who had worked for the Shen family for thirty years and had once, when Yu Jie was nine, given her a biscuit from her desk drawer and told her not to tell her mother.

She stood up when Yu Jie came out of the lift.

“Miss Shen,” she said. She looked at the dark blue dress, and then at the four pens in the claw clip, and something moved at the corner of her mouth. “He’s waiting for you. He cleared his morning.”

Yu Jie stopped.

“He cleared his morning?”

“Yes.” Madam Kong came round her desk. “He has never cleared his morning for anyone. Not the Minister of Commerce. Not your mother.” She paused at the tall double doors. “He told me to say, if you asked, that he has been expecting you for four years.”

She opened the doors.

✦ ✦ ✦

Shen Guoqiang was standing at the window.

His office was the size of her apartment, mostly glass, with the whole city spread out below it like a map. There was a long dark desk with nothing on it except a closed laptop and a single file. There was a sofa that nobody had ever sat on. There was a painting on the one wall that wasn’t glass, of mountains in mist, that she recognised: it had hung in her grandmother’s house, in the kitchen, above the stove, where she had set things on fire every Sunday.

She hadn’t known he’d kept it.

He turned round.

He was sixty-two, tall and silver-haired and expressionless, in a dark suit. He had never once in her life shouted at her. He had never once in her life hugged her. He had never once in her life asked her about a single equation. At dinner, he looked at his phone. At galas, he talked to men about money. At New Year, he gave her a red envelope with exactly the same amount in it as he gave her brother, and said “study hard,” and went to take a call.

He looked at her now, standing in the doorway of his office in a dark blue dress with four pens in her hair.

“Sit down, Yu Jie,” he said.

She didn’t sit down.

“I came about Grandmother’s money,” she said.

“I know.” He gestured to the file on his desk. “My lawyers told me in January. The trust. The Bending Light Foundation.” His face didn’t change at all. “Four million, two hundred thousand. All of it.”

She went cold.

“You knew,” she said.

“Of course I knew. The lawyers who manage your grandmother’s estate are mine. When you moved the money, they told me within a day.” He looked at her across the long dark desk. “I didn’t tell your mother.”

She stared at him.

“Why not?”

He didn’t answer. He turned and looked out of the window for a while.

“Sit down,” he said again, more quietly. “Please.”

She sat down.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I want to give it back,” she said. “The money. I want to dissolve the foundation and give it back to the trust. I want to do it myself. Not through your lawyers. Not through Mother. Me.” She held her hands together in her lap so that they wouldn’t shake. “And I want it done before the fourteenth of April. Before the university council meets.”

Her father turned from the window.

“Why?”

She had prepared for this. She had prepared for days, at two in the morning, in Professor Gao’s dark office. She had a speech. It was logical and calm and had three parts.

She opened her mouth, and the speech didn’t come.

“Because I didn’t ask him,” she said instead.

Her father waited.

“There’s a lecturer,” said Yu Jie. “At the university. Dr. Miles Wei. You met him at the gala. You won’t remember. He was by the food.” She swallowed. “Mother has been writing to the Vice-Chancellor, to stop him getting a permanent post. Because of a photograph. Because he gave me his jacket when I was cold. Because he wrote an honest letter to his head of department saying that nothing had happened between us, and nothing would, while I was his student.” Her voice wavered. “And I found out, and I was so angry, and so frightened, that I took Grandmother’s money and put it in front of him like a wall. So she couldn’t touch him.”

Her father’s face didn’t move.

“Is he kind to you?” said Shen Guoqiang.

It was so unexpected that she laughed, a small cracked sound.

“He walked me home from the gala the long way,” she said. “Along the old wall. Because it was flatter, for my shoes. He said it was the optimal route.” She looked at her hands. “It took forty-one minutes. He counted.”

Her father was silent for a moment.

“Your grandfather,” he said, “never once in fifty years noticed what shoes my mother was wearing.”

“And he was angry,” said Yu Jie. “Because I didn’t ask him. Because I decided what he needed and arranged it with lawyers, in secret, the way—” She stopped. She made herself say it. “The way Mother does. The way this family does. Deciding what people are for.”

She looked at her hands.

“He was wrong about some of it,” she said. “He said I was like her. I’m not. But he was right about the asking. I didn’t ask. And if I let it stand, then every single thing he does for the next five years, people will say the Shen girl paid for that. And he’ll never know, himself, whether he got it because he’s brilliant or because of me.” She looked up. “He is brilliant. He’s the most brilliant person I’ve ever met. He deserves to know it. He deserves to get his job because of what he is. Not because I bought him a wall.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father was silent.

Then he did something she had never seen him do. He came round from behind his long dark desk, and sat down on the sofa that nobody ever sat on, across from her chair, so that they were at the same height.

He looked at her.

“If you take the money back,” he said, “your mother may still win. The council may still refuse his post. He may lose his job.”

“I know.”

“And you’ll have nothing. Your mother’s allowance. Your mother’s apartment. Your mother’s clothes. Nothing of your own.”

“I know.”

“And you want to do it anyway.”

“Yes,” said Yu Jie.

Her father looked at her for a long time with his expressionless face.

“Your grandmother,” he said finally, “said you would come here one day and ask me for something.”

She went still.

“She said it at her eightieth birthday. The lunch, in the private dining room. You were fourteen. You’d set fire to a napkin with a candle, trying to show your cousin something about oxygen, and your mother sent you to the bathroom in disgrace.” Something moved at the very corner of his mouth. “And while you were gone, your grandmother leaned over to me and said, That one is going to come to your office one day and ask you for something, Guoqiang. When she does, you will listen. You didn’t listen to me when you were her age, and look what you became.”

Yu Jie couldn’t speak.

“I didn’t know what she meant,” said her father. “I thought she was being sentimental. She was eighty.” He looked at the painting on the wall, the mountains in mist. “Then she died, and left you the money, not me, not your brother, and the will said the money was for you to use for whatever you want to be. And the lawyers asked me whether I wanted to contest it. And I said no.”

He looked back at her.

“And then in January, when you moved it, all of it, to fund a laboratory for a young physicist your mother was trying to destroy—” He stopped. “I sat in this office and read the purpose clause that you made the lawyer rewrite. A scientist who takes students’ questions seriously. And I thought about my mother saying, Look what you became.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“What did you want to be?” said Yu Jie.

It came out before she could stop it. She had never in her life asked her father a question like that.

He looked at her in surprise. Then, for the first time she could remember, he smiled. It was very small and very tired and it changed his whole face.

“An engineer,” he said. “Bridges. I wanted to build bridges. I had a place at the university to study it. My father said no. Shen Holdings needed a son. So I went into shipping.” He looked out of the window, at the harbour, at the long grey bridge across it that she had driven over a thousand times without thinking. “I build very good ships. I’ve never built a single bridge.”

She had not known. Twenty-two years, and she had not known.

“Grandmother bought me a chemistry set,” she said quietly. “When Mother threw the first one away.”

“I know,” said her father. “I paid for the second one. Your grandmother told me to. She said, If you won’t do it yourself, at least give me the money.” He looked down at his hands. “It was the only thing I ever did. Paying for it. I never once went to her kitchen on Sunday to watch you set things on fire.” His voice was very level. “I should have.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They sat in silence for a while. Forty floors above the city.

Then her father stood up, and went to his desk, and opened the single file, and took out a document and a pen.

“The dissolution of the foundation,” he said. “My lawyers drew it up in January. In case.” He held it out to her. “It returns the money to your grandmother’s trust, in your name. It needs only your signature. Nobody needs to know it was ever moved, except the university, and Professor Zhou has already said he will be discreet.”

She stared at him.

“You drew this up in January?”

“I thought you might come,” said her father. “Your grandmother said you would.”

She took the pen. Her hand was shaking. She signed it anyway. S.Y.J. Small and round and quick.

He took it back, and looked at the signature for a moment, and put it in the file.

“Your mother,” he said, without looking up, “has written two letters to the Vice-Chancellor. On Shen Foundation paper. With my name at the top.”

Yu Jie held her breath.

“I can’t stop your mother,” said Shen Guoqiang. “Nobody has ever stopped your mother. I married her thirty-six years ago, and I have never once won an argument with her.” He closed the file. “But I can stop her using my name to do it. And I can write to the Vice-Chancellor myself, this afternoon, to say that the Shen Foundation has no view whatsoever on the employment of any member of the university’s staff, and never will, and that any letter suggesting otherwise was sent without my knowledge.”

He looked at her.

“After that,” he said, “your lecturer will have to get his job by being brilliant. If he is as brilliant as you say, he will.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She stood up.

She didn’t know what to do. She had never known what to do with her father. She stood in front of him in the dark blue dress with four pens in her hair, forty floors above the city, and didn’t know whether she was allowed to cry.

“Thank you,” she said.

“Don’t thank me.” He turned back to the window. “I’ve done nothing. I should have done it four years ago. Twenty-two years ago.” He was quiet for a moment. “Is there anything else?”

She thought about it.

She thought about the second thing on her list, written at her desk the night of the rain. Tell them no.

“Yes,” she said. “But not to you. To Mother. And the Lus.” She lifted her chin. “I’m not going to marry Lu Zhiyuan. Not in June. Not ever.”

Her father didn’t turn round.

“I know,” he said.

“You know?”

“Lu Zhiyuan came to see me,” said her father, to the window. “Three weeks ago. Privately. He sat in that chair and told me, very politely, that he had the greatest respect for my daughter, and that he would not be marrying her, and why.” A pause. “He is a very brave young man. Braver than I was at his age. His father doesn’t know.”

Yu Jie put her hand over her mouth.

“Tell your mother,” said Shen Guoqiang. “Not me. I won’t take her side.” He paused, and then said, very quietly, still to the window, so that she almost didn’t hear it: “I won’t take yours either, in front of her. I’m not brave enough for that. I’m sorry. But I won’t take hers.”

It was the most he had ever said to her in one morning in twenty-two years.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the doors, she stopped and looked back.

Her father was still standing at the window, looking down at the harbour, at the long grey bridge across the water. His back was very straight.

“Father,” she said.

He turned his head.

“The tank,” she said. “At the university. In the basement. He’s already got it. The money bought it, before I took it back. It’s four metres long and made of clear acrylic and when it’s filled with water and the pumps are on, it makes a horizon, like a black hole. An edge where the waves can’t get back.” She paused. “It’s a kind of bridge. Between the maths and the real thing. Between what you can write on a board and what you can see.”

Her father looked at her.

“Will he keep it?” he said.

“I don’t know. It’s his choice.”

Something moved in her father’s expressionless face.

“Good,” said Shen Guoqiang. “Let it be his.”

She went out. The doors closed behind her.

Madam Kong was at her desk. She looked at Yu Jie’s face. Then she opened her desk drawer, and took out a biscuit, and held it out without a word.

Yu Jie took it.

She ate it in the glass lift on the way down, forty floors, with the whole city rising up to meet her, crying and laughing at the same time, with crumbs on her dark blue dress.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 4:15 that afternoon, Professor Zhou walked into the glass seminar room on the third floor and found Miles at the whiteboard, alone, on a Friday, looking at the two small words in the bottom right-hand corner.

“The Bending Light Foundation,” said Professor Zhou, “was dissolved at eleven o’clock this morning. By its settlor. In person.”

Miles turned round very slowly.

“The money has gone back to the trust it came from,” said Professor Zhou. “The equipment already purchased remains the property of the department. That includes, I’m told, a four-metre acrylic tank currently in the basement of the east wing.” He paused. “At two o’clock, the Vice-Chancellor received a letter from Shen Guoqiang personally, stating that the Shen Foundation has no view on any staff appointment. Your review will go ahead on the fourteenth of April. On your record. Nothing else.”

Miles didn’t say anything.

“You may lose,” said Professor Zhou. “I don’t think you will. But you may. I want you to know that.”

“I know,” said Miles.

“And I was asked to give you this.”

He held out a yellow sticky note. Miles took it.

It was in small round handwriting. A little uneven, as if written in a moving lift.

I asked my father. Not you. I should have asked you in January. I’m asking now.

The tank is yours. Keep it or don’t. Your choice.

Still angry. Still peeling oranges.

Professor Zhou watched the youngest lecturer in his department read a sticky note four times, standing at a whiteboard on a Friday afternoon, and then sit down very suddenly on the edge of the long white table, as if his legs had made a decision without him.

He read it a fifth time. Then he looked up at Professor Zhou with an expression Professor Zhou had never seen on a member of staff in thirty-four years: helpless, dazzled, and entirely unprofessional.

“She’s still peeling oranges,” said Miles, as if reporting a result.

Professor Zhou considered this.

“I gather,” he said, “that is good.”

“It’s the best data I’ve had in sixteen days.” He held the note very carefully by its edges, so as not to smudge the ink. “She asked. She asked me.” He swallowed. “Nobody ever asks.”

“Professor Zhou,” said Miles, after a long time.

“Yes?”

“I’d like to keep the tank,” said Miles. “And I’d like to find a way to pay for the rest of it myself.”

Professor Zhou smiled. It was the first time Miles had ever seen him do it.

“Good,” he said. “Write the proposal. I’ll sign it.” He went to the door. “And Miles. Ask about the boundary conditions. The funding council always does.”

chapters.title: The Perfect Jewel Says No
chapters.desc: Sunday dinner at the museum, with the Lus, a seating plan for two hundred, and a sample of engagement silk. She puts down her chopsticks. Then the diplomat puts down his.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m not a jewel, Mother. I’m a physicist. You can’t wear me.”
chapters.content:
Sunday dinner was at seven.

It was always at seven. It had been at seven every Sunday of her life, in the big dining room of the house on the hill that Tao Tao called the museum, because of the glass cabinets and the Ming vases and the fact that you weren’t allowed to touch anything.

This Sunday, the twenty-second of March, the Lus came too.

They came at half past six, all three of them, and her mother met them at the door in pale blue silk, glowing. There were flowers on every surface. White peonies, out of season, flown in. On the long dining table, beside each place setting, there was a small square of heavy ivory silk, embroidered with a gold pattern of entwined letters: an S, and an L.

“Samples,” said her mother, smiling round the table as they sat. “For the invitations. I thought we could choose tonight. Two hundred guests. The last Saturday of June. Here, in the garden.” She touched the silk beside her own plate. “I’ve already spoken to the florist.”

Lu Zhiyuan’s mother picked up her square of silk with trembling fingers and looked at it as if it were the most beautiful thing she had ever seen.

Lu Zhiyuan, beside Yu Jie, very correct, at exactly the right distance, did not look at his.

Under the table, his phone was dark.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had not slept.

She had lain awake in her old canopy bed in the house on the hill, where her mother had insisted she stay on Saturday night so that we can talk about the dress, and looked at the dolls in their glass cases, and thought about Friday. About her father on the sofa nobody sat on, saying I won’t take hers. About a yellow sticky note in a lift.

About a whiteboard. Still here.

At four in the morning she had texted Lu Zhiyuan: tomorrow. at dinner. i’m going to tell them.

He had replied at once, as if he had been awake too.

I know. Your father told me. I’ll be there.

Then, a minute later:

Jie. Whatever happens at that table, you won’t be the only one saying no.

She had read it six times. She didn’t know what it meant. She was too afraid to ask.

She had typed a message to Miles, too. Four times. tomorrow at dinner i’m going to and then nothing, because there was no way to end the sentence that didn’t ask him for something, and she had promised herself she would do this one thing without asking anyone. She had deleted it four times. The fifth time she had typed only are you awake, and looked at it, and deleted that too.

Then she had lain in the canopy bed with the phone face down on her chest, over her heart, as if it could hear, and thought about a man in a grey cardigan who would, she knew perfectly well, have been awake.

✦ ✦ ✦

They got through the soup.

They got through the cold plates, the phoenix, and the steamed fish, which nobody turned over. They got through her mother describing the marquee, and the string quartet, and the cake, which would be seven tiers, from a patissier in Shanghai. They got through Lu Zhiyuan’s father asking her father about the new container terminal, and her father answering in one word at a time, and her brother looking at his phone.

They got to the silk.

“Now,” said her mother, picking up her sample. “Yu Jie, darling. Which do you prefer? The gold thread, or the silver? I think gold. Gold is warmer. Zhiyuan, what do you—”

Yu Jie put down her chopsticks.

She put them down very carefully, side by side on the rest, the way she had been taught to at four years old, so that they made no sound at all.

The table didn’t notice. Her mother was still talking about thread.

She put her hands in her lap. They were shaking. She held them together.

Professor Zhou will ask about the boundary conditions. When he does, I want you to smile.

She didn’t smile.

“Mother,” she said. “I’m not going to marry Lu Zhiyuan.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The table went silent.

Not all at once. In a wave, the way a room went silent in a seminar when someone stood up in the second row. Her mother stopped first, with the silk in her hand. Then Lu Zhiyuan’s mother, her fingers frozen on the gold thread. Then his father, mid-sentence about the container terminal. Then her brother, who actually looked up from his phone.

Her father did not stop, because he had not been speaking. He was looking at his plate.

“Darling,” said her mother pleasantly. “What did you say?”

“I said I’m not going to marry Lu Zhiyuan.” Her voice was very steady. She was surprised by how steady it was. “Not in June. Not in the garden. Not ever. I’m sorry, Auntie Lu.” She looked across the table at Lu Zhiyuan’s mother, who had gone pale. “I’m very sorry. It isn’t because of anything he’s done. He’s been kinder to me than anyone at any party I’ve ever been to. But I don’t love him, and he doesn’t love me, and I won’t marry a man I don’t love so that two hundred people can look at a silk invitation.”

Her mother was still smiling. The smile had not moved at all.

“Yu Jie,” she said softly. “You’re tired. You’ve been working too hard on your little thesis. You’re not yourself.”

“I am myself,” said Yu Jie. “For the first time in twenty-two years, I think I am completely myself.”

She looked at her mother across the table, across the peonies flown in out of season.

“I’m not going to stop physics,” she said. “Not after graduation. Not ever. I’m going to do a doctorate. I’m going to do research. I’m going to stand at chalkboards and get chalk dust on my clothes and be wrong in front of famous people and work out how electrons move along the edges of things that nobody has ever thought about before.” Her voice shook at last. “I’m not going to Geneva. I’m not going to be worn. I’m not a jewel, Mother.”

She took a breath.

“I’m a physicist. You can’t wear me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Nobody moved.

Across the table, Lu Zhiyuan’s mother had put the square of silk down very slowly, as if it had become heavy. His father was looking at Shen Ruolan with an expression of polite, freezing displeasure: the face of a diplomat watching a treaty fall apart.

Her brother said, “Oh, for God’s sake, Jie,” and put his phone down on the table with a clatter.

Her mother still did not stop smiling.

She turned to Lu Zhiyuan.

“Zhiyuan,” she said, very sweetly. “I’m so sorry. She’s overwrought. She’s been under a great deal of strain, with her examinations. And there’s been some—unpleasantness, at the university. A man who took advantage of her—”

“No one took advantage of her,” said Lu Zhiyuan.

His voice was perfectly calm. His reception voice. It cut across the table like a knife through silk.

Shen Ruolan stopped.

“Forgive me, Auntie,” said Lu Zhiyuan. “I don’t mean to contradict you at your own table. But I’ve met the man you mean. I sat in his office for half an hour. I’ve never met anyone less capable of taking advantage of anyone. He wrote a letter to his head of department declaring everything he felt, so that she would never be blamed for any of it.” He looked at Shen Ruolan with his calm, tired eyes. “He’s the most honourable man I’ve met in this city. And I would like that to be said, at this table, out loud, at least once.”

His father said, “Zhiyuan,” very quietly. A warning.

Lu Zhiyuan didn’t look at him.

He put down his own chopsticks. Side by side on the rest. No sound.

“And Yu Jie isn’t the only one saying no tonight,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Jie turned and stared at him.

He was sitting very straight beside her, at exactly the right distance, in a perfect grey suit. His face was calm. His hands were flat on the white tablecloth on either side of his plate. They were very slightly trembling.

She understood, suddenly, what his text had meant at four in the morning. You won’t be the only one saying no.

“Zhiyuan,” she whispered. “You don’t have to.”

“I know,” he said, without looking at her. “That’s why I’m going to.”

He looked across the table. Not at her mother. At his own parents. His father, stiff and grey and furious. His mother, pale, her hand still on the square of ivory silk.

“Mother,” said Lu Zhiyuan. “Father. I’m not going to marry Yu Jie. And I’m not going to marry anyone you find for me after her. I should have told you this six years ago. I was a coward. I was afraid of exactly this: this table, these faces, this silence.” His voice was quiet and very clear. “I’m in love with someone. I have been for six years. I can’t marry him, in this country. But I won’t marry anyone else.”

The silence that followed was the loudest thing Yu Jie had ever heard.

“His name is Kai,” said Lu Zhiyuan. “He’s a translator. He lives in a flat above a shoe shop on Wen Street and he makes terrible coffee. He’s the best person I know.” He looked at his mother. “I’m sorry I didn’t tell you. I’m not sorry about him.”

✦ ✦ ✦

His father stood up.

He did it slowly. Very correctly. He pushed his chair back without scraping it on the floor. He folded his napkin and put it on the table beside his plate. He did not look at his son.

“Ruolan,” he said. “Guoqiang. Thank you for dinner. Please excuse us.”

He walked out of the dining room. His footsteps went down the long marble corridor toward the front door, past the glass cabinets, without hurrying, and the front door opened, and closed.

Nobody at the table breathed.

Lu Zhiyuan sat very straight, looking at his plate. His hands on the tablecloth had stopped trembling. They were perfectly still now, the way things are still after they break.

His mother did not stand up.

She sat across the table from her son with her hand on the square of ivory silk and looked at him for a long, long time. Her eyes were full.

Then she let go of the silk. She reached across the table, past the peonies, past the cold fish that nobody had turned over, and put her hand on top of her son’s hand on the tablecloth.

She didn’t say anything. She didn’t need to.

Lu Zhiyuan looked down at her hand on his.

And the perfect diplomat, who had sat through a thousand receptions in a dozen countries without letting his face move once, put his other hand over his eyes.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Well,” said Shen Ruolan.

Her voice was perfectly pleasant. Perfectly calm. Her smile had not moved at all through any of it.
