She put down her square of ivory silk with the gold thread. She put it down very precisely, squared to the edge of the table.

“Yu Ming,” she said. “Please see Auntie Lu and Zhiyuan to the door.”

Her brother stood up at once. Lu Zhiyuan’s mother rose, still holding her son’s hand. Lu Zhiyuan stood beside her. At the door of the dining room, he stopped and looked back at Yu Jie.

Are you all right? said his face.

She nodded. Very slightly.

He went.

Then it was just the three of them. Her mother, her father, her. And the peonies, and the cold fish, and two hundred silk invitations that would never be sent.

Her mother turned to her.

“You have humiliated me,” said Shen Ruolan, in the same pleasant voice, “in front of a family whose friendship this family has cultivated for twenty years. You have made me look like a fool. You have made me look like a mother who cannot control her own child.” She smiled. “And you have done it for a man who eats egg sandwiches in an office with a cactus.”

“I didn’t do it for him,” said Yu Jie. “I did it for me.”

“Did you,” said her mother.

She stood up. She came round the table, the way she had at New Year, and stood beside her daughter’s chair, and looked down at her.

“I made you,” said Shen Ruolan softly. “Everything you are. The way you walk. The way you sit. The way you smile at a man you don’t like so that he never knows. The languages. The piano. The posture. The clothes on your back, the apartment you live in, the food you eat, the university you chose against my wishes. The allowance that pays for your White Rabbit sweets and your terrible shoes.” Her voice didn’t rise at all. “I made you. And I paid for you. Every single thing.”

She bent closer. Her perfume was very cold.

“If you leave this table tonight and do not marry the man I chose,” she said, “then you will do it without any of it. Do you understand? Not one thing. Not one yuan. You will find out what you are without me.”

Yu Jie looked up at her.

At the perfect face. The perfect smile. The diamonds.

Across the table, her father was looking at his plate. He had not moved. He had not spoken. He had not taken her mother’s side.

He had not taken hers either. He had said he wouldn’t. He had told her he wasn’t brave enough. She had believed him.

She stood up.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stood up from the table without scraping her chair, the way she had been taught.

She looked at her mother, very close, at eye level.

“I know what I am without you,” she said. “I found out on the second Wednesday of September, at 3:47 in the afternoon. I’m a physicist.” She picked up her bag from the back of the chair. “And I’m not afraid of you any more.”

It wasn’t true. She was terrified. Her legs were shaking so badly she could barely stand. Her heart was going so fast she could hear it.

But she said it, and her voice didn’t shake, and her mother’s smile, for the first time in twenty-two years, moved.

Only a little. Only at one corner. But it moved.

Yu Jie walked to the dining-room door.

“Yu Jie,” said her father.

She stopped. She didn’t turn round.

He didn’t say anything else for a long moment. She could feel him behind her, at the long table, with the peonies and the cold fish and her mother standing very still beside the empty chair.

“Your grandmother,” said Shen Guoqiang finally, very quietly, “would have been very proud.”

That was all.

Her mother turned and looked at her husband across the table as if she had never seen him before.

Yu Jie walked out.

✦ ✦ ✦

She walked down the long marble corridor past the glass cabinets. Past the small sitting room, where the single pearl sat on its silver stand under its own little light. She didn’t look in.

She walked out of the front door. Down the steps. Down the long drive, between the trimmed hedges, to the gates.

Lu Zhiyuan was standing outside them, under the streetlamp. Alone. His mother had gone home in the car. His father had gone ahead. He was standing on the pavement in his perfect grey suit with his hands in his pockets, looking at nothing.

He looked up when she came out.

They stood and looked at each other under the streetlamp, outside the gates of the museum.

“Well,” said Lu Zhiyuan. His voice was rough. “That went exactly as badly as I expected.”

“Your mother held your hand.”

“She did.” He looked away. His eyes were wet. “I didn’t expect that. I’ve spent six years planning for every possible outcome of that conversation, and I didn’t once plan for that.”

“Your father—”

“Will not speak to me for a very long time,” said Lu Zhiyuan. “Possibly ever. I knew that too.” He took a long breath. “And Kai is going to be furious that I did it without telling him first. And then he’s going to make me terrible coffee and not say anything for three hours, which is how he forgives people.” He looked at her. “And you?”

“I’m cut off,” said Yu Jie. “Everything. Tomorrow, probably. She said I’d find out what I am without her.”

Lu Zhiyuan looked at her under the streetlamp.

“And what are you?” he said.

She thought about it. Properly. The way she had learned to, on Wednesdays.

“Frightened,” she said. “And free.”

He laughed. Rough and wet and real.

Then he held out his arms, and she walked into them, and the two of them stood on the pavement outside the gates of the Shen house under the streetlamp and held on to each other like two people who had just jumped off the same cliff and found, to their astonishment, that they could both still breathe.

“Thank you,” she said into his perfect grey shoulder. “For not making me be the only one.”

“Thank you,” said Lu Zhiyuan, “for making me brave enough.”

chapters.title: Cut Off
chapters.desc: The bank card fails at the canteen. A letter from the family office. Seven days to leave. She packs one suitcase, and finds out what she owns.
chapters.epigraph: “Insufficient funds.” — card reader, City University canteen, Monday, 12:41 p.m.
chapters.content:
The card failed at the canteen on Monday at 12:41.

She was buying congee. A small bowl, with pickles, eleven yuan, the same thing she had bought most Mondays for four years. The woman at the till, who knew her, smiled and held out the card reader. Yu Jie tapped her card.

The reader beeped. A red light.

Insufficient funds.

The woman frowned and said, “Try again, love, it does that,” and Yu Jie tried again, and it did it again, and the queue behind her shifted, and somebody sighed.

She stood there with the tray in her hands and the red light on the reader and understood, very calmly, that it had begun.

“I’m sorry,” she said to the woman. “I’ll put it back.”

“Don’t be silly.” The woman waved her hand. “Pay me tomorrow.”

“I don’t think I can pay you tomorrow,” said Yu Jie.

She put the congee back on the counter. She walked out of the canteen. She stood outside in the March sunshine with her bag on her shoulder and eleven yuan of nothing in her hands, and laughed, because she didn’t know what else to do, and two first-years walking past looked at her as if she were mad.

✦ ✦ ✦

The letter was waiting at the apartment when she got home.

It was on the mat inside the blue door, in a heavy cream envelope with the Shen crest in dark red wax. Not from her mother. From the family office, which managed the family’s property: the buildings, the cars, the apartments in good areas where the children of the family lived while they were at university.

Dear Miss Shen,

We write on behalf of the owners of Flat 6A, 14 East Gate Road, to inform you that your licence to occupy the property has been withdrawn with effect from today’s date. You are requested to vacate the property, with your personal belongings, no later than 5 p.m. on Monday 30 March.

Furniture, fittings, and household items belonging to the owners must remain in the property.

We would be grateful if you would leave the keys with the building’s security.

Yours faithfully,

And a signature she didn’t recognise.

She read it standing in the hallway, with her bag still on her shoulder.

Seven days.

She went into the kitchen, and sat down at the table, and put the letter in front of her, and looked at it for a very long time.

✦ ✦ ✦

Tao Tao came home at six and found her still sitting there.

She read the letter over Yu Jie’s shoulder. She read it twice. Then she said a word that Yu Jie had never heard her say before, a word from her grandmother’s village, which meant something very bad about someone’s ancestors.

“Seven days,” said Tao Tao. “Seven days? After four years? She can’t—”

“She can. It’s her flat. It always was.” Yu Jie looked round the kitchen. At the good knives, the expensive coffee machine, the copper saucepans nobody used. “I knew that. I always knew it. I just never thought about it.”

Tao Tao sat down across from her.

“Then I’ll find us somewhere,” she said fiercely. “Somewhere else. A flat. A room. I’ve got my scholarship. It’s not much, but—”

“Tao Tao.” Yu Jie looked at her. “Your scholarship pays for your tuition and your books and your share of nothing, because you never paid rent here, because it was my mother’s flat. You send half your stipend home to your grandmother. I know you do. I’ve seen you do it.” She reached across the table and took her friend’s hand. “You can’t pay for both of us. I won’t let you.”

Tao Tao’s fierce small face crumpled.

“Then where will you go?”

Yu Jie didn’t answer.

She didn’t know.

✦ ✦ ✦

She made a list that night. She was good at lists.

Things I own.

She sat on her bedroom floor and went through the room, and the wardrobe, and the drawers, and the bathroom, and wrote down everything that was hers. Not bought by her mother. Not chosen by her mother. Not paid for with her mother’s money.

It took her forty minutes. The list was very short.

1. Laptop. (Bought with prize money, first-year physics prize. Mine.)

2. Notebooks. Eleven. Everything since first year.

3. Calendar. Graph paper. Atoms.

4. One yellow sundress. (Bought at the night market for forty yuan, second year. Mother has never seen it.)

5. Grey cardigan. (Tao Tao’s grandmother knitted it. She said it was a present.)

6. Trainers. Biro on them.

7. Pens. All of them.

8. A napkin. A box with a wall. Dots.

9. A brown envelope. 212 notes.

10. Sticky notes. Yellow. All of his.

11. A red envelope with 20 yuan in it, from Tao Tao’s grandmother.

12. A purple pen with a cat on it.

She stopped there.

She looked at the list. Then at the room. The wardrobe full of silk. The jewellery box. The dawn-coloured dress from the gala, hanging in its plastic cover. The Italian shoes. The perfume bottles on the dresser, each one a birthday. Twenty-two years of birthdays.

None of it was hers.

She sat on the floor with the list on her knee and thought: twelve things. Twenty-two years, and I own twelve things.

And then, slowly, she thought: But I chose every one of them.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t tell Miles.

Tao Tao wanted her to. Tao Tao said it at breakfast on Tuesday, and at dinner on Tuesday, and again on Wednesday morning, very loudly, while Yu Jie was trying to drink her coffee.

“Tell him. He’d help. You know he would. He’d—”

“He’d find a way to pay for it,” said Yu Jie. “Or he’d offer me his flat. Or he’d go and stand outside my mother’s house in the rain. And then there’d be another photograph, and another forum, and his review is in twenty days.” She put down her cup. “And I said I was angry with him. I am angry with him. I don’t want him to come and save me because he feels guilty.”

“That isn’t why he’d come.”

“I know,” said Yu Jie quietly. “That’s the other reason I can’t tell him.”

Tao Tao looked at her for a long time.

“You’re as bad as he is,” she said.

“I know.”

She didn’t go to the glass room on Wednesday. Not because she was still angry, although she was, a little. Because she was afraid that if she sat at that long white table across from him, three metres away, with Fang Hao eating croissants at the end, he would look at her the way he always looked at her—as if he could see everything—and see this too.

She walked past the glass room at 3:45 on her way to the lab. She didn’t look in.

She heard, as she passed, his voice. Talking to Fang Hao. Low, about something to do with pumps.

She kept walking. She didn’t stop. But she had seen, in the corner of her eye, through the glass, without meaning to: the white mug at her place at the long table. Full. Steaming. With something small and yellow stuck to the side of it.

He had made her tea. On a Wednesday when she hadn’t come, he had made her tea anyway and written her a note, and was talking to Fang Hao about pumps as if it weren’t there.

She didn’t let herself go back and read it. Her eyes stung all the way to the second floor.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday, Lu Zhiyuan offered her his sofa.

He called at nine in the evening. He sounded tired but steady.

“It’s not a very good sofa,” he said. “It’s in Kai’s flat, above the shoe shop. I’ve been staying there since Sunday. My father had my things sent over from the house in boxes.” A pause. “Kai says you’re welcome. He says it in a very grumpy voice, which means he means it. He also says the shoe shop opens at seven and the owner plays opera very loudly while he unpacks deliveries.”

She sat on her bedroom floor and closed her eyes.

“Thank you,” she said. “Thank you. But you’ve only just—you two need—”

“We need nothing,” said Lu Zhiyuan, “except to not see you on the street.”

“I won’t be on the street. I’ll go to Professor Gao’s sofa. She already lets me sleep there three nights a week.”

“Jie.”

“I’ll be fine,” said Yu Jie. “I promise.”

There was a long pause on the line.

“You’re talking about the weather,” said Lu Zhiyuan gently.

She put her hand over her mouth.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday night, she packed.

One suitcase. It was Tao Tao’s, old and blue, with a broken wheel, from the year she came to the city on the train with her grandmother. Yu Jie’s own suitcases were leather, and monogrammed, and belonged to the family office.

She packed the twelve things.

The laptop. The eleven notebooks, wrapped in the grey cardigan. The yellow sundress, folded small. The trainers. All the pens, in a pencil case. The napkin, flat between two pages of the thickest notebook. The brown envelope. The sticky notes in a plastic bag, all of his, yellow. The red envelope with twenty yuan. The purple pen with the cat on it, in her claw clip, in her hair.

And the calendar.

She took it down from the wall last. She did it carefully, peeling the tape off slowly so the paper wouldn’t tear. Two hundred and sixty-six squares of graph paper, and then the new row she had drawn after the stairwell, going off the edge onto the wall. She had to leave that part. It was drawn on the wall in pencil. She looked at it. Not a pearl.

She rolled the calendar up very carefully and put it in the suitcase on top of everything else.

There was room left over. A lot of room.

She closed the suitcase anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday, the thirtieth of March, at 4:30 in the afternoon, she gave her keys to Old Huang.

He took them in his little lit-up box. He looked at them in his hand. Then at her, standing in front of the blue door in jeans and the grey cardigan and her trainers with biro on them, with a battered blue suitcase with a broken wheel.

“Miss Shen,” he said. “Where will you go?”

“I have a sofa,” she said. “In my supervisor’s office. She says I can stay as long as I need.”

Old Huang looked at her.

“A sofa,” he said.

“It’s a very good sofa,” said Yu Jie. “It’s leather. Professor Gao says it’s older than me. She says it once survived a fire.”

Old Huang didn’t say anything.

Then he reached under the counter of his little box and took out a plastic bag. Inside were six steamed buns, still warm, wrapped in a tea towel.

“My wife made too many,” he said gruffly.

She looked at them. Then at him.

She had walked past Old Huang every day for four years. She had said good morning and good evening and thank you. She had never once asked him his wife’s name.

“What’s her name?” she said. “Your wife.”

“Lin Ping,” said Old Huang, surprised.

“Please tell Lin Ping thank you,” said Yu Jie, “from me.”

She took the buns.

Tao Tao was waiting by the gate with her own bag; she was going to her cousin’s in the east of the city, two hours on the bus. They had said goodbye three times already, upstairs, and both cried, and promised to see each other every day at the university, which they would. Tao Tao hugged her one more time, very hard, and said into her shoulder, “If you don’t tell him, I will,” and Yu Jie said, “Don’t you dare,” and Tao Tao said, “Watch me,” and went to catch her bus.

Yu Jie stood outside the blue door, alone, with a blue suitcase and a bag of buns.

Then she turned toward the university, up the road, past the east gate, toward the Hall of Science on the hill. It was a kilometre. The suitcase had a broken wheel. She would have to drag it.

She started walking.

✦ ✦ ✦

She got as far as the convenience shop on the corner.

The one with the bright windows, where a boy buying instant noodles had once taken a photograph through the glass.

She stopped there, because the broken wheel had come off completely and was rolling away down the pavement.

She watched it go. It rolled down the hill, wobbling, all the way to the bottom, and into a drain, and was gone.

She stood on the corner with a suitcase that wouldn’t roll and a bag of buns and looked at the drain.

And then, because there was nobody to see, and because it had been a week since the canteen and she had not cried once, not at the letter, not at the list, not at the twelve things, not at taking the calendar off the wall—she sat down on the suitcase, on the corner, by the bright shop window, in the cold, and cried.

She cried for the room she had lived in for four years. For the twelve things. For her grandmother. For her father at the long table, saying She would have been very proud, and not getting up. For her mother’s smile moving, just at one corner. For Lu Zhiyuan’s mother’s hand on his.

She cried the way she had not let herself cry since she was small: with her whole body, bent over the bag of buns in her lap, her shoulders jerking, her breath coming in ugly, hiccupping gulps that hurt her ribs. The suitcase was hard and cold under her. The buns were still warm through the plastic, and somehow that was the worst thing of all, that a woman whose name she had only just learned had made them warm for her, and she held them against her stomach like a hot-water bottle and cried until her nose ran and her eyes swelled shut and the bright shop window behind her turned into a smear of white light.

People walked past. A woman with shopping. A boy on a scooter. A man on his phone, who stepped round her as if she were a bin. Nobody stopped.

Then somebody did.

✦ ✦ ✦

She heard the bicycle first. An old bicycle, with a squeaking chain. It came down the road from the university, slowly, and stopped at the corner.

She didn’t look up.

The bicycle was leaned against the lamppost, very carefully. Footsteps came across the pavement. Not close. They stopped about three metres away.

Then nothing. Just waiting.

She looked up.

Miles was standing on the corner, by the lamppost, in his grey cardigan and his old coat, with his glasses slightly crooked and his hair sticking up at the back and his face completely white.

“Tao Tao,” he said, before she could ask. “She came to my office at three o’clock. She shouted at me for eleven minutes. Fang Hao timed it. She said you were being stupid and noble, and that you’d rather sleep on a sofa that survived a fire than tell me, and that if I let you do it, she’d bite me.” He swallowed. “She said the suitcase had a broken wheel.”

Yu Jie looked down at the suitcase.

“It’s in the drain,” she said. “The wheel.”

“Ah,” said Miles.

He looked at the suitcase. At her, sitting on it, in the grey cardigan, with her face wet and a bag of steamed buns in her lap.

He didn’t come any closer.

He unwound the scarf from his neck instead. It was grey, and old, and had been knitted by his mother in a year when she believed he would grow into a wider man. He folded it once, the way you would fold a letter, and laid it over the handle of the suitcase, at the very end, where it stuck up beside her shoulder. Then he stepped back to exactly where he had been.

“It’s March,” he said. “You’re sitting on a pavement. The pavement is approximately four degrees.”

She looked at the scarf. She didn’t touch it.

“I’m not cold,” she said.

“Your hands are shaking.”

“That isn’t the cold.”

“I know,” said Miles. “Put it on anyway. Please. I’ll stand here and be unbearable until you do.”

She put it on. It smelled of chalk, and jasmine tea, and the inside of office 412. She pulled it up over her mouth so that he wouldn’t see what her face did.

“I’m not going to ask if you’re all right,” he said. “Because you’re not. And I’m not going to offer you my flat, because I know you’ll say no, and you’d be right to. And I’m not going to say anything about your mother, because if I start I won’t be able to stop, and some of the words are ones my sister uses.”

She laughed. Wet and shaky.

“Then what are you going to do?” she said.

Miles looked at her.

“I’m going to carry your suitcase,” he said. “If you’ll let me. Because it doesn’t have a wheel any more, and it’s a kilometre up the hill, and you have buns.” He paused. “And then I’m going to take you somewhere. It isn’t my flat. It isn’t a sofa. It’s a room. With a door and a window and a bed and a lock. I found it this afternoon, in the forty minutes after Tao Tao left. It’s yours if you want it. You don’t have to say yes.” His voice was very quiet. “I’m asking. This time I’m asking first.”

She looked up at him on the corner by the bright shop window, three metres away, in the cold.

This time I’m asking first.

She was still angry with him. A little.

She stood up.

“Yes,” said Shen Yu Jie.

chapters.title: Miles Finds Her a Room
chapters.desc: Not his. A slanted attic above a bakery on Bell Street, a landlady who once threw a rolling pin at a health inspector, and bread at four in the morning. He carries the suitcase, and doesn’t go in.
chapters.epigraph: “Rent is two hundred a month and four mornings a week on the counter. Fair is fair. Nobody in my house lives on charity.” — Su Mei, baker
chapters.content:
He couldn’t carry the suitcase and push the bicycle at the same time, so he put the suitcase on the bicycle.

He balanced it on the saddle, sideways, and held it there with one hand, and pushed the bicycle with the other hand on the handlebars, and walked. It wobbled. It wobbled a great deal. Twice on the way down the hill it nearly fell off, and twice he caught it, and the second time he caught it he also caught the bicycle, and himself, and a lamppost, all at once, and stood there with his arms full of everything, breathing hard.

Yu Jie walked beside him with the bag of buns.

Three metres away. Then two. By the bottom of the hill, without either of them noticing, one and a half.

“Where are we going?” she said.

“Bell Street,” said Miles. “By the old wall. Near where we—” He stopped. “Near the park.”

“Near where we walked the long way.”

“Yes,” said Miles, to the suitcase.

She didn’t say anything. But she walked a little closer.

The suitcase lurched. He caught it.

“You’re going to drop it,” she said.

“I’m not going to drop it.”

“You’ve nearly dropped it twice.”

“Three times,” said Miles, to the suitcase. “You didn’t see the third. I recovered very quickly.” He adjusted his grip. “It’s a stable system. It just doesn’t know that yet.”

She made a small sound that might have been a laugh. It was the first one in a week that didn’t hurt.

✦ ✦ ✦

The bakery on Bell Street was called Fang’s, in red letters on a white sign, and it was closed, because it was six o’clock on a Monday evening, and bakers go to bed early.

But the lights were on. And the door opened before Miles had finished leaning his bicycle against the wall, and a woman came out who was nearly as tall as he was and twice as wide, in a flour-covered apron over a black T-shirt, with her hair tied up in a red scarf and her arms folded.

She looked at Miles. At the bicycle. At the battered blue suitcase balanced on the saddle with no wheel.

Then she looked at Yu Jie.

She looked for a long time. Up and down. At the grey cardigan and the biro trainers and the pens in the claw clip and the red eyes and the bag of buns.

“So you’re the orange girl,” said the woman.

Yu Jie opened her mouth. Nothing came out.

“The tub of oranges on my pastry counter,” said the woman. “Seven a.m., two weeks ago. Every bit of pith off. You ran away in a yellow raincoat before I could ask your name.” She unfolded her arms. “I’m Su Mei. I’m married to the croissant man. He told me everything at dinner, at length, with diagrams. I made him stop at the diagrams.”

She came down the step and took the suitcase off the bicycle with one hand as if it weighed nothing.

“Come in,” said Su Mei. “You look like a girl who hasn’t eaten. And you—” she looked at Miles, “—look like a man who forgot his umbrella in March.”

“It isn’t raining,” said Miles.

“You look like you forgot it anyway,” said Su Mei, and went inside.

✦ ✦ ✦

The room was at the top of the house, up three flights of narrow wooden stairs that creaked on every step.

It was small. The ceiling sloped down on one side, so steeply that you could only stand up straight in half of it. There was a single bed against the low wall, made up with a patchwork quilt. A small desk under the window. A wooden chair. A wardrobe with a door that didn’t quite shut. A sink in the corner. A radiator painted white, which ticked.

And the window. A round window, like a ship’s porthole, that looked out over the rooftops of Bell Street, and the dark line of the old city wall, and beyond it the bare trees of the park, and far away, lit up at the top of the hill, the Hall of Science.

Yu Jie stood in the doorway and looked at it.

“My mother lived up here,” said Su Mei, behind her, “for eleven years, until she died. Then it was storage. Then the croissant man cleared it this afternoon in forty minutes, after your physicist turned up at the shop at half past three looking like a ghost and asked me if I had a room.” She put the suitcase down on the floor. “He didn’t even say hello. He just said, Su Mei, do you have a room with a door and a lock, and how much is it.”

Yu Jie looked back down the narrow stairs.

Miles was standing on the landing below. He had not come up the last flight. He was standing at the bottom of it, one hand on the banister, looking up at the doorway, at her, and not coming any closer.

“How much is it?” said Yu Jie.

Su Mei looked at her.

“Rent is two hundred a month,” she said. “And four mornings a week on the counter. Five to nine. Saturday, Sunday, and two weekdays when you don’t have lectures. I pay you for the counter. You pay me rent out of what I pay you.” She folded her arms. “Fair is fair. Nobody in my house lives on charity. My mother didn’t, I don’t, and you won’t.”

Yu Jie stared at her.

“You’re paying me,” she said.

“For work. Yes.”

“A wage.”

“Twenty an hour. It’s what I pay everyone.” Su Mei looked at her sharply. “Have you never had a job, girl?”

“No,” said Yu Jie.

She had never had a job. She had never had a wage. She had never had a single yuan in her life that had not come from her mother, except the physics prize and a red envelope with twenty yuan in it from Tao Tao’s grandmother.

Twenty an hour.

Something came up in her chest that she didn’t have a name for.

“I’ll take it,” she said. “I’ll take it. Thank you. I’ll be very good at the counter. I’m very good at counting. I can do the change in my head. I can—”

“I know,” said Su Mei. “The croissant man told me. He said you can do quantum mechanics in your head and that you make his friend laugh.” She looked down the stairs at Miles on the landing. “He said that was the most important part.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Su Mei went down to make dinner. She went past Miles on the landing and said something to him very quietly that made him go red to his collar, and then she was gone, and the stairs creaked all the way to the bottom.

Yu Jie stood in the doorway of the attic room.

Miles stood on the landing, at the bottom of the last flight.

Eight steps between them. Narrow wooden ones, worn in the middle.

“You’re not coming up,” she said.

“No.”

“Because of the rule.”

“Because it’s your room,” said Miles. “You haven’t asked me in.” He looked up at her. “And because of the rule. Both.”

She looked at him.

Then she went into the room and put the bag of buns on the desk and knelt down by the suitcase and opened it.

She heard him on the stairs. He came up three steps. Then stopped. Then five more. He stopped at the top step, just outside the door, on the landing, with one hand on the frame.

He didn’t come in.

She took out the calendar.

She unrolled it carefully on the bed, and smoothed it flat with her hands. Two hundred and sixty-six squares. Purple atoms in all of them, up to today. A gold one at the end.

Beside the squares for some of the days, very small, there were other drawings. He could see them from the doorway. A box with a wall down the middle and dots. A tub. An orange. A lamp, three lamps, a long curved line along the bottom of the square. A tiny chalkboard with a mark in the corner.

He stood in the doorway and looked at them.

“You drew the long way,” he said.

“I drew all of it,” said Yu Jie, without looking up. “Every day that something happened. I’m a scientist. I keep records.”

She stood up. She looked round the slanting room for somewhere to put the calendar. The low wall over the bed was sloped. The wall by the desk had a window in it. The only straight wall was beside the door.

She went to it. She held the calendar up against it, at eye level. Right beside the doorframe. Right beside his hand.

“Hold this,” she said.

He held it. Flat against the wall with both palms. She found tape in the pencil case and taped the corners, one, two, three, four. Her hands were very close to his. Close enough to feel the warmth coming off his knuckles through the cold paper, close enough to see the chalk in the creases of his fingers. At the third corner her thumb came within a millimetre of his little finger, and he stopped breathing, and so did she, and neither of them closed the last millimetre. Neither of them said anything. When she had taped the fourth corner, he took his hands away.

She looked at the calendar on the wall.

Then she took a pencil, and after the gold square at the end, she drew a line. And another square. And another. A new row, going off the edge of the paper and onto the plaster wall of Su Mei’s mother’s attic.

In the first new square, the twenty-first of June, very small, she wrote again:

Not a pearl.

He looked at it.

“Not a pearl,” he said quietly.

“I wrote it on the wall at the old flat, too,” said Yu Jie. “After the stairwell. I had to leave it there. It was on the wall.” She put the pencil down. “I didn’t want to start here without it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She sat down on the bed under the low sloping ceiling. He stayed in the doorway.

“I saw the whiteboard,” she said. “In the glass room. Still here.”

He went very still.

“I didn’t know if you’d go in,” he said.

“I didn’t go in. I walked past. I saw it through the glass.” She looked at her hands. “I walked past every day for two weeks without looking. And then one day I looked, and you’d written that.” She swallowed. “I went to see my father the next morning.”

Miles was silent.

“I’m sorry,” he said. “For what I said. I keep saying it.”

“I know. Tao Tao says you’ve said it eleven times. Fang Hao told her. He keeps a tally.” She looked up at him. “You don’t have to say it any more.”

“I want to.”

“I know. But you don’t have to.” She looked at him in the doorway, with one hand on the frame, in his grey cardigan, with his glasses crooked. “I’m still a little angry. Not about the money. About what you said. Being angry about that is going to take a bit longer.” She took a breath. “But I’m not angry with you. Do you understand the difference?”

He thought about it, properly.

“The anger is about what I said,” he said slowly. “The oranges are about who I am.”

She stared at him.

“Who told you that?”

“Fang Hao,” said Miles. “He said it as if it were a theorem. Then he admitted he had no idea if it was true.”

She laughed. She put her face in her hands and laughed and cried at the same time, sitting on the patchwork quilt in the slanting room, and he stood in the doorway and didn’t come in, and didn’t go away.

“It’s true,” she said, muffled. “It’s true, it’s true, I hate that it’s true.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She held out a bun.

One of Lin Ping’s steamed buns, from the bag on the desk. She held it out to him across the room. Her arm wasn’t long enough. She had to get up, and walk to the door, and hold it out to him there, on the threshold, him on the landing, her in the room, the doorframe between them.

He took it.

They ate the buns standing either side of the doorframe. Him on the landing. Her inside. Pork and cabbage, still faintly warm. Neither of them said anything for a while.

He finished his in four bites.

She watched him. Then she held out a second one across the threshold.

“I’ve had one,” said Miles.

“When did you last eat? Before that one.”

He thought about it. Properly. She watched him do it, and saw the exact moment he realised he didn’t know.

“Breakfast,” he said, without conviction.

“What did you have?”

“…An egg.”

“Your one egg,” said Yu Jie. “Eat the bun, Dr. Wei.”

He ate the bun. She watched him eat all of it, with her arms folded on her side of the doorframe, exactly like Su Mei, and when he had finished she nodded once, satisfied, and he went red to his collar and didn’t know why.

From downstairs came the smell of dinner, and Fang Hao’s voice saying something about croissants, and Su Mei’s voice telling him to be quiet.

“Old Huang’s wife made these,” said Yu Jie. “Lin Ping. I never knew her name before today.”

“They’re very good.”

“I know.” She looked at the bun in her hand. “I walked past him every day for four years. I never once asked. And today when I asked, he looked so surprised.” She was quiet for a moment. “There are a lot of things I never asked about. Living in that flat. I’m going to ask about them now.”

Miles looked at her across the threshold.

“You’ll be very good at it,” he said. “You ask the best questions of anyone I’ve ever met.”

She looked at him for a long time over the half-eaten bun.

Then she said, very softly:

“Eighty-two squares.”

He knew exactly what she meant.

“Eighty-two,” he agreed.

✦ ✦ ✦

He went home at nine.

He didn’t go home. He went to the Hall of Science, and down to the basement under the east wing, with his torch, and stood in front of the long clear tank against the north wall.

He had not done anything with it. Not since the glass room. He had not ordered the pumps or the cameras or the laser. He had not filled it.

He found a hose in the cleaner’s cupboard. He connected it to the tap in the corner of the basement, where the old storage room still had a sink. He put the other end in the tank.

He turned the tap on.

It took two hours. He sat on a broken chair from 1997 and watched it fill, slowly, the water rising up the clear acrylic sides in the torchlight, the bare bulb in the ceiling reflected in it, wobbling, getting steadier as the tank got fuller.

There were no pumps. No flow. No horizon. Just a long clear tank full of still water in the dark.

But when it was full, he turned off the tap and shone the torch into it from one end, low, along the length of the tank, and the beam went through the water and came out the other side and hit the far wall, slightly lower than it went in. Bent. Just a little. The way light bends whenever it goes from one thing into another.

Not a black hole. Not yet. Just light, going through water, and bending.

He sat on the broken chair and looked at it for a long time.

At 11:20 his phone buzzed. A message.

Not from her. From an unknown number.

Dr. Wei. This is Su Mei. She’s asleep. She ate two bowls of noodles and a piece of the cake I made for tomorrow that I told her not to touch. She put a calendar on my mother’s wall and wrote something on it in pencil that I won’t tell you because it isn’t mine to tell. She’s starting on the counter on Saturday at five. I’ll teach her the till.

She asked me before she went to sleep if you were all right. I told her you were a grown man and could look after yourself. She said, “He can’t, though. He only has one egg.”

Buy more eggs.

Miles read it three times in the basement, by the light of the torch and the long tank of still water.

Then he typed back: Thank you. I will.

And then, after a long moment: Please tell her I filled the tank.

✦ ✦ ✦

His review was on the fourteenth of April.

He was not allowed to attend. The university council met in the old council chamber in the administration building, under portraits of dead vice-chancellors, and went through forty-one staff reviews in one afternoon, one after another, and he was number twenty-seven.

He spent the afternoon in the basement. The pumps had come. He had ordered them with his own small research budget, the one every lecturer got, which would not pay for much else. He was on his back under the tank with a spanner, connecting them, when his phone rang at 4:52.

It was Professor Zhou.

“Twenty-seven,” said Professor Zhou. “Wei, Miles. Lecturer, Department of Physics. Recommendation of the department: permanent appointment.” A pause. “There was a question from one member of the council. She asked whether a lecturer who had declared a personal interest in a student should be considered. Very politely.”

Miles lay on his back under the tank with the spanner on his chest and didn’t breathe.

“Professor Gao answered,” said Professor Zhou. “She stood up, which you are not supposed to do at council. She said that in twenty years she had never seen a member of staff behave with more integrity under more pressure than you had, and that if the council was going to punish people for being honest, she would like it minuted so she could read it out at her retirement dinner.” Another pause. “Then a second member of the council spoke. Shen Guoqiang. He doesn’t usually attend. He said that the Shen Foundation had no view on the matter, and that he personally had no view on it either, except that he had read your paper on lensing in galaxy clusters, and had not understood it, and thought that was probably a good sign.”

Miles put his hand over his eyes, under the tank.

“The vote was nineteen to one,” said Professor Zhou. “Congratulations, Dr. Wei. You’re permanent. You’re stuck with us.”

“Thank you,” said Miles. His voice didn’t work properly. “Thank you.”

“Don’t thank me. I didn’t stand up. I’m much too old to stand up at council.” A pause. “Meiling’s gone to the balcony. She’s smoking two at once.”

He hung up.

Miles lay on his back under the four-metre tank of still water, looking up through the clear acrylic at the bare bulb in the ceiling, wobbling through the water.

Then he took out his phone and sent one message, to Su Mei’s number, because he didn’t have any other way.

Please tell her: permanent. Nineteen to one. Her father came.

The reply came in four minutes. Not from Su Mei. Typed on Su Mei’s phone, but not in Su Mei’s voice.

I know. Gao called me first. I’m helping Su Mei with tomorrow’s dough, I’m not supposed to have my phone, she’s pretending not to see.

My father came.

Sixty-seven squares.

(I’m still a little angry.)

(I’m so happy I dropped a tray of egg tarts.)

chapters.title: The Thesis Defence
chapters.desc: Nearly three hours in room 301, with an external examiner from the capital who has a score to settle. Miles waits in the corridor and doesn’t sit down.
chapters.epigraph: “Miss Shen. Tell me about your boundary conditions.” — Professor Zhou Lin, 10:47 a.m.
chapters.content:
The thesis defence was on the fifteenth of May, at ten in the morning, in room 301.

Room 301 was on the third floor, at the other end of the corridor from the glass seminar room. It was small and wood-panelled, with a long table, four chairs on one side for the examiners and one on the other for the candidate, a projector, and a blackboard. A real one. Chalk. Professor Zhou had insisted on it in 1994 and nobody had dared to change it since.

The examiners were four. Professor Gao, supervisor. Professor Zhou, internal. Dr. Fang Hao, internal, replacing Dr. Wei. And the external examiner, who was always a professor from another university, appointed by the faculty to make sure the department wasn’t being too kind to its own students.

The faculty had appointed him in March, from a shortlist of three.

Professor Huang Zhenhai. From the capital.

The man with slide nineteen.

✦ ✦ ✦

“He asked for it,” said Fang Hao, on the Monday before, in the glass seminar room. “Huang. He asked the faculty specifically. He said he had a particular interest in the candidate’s work.” He put down his croissant. “That’s academic for I want blood.”

Miles was at the whiteboard. He didn’t turn round.

“She’ll be fine,” he said.

“He’s the most famous person in her field in the country. He’s on every grant committee. He’s on the editorial board of the journal she wants to publish in. And she corrected him in front of thirty people and then made a joke about it that went round three universities.” Fang Hao looked at him. “He has not forgotten my gap doesn’t close, Miles.”

“She’ll be fine,” said Miles again.

He said it very calmly. He was drawing a diagram of a pump.

His hand was shaking so badly the line came out wavy.

✦ ✦ ✦

He arrived at 9:20.

He wasn’t supposed to be there. He had withdrawn from the panel. He had no reason to be on the third floor at all. He told himself he was going to the glass seminar room to work, and walked down the corridor toward it, and walked past it, and kept walking, and stopped at the other end, outside room 301, where there was a window and a noticeboard and nothing else.

He stood by the window.

At 9:40 Professor Gao came up the stairs, in a black jacket instead of her lab coat, which Miles had never once seen her wear. She stopped when she saw him.

She looked at him for a long moment.

She didn’t say anything. She nodded once and went into room 301.

At 9:45, Fang Hao came, with no croissant, which was alarming. He squeezed Miles’s shoulder as he went past.

At 9:50, Professor Zhou, in his cardigan, with his reading glasses in his pocket. He looked at Miles by the window and raised his eyebrows very slightly and went in.

At 9:52, Professor Huang came up the stairs.

He was exactly as he had been in December: tall, silver-haired, beautifully dressed, with a leather folder under his arm and the air of a man who was used to rooms going quiet when he walked into them. He saw Miles by the window, and stopped.

“Dr. Wei,” he said.

“Professor Huang.”

“I was told you had withdrawn from this panel.”

“I have,” said Miles. “I’m standing in a corridor.”

Professor Huang looked at him for a moment with an expression Miles couldn’t read. Then he looked at the door of room 301.

“I read her thesis,” he said. “Twice. On the train, and again last night in the hotel.” He paused. “The section on corners. Chapter three.”

Miles said nothing.

“I spent eleven years on that problem,” said Professor Huang, “and never once thought about corners.”

He went into room 301. The door closed.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 9:57, she came up the stairs.

She was in a dark grey suit. Not her mother’s. Su Mei had taken her to a shop near the harbour on Saturday afternoon, after the counter, and stood over her while she tried things on, and paid for half of it, and refused to discuss the other half. Her hair was up in the claw clip. There were four pens in it. One of them was purple, with a plastic cat on the end.

She saw him by the window and stopped at the top of the stairs.

He was standing very straight in his grey cardigan, with his hands at his sides.

They looked at each other down the corridor. About ten metres.

She didn’t come any closer. He didn’t either.

Then he frowned, very slightly. He touched his own collar, on the left side, with one finger, and looked at her.

She looked down. Her collar was folded in on itself on the left, where the stairs had undone Su Mei’s pressing.

She fixed it. He watched her fix it. When it lay flat, he nodded once, gravely, as if she had corrected a sign error, and something in her chest that had been clenched since five in the morning let go a single notch.

But there was nothing either of them could say, here, outside room 301, with four examiners on the other side of the door.

So he held up one hand. Flat. Palm toward her. The way he had put it flat on the cold concrete step in February, a finger’s width from hers.

She looked at it.

Then she held up her own hand, palm toward him, flat. Ten metres apart. In an empty corridor.

Neither of them smiled.

Then she put her hand down, and turned, and knocked on the door of room 301, and a voice said “Come in,” and she went in, and the door closed.

It was 10:00 exactly.

✦ ✦ ✦

He did not sit down.

There was a bench in the corridor, under the noticeboard. He didn’t sit on it. He stood by the window, with his back to the wall, and looked at the door of room 301.

The walls in the Hall of Science were cardboard. Everybody knew that. But room 301 had been built in 2004, when Professor Zhou was head of department for the first time, and Professor Zhou had insisted on two things: a blackboard, and proper walls. Through proper walls, you could hear voices but not words. A low rumble. Someone speaking. A pause. Someone else.

He listened to the rumble.

At 10:20, he recognised her voice. Fast and clear, rising and falling. Presenting. She would be on slide four, or five. The overview.

At 10:31, a man’s voice. Deeper. Slower. Huang. He spoke. Then her voice again, quicker. Then Huang again. Then her. Then a long silence.

Miles realised he was holding his breath, and let it out.

At 10:40, Bai Tianyu came along the corridor with a cup of bubble tea, on his way to the second-year computing lab, and saw Miles standing by the window and stopped.

“Dr. Wei,” he said. “Are you okay? You look like you’re waiting for exam results.”

“I am,” said Miles. “In a way.”

Bai Tianyu looked at the door of room 301. At the sign on it: THESIS DEFENCE IN PROGRESS. DO NOT DISTURB.

He looked back at Miles. His face changed. Slowly. Bai Tianyu, who asked whether gravity was real, was not, it turned out, entirely stupid.

“Oh,” he said.

He didn’t say anything else. He stood beside Miles by the window for a moment, sipping his bubble tea. Then he took a small packet of dried mango out of his backpack and held it out.

“For energy,” he said.

Miles took it.

Bai Tianyu went off to the computing lab. At the corner, he turned round and gave Miles a solemn thumbs-up, and nearly walked into a pillar.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 10:47, through the proper walls, Professor Zhou’s voice.

Miles knew it immediately. Mild. Unhurried. Slightly higher than the others. He couldn’t hear the words. He didn’t have to.

He knew exactly what Professor Zhou was saying, because Professor Zhou always said it. In every seminar for thirty-four years. In every interview. In every defence.

Tell me about your boundary conditions.

There was a pause in room 301.

Miles closed his eyes.

And then, through the proper walls, faintly, something he had not expected to hear.

Laughter.

Not from her. From the room. From several people at once. Fang Hao’s, unmistakable. Professor Gao’s short dry cough of a laugh. And a deeper one, slower, more reluctant, that could only be Huang’s.

Then her voice. Fast and clear and absolutely steady. Going on for a long time.

He didn’t know what she had said. He would find out later. Fang Hao would tell him, that evening, with enormous satisfaction, word for word.

When Professor Zhou had asked about her boundary conditions, Shen Yu Jie had smiled at him across the long table in room 301, exactly as instructed in red ink on page 69, and said:

“I was hoping you’d ask, Professor Zhou. Everybody told me you would. I’ve been looking forward to it since January.” Then, without looking at anyone else: “Can I use the blackboard? I’m better with chalk.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At 11:30, a long silence.

It went on. A minute. Two. He found that he had put his palm flat against the window, that the glass was cold, and that he was pressing hard enough to hurt his wrist. He could feel his own pulse in his fingertips against it. He thought: she has stopped talking. He knew every way a defence could go wrong in a silence; he had sat on panels; he knew them all. He made himself list them, one by one, because a list was something to hold on to.

Three minutes.

Then chalk. Faint, through the proper walls. A long, steady scrape, and a tap, and another scrape.

He took his hand off the glass. It left a print that faded slowly in from the edges.

At 11:45, Huang again. For a very long time. Then her. Then Huang. Then her. Back and forth, fast, like a game of something. Then Fang Hao said something, and everybody laughed again.

At 12:05, silence.

At 12:20, the door opened.

She came out.

She came out alone, as candidates always did, while the examiners stayed behind to decide. She shut the door behind her. She stood in the corridor with her back against it, in her dark grey suit with chalk dust all down the front of it, and four pens in her hair, and her face completely white.

She looked down the corridor at him.

He hadn’t moved from the window. Two hours and twenty minutes. He had not sat down once.

She didn’t say anything. Neither did he.

She walked down the corridor. She stopped two metres away from him. Exactly two metres. She leaned on the wall beside the window.

“I used the blackboard,” she said.

“I heard,” said Miles. “Not the words. The chalk. I could hear the chalk.”

She looked down at the dust on her suit.

“Professor Huang asked me about slide nineteen,” she said. “His slide nineteen. From December. He asked me what I would have done, if I’d been him.” Her voice was very small. “I told him. He took notes.”

Miles closed his eyes.

“He took notes, Miles.”

“I know,” said Miles, with his eyes closed. “I know he did. I know.”

Then he opened his eyes, and put his hand in his cardigan pocket, and took out a White Rabbit sweet. He held it out to her at the full length of his arm.

She stared at it.

“I bought a bag,” said Miles. “On Monday. I’ve had one in my pocket all morning. In case your blood sugar—” He stopped. “In case.”

She took half a step in, and took it from his fingers without touching them, which needed a great deal of care from both of them, and stepped back to exactly two metres. She unwrapped it. She put it in her mouth. A little of the white went out of her face.

“You carried a sweet,” she said, round it, “for two hours and twenty minutes.”

“It was a very long two hours and twenty minutes,” said Miles.

✦ ✦ ✦

They waited.

Side by side by the window. Two metres apart. Not talking. Fifteen minutes, then twenty.

At 12:38, Tao Tao came running up the stairs in a lab coat with a pipette still in her pocket, and stopped dead at the top, and stared at them, and said “Well?” in a whisper that could be heard on the fourth floor.

“They’re deciding,” said Yu Jie.

Tao Tao came and stood on the other side of her, and held her hand very tightly, and glared at the door of room 301 as if she could make it open by force of will.

At 12:44, Lu Zhiyuan came up the stairs in a perfect suit, with a man beside him. A slightly shorter man, in a rumpled jacket, with untidy hair and kind eyes behind thick glasses and a paper cup of coffee in each hand. He handed one to Yu Jie without a word.

“This is Kai,” said Lu Zhiyuan. “He made you coffee. I’m sorry.”

Yu Jie tasted it.

It was the worst coffee she had ever had in her life.

She started to laugh, and couldn’t stop, and Kai looked pleased, and Lu Zhiyuan put his hand over his face.

And Miles, by the window, looked at them all: the fierce small biologist and the diplomat and the translator with the terrible coffee, standing around Shen Yu Jie in a corridor outside room 301, holding her hands and making her laugh. People who had chosen her. Not people she had been born to.

He had never seen her so surrounded.

He stood two metres away and watched, and didn’t come any closer, and was happier than he had been in his whole life.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 12:51, the door of room 301 opened.

Professor Gao came out first.

She looked at the little crowd by the window. At Tao Tao with the pipette and Lu Zhiyuan and the man with the coffee, and at Miles, two metres from the rest, standing very straight. She looked at her student.

She didn’t smile. Professor Gao never smiled.

“Shen Yu Jie,” she said. “Come in. The panel would like to tell you its decision.”

Yu Jie put down the terrible coffee. She let go of Tao Tao’s hand. She went back down the corridor, past the noticeboard, and into room 301, and the door closed again.

It was only closed for four minutes.

Then it opened, and she came out, and she was crying, and behind her in the doorway Fang Hao was grinning so widely his face looked as if it might break, and Professor Zhou was polishing his reading glasses, and Professor Huang was standing at the blackboard looking at the chalk diagrams she had left behind with an expression of a man who had just seen something he would think about for the rest of the year.

“Distinction,” said Professor Gao, to the corridor, in a flat voice that didn’t quite manage to stay flat. “The highest mark this department has given a final-year thesis in twenty-three years. The panel recommends immediate publication of chapter three. The external examiner—” She stopped. She looked back over her shoulder into the room. “The external examiner would like to know whether the candidate has considered a doctorate. In the capital. With him.”

Tao Tao screamed.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the noise afterwards—Tao Tao screaming, Lu Zhiyuan laughing, Kai saying something gentle in a language Miles didn’t know, Fang Hao coming out and shaking everybody’s hand, including, by mistake, a passing cleaner’s—Yu Jie stood in the middle of the corridor in her chalk-covered suit, crying, and looked for him.

He was still by the window. Two metres from everyone.

He hadn’t moved.

She came through the crowd toward him. She stopped two metres away. Then, for a second, one and a half. Then she stopped herself, and stepped back to two.

Thirty-six days.

“Distinction,” she said.

“I heard.”

“Professor Huang wants me in the capital.”

“I heard that too.”

She looked at him, standing very straight by the window in his grey cardigan, with a packet of dried mango in his hand that he had forgotten he was holding.

“You didn’t sit down,” she said. “The whole time. Fang Hao said you didn’t sit down.”

“I couldn’t,” said Miles simply. “You were standing up.”

She made a sound that was half a laugh and half something else.

Then she held up her hand. Flat. Palm toward him. The way she had at ten o’clock.

He held up his.

Two metres apart, in a crowded corridor, two hands. Not touching. A finger’s width, and two metres, and thirty-six days.

Behind her, Professor Gao, who never smiled, looked at the two raised hands across the corridor outside room 301.

And turned away, quickly, toward the window, and took out a cigarette that she was not allowed to smoke in the building, and didn’t light it, and held it, looking out at the trees.

chapters.title: Graduation Day, 4:01 P.M.
chapters.desc: The ceremony ends at four. Eighty-seven steps from the Great Hall to the fourth floor. The first minute she stops being a student in his department.
chapters.epigraph: “It’s open. Unless you’re from facilities.” “I’m not from facilities.” “No. I know.”
chapters.content:
The graduation ceremony for the Faculty of Science was on Saturday the twentieth of June, in the Great Hall, from two o’clock until four.

It said so on the programme. 14:00–16:00. It had said so in September, when she had looked it up on the university website at two in the morning, sitting on her bedroom floor, the night after she had drawn a mark in the bottom right-hand corner of a chalkboard. Ceremony concludes 16:00.

She had built a calendar on it. Two hundred and sixty-six squares.

She woke at five, because Su Mei’s ovens started at four and the whole house smelled of bread, and because she had been waking at five for twelve weeks to stand at the counter. She lay on the narrow bed under the sloping ceiling and looked at the calendar taped to the wall beside the door.

Every square full. A purple atom in each one. Two hundred and sixty-five of them.

And the last one. Gold. Empty.

She lay there and looked at it until the sun came up over the rooftops of Bell Street and shone through the round window onto the wall.

Then she got up and went down to help with the morning bread, because it was Saturday, and Saturdays were hers on the counter, and she was not going to stop being herself just because it was the most important day of her life.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You’re not working today,” said Su Mei, at 5:04, in the doorway of the kitchen, with her arms folded.

“It’s Saturday.”

“It’s your graduation.”

“It doesn’t start until two.”

Su Mei looked at her for a long moment. Then she unfolded her arms and handed her an apron.

“Till,” she said. “Until nine. Then you go upstairs and you have a bath and you put on that dress, and you don’t come down again until Tao Tao arrives with the car.” She paused. “And you eat breakfast. A real one. Not White Rabbit sweets.”

“Yes, Su Mei.”

“And you don’t think about him.”

Yu Jie tied the apron.

“That,” she said, “I can’t promise.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At the Hall of Science, on the fourth floor, the door of office 412 was propped open with Principles of Quantum Mechanics.

It was Saturday. There were no office hours on Saturday. The building was nearly empty, except for one PhD student in the basement checking on a cryostat and a cleaner on the second floor and, in office 412, Dr. Miles Wei, permanent lecturer, who had arrived at 7:15 in the morning and had been sitting at his desk ever since, doing nothing at all.

He had tried to do something. He had brought a paper to referee. He had read the first page six times. He had tried to mark the last of the second-year exam scripts. He had found Bai Tianyu’s, and read his answer to a question about the uncertainty principle, which said we can never really know anything for sure, and that’s okay, and given it full marks, and then wondered whether he was in the right frame of mind to be marking anything.

He had watered Schrödinger. Twice.

At 9:30, Fang Hao came in.

He wasn’t supposed to be there either. He was supposed to be at the bakery, helping Su Mei with the graduation orders. He was carrying a paper bag. He put it on the desk.

“Breakfast,” he said. “From my wife. She says if you don’t eat it, she’ll know.”

Miles looked in the bag. An egg sandwich, on proper bread, cut into triangles. A tub of peeled orange segments, every bit of pith picked off.

“She made the sandwich,” said Fang Hao. “The oranges came from the counter. At six this morning. Somebody in an apron with four pens in her hair peeled them between customers. My wife pretended not to see.”

Miles ate the orange segments one by one.

“What time is it?” he said.

“Nine thirty-two.”

“Six and a half hours.”

“Six hours and twenty-nine minutes,” said Fang Hao. “But who’s counting.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The Great Hall was full.

Four hundred graduates in black gowns with green hoods, for science. Their families in the seats behind them: grandparents in their best clothes, mothers with tissues, fathers with cameras. The university orchestra playing something stately. Banners. Flowers. The Vice-Chancellor on the stage in robes so heavy with gold that he moved like a ship.

Yu Jie sat in the fourth row, between a chemist and a mathematician, in a black gown with a green hood over a yellow sundress.

The yellow sundress. Forty yuan from the night market. The one from the list.

Under her gown, her feet were in her trainers. With biro on them.

In her hair, the claw clip. Four pens. One purple, with a cat.

Behind her, in the family seats, there was a little group of people who were not her family and who were. Tao Tao, in a borrowed dress, with her grandmother beside her, who had come in on the train that morning and was holding a red envelope. Su Mei, enormous and fierce, in her one good blouse, with flour still on one sleeve. Lu Zhiyuan, in a perfect suit, and Kai beside him, in a rumpled one. Old Huang and Lin Ping, who had asked if they could come and been told yes.

And Professor Gao, at the end of the row, in her black jacket, sitting very straight, not smiling.

Her mother had not come.

Yu Jie had known she wouldn’t. She had sent the invitation anyway, by post, to the house on the hill. One ticket. The university gave each graduate four. She had sent one to her mother and one to her father and kept the others for Tao Tao’s grandmother and Su Mei.

She did not look round to see if the seats were empty. She had promised herself she wouldn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

The names took an hour and a half.

One by one, in alphabetical order by department, the graduates went up onto the stage and shook the Vice-Chancellor’s hand and took a scroll and walked off the other side, and their families cheered, and the orchestra played a few notes, and the next name was called.

Physics was ninth. S was near the end.

At 3:41, a voice said into the microphone: “Shen Yu Jie. Bachelor of Science, Physics. First Class, with Distinction. The Departmental Prize for Physics. The Faculty Medal.”

She stood up.

She walked up the steps onto the stage in her gown and her trainers. The Vice-Chancellor shook her hand and gave her the scroll and a small blue box with the medal in it and said something about being very proud. She didn’t hear him.

Behind her, in the family seats, Tao Tao’s grandmother stood up and shouted something in her village dialect that made half the hall turn round. Su Mei whistled through her fingers. Lu Zhiyuan and Kai stood up and clapped. Old Huang stood up. Lin Ping stood up. Professor Gao did not stand up, but she clapped once, very hard, like a gunshot.

And then Yu Jie, crossing the stage, with the scroll in one hand and the blue box in the other, looked out at the hall, because she couldn’t help it.

At the very back. In the last row. By the door.

Alone.

A tall, silver-haired man in a dark suit, standing up, clapping.

Her father.

He didn’t wave. He didn’t smile. He stood at the back of the Great Hall by the door, where nobody would see him, and clapped, slowly, with his expressionless face.

She stopped in the middle of the stage.

He looked at her across four hundred people and gave one small nod.

And then he turned, and opened the door at the back of the hall, and went out, before anybody could see him, before her mother could ever be told.

She walked off the stage. She sat down in the fourth row. The chemist beside her said, “Are you okay? You’re shaking.”

“Yes,” said Yu Jie. “Yes. I’m okay. I’m okay.”

It was 3:44.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the fourth floor of the Hall of Science, Miles had stopped pretending to do anything.

He was standing at the chalkboard.

He had been standing there since 3:30. Fang Hao had gone at three, very quietly, without saying anything, and closed the door of office 413 behind him, and Miles had heard him go down the stairs.

The chalkboard was clean. He had cleaned it that morning, at 7:20. Every equation. Every diagram. Every grey ghost of a calculation from a whole year of Wednesdays.

Everything except one thing.

In the bottom right-hand corner, in small round handwriting that wasn’t his, which had been there since the last week of September and which he had worked around all year like a man stepping round a sleeping cat: 20 June, 16:00.

He had wiped the flat line off in September, the same afternoon she drew the mark. At half past seven this morning, he had drawn it again. The same line, in the same place. Professional distance (constant). Running across the board from the left-hand edge and stopping exactly at her small vertical mark. And after the mark, nothing.

Empty board.

He stood in front of it with a piece of chalk in his hand.

3:52.

He thought about the second Wednesday of September, at 3:47 in the afternoon. A knock on the door. It’s open. Unless you’re from facilities.

He thought about the harmonic oscillator, the long way, twenty-five minutes, with Hermite polynomials. You need a different excuse for coming on a Wednesday.

He thought about a cactus. A sticky note on his tea. A study group of one. Oranges. A seminar room going silent. A terrace, and Elowen asking, Are you happy? A walk along the old wall, the long way, forty-one minutes. Two hundred and twelve notes in red ink. A kitchen, and his own voice saying Say it again. A letter at four in the morning. A stairwell, and two hands flat on a cold step, a finger’s width apart. A glass room. You bought me a lab. I bought you time. An intercom in the rain. A whiteboard. Still here. A suitcase with no wheel. A corridor outside room 301, and two hands raised, two metres apart.

Two hundred and sixty-six days.

3:58.

He put the chalk down on the ledge.

He picked it up again.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 3:59 in the Great Hall, the Vice-Chancellor stood up for the closing words.

At 4:00, the orchestra played the last note.

At 4:00 and five seconds, before the four hundred graduates had finished standing up, before the families had finished clapping, before the Vice-Chancellor had made it off the stage in his gold robes, a girl in the fourth row in a black gown over a yellow sundress put down her scroll and her medal in the lap of a very surprised chemist, and said “Hold these, please,” and ran.

She ran down the aisle. Past her friends, who were all standing, who all saw her go, and none of whom tried to stop her. Tao Tao shrieked. Su Mei shouted GO. Professor Gao, at the end of the row, did not stand up, but turned her head and watched her student run, and for the first time in twenty years, in public, smiled.

She ran out of the Great Hall into the June sunshine. Down the steps. Across the square, where families were coming out with cameras. Down the long path between the trees.

She had timed it in October. Eighty-seven steps from the door of the Great Hall to the main entrance of the Hall of Science, and then four flights of stairs. Three minutes, walking. She had planned to walk. She had planned to be calm and dignified and graceful, and to climb the stairs slowly, and to arrive at exactly 4:01, at the door of office 412, composed.

She ran.

She ran with her gown flying open over the yellow sundress, in her trainers with biro on them, with four pens in her hair and the green hood bouncing on her back. She ran into the Hall of Science and past the empty porter’s desk and up the stairs. Not the lift. The stairs. The back stairs, the old concrete ones at the north end. Past the first floor. Past the second, where the lab smelled of toast. Past the third, where the glass room was, and room 301. Past the landing between the third and fourth floors, with the narrow window, where she had cried in February.

She burst through the fire door at the top.

The fourth-floor corridor. Empty. Long. The kitchen. Office 413, door closed, very quiet, as if someone inside were holding his breath.

Office 412.

The door was propped open with Principles of Quantum Mechanics.

She stopped.

She stood in the corridor outside, with her chest heaving and her gown hanging off one shoulder and her face burning, and looked at her phone.

16:00.

She stood there and watched it.

She was a physicist. She was precise. She had built a calendar on a number, and she was not going to cheat on the last minute.

She waited.

16:01.

She knocked.

✦ ✦ ✦

“It’s open,” said a voice inside. Quiet. Not quite steady. “Unless you’re from facilities.”

She went in.

He was standing at the chalkboard, with his back to her, with a piece of chalk in his hand.

He didn’t turn round.

“I’m not from facilities,” said Yu Jie.

“No,” said Miles. “I know.”

She stood just inside the door. Three metres. The same three metres as every Wednesday since September. The radiator whale was silent; it was June, the heating was off. The cactus sat on the windowsill, alive and dead. The sun came through the window and lay across the floor between them in a long gold bar.

“I’m not a student in your department,” she said.

He looked at his watch. Then at the clock on the wall. Then, very slowly, he turned round.

He looked at her. In the black gown, falling off one shoulder, over a yellow sundress. In her trainers. With four pens in her hair, and her face flushed from running, and her eyes very bright.

“It’s 4:01,” he said.

“I know,” said Shen Yu Jie. “I waited outside. For the minute.”

He looked at her.

Then he turned back to the chalkboard. To the bottom right-hand corner. To the flat line, professional distance (constant), running across the board and stopping at the small vertical mark, 20 June, 16:00. And after the mark, nothing. Empty board.

He put the chalk to the board at the end of the line.

And he drew.

The line went on from the mark. Not flat. Up. It curved upward, slowly at first, and then more steeply, and more, and more, a long sweeping curve going up and up across the empty board, toward the top right-hand corner, and off the edge of the chalkboard, and onto the painted wall beside it, where he had painted the board himself five years ago and the roller had stopped. He kept drawing. Onto the wall. Up past the edge of the paint, toward the ceiling, until he couldn’t reach any further, and stood on his toes, and the chalk ran out, a stub in his fingers, and he stopped.

He stood there with his arm up and the stub of chalk against the wall, breathing hard.

Then he wrote beside the curve, in small, neat, slightly shaking letters:

Not constant.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was crying. She didn’t notice. She stood by the door and looked at the line going up off the edge of the board and onto the wall, and couldn’t see it properly any more.

He turned round.

He put the stub of chalk down on the ledge. Very carefully. He wiped his hands on his trousers, which left white streaks. He pushed his glasses up his nose.

He looked at her across the three metres.

“I’ve thought about this,” he said. His voice was not steady at all. “For two hundred and sixty-six days. What I’d say. I wrote it down. Eleven drafts. I had it in order. Assumptions. Steps. Conclusion.” He swallowed. “I can’t remember any of it.”

“That’s all right,” she said.

“It was very good. The ninth draft especially.”

“Miles.”

“Yes.”

“You’re standing three metres away.”

He looked down at the floor. At the long gold bar of sunlight between them.

“Yes,” he said. “I don’t know how to stop.”

She laughed. Through the tears. And she took one step forward, across the gold bar of light, and then another, and another, and he didn’t move, he stood absolutely still by the chalkboard and watched her come, and she stopped in front of him.

Close. Closer than the stairwell. Closer than the jacket on the dark corner. Close enough that she could see the chalk dust on his glasses and the white streaks on his trousers and his heart going in the pulse at his throat.

Close enough to touch.

Neither of them did.

“Ask me,” she said. “You said in March. This time I’m asking first. So ask me.”

He looked down at her. At her wet face and her bright eyes and the purple pen with the plastic cat in her hair.

“May I,” said Miles Wei, very quietly, “touch you?”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t answer.

She took his hand instead.

She reached out and found it, at his side, his right hand, the one with chalk on the fingers, and took it in hers. Just that. Her hand around his. Warm. Ink on her middle finger. Chalk on his.

He went completely still.

Two hundred and sixty-six days, and they had never once touched. Not in the office. Not at the gala. Not in the stairwell, where their hands had lain flat on the cold concrete a finger’s width apart.

His hand was shaking. She held it tighter.

He looked down at their two hands together. As if it were an experiment that had done something no theory predicted.

Then he lifted his other hand. Slowly. The way he did everything, as if working it out as he went. He put it, very lightly, against the side of her face. His thumb on her cheekbone. Chalk on her skin. He brushed away a tear with it, and left a white smudge behind.

“You’re crying,” he said.

“So are you.”

He hadn’t noticed. He was.

“Oh,” said Miles.

She laughed again, and it broke in the middle, and she stood on her toes in her trainers with biro on them, and he bent his head—he was so much taller than her, she had never been this close, she had never realised how far she would have to reach—and they met in the middle.

✦ ✦ ✦

It wasn’t like the films. It wasn’t like anything.

It was careful, at first. Very careful. As if neither of them believed it was allowed. His mouth was warm, and tasted faintly of oranges, and he kissed her the way he did physics: slowly, and properly, paying attention to everything, as if he wanted to understand it completely and had all the time in the world to do it.

He barely moved, at first. Just his mouth on hers, warm and still, as if he were waiting to see whether the world would end. It didn’t. So he moved, very slightly: a soft, slow pressure, then a little less, then a little more, learning her. His thumb stayed on her cheekbone the whole time, tracing it, back and forth, back and forth, so lightly it was almost not there, and every pass of it sent something shivering down through her, through her ribs, into her stomach, where it turned over and over like a coin spun on a table.

She had imagined this. Of course she had. For two hundred and sixty-six days, in the dark, on her bedroom floor under the calendar. She had imagined it a hundred different ways.

She had not imagined that he would kiss her as if she were the only problem he had ever wanted to solve.

She had not imagined that her knees would actually go. That was a thing that happened in books, she had thought. It was not physics. And then his lower lip moved against hers, slow and soft, and her knees went, and she had to hold on to the front of his cardigan to stay standing, and he felt it, and made a small surprised sound against her mouth, as if he hadn’t known he could do that to anyone.

Then she made a small sound against his mouth, and something in him that had been held very still for two hundred and sixty-six days let go.

His hand went from her cheek into her hair. The claw clip came loose. Four pens fell onto the floor of office 412 one after another, clattering—the purple one last, the little plastic cat bouncing across the floorboards—and neither of them noticed. She had both her hands in the front of his grey cardigan, holding on, pulling him down. He made a sound she had never heard him make, low and helpless, and put his arm round her waist and lifted her clean off her feet against him, the black gown sliding off her shoulders onto the floor, and turned, without meaning to, and her back hit the chalkboard.

The whole board shook.

Chalk dust came down on both of them like snow.

He stopped. He pulled back, an inch. He was breathing as if he had run up four flights of stairs too.

“Sorry,” he said, against her mouth. “Sorry. The board. Are you—”

“If you apologise to the chalkboard,” said Yu Jie, breathless, “I will never forgive you.”

He looked at her. White chalk dust in her loose hair, on her eyelashes, all down the back of her yellow sundress where she had been pressed against the board.

He started to laugh.

Not the laugh in the seminar. Not the one on the terrace. A new one. Breathless and helpless and so happy it sounded almost like pain, with his forehead against hers and his arms around her and her feet still off the floor.

She laughed too. She couldn’t stop.

Through the cardboard wall, from office 413, very faintly, came the sound of Dr. Fang Hao, who had not gone down the stairs after all, who had gone down one flight and come straight back up and been sitting very quietly at his desk since 3:05, blowing his nose.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later—a long time later, with the sun gone round to the other side of the building and the gold bar on the floor turned orange and then grey—they were sitting on the floor of office 412, under the window, with their backs against the wall.

She was leaning against his shoulder, in his grey cardigan, which was much too big for her, the sleeves over her hands. He had put it on her himself, when the sun went round and she shivered in the thin sundress: very carefully, one arm and then the other, as if dressing someone were an experiment with a high chance of error. He had done the buttons up wrong. One out. She had not let him fix it. He had his arm around her. Neither of them had said anything for a while. They didn’t need to. It was the same silence as every Wednesday at five o’clock, when the problem was finished and neither of them wanted to leave.

Except now they didn’t have to.

The four pens were scattered across the floorboards. The black gown was in a heap by the chalkboard. On the board above it, the long curve went up and up and off the edge and onto the painted wall.

Not constant.

“Miles,” she said.

“Mm.”

“What happens now?”

He thought about it. Properly. The way he thought about everything.

“I don’t know,” he said. “I’ve never got this far.” He was quiet for a moment. “I want to do it properly. Ask you properly. Take you somewhere. I want to—” He stopped. “I’ve been thinking about how to ask since October. I have a plan. It’s a proof.”

She lifted her head from his shoulder and stared at him.

“A proof?”

“By induction,” said Miles, a little defensively. “It’s the right method. You establish the base case. Then you show that if it’s true for one day, it’s true for the next. Then it’s true for all of them.” He looked at her. “I was going to do it tomorrow. On the board. I’ve got the base case already.”

“What’s the base case?”

“The second Wednesday of September,” said Miles. “3:47 p.m.”

She looked at him for a long time in the grey light.

Then she put her head back on his shoulder and laughed so hard she couldn’t breathe, and he held on to her, and didn’t understand what was funny, and didn’t mind at all.

“Tomorrow,” she said, when she could speak. “Do it tomorrow. I want to see it.”

“It’s Sunday.”

“I don’t care.”

“The building’s closed on Sunday.”

“You have a key,” said Shen Yu Jie. “You’re permanent.”

He looked down at her, at the chalk dust still in her hair.

“Yes,” said Miles Wei, and something in his face, that had been shut since he was seventeen, opened all the way. “I am.”

chapters.title: A Proof by Induction
chapters.desc: Sunday, a closed building, a key. Miles asks her out the only way he knows how: on a chalkboard, with a base case, an inductive step, and a very small mistake he made on purpose.
chapters.epigraph: “Let P(n) be the statement: on day n, I want to see you on day n + 1.”
chapters.content:
The Hall of Science was closed on Sundays.
