There was a sign on the main door that said so, and a chain across the car park, and a security guard called Mr. Pan who sat at the porter’s desk reading martial arts novels and let nobody in unless they had a key card and a very good reason.

At ten o’clock on Sunday the twenty-first of June, Mr. Pan looked up from chapter forty-one and saw Dr. Miles Wei coming through the main door with his key card in one hand and a carrier bag in the other, and, behind him, a girl in a yellow sundress.

Mr. Pan had worked at the Hall of Science for nine years. He had seen Dr. Wei come in on Sundays before, many times, always alone, always to work. He had never once seen him with anyone.

He had certainly never seen him holding someone’s hand.

Dr. Wei saw him looking. He went red. He did not let go.

“Good morning, Mr. Pan,” he said. “This is Shen Yu Jie. She’s—” He stopped. He clearly had not thought about what she was. “She’s not a student,” he said finally. “As of yesterday. At 4:01.”

Mr. Pan looked at the girl. The girl looked back at him, perfectly composed, with four pens in her hair and her hand in Dr. Wei’s.

“Very good reason,” said Mr. Pan, and went back to chapter forty-one.

✦ ✦ ✦

Office 412 was exactly as they had left it.

The black gown was still in a heap by the chalkboard. The four pens were still on the floor, where neither of them had picked them up. On the board, the long curve still went up and up off the edge and onto the painted wall. Not constant.

Yu Jie stood in the doorway and looked at it all, and went pink.

“You didn’t tidy up,” she said.

“I didn’t want to,” said Miles. He put the carrier bag on the desk. “I wanted it to stay the way it was. I know that’s not scientific.”

“It’s entropy,” said Yu Jie. “Messy is more likely than tidy.”

He looked at her. Then he smiled, slowly, the smile she had seen for the first time in the third week of September, at the bent oscillator, and had been collecting ever since.

“There are more ways to be messy,” he agreed.

He took out of the carrier bag a box of new chalk, white, still in its wrapper. He unwrapped it very carefully. He took out one stick.

Then he went to the chalkboard, and stood in front of it, and didn’t look at her.

“Sit down,” he said. “Please. In the chair.”

She sat in the chair. The Wednesday chair. She had sat in it for nine months. She had never once sat in it feeling like this.

He picked up the rubber and wiped the left half of the board clean. Not the curve. Not Not constant, or the mark in the corner. Just the left side, where there was room.

Then he wrote, at the top, in neat white capitals:

THEOREM.

✦ ✦ ✦

She put her hand over her mouth.

He didn’t turn round. He wrote underneath, slowly, the chalk squeaking a little on the paint:

For all n ≥ 1: I want to see you on day n.

He underlined it.

“A theorem,” he said, to the board, “is a statement you want to prove is true. Always. Not just once. Not just on Wednesdays. For every case.” He cleared his throat. “There are lots of ways to prove a theorem. You can do it directly. You can do it by contradiction. You can do it by drawing very large pictures, which is what Fang Hao does.”

She laughed behind her hand.

“But when you want to prove something is true for every number, one after another, forever,” said Miles, “the best way is induction.” He wrote: PROOF (by induction). “You do two things. First, you show it’s true for the first one. That’s called the base case. Then you show that if it’s true for any one, it must be true for the next one. That’s called the inductive step. And if you can do both, then it’s true for all of them. Like dominoes. If the first one falls, and each one knocks over the next, then they all fall.”

He turned round, finally, and looked at her.

“I’m going to do the base case first,” he said. “Is that all right?”

She nodded. She couldn’t speak.

✦ ✦ ✦

He turned back to the board.

Base case (n = 1).

Day 1: the second Wednesday of September. 3:47 p.m.

He wrote it in small neat letters.

A student came to my office on a Wednesday. Office hours are Tuesdays and Thursdays. She brought the harmonic oscillator. She had already solved it. The answer was hidden in the margin.

I solved it the long way. Twenty-five minutes. Hermite polynomials. I did it to prove she didn’t need my help.

Then I told her she needed a different excuse for coming on a Wednesday.

He stopped. He held the chalk against the board for a long moment.

Then he wrote:

After she left, I sat at my desk for forty minutes. I didn’t do any work. I kept looking at the door. She had left a purple pen with a cat on it. I put it in my top drawer.

I wanted to see her again.

So P(1) is true.

He drew a small box after it. A neat little square. Then he turned round.

She was crying. Silently. Sitting in the Wednesday chair with tears running down her face.

“Is that—” he said. “Should I stop? I can stop.”

“Don’t you dare stop,” said Yu Jie.

✦ ✦ ✦

He turned back to the board.

Inductive step.

Suppose P(k) is true for some day k. That is: on day k, I want to see you on day k + 1.

We must show P(k + 1) is true: that on day k + 1, I want to see you on day k + 2.

He paused. He tapped the chalk against the board, once, twice.

“This is the hard part,” he said, without turning round. “In a real proof. You have to show that one thing causes the next. Not just that it happens to be true. That it has to be.” He was quiet for a moment. “I’ve been thinking about how to do this part since October. I tried it nine different ways.”

“What happened to the other eight?”

“They were all true,” said Miles. “But they weren’t proof.”

He wrote:

On day k + 1, I see you.

Every time I have seen you, I have learned something about you I didn’t know before. (See: the long way home. The oranges. The corners. A stairwell. Your father. Twelve things in a suitcase.) There has never been a day I have seen you and not learned something new.

Every time I learn something new about you, I want to know what the next thing is.

Therefore: on day k + 1, having seen you, I want to see you on day k + 2.

So P(k) implies P(k + 1).

He drew another small box.

✦ ✦ ✦

“So,” said Miles. He was standing very straight, with his back to her, holding the chalk. “By the principle of mathematical induction. Since P(1) is true. And P(k) implies P(k + 1) for all k. Then P(n) is true for all n.”

He wrote it underneath.

Therefore, for all n ≥ 1: I want to see you on day n.

He looked at it.

Then, below it, smaller, he wrote one more line.

Corollary: Would you have dinner with me? Tonight. And then, by induction, tomorrow.

He put the chalk down on the ledge.

He didn’t turn round.

✦ ✦ ✦

The office was very quiet.

The radiator was silent; it was June. The cactus sat on the windowsill. The sun came through the window, the way it had yesterday, and lay across the floorboards, and across the four pens nobody had picked up.

Behind him, he heard the chair scrape.

He heard her footsteps cross the floor. Not to him. To the chalkboard, beside him. He heard her pick up a piece of chalk from the new box.

He turned his head.

She was standing at the board next to him, with tear tracks on her face and the chalk in her hand, looking at his proof with the same expression she had worn on the second Wednesday, at the bent oscillator, when she had found the mistake in four seconds.

Ferocious, delighted, absolutely focused.

“There’s an error,” said Shen Yu Jie.

He went very still.

“Where?”

She pointed with the chalk. At the top. At the theorem.

For all n ≥ 1: I want to see you on day n.

“You only proved it for you,” she said. “I want to see you. It’s one direction. It’s a very nice proof. It’s very rigorous. The base case is beautiful. But it’s only half the theorem.” She looked at him sideways. “You did it on purpose. Didn’t you. You left it out on purpose, so I would have to fix it.”

He looked at her.

“Yes,” said Miles.

She laughed, wet and shaky. Then she put the chalk to the board, under his base case, and began to write in her small round quick handwriting.

Base case, second half (n = 1).

Day 1: the second Wednesday of September. 3:47 p.m.

I went to a lecturer’s office with a problem I had already solved, because I had watched him from the back of Lecture Theatre C for two weeks and he was the only person in the building who said “I don’t know” out loud.

He solved it the long way, to prove I didn’t need him. He told me I needed a different excuse.

I went back to my apartment and lay on my bed and looked at the ceiling for three hours. Tao Tao asked if I was ill. I said I was in a superposition.

I wanted to see him again.

So P(1) is true. For both of us.

She drew a box. Bigger than his. Slightly crooked.

Then, under his inductive step, she wrote:

Inductive step, second half: see above. Same reasoning. Also, he peels oranges badly and I need to supervise.

Box.

Then she went down to his corollary. Would you have dinner with me? Tonight. And then, by induction, tomorrow.

And underneath it, she wrote one word.

Yes.

And then, because she was a physicist, and precise, and she was not going to leave anything unproved:

(for all n.)

✦ ✦ ✦

He was looking at the board.

He looked at it. At the two proofs, his and hers, side by side, in two different handwritings, his small and neat and hers small and round and quick. At the two boxes. At the Yes.

(for all n.)

“That,” he said finally, in a voice she had never heard from him before, “is a very strong statement.”

“I know.”

“For all n. You’ve claimed it for every day. Indefinitely. That’s an infinite set.”

“I know.”

“You’d have to be very sure.”

She put the chalk down on the ledge next to his.

“Miles,” she said. “I made a calendar with two hundred and sixty-six squares on it, and I drew an atom in every single one. I’m very good at being sure.”

He turned round. He looked down at her, standing beside him at the chalkboard in her yellow sundress, with chalk dust on her fingers and four pens on the floor.

Then he did something he had never done in office 412. He laughed out loud, and pulled her into his arms, and lifted her off her feet, and spun her round, once, right there in the middle of the room, so that her sundress flew out and her heel caught the stack of second-year homework on the corner of the desk and sent it flying, a hundred and forty scripts fluttering down across the floor like enormous white leaves.

He put her down.

They both looked at the floor. At the scripts everywhere. Bai Tianyu’s, on top, open at the uncertainty principle. We can never really know anything for sure, and that’s okay.

“Oh no,” said Miles.

“Entropy,” said Yu Jie.

And they stood among the scattered homework in the June sunshine and laughed until they had to hold on to each other, and then they stopped laughing, and he kissed her against the chalkboard again, more slowly this time, and the proof got smudged at one corner, the bottom of her box, and neither of them noticed until much later.

✦ ✦ ✦

He did not wipe the left-hand side of that board for the rest of the year.

He taught around it. When term started again in September, he wrote his second-year quantum mechanics on the right-hand side and left the left-hand side alone. Students asked him about it. Bai Tianyu asked him about it every single office hour, on Tuesdays and Thursdays, until in the end Miles told him: “It’s a proof by induction. It’s the most important one I’ve ever done.”

“What does it prove?”

“That something is true for every day.”

Bai Tianyu read it. He read it twice, slowly, his lips moving. He got to the bottom. To the Yes. To the (for all n).

He looked at Miles. His eyes went very wide.

“Dr. Wei,” he said. “Is that—”

“Yes,” said Miles.

Bai Tianyu stared at him.

Then he went out into the corridor, and Miles heard him, through the cardboard walls, all the way down the fourth floor, saying to someone, in a voice of awe: “He proved he’s in love with her. By induction.”

And from office 413, through the wall, Fang Hao said: “It took him nine months to get the base case.”

And Miles sat at his desk in office 412 with his face in his hands, red to the ears, smiling so much it hurt.

chapters.title: The First Date Has a Lesson Plan
chapters.desc: Four pages, timed to the minute, with learning objectives. She reads it, folds it into a paper plane, and takes him to the night market instead.
chapters.epigraph: “Learning objective 3: by the end of the evening, the participant will feel comfortable.” “Miles, I’m going to throw this into the harbour.”
chapters.content:
He had a lesson plan.

He had written it on Sunday afternoon, after the proof, after they had picked up the hundred and forty scripts together and he had walked her back to Bell Street and Su Mei had opened the door before they had even knocked. He had gone home and sat at his one table and written it out by hand on graph paper, and then typed it up, and printed it, because he wanted it to be right.

It was four pages long.

FIRST DATE: PROPOSED STRUCTURE

Date: Sunday 21 June. Duration: approx. 4 hours.

Learning objectives: 1. Participant will experience a pleasant evening. 2. Participant will not be cold. (Bring jacket. Note: own jacket. Not borrowed.) 3. By the end of the evening, participant will feel comfortable.

18:00 — Meet at Bell Street. Walk (flat route) to tram stop. 6 mins. 18:15 — Tram to Harbour Road. 11 mins. 18:30 — City Planetarium. Evening show: “The Life of Stars.” 45 mins. (Note: I have checked the script. Two errors regarding white dwarfs. Do not mention unless asked.) 19:30 — Dinner. Restaurant: The Lantern, Harbour Road. Booked: table by window. Menu reviewed in advance. Participant has expressed preference for dumplings (see: New Year, Tao Tao’s grandmother). Dumplings available. 21:00 — Walk along harbour front. Weather forecast: clear, 22°C. Low tide 21:47. Possible to see stars if light pollution permits (unlikely). 21:45 — Return to Bell Street. Long route (along old wall). 38 mins.

Contingencies: If rain: umbrella (REMEMBER UMBRELLA). If participant is bored: see appendix (topics of conversation). If I say something stupid: apologise once. Do not apologise eleven times.

Appendix A: Topics of conversation (non-physics). 1. Food. 2. Tao Tao. 3. Books (non-physics). 4. Ask about the bakery. 5. ...

The appendix went on for a page and a half.

✦ ✦ ✦

He gave it to her at 18:00 on Bell Street, on the step outside Fang’s, in a plastic folder.

He had thought about whether to give it to her. For a long time. He had decided that it would be dishonest not to, because she would see him checking his watch and wonder why.

She took the folder. She opened it.

She read the first page. Then the second. Then the third. Then she got to the appendix, and Topics of conversation (non-physics), item 14, Ask whether she likes cats (see: pen), and she sat down on the step outside the bakery and put her face in her hands and made a sound like something being strangled.

“Are you—” said Miles, alarmed. “Is it wrong? I can change it. I have a pen.”

She lifted her face. She was laughing so hard there were tears on it.

“Miles,” she said. “Learning objectives.”

“It’s a structure,” said Miles, going red. “It helps. I always do it for lectures. If you know what you want people to get out of something, you can plan it better.”

“You planned the tide.”

“Low tide is relevant if we walk on the harbour front. There are steps down to the sand.”

She looked up at him from the step. He was in a clean white shirt, ironed. His hair had been cut again. He had a jacket over his arm, his own, and an umbrella under the other arm, even though the sky was perfectly clear and blue, and his face was earnest and anxious and red.

He had planned the tide.

She stood up. She took the four pages out of the plastic folder.

And she folded them. Very carefully. Into a paper plane. A good one, with sharp wings, the kind Tao Tao had taught her to make in first year, during a very boring lecture on statistics.

He watched her do it in silence.

She held the plane up. She looked at him over it.

“Learning objective three,” she said. “By the end of the evening, participant will feel comfortable.”

“Yes?”

“The participant,” said Shen Yu Jie, “will feel comfortable when the lecturer stops reading from his notes.”

And she threw the plane.

It went beautifully. It flew down Bell Street in the evening sunshine, over the parked bicycles and the fruit stall and an old man walking his dog, past the noodle shop, all the way to the corner, where it banked to the left, very gracefully, and went straight into the open window of a passing tram.

They both watched it go.

“That was four hours of planning,” said Miles faintly.

“I know,” said Yu Jie, and took his hand. “Come on. I’m taking you somewhere. I didn’t plan it at all.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She took him to the night market.

Not the tourist one by the harbour, with the lanterns. The other one. The real one, on the waste ground behind the old railway station, where the stalls went up at six every evening out of the backs of vans and came down again at midnight, and the air was full of smoke and frying oil and someone’s radio playing Cantonese opera, and nobody had ever heard of a learning objective.

She had found it in second year. By accident, getting lost on the way back from a lecture. It was the first place she had ever bought anything with her own choice: a yellow sundress, from a woman with a rail of clothes and a hand-painted sign, for forty yuan.

She took him there by the hand, through the crowd, and he came, stumbling slightly, looking at everything.

“I’ve never been here,” he said.

“I know. I could tell. You’re looking at everything like it’s an experiment.”

“It is an experiment,” said Miles. “There are at least sixty stalls. There’s no system. That man is cooking squid on a car battery. That’s—” He looked at it. “That’s actually quite clever.”

She laughed.

They ate everything.

Squid on sticks from the car-battery man. Stinky tofu, which Miles approached the way he approached a new equation, with great caution and respect, and then ate four pieces of. Egg waffles from a woman who knew Yu Jie by sight and gave her an extra one. Sugar-cane juice from a man with a machine that crushed the cane right in front of them, which Miles watched for six full minutes with deep fascination while she held both cups.

“The pressure,” he said. “It’s a very simple lever. But the efficiency—”

“Miles.”

“Sorry.”

“No,” said Yu Jie. “Don’t be sorry. Keep going. I want to hear about the efficiency.”

He looked at her.

He kept going.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the far end of the market, under a string of bare light bulbs, there was a dumpling stall run by a very old woman and her very old husband. They had four plastic tables and a pot of boiling water and a wooden board, and the old woman sat on a stool making dumplings faster than anyone could eat them, her thumbs moving like a machine.

Yu Jie stopped in front of it.

“Here,” she said.

They sat at a plastic table. The old man brought them a plate of pork-and-chive dumplings and a dish of black vinegar and two pairs of wooden chopsticks, and went back to his pot.

Miles ate a dumpling. He stopped.

“These are better than the Lantern,” he said. “I read the Lantern’s reviews. These are better.”

“I know,” said Yu Jie. She was watching the old woman’s hands. “Watch her. Watch how she does it.”

He watched. The old woman took a round of dough. A spoon of filling. Folded it once. Then her thumbs went round the edge, pleating it, seven small pleats, so fast you could hardly see them.

“Tao Tao’s grandmother taught me,” said Yu Jie. “In first year. The New Year I went to their flat. I’d never folded a dumpling. In my family you have a cook.” She was quiet for a moment. “She showed me how to do the pleats with my thumbs, and I got it wrong eleven times, and she didn’t mind at all. And on the twelfth one I got it right and she clapped. And I was so happy I nearly cried.”

Miles looked at her across the plastic table.

The old woman had stopped making dumplings. She was looking at them.

“You want to make?” she said to Yu Jie, in a heavy accent from somewhere in the north.

Yu Jie went pink. “I—no, I—”

“Come.” The old woman patted the stool beside her. “Both. Come. Your man too. Big hands, he will be bad. Come anyway.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He was bad.

He was very, very bad. He had long thin fingers that could write a perfect integral sign in chalk and draw a diagram of a harmonic oscillator freehand, and he could not, it turned out, pleat a dumpling to save his life. His first one fell apart. His second one exploded in the pot. His third one, the old woman held up to the light of the bare bulb, and looked at, and said something in her northern dialect to her husband, who laughed so hard he had to sit down.

“What did she say?” said Miles.

“She said it looks like a bicycle accident,” said Yu Jie, who had grown up with three languages and had a fourth from Tao Tao’s grandmother.

Miles looked at his dumpling. It did look like a bicycle accident.

“It’s topologically correct,” he said with dignity. “All the filling is on the inside. It’s just—”

“Ugly,” said the old woman.

“Ugly,” agreed Miles.

Yu Jie was laughing so hard she couldn’t hold her own dough.

He picked up another round of dough. He watched her hands. He watched the old woman’s. He tried again, slowly. He got it wrong. He tried again.

On the twelfth one, Yu Jie reached over and put her hands over his.

She didn’t say anything. She just put her small hands, with flour on them, over his big clumsy ones, and moved his thumbs. Fold. Pleat. Fold. Pleat. Slowly, the way Tao Tao’s grandmother had done it with her. Seven pleats, round the edge.

He held very still and let her.

They looked down at it together. A dumpling. Not perfect. A little lopsided. But closed, and pleated, and whole.

The old woman leaned over and looked at it.

Then she clapped. Once. Very loudly.

And Miles, sitting on a plastic stool under a string of bare light bulbs at the back of a night market, with flour on his hands and a girl’s hands still over his, looked at the twelfth dumpling and felt something come up in his chest that he didn’t have a name for.

“Thank you,” he said to the old woman. His voice came out strange.

“Not me,” said the old woman. She pointed her rolling pin at Yu Jie. “Her. Good teacher. You keep her.”

“I’m going to,” said Miles.

He said it without thinking, before he could stop himself.

Yu Jie looked at him sideways, with flour on her nose.

The old woman nodded once, satisfied, as if some important business had been concluded, and went back to her dumplings.

✦ ✦ ✦

They walked home the long way.

Not along the old wall. A different long way, that she found by turning left whenever she felt like it. Through the backstreets behind the railway station, where washing hung between the buildings and old men played chess under streetlamps and somebody was practising the erhu very badly in an upstairs window. Past a temple. Past a park where a group of grandmothers were doing a fan dance to a portable speaker at ten o’clock at night. Past a shop that sold nothing but brooms.

He didn’t check his watch once.

She noticed. Somewhere around the shop that sold brooms, she looked at his wrist and saw that he wasn’t wearing a watch at all.

“Where’s your watch?” she said.

“In my pocket,” said Miles. “I took it off at the sugar cane.” He was quiet for a moment. “I didn’t want to know what time it was.”

She stopped walking.

He stopped too. They were on a narrow street with no lamps, between the broom shop and a closed tailor’s, and the only light came from an upstairs window where someone was watching television, flickering blue.

“Miles,” she said.

“Yes?”

“Is the participant comfortable?”

He looked down at her in the flickering blue light. At the flour still on her nose. At the claw clip, slipping. At her face, turned up to his, waiting.

“No,” said Miles honestly. “The participant is not comfortable at all. The participant’s heart is going at about a hundred and forty beats per minute. The participant has wanted to kiss you since the sugar cane and has been trying to work out whether it would be appropriate in front of the old woman with the rolling pin.”

She started to laugh.

He didn’t wait for her to finish.

✦ ✦ ✦

He kissed her in the dark street between the broom shop and the tailor’s, under the flickering blue window, with flour on both their hands.

Not carefully, this time. Not like the chalkboard. Not like a man who wasn’t sure he was allowed.

He put one hand in her hair, where the claw clip was slipping, and it slipped the rest of the way and fell, and her hair came down over his wrist. He put his other hand flat against the small of her back, over the yellow sundress, and pulled her in until there was no space at all, none, not a finger’s width, and kissed her as if he had been thinking about nothing else for nine months, which he had.

She made a small sound against his mouth and put both her arms round his neck and held on.

He walked her backwards. He didn’t seem to decide to. Two steps, three, until her shoulders met the shutter of the tailor’s shop with a soft metal rattle, and he followed her there and kept kissing her, one forearm braced on the shutter above her head, the other hand spread on her back, holding her against him. It was dark and the street was narrow and he was so much taller than her that she had to tip her head right back, and he bent to her, and his mouth opened hers, slow and deep and thorough, the way he did everything, and her stomach dropped as if the street had tilted.

She had not known he could kiss like this. She was fairly sure he hadn’t known either.

He broke away for one second, breathing hard, and looked down at her in the flickering blue light.

“Is this—” he said. “Am I—”

“If you stop to ask,” said Yu Jie, “I will bite you.”

Something went across his face. Surprise, and then something much darker, and much less polite.

“Noted,” said Miles Wei, and kissed her again, harder, until the shutter rattled behind her and she had both hands fisted in his shirt and had forgotten the dumplings and the night market and her own name.

Above them, the television went to an advertisement. The blue light flickered. Someone in the window laughed at something. Down the street, the erhu player hit a terrible note and stopped.

Neither of them noticed.

When they came apart, finally, she was breathing hard and he was breathing harder, and his glasses were crooked and fogged, and she reached up and took them off his face very gently, the way she had done once in his flat when he was asleep with a fever.

“There,” she said. “Now you can’t see anything.”

“I can see you,” said Miles. “You’re very close. That’s within my focal range.”

“That,” said Shen Yu Jie, “is the most romantic thing anyone has ever said to me.”

“Really?”

“No,” she said, and kissed him again, and he forgot his glasses entirely.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was midnight when they got back to Bell Street.

The bakery was dark. Su Mei went to bed at nine. But there was a light on in the round window at the top of the house, and the front door was unlocked, which it never was.

They stood on the step outside Fang’s.

“I had a very good time,” said Miles.

“I know,” said Yu Jie. “I watched you have it.”

“The dumplings,” said Miles. “I’m going to practise. I’m going to get better. I’m going to learn the pleats properly.”

“I’ll teach you.”

“Yes,” said Miles. “Please.”

He looked at her for a long time on the step, in the light from the round window.

“Can I see you tomorrow?” he said. “By induction.”

She smiled.

“You don’t have to ask every day,” she said. “I already said yes. For all n.”

“I know,” said Miles. “I want to ask anyway. I like asking.” He paused. “I like it when you say yes.”

She stood on the step and looked at him with her hair down and flour on her nose.

“Yes,” she said.

He kissed her once more, very lightly, on the step. Then he went down the street. At the corner, by the noodle shop, he turned round and walked backwards for a few steps, looking at her, and walked into a bicycle.

She heard him say “Sorry” to it.

She went inside, and closed the door, and leaned against it in the dark hallway of the bakery, and put both her hands over her face, and laughed.

From the top of the stairs, a voice said: “Did he plan the tide?”

Su Mei was standing on the landing in a dressing gown and curlers with her arms folded.

“Yes,” said Yu Jie.

“I knew it,” said Su Mei, and went back to bed.

Upstairs, in the attic room, on the wall beside the door, Yu Jie took a pencil and found the new row of squares after the gold one. The first one said Not a pearl. The second one was the twenty-second of June. It was after midnight. Today.

She looked at it for a long time.

Then she drew in it, very small: a dumpling. Not perfect. Lopsided. Closed and pleated and whole. Twelfth try.

chapters.title: Holding Hands in Public
chapters.desc: Across the campus in July, past the canteen, the library café and the department kitchen. He keeps checking whether anyone is looking. Everyone is. Then a society photographer gets the picture the forum never did.
chapters.epigraph: “Dr. Wei. You can stop looking over your shoulder. You’re allowed.” “I know I’m allowed. My shoulders don’t.”
chapters.content:
The first time they held hands on campus, he let go four times in two hundred metres.

It was the first Monday in July. The summer term was over, but the campus wasn’t empty. There were summer-school students, and staff, and PhD students who never went home, and parents being shown round by student guides in red T-shirts, and the canteen was open, and the library café, and the gardeners were cutting the grass on the big lawn in front of the Hall of Science.

They came out of the east gate together at nine in the morning. She had walked up from Bell Street after her shift on the counter, with flour still on the cuff of her cardigan, and he had been waiting by the gate, very straight, in his grey cardigan, looking as if he were about to give a lecture on a subject he hadn’t prepared.

She took his hand.

He looked down at it. Then up, quickly, at the path ahead, at a gardener on a ride-on mower, at two summer-school students with ice creams.

He let go.

“Sorry,” he said. “Sorry. Reflex.”

She took his hand again.

They walked twenty metres. A man in a suit came out of the administration building. Miles let go.

“Sorry.”

She took it again.

Forty metres. The canteen. A group of second-years from his quantum course, eating breakfast outside at a plastic table. One of them looked up and saw them and her mouth fell open.

He let go.

“Miles,” said Yu Jie.

“I know. I know. I’m sorry.” He pushed his glasses up. “It’s nine months. Nine months of three metres. My hand doesn’t know yet. It’s like—you know when you’ve been carrying something heavy for a long time, and you put it down, and your arm still feels like it’s holding it?”

She looked at him.

Then she took his hand again, and this time she laced her fingers through his, all the way, so that he would have to actually undo them to let go.

“There,” she said. “Now you have to make a decision.”

He looked down at their laced fingers.

He didn’t let go.

They walked the rest of the way to the Hall of Science like that. Past the canteen, where the first-years from mechanics had stopped eating entirely. Past the library café, where someone inside dropped a cup. Past the gardener on the ride-on mower, who turned the mower off to watch them go by. Past the big lawn. Up the steps.

He checked over his shoulder eleven times. She counted.

He didn’t let go once.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mr. Pan, at the porter’s desk, looked up from his martial arts novel.

He looked at the laced fingers.

He looked at Dr. Wei’s face, which was the colour of a tomato.

“Good morning, Dr. Wei,” he said. “Good morning, Miss Shen.”

“Good morning, Mr. Pan.”

Mr. Pan went back to his book. As they went past to the stairs, he said, without looking up:

“My wife said three to one you’d have done it by the end of May.”

Miles stopped on the bottom step.

“Done what?”

“Held hands. In public.” Mr. Pan turned a page. “Dr. Fang’s pool. The security staff had our own. I said July. She said May. She owes me fifty.”

They stood on the bottom step and stared at him.

“How many pools were there?” said Yu Jie faintly.

Mr. Pan considered it.

“Seven,” he said. “That I know of.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the fourth floor, Fang Hao opened the door of office 413 as they came out of the stairwell, and looked at the hands, and said nothing at all.

He went back into his office.

A second later he came out again with a large piece of card. He had clearly made it some time ago and been keeping it. It said, in thick black marker, in his big careless handwriting:

DAY 1 (PUBLIC).

He stuck it on the door of office 412 with tape, beside the sign about office hours with the green cat in a box, and stood back and admired it.

“Hao,” said Miles.

“Yes?”

“Take that down.”

“No,” said Fang Hao serenely, and went back into 413 and shut the door.

Through the cardboard wall, they heard him say, apparently on the phone: “Yes. Both hands. Laced. Mei, I’m telling you, laced. Pay Mr. Pan’s wife.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the fourth-floor kitchen, at 12:30, Dr. Ren Bo was making instant noodles.

He looked up when they came in. Miles had his WORLD’S OKAYEST SON mug. Yu Jie had the white one. She had brought it from the glass seminar room, where it had sat on the drying rack for three months, unused.

They were holding hands. Still. Because she had refused to let go at the kitchen door, and he had stopped trying.

Ren looked at them. His face went through several things.

Then he turned back to his noodles.

“Congratulations on your distinction, Miss Shen,” he said, to the kettle. Stiffly. “I read chapter three. It was very good.”

Yu Jie looked at the back of his head.

“Thank you, Dr. Ren,” she said. “I read your paper on spin chains last year. The second section was very elegant.” She paused. “The fourth one had a sign error.”

Ren’s shoulders went rigid.

Then, slowly, they came down.

“Yes,” he said, still to the kettle. “It did. Somebody wrote in. I’ve been trying to forget.”

He picked up his noodles and walked out of the kitchen past them, carefully not looking at their hands, and at the door he stopped and said, without turning round:

“Wu Na got married in May. Did you know? To a chemist. I went to the wedding. She said she forgave me, but only because I helped carry the cake.”

He went out.

Yu Jie looked at Miles.

“That was almost nice,” she said.

“That was the nicest thing I’ve ever heard him say,” said Miles. “I think you broke him.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They had lunch on the big lawn, because she said that if they were going to be looked at, they might as well be looked at in the sunshine.

They sat on the grass in front of the Hall of Science with an egg sandwich each, cut into triangles, and a tub of oranges, and she lay back on the grass with her head on his knee, and he sat very straight with his back against a tree and her head on his knee and looked down at her and didn’t know what to do with his hands at all.

“You can put one on my hair,” said Yu Jie, with her eyes closed. “If you like. It’s allowed.”

He put one on her hair.

It lay there, very still, like a paperweight.

“You can move it,” said Yu Jie, with her eyes still closed.

He moved it. Once. Down, very slowly, from her temple to the end of a strand, and stopped, as if waiting for a result.

“Is that—”

“You’re doing it like you’re calibrating something.”

“I am, a little,” said Miles. “I’ve never done this. I don’t know the correct pressure.”

She opened one eye and looked up at him from his knee.

“Whatever you’re doing,” she said, “keep doing it, and don’t write it down.”

He kept doing it. After a while his hand stopped being careful and simply moved, slowly, through her hair, and she made a small contented sound like a cat in the sun, and he looked down at her and forgot that anybody else was on the lawn at all.

People went past. Summer-school students. Parents with guides in red T-shirts, who pointed at the Hall of Science and said, this is the physics building, and then looked at the lecturer under the tree with a girl’s head on his knee and lost their place in the script.

At one o’clock, Professor Zhou came down the steps of the Hall of Science in his cardigan.

Miles saw him and went rigid. His hand stopped moving in her hair.

Yu Jie opened her eyes.

Professor Zhou came down the path toward them. He didn’t hurry. He walked the way he always walked, mildly, his reading glasses in his top pocket. He reached the tree. He stopped.

He looked down at Dr. Miles Wei, permanent lecturer, sitting very straight against the tree with a former student of his department lying on the grass with her head on his knee.

Miles opened his mouth.

“Good afternoon, Dr. Wei,” said Professor Zhou. “Good afternoon, Dr.-to-be Shen.”

He walked on.

He got three steps down the path. Then he stopped, and turned, and came back, and looked down at Miles again over his glasses.

“Miles,” he said. “Stop looking over your shoulder. You’re allowed.”

“I know I’m allowed,” said Miles. “My shoulders don’t.”

Professor Zhou looked at him for a long moment. Then something happened to his mild face that Miles had seen exactly once before, in the glass seminar room, the day the foundation was dissolved.

He smiled.

“Then teach them,” he said, and went on toward the canteen.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday evening, they went to the harbour.

Not for anything. Just to walk. She wanted to see the place where she had stood barefoot on the steps of the Harbour Hotel in December with her shoes in her hands and no coat. She wanted to stand there in July in her yellow sundress, holding his hand, and not be cold.

They stood on the steps of the Harbour Hotel at eight o’clock in the evening, in the warm summer dusk, and looked at the harbour, and the ships, and the Shen Building across the water with its name lit up in white at the top.

“There,” said Yu Jie. “That’s where I was standing. By the pillar.”

“I know,” said Miles. “I remember.”

“You gave me your jacket.”

“I gave you my jacket.”

“Miss Shen!”

A man had come down the steps from the wedding party. Young, sleek, in a white dinner jacket, with a glass of champagne. She knew him. Mr. Huo. His family owns the airport. The eighth of the nine.

“I thought it was you,” said Mr. Huo, delighted, and took her free hand and bent over it as if he meant to kiss it. “Your mother told everyone you’d grow out of physics. Have you? You must come in. Everyone’s here.”

Yu Jie opened her mouth.

Miles got there first.

He didn’t raise his voice. He barely moved. He only stepped half a pace forward, so that his shoulder was very slightly in front of hers, and looked down at Mr. Huo from his full height with an expression she had only ever seen him use on a referee who had not read the paper.

“She hasn’t,” said Miles. “She’s grown into it. She has the Faculty Medal.” A pause. “And she’s busy.”

Mr. Huo looked at him. Then at the hand Miles was holding. He let go of the other one.

“Of course,” he said, and went back up the steps rather faster than he had come down.

Yu Jie turned to Miles.

“She’s busy,” she said.

“You were,” said Miles. His ears had gone red. “You were standing on some steps with me. That’s a valid use of time.”

She looked up at him.

“Kiss me,” she said. “Here. On the steps. Where you didn’t, in December.”

He looked down at her. Then at the steps. At the doormen. At the line of black cars. At the rich people in evening clothes coming out of a wedding party in the ballroom, laughing, with their breath not white at all.

He kissed her.

On the steps of the Harbour Hotel. In front of everybody. With his hand on her face and her hand in the front of his shirt.

And at the bottom of the steps, a man with a camera, who had been waiting to photograph the wedding party for the society pages of the Harbour Daily, turned round, and saw who it was, and took eleven photographs very fast.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was on page six on Sunday.

Not page one. Page six. Society. Between a photograph of a charity auction and a photograph of a new restaurant opening.

It was a good photograph. Much better than the forum. In focus, in the warm dusk light. The steps of the Harbour Hotel. A tall thin man in a white shirt with his head bent and his hand on the face of a girl in a yellow sundress, who was on her toes in trainers with biro on them, kissing him, with her hand fisted in the front of his shirt. Behind them, blurred, the harbour, and the lights of the Shen Building across the water.

The caption said: Shen heiress Shen Yu Jie, 22, and City University physicist Dr. Miles Wei, 32, on the steps of the Harbour Hotel on Friday. Miss Shen graduated last month with the Faculty Medal. Sources say she has turned down an engagement to diplomat Lu Zhiyuan, and that her family is “not commenting.”

Su Mei showed it to her at five in the morning, on the counter, between the first batch of buns and the second.

Yu Jie looked at it.

“Are you all right?” said Su Mei.

“Yes,” said Yu Jie slowly. “Yes. I think I am.” She touched the photograph. “It’s the same steps. The same pillar. In December I stood there alone and nobody saw.”

“And now the whole city has.”

“Yes.” She looked at the girl on her toes in the photograph, in her forty-yuan sundress, kissing a physicist in front of the Shen Building. “I don’t mind,” she said, sounding surprised. “I thought I’d mind. I don’t mind at all.”

Su Mei looked at her.

Then she took the newspaper, and cut the photograph out with the bread knife, very neatly, and stuck it to the wall behind the till with a piece of tape, next to the health-and-safety certificate and a postcard from her sister in Chengdu.

“There,” she said. “Now every customer sees it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles bought ten copies.

He went to the newsagent at the bottom of the hill at eight o’clock on Sunday morning and bought ten copies of the Harbour Daily and carried them home under his arm. The newsagent, who had sold him one newspaper a week for five years, looked at the stack and then at page six and then at Miles, and gave him the eleventh one free.

He sent one to his sister. By post, because she would want to hold it.

He sent one to his parents, in the small flat by the sea, with a note on graph paper that said: This is Yu Jie. I’ve told you about her on the phone. I’d like to bring her to meet you. In August, if she says yes. She probably will. She says yes a lot.

He kept one. He put it in the drawer of his one table, the drawer where he kept nothing important, with two letters he had written in March and never sent.

The other seven he took to the Hall of Science on Monday morning and left in the fourth-floor kitchen, in a neat stack, beside the kettle, for anyone who wanted one.

By ten o’clock, they were all gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

His sister called on Wednesday.

“It came,” said Wei Lan. “The newspaper. I’ve put it on the fridge.” A pause. “Miles. You’re kissing someone. On the steps of a hotel. In a newspaper.”

“Yes.”

“In front of the whole city.”

“Yes.”

“You.”

“Yes,” said Miles.

There was a long silence on the line. When Wei Lan spoke again, her voice had gone strange.

“Mum cried,” she said. “When she opened hers. She sat down at the kitchen table and cried for twenty minutes. Dad had to make her tea.” Another pause. “She said, ‘He’s laughing. Look, Lan. In the photograph. He’s laughing while he’s kissing her.’”

Miles hadn’t noticed. He went and got his copy out of the drawer and looked at it.

He was. Very slightly. At the corner of his mouth, under her hand.

“Bring her in August,” said Wei Lan. “Mum’s already planning the food. She’s planning eleven dishes. She’s asked me what the girl likes and I said I didn’t know, I’ve only spoken to her once, about your fever, and Mum said, ‘Then ask him, Lan, honestly, what is the point of you.’”

“Dumplings,” said Miles. “She likes dumplings. Tell Mum she’ll want to help fold them.”

“Help fold them? She’s a Shen. They have cooks.”

“She’s not a Shen,” said Miles. “Not that kind. She’s a physicist. She folds them better than anyone I know.” He looked at the photograph. “She taught me. On the twelfth try.”

Another long silence on the line.

“Oh, Miles,” said his sister. And then, in a completely different voice, the one she used at the hospital for bad news and good news both: “I’m so glad. I’m so glad. I’m going to cry now. I’m going to hang up so you don’t hear.”

She hung up.

He sat at his one table with the newspaper and laughed, out loud, alone in his flat, at nothing. At the cactus on the windowsill. At the eleven eggs in his fridge, now. Twelve, until breakfast.

At the fact that he could.

chapters.title: Yu Jie Gets a Job
chapters.desc: A research assistant post in the capital, five hours north. He asks her what she wants, and makes himself listen to the answer. Then the last night of August, the door of the staff flat, and a question he asks at every step.
chapters.epigraph: “What do you want?” “I want both.” “Then we’ll find out how to have both. I’m a physicist. I’m good at problems with two variables.”
chapters.content:
The letter from the capital came in the last week of July.

It was from Professor Huang Zhenhai, and it was two pages long, and it said, in very formal language, that the Institute for Condensed Matter Physics was pleased to offer Miss Shen Yu Jie a one-year post as Research Assistant in his group, beginning on the first of September, with a salary, and a room in the institute’s residence, and a guaranteed place on the doctoral programme the following year.

At the bottom, in his own hand, he had written:

I have been thinking about corners since May. I would like very much to think about them with you. — H.

She read it on the counter at Fang’s at half past six in the morning, between customers, and then put it face down under the till and didn’t look at it again for three days.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t tell him.

Not because she was hiding it. She just didn’t know how to say it. I’ve been offered the best job anyone in my year has been offered, in the best group in the country, by a man who took notes at my defence. It’s five hours away on the train. It starts in five weeks.

Five weeks. They had had five weeks. Since 4:01 on the twentieth of June. Five weeks of holding hands in public, and dumplings, and the night market, and kissing on the steps of the Harbour Hotel, and lying on the big lawn with her head on his knee. Five weeks of him laughing.

She had waited two hundred and sixty-six days for five weeks.

She didn’t tell him.

On the fourth day, Su Mei found the letter under the till, and read it, which she had no right to do and did anyway, and put it in front of her at the kitchen table at eight in the evening, and folded her arms.

“Tell him,” said Su Mei.

“I know.”

“Tonight.”

“I know.”

“If you don’t, I’ll tell the croissant man, and the croissant man will tell him in four minutes, and then you’ll have a much worse conversation than the one you’re going to have.” Su Mei looked at her. “Do you want to go?”

Yu Jie looked at the letter.

I have been thinking about corners since May.

“Yes,” she said, very quietly. “Yes. I want to go. I want it so much I can’t breathe.” She put her hands over her face. “And I want to stay. I want both. I can’t have both.”

“Who says?”

Yu Jie looked up.

“You’re twenty-two,” said Su Mei. “You think everything is one thing or the other. Physics or a husband. Your mother or the street. Him or the capital.” She unfolded her arms. “I married a theorist who eats croissants for breakfast, lunch and dinner and talks about string theory in his sleep. My mother told me I’d starve. I’ve been running this bakery for eleven years and he’s been in that building for nine and we have never once lived the life anybody told us we had to.” She stood up. “Go and ask him. Don’t tell him. Ask him. You two are good at asking.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went to the basement.

He was there. He was always there, that summer, in the evenings. The pumps were connected now, and a small camera he had borrowed from the engineering department, and a laser pointer on a stand, and a laptop on a broken chair from 1997. The tank was full. When the pumps were on, the water ran the length of the tank and sped up over a smooth hump in the middle, faster and faster, and you could drop a little wave in at the downstream end and watch it try to swim upstream against the flow, and slow, and slow, and at one point, stop.

He was lying on his back under the tank with a spanner when she came down the ramp.

“Yu Jie,” he said, from under the tank. He always knew her footsteps. “Come and look. I’ve got the flow steady. It holds for nearly a minute now. If you put a wave in from the left—”

“Miles,” she said. “Can you come out?”

He came out. He looked at her face. He put the spanner down.

She held out the letter.

He read it standing by the tank, in the light of the bare bulb, with the pumps humming. He read it twice. She watched his face. She had spent nine months watching his face at a chalkboard. She knew what it did when something hurt.

It didn’t do that.

It did something else. Something she hadn’t seen before. It went very still and very bright, the way it had in the corridor outside room 301, when Professor Gao said distinction.

“Huang,” he said. “The Institute. Research assistant. And the doctorate after.” He looked up at her. “That’s the best group in the country. That’s—Yu Jie, that’s the best possible thing. That’s exactly where you should be. That’s—”

He stopped.

He looked at her face.

“You haven’t said yes,” he said slowly.

“No.”

“Why not?”

She couldn’t answer.

He looked at her for a long moment, standing by the long tank with the water flowing and the letter in his hand.

Then he folded the letter, very carefully, and gave it back to her. And he did a thing that, later, she would think of as the moment she was certain. Not the proof. Not the kiss against the chalkboard. This.

He didn’t tell her to go.

He didn’t tell her to stay.

He asked.

“What do you want?” said Miles.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stood in the basement with the letter.

“I want to go,” she said. Her voice shook. “I want to go so much it frightens me. I want to work with him. I want to think about corners. I want to be in a building full of people who are better than me and find out how good I can get.” She swallowed. “And I want to stay. With you. I waited two hundred and sixty-six days and I’ve had five weeks, Miles. Five weeks. I want to be able to walk to the basement and watch you lie under a water tank with a spanner. I want—” She stopped. “I want both.”

He looked at her.

“Then we’ll find out how to have both,” he said.

She stared at him.

“It’s five hours on the train,” said Miles. “That’s a distance. It’s not infinity. It’s a number. You can do things with a number.” He was thinking now; she could see it. The way he thought about a problem. “There are trains every two hours. The last one back on a Sunday is at 21:10. I teach Tuesday and Thursday. You’ll work all week, but researchers don’t work Saturdays, not properly, not unless they’re mad, and Huang isn’t mad, he’s just famous. So that’s Friday night to Sunday night. Every other weekend I come to you. Every other weekend you come to me. Holidays. Conferences. I have a conference in the capital in November, I was going to say no to it, now I’ll say yes.” He took a breath. “It’s one year. Then you start the doctorate. And doctorates can be co-supervised. Huang could supervise you from there. Gao could supervise you from here. If you wanted. If it worked. That’s for later. That’s a different problem.”

She was staring at him.

“You’ve thought about this,” she said.

“For about forty seconds,” said Miles. “Since you said both.” He pushed his glasses up. “I’m a physicist. I’m good at problems with two variables.”

She made a sound. Half a laugh, half a sob.

“You’re not going to tell me to stay?”

“No.”

“Even though you want me to.”

“I want you to be in the best group in the country thinking about corners,” said Miles. “I want that more than I want you in the basement watching me fix a pump. I’ll be sad. I’ll miss you every day. I’ll make you tea on Wednesdays and nobody will drink it.” His voice went quiet. “But I waited two hundred and sixty-six days to stop being a reason you couldn’t do something. I’m not going to start again now.”

She walked across the basement and put her arms round him and her face in his chest and held on.

He held her. Next to the long clear tank, with the water flowing toward the middle, and the little waves slowing, and slowing, and stopping at the edge.

“Say yes to Huang,” he said into her hair.

“Yes,” said Yu Jie, into his shirt.

“By induction?”

She laughed, and cried, and held on.

“Yes,” she said. “For all n.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She was leaving on the first of September, on the 7:40 train.

On the thirty-first of August, at nine o’clock at night, she knocked on the door of number fourteen, third floor, the staff flats behind the sports ground.

She had been to the flat many times that summer. For dinner, which he cooked badly and she fixed. For breakfast, on Sundays, when he made eggs, because there were always eggs now, a full box of twelve, he replaced them every Saturday. To sit on his sofa and read while he worked at his one table, with her feet in his lap.

She had never stayed.

He had never asked. She had never asked. They had kissed on the sofa until it was very late and both of them were breathing hard and his glasses were somewhere on the floor, and then he had walked her home to Bell Street, the long way, every time. Neither of them had said anything about it. It was just something they hadn’t done yet.

She knocked on the door. She was holding nothing. No bag. No suitcase. Her one suitcase was packed and waiting at the bakery for the morning.

He opened it.

He looked at her on his doormat, beside the small cactus in its blue pot. In the yellow sundress. With her hair down. No pens.

He knew. She saw him know. It went through his whole face.

“Hello,” said Miles.

“Hello,” said Yu Jie. “I’m not going home tonight.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say anything.

Then he stepped back, and held the door open, and she came in, and he closed it behind her, and they stood in his small clean flat full of books with the light from the one lamp, and neither of them moved.

“Are you sure?” he said.

“Yes.”

“You can change your mind. At any point. Any point at all. I mean that.”

“I know.” She looked at him. “I’ve been sure since about the sugar cane.”

He let out a breath that was almost a laugh.

“I’ve never—” he said. Then stopped. Then made himself go on, because he had promised himself, in September, that he would be honest with her. “Not since I was very young. Once. At university. It wasn’t—it didn’t mean anything. I’ve never done this with anyone who meant anything.” He pushed his glasses up. His hand was shaking. “I don’t know if I’ll be any good at it.”

She came across the room to him.

She stood in front of him and reached up and took his glasses off, very gently, and folded them, and put them on the bookshelf beside the door, on top of a stack of journals.

“You did the harmonic oscillator the long way,” she said, “to prove I didn’t need help. You did it perfectly. With Hermite polynomials. Twenty-five minutes.” She put her hands flat on his chest. “I think you’ll be good at the long way.”

He looked down at her. Without his glasses, his eyes looked different. Younger. Less guarded.

“May I?” he said.

It was what he had asked at 4:01. May I touch you?

“You don’t have to ask every time,” said Yu Jie softly.

“I want to,” said Miles. “I like asking. I like it when you say yes.”

She smiled. Her eyes were wet.

“Yes,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He kissed her first. Before anything else. Standing just inside the door of his small flat, with one hand on the side of her face and the other not touching her at all, held a little away, as if he had to keep one hand back in case he forgot himself.

Not the way he had kissed her against the chalkboard at 4:01, all at once, two hundred and sixty-six days breaking open. Not the way he had kissed her by the broom shop, hungry and laughing. Slowly. As if he had decided, somewhere in the ten weeks since June, that he was going to learn this the way he learned everything: properly, from first principles, one step at a time.

He kissed the corner of her mouth. Then the other corner. Then her mouth, very lightly, barely touching, and stayed there, his breath on her lips, until she was the one who leaned in. He let her. He let her deepen it, and when she did, he made a sound low in his throat that she felt more than heard, and his held-back hand finally came to her waist, and spread there, warm through the thin cotton of the sundress.

Her stomach dropped as if she had missed a stair.

He kissed her for a long time. Long enough that she stopped thinking. Long enough that her hands, which had been flat on his chest, curled into his shirt, and then crept up to his neck, and into his hair, which was soft and would not lie down, and she pulled, very slightly, and he broke away from her mouth with a gasp and put his forehead against hers.

“That,” he said unsteadily, “was not in the plan.”

“You had a plan?”

“I had a very vague plan,” said Miles. “I didn’t write it down. I want that noted.” He was breathing hard. “It said, go slowly. That’s all it said. I’m already failing.”

“You’re not failing,” she whispered. “Do that again.”

He did it again.

✦ ✦ ✦

He asked at every step.

At the first button of the yellow sundress, which had seven, small and white, down the front. May I? Yes. He undid it, and kissed the skin it showed, just below her collarbone, and she shivered. At the second. May I? Yes. Another kiss, lower, slower, his mouth warm, his breath warmer. At the third her knees had gone strange and she had to hold on to his shoulders. At the fourth she started to laugh, shakily, and said Miles, you can assume yes for the remaining three, and he said, against her skin, that isn’t how proofs work, and she laughed so hard she had to hold on tighter, and he undid the fifth, and the sixth, and the seventh, slowly, looking up at her the whole time from where he had knelt down in front of her without either of them noticing, and she stopped laughing.

The yellow dress slid off her shoulders and down, and pooled on the floor of the staff flat beside a stack of journals.

He stayed on his knees for a moment and just looked at her.

Not the way the men at the gala had looked at her diamonds. Not the way her mother looked at her, checking for flaws. He looked at her the way he would look, five months later, at the first stable horizon in the tank: as if he couldn’t believe it was real, and was terrified that if he blinked it would go away.

“You’re staring,” she said. Her voice wasn’t steady at all.

“Yes,” said Miles. “I’m sorry. I’ve wanted to for a year. I’m catching up.”

She pulled him up by the front of his shirt and kissed him.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was very slow.

He was the slowest, most careful, most attentive thing that had ever happened to her. He touched her as if she were a problem he had been waiting his whole life to be given: patiently, thoroughly, missing nothing, and he talked while he did it, very quietly, without seeming to know he was doing it. Small facts. Observations. As if he were taking notes.

You have a freckle here. Just here. I didn’t know.

Your heart is going very fast. I can feel it.

When I do this—your breath stops. Every time. Did you know that?

She hadn’t known. Nobody had ever told her anything about herself that wasn’t about how she looked.

He found the place below her ear that made her breath catch, and stayed there until she was clutching his shoulders. He found the ink on her middle finger and kissed it, and then kissed the inside of her wrist, and then the inside of her elbow, slowly, all the way up, until she was laughing and gasping at once. He found the scar on her knee from falling off a bicycle at nine, which nobody had ever noticed, and asked about it, and listened to the whole story of it with his mouth against the scar, while she tried to tell it and kept losing the words.

He noticed everything. He couldn’t stop. He had told her so on the old city wall in December, three metres away under a lamp. I notice things. I can’t stop.

She had not known, then, what it would be like to be noticed like this.

When she pushed his grey cardigan off his shoulders and pulled his shirt over his head, his hair stood straight up, all of it, and she laughed again, and he laughed too, and she put both her hands flat on his bare chest and felt his heart going under them like something trying to get out. He was thin and warm and there was a dusting of chalk on one shoulder from the basement chalkboard, and she kissed it, and tasted it, and he made the low sound again and stopped laughing.

She took his hand and walked backwards, into the small bedroom, with the window open on the warm August night, and the sound of a radio from somewhere across the sports ground, and the smell of cut grass. And him.

✦ ✦ ✦

She pulled him down to her on the narrow bed.

For a while it was only kissing. Lying down, it was different. Slower and deeper and closer, the whole length of him against her, the sheets cool under her back and his skin warm everywhere else. His hand moved down her side, over her ribs, her waist, the curve of her hip, and back up, as if he were memorising the shape of her, and every time he reached the place where her ribs ended she felt it in her stomach, a slow, bright, falling flutter, like the moment at the top of a swing.

His hands were shaking at first. She felt it. She took one of them and held it flat against her, over her heart, and said, Feel. Mine’s worse, and he laughed into her neck, and after that his hands were not shaking any more.

He asked once more. At the very end of asking. He lifted his head and looked down at her face in the light from the window, his eyes dark without his glasses, and said, very quietly, Jie. Are you sure?

He said Jie. Not Yu Jie. The way only Tao Tao said it, as if he had been keeping it for a long time and had only now been allowed.

She put her hands on either side of his face.

For all n, she said.

And then there was no more asking.

✦ ✦ ✦

It wasn’t like anything she had imagined. It was clumsier, and gentler, and far more real.

He was careful with her, and then less careful, because she pulled him closer every time he tried to be. The fourth time she did it, he caught her wrists and pressed them down into the pillow on either side of her head, gently, and held them there, and looked down at her, breathing hard.

“Jie,” he said. “I’m trying to go slowly.”

“I know. Stop.”

“I’ve been waiting a year.”

“So have I.” She lifted her head off the pillow until her mouth was almost on his. “I made a calendar, Miles. Two hundred and sixty-six squares. I drew an atom in every one.” She bit his lower lip, softly. “Don’t make me draw any more.”

He made a sound she had never heard him make. Low, and rough, and not polite at all.

After that, he wasn’t careful. They found each other slowly, in the narrow bed, in the warm dark, learning as they went—when to hold still, when not to, where her breath caught and where his did. At one point her elbow hit the wall and they both froze and then dissolved into laughter, foreheads together, and the laughter turned into something else halfway through, low and breathless and urgent, and neither of them was laughing any more.

He stopped, once, and looked at her face, and said Are you all right?, and she said Miles, if you stop now I will never forgive you, and he laughed into her shoulder, helplessly, and didn’t stop.

She would remember, afterwards, how it felt to be held by someone who had spent a year not touching her. As if every one of those two hundred and sixty-six days had been kept somewhere in him, saved, and were being given to her now, all at once, in his hands and his mouth and the way he said her name against her throat, over and over, like the answer to something.

She would remember his heart, against hers, going so fast she thought it might break, and the moment when everything in her went bright and still and far away, and his arms tightening round her as if he could feel it too, and his voice, breaking on her name.

And then the quiet.

The radio across the sports ground, playing something old. The cut grass. His breathing, ragged, slowing. His face in her hair. His arms round her, all of her, against him, so tightly, as if he were afraid that if he let go the five hours would start right now.

Her own heart, going very fast, and then slower, and slower, against his.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Jie,” he said, a long time later, into her hair, in the dark.

“Mm.”

“That wasn’t the long way.”

She opened her eyes.

“What?”

“I had a plan,” said Miles. “I’d thought about it. Not a lesson plan. I learned my lesson. But I’d thought about it. And I was going to go very slowly, and take as long as you wanted, and—” He stopped. “And then you did the thing with the—and I—it wasn’t the long way at all. Not the second half.” His voice was mortified. “I’m sorry.”

She turned over in his arms. She looked at him in the dark, at his face very close, without his glasses, with his hair still standing straight up.

“Miles,” she said. “Are you apologising to me for being too in love with me?”

He thought about it.

“…Yes,” he said.

She started to laugh. She couldn’t stop. She laughed so hard the narrow bed shook, and he put his face in the pillow and groaned, and she laughed harder, and pulled his face out of the pillow, and kissed him, and kept laughing against his mouth.

“We can do the long way,” she said, when she could speak. “We have time. The train isn’t until 7:40.”

He looked at her.

“That’s eight hours and eleven minutes,” he said.

“Yes.”

“That’s a lot of time.”

“Yes,” said Shen Yu Jie, and pulled him back down.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second time, he did it the long way.

He started at her ankle. He said so, out loud, very seriously, like the first line of a proof: I’m going to start here. And she laughed, and then she stopped laughing, because he meant it. Her ankle. The back of her knee, which turned out to be a place nobody had ever told her about. The scar again. Her hip. The curve of it, where his breath made her whole body tighten. The dip of her waist. Every one of her ribs, one at a time, counting them under his breath until she pulled his hair and told him he was a menace.

Seven, he said. Eight. You have the standard number. I’m very relieved.

She would have laughed if she could have breathed.

He took so long that the radio across the sports ground went off, and the sky outside the window changed from black to the deep blue that comes just before the grey, and she was the one who broke first, who said his name in a voice she had never heard herself use, and pulled him up to her, and said Now. Please. Now.

He looked down at her in the blue light.

May I? he said, and she could have killed him, and she said yes, and yes, and yes, and this time it was slow from the very beginning to the very end, slow enough that she felt every second of it, slow enough that she was crying a little by the end and didn’t know why, and he kissed the tears away one by one and didn’t stop, and didn’t hurry, and held her face in his hands the whole time, looking at her, as if he never wanted to look at anything else.

Afterwards, she lay with her head on his chest and listened to his heart slowing down, and watched the window go grey, and then pale gold.

That, he said into her hair, was the long way.

I know, she said. I was there.

Was it all right?

She lifted her head and looked at him. At his hair, standing straight up. At his face, which had been shut for fourteen years, open all the way.

Miles, she said. I’m going to think about that on the train for five hours, and I’m not going to be able to look at Professor Huang.

He went red to the collar.

She laughed, and put her head back down, and he held her until the alarm went off at six.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning, he made eggs.

He made them very badly. He burned the first two and dropped the third and the fourth came out shaped like the coast of Norway. She sat on his one chair at his one table in his grey jumper, which came down to her knees, with her hair everywhere and her feet bare, and watched him, and didn’t help, because she wanted to watch.

He put the Norway-shaped egg in front of her with great ceremony.

“I bought twelve,” he said. “Every Saturday. Since March. Since Su Mei told me to.”

She looked at the egg. Then at him, at the stove, in his pyjama trousers and nothing else, with his hair still standing up, looking at her with an expression she had never seen on anybody’s face in her whole life. Not on a man at a gala. Not on her mother. Not on anyone.

As if she were the answer to a question he had been asking since he was nine.

“Miles,” she said. “I love you.”

She hadn’t said it before. Neither had he. Not in ten weeks. Not at 4:01. Not on the steps of the Harbour Hotel. It had been in everything, and neither of them had said it, because both of them, she thought, had been afraid that saying it would make it real enough to break.

He stood at the stove with the spatula in his hand.

He didn’t say anything.

Then he put the spatula down. He came across the small kitchen. He knelt down beside her chair, on the floor, so that his face was below hers, and looked up at her.

“I’ve loved you since the second Wednesday of September,” he said. “At about 3:51. When you told me the radiator was lonely. I spent nine months trying to call it something else.” His voice was very quiet. “I love you. I’ve loved you for a year. I’ll love you on the train, and in the capital, and on every other weekend, and on every Wednesday when you don’t drink the tea I make you.” He took her hand. “For all n.”

She was crying into her Norway egg.

“That’s my line,” she said.

“I know,” said Miles. “I stole it. I’m sorry.”

“Don’t you dare be sorry.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He took her to the station on his bicycle. Her suitcase on the back, strapped down with bungee cords, which Fang Hao had lent him. Her on the crossbar. Through the morning streets, in the early September sunshine, by way of the bakery on Bell Street, where the suitcase was waiting and Su Mei was standing outside with her arms folded and a bag of buns, which she threw into Yu Jie’s lap as they pushed off again.

On the platform, at 7:36, she stood at the open door of the carriage.

He stood on the platform. Not three metres away. Not two. Right there.

“Two weeks,” she said. “Friday after next. You come to me.”

“The 18:20. Arriving 23:15. I’ve booked it.”

“Of course you have.”

“I’ve booked all of them,” said Miles. “Until Christmas. Every other weekend. I did it last night. While you were asleep.” He looked faintly embarrassed. “I couldn’t sleep. I wanted to do something with my hands.”

She looked at him.

Then she stepped down off the train, and kissed him on the platform, in front of the guard, and the passengers, and a family with four children who all said ewwww in perfect unison, and the guard blew his whistle twice, and she got back on.

The doors closed.

She stood at the window as the train pulled out. He walked beside it along the platform, as far as he could, and then stopped at the end, by the yellow line, and stood there with his hands in his pockets, getting smaller and smaller.

She put her palm flat against the window.

At the end of the platform, as if he had felt it through the glass, he took one hand out of his pocket and held it up. Flat. Palm toward her. The way he had in a corridor outside room 301, two metres apart, when they weren’t allowed.

They were allowed now. It didn’t help at all.

The glass was cold under her hand. She kept it there until he was a grey shape, and then a dot, and then nothing, and the train went round a curve, and there were only the backs of houses and washing lines and her own face in the window. She had to press her other hand hard against her mouth. Two weeks was fourteen days. Fourteen days was three hundred and thirty-six hours. She knew, because she had worked it out at 7:39 and wished she hadn’t.

Then she sat down in her seat, and opened her bag, and took out a sticky note. Yellow. She had found it in the pocket of her cardigan that morning. She didn’t know when he had put it there.

Why did the photon take the train?

Because it was travelling light, and it had five hours to think about someone.

(It isn’t a very good joke. I didn’t sleep. I’ll do better in two weeks.)

(I love you.)

She held it in both hands all the way to the capital.

chapters.title: Long Distance Is Just a Variable
chapters.desc: The 18:20 and the 21:10. Calls at midnight. A whiteboard screwed to his kitchen wall. A storm, a cancelled train, a handsome postdoc, and a black hole made of water that finally holds.
chapters.epigraph: “I’d like to report that I’m jealous. I don’t think it’s rational. I’m reporting it anyway, in the interests of transparency.”
chapters.content:
The 18:20 to the capital left from platform four.

By October, the guard on platform four knew him. By November, the woman at the noodle stall on the station concourse had started making his order when she saw him come through the doors at 17:55: beef noodles, no coriander, extra chilli, which he didn’t like but ate because she had decided he needed it. By December, the ticket inspector on the train, a cheerful man called Wang with a gold tooth, had stopped asking for his ticket at all, and instead asked, every other Friday, at the same point past the river bridge:

“Same girl?”

“Same girl,” said Miles.

“Good,” said Wang, and went on down the carriage.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was five hours and three minutes. He had measured it. On a good night, with no delays, it was five hours and one minute, and once, in November, with a tailwind and a driver who seemed to be in a hurry, it was four hours and fifty-two. He had written it down. He wrote all of them down, in a small notebook he kept in his coat pocket, with the date and the departure time and the arrival time and, in a column on the right, a single word for each one.

She found the notebook in November, in the pocket of his coat, which she had stolen to wear to the shops because it was cold in the capital and he had come up without remembering she had no winter coat yet.

She read it standing in the queue at the bakery on the corner of the institute.

9 Oct. 18:20–23:23. Delayed (signal). Rain.

23 Oct. 18:20–23:21. Wang asked. Moon.

6 Nov. 18:20–23:12. Tailwind? She was on the platform. Didn’t expect. Ran.

20 Nov. 18:20–23:24. Fog after the river. Couldn’t see anything. Thought about her the whole way.

She stood in the queue with the notebook and the line went forward without her.

“Miss?” said the woman at the counter. “Miss? Are you all right?”

“Yes,” said Yu Jie. “Sorry. My boyfriend writes things down.”

The next time he came up on the 18:20 he had a carrier bag, and on the platform at 23:12, before he had even kissed her, he took a winter coat out of it. Navy. Wool. Bought, he said, from a shop near the harbour, after measuring the sleeve of her cardigan while she was asleep. It was slightly too big. He had allowed, he explained, for jumpers.

He held it open for her on the platform, the way men did in films, and she turned round and put her arms into it, and he did up every button himself, from the bottom to the top, very seriously, while a guard watched, and turned up the collar, and stood back to look.

“Now you can give me mine back,” he said.

She gave it back. On Sunday morning she stole it again anyway, because it smelled of him, and he let her, and went out for buns in his jumper and came back blue with cold and extremely happy.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the weekends she came to him, she took the 18:15 from the capital and arrived at 23:18, and he was always on the platform. Always. Even in the rain. Even the night the train was two hours late because of a fault on the line, and she texted him at nine to say don’t wait, go home, I’ll take a taxi, and he texted back I don’t know how to call a taxi either, which wasn’t true, and was there when she got off at 01:20, asleep on a bench on platform four with his coat over him and a flask of ginger tea in his lap.

She woke him up. He opened his eyes and saw her and smiled, before he was even properly awake, before he knew where he was.

That was the thing she would remember, years later. Not the kissing on the platform, though there was a great deal of kissing on the platform, and a great many families with small children who said ewwww. Not the long nights in the narrow bed in the staff flat with the window open. Not the breakfasts.

The way he smiled before he knew where he was. As if the first thing his body knew, before his brain caught up, was that she was there.

✦ ✦ ✦

In between, they talked on the phone.

Every night. Eleven o’clock, when she got back to her room in the institute residence and he had finished marking. Sometimes for ten minutes. Sometimes until three in the morning, when one of them fell asleep mid-sentence and the other one didn’t hang up, and listened to the breathing on the line, and fell asleep too.

And on Wednesday nights, they worked.

That had been his idea. In the second week, he had gone to a hardware shop at the bottom of the hill and bought a whiteboard, a real one, a metre and a half wide, and screwed it to the wall of his tiny kitchen, beside the fridge, so that it took up the whole wall. Then he propped his laptop on the kitchen counter, facing it, and called her.

“What is that?” she said, when the video came through.

“It’s a whiteboard,” said Miles.

“It’s on your kitchen wall.”

“Yes. It’s the only wall big enough.” He picked up a marker pen. It squeaked. He winced. “I know. I hate them too. But I can’t get a chalkboard into a staff flat, facilities would kill me.” He held up the pen to the camera. “It’s Wednesday. 3:45 was hours ago, but it’s still Wednesday. You said there was a second paper in the corners. I thought—”

She was laughing. On the screen, in her small room at the institute, with her hair in the claw clip and four pens in it and a cup of tea.

“Every Wednesday?”

“If you want.”

“I want.”

So every Wednesday, at nine o’clock at night, five hours apart, they did physics. Him at the whiteboard in his kitchen, with the laptop on the counter. Her at her desk in the capital, with a notebook and the camera tilted down so he could see what she was writing. She talked. He drew. He got it wrong; she corrected him. She got stuck; he asked a question. Sometimes they didn’t talk at all for twenty minutes, just worked, him on the whiteboard and her on paper, and the only sound was the squeak of the marker and the scratch of her pen.

It was the same silence as office 412 at five o’clock.

Except that at about half past ten she would look up from her notebook and say, “You’ve got marker on your face,” and he would wipe it, and make it worse, and she would take a screenshot and refuse to delete it. By Christmas she had eleven. She kept them in a folder on her phone called Data. He was blue in nine of them, and in all eleven he was looking not at the camera but slightly to the side of it, at the place on the screen where her face was.

Over five hours of railway line, through a phone.
