The second paper went to the journal in January. Two names on it. Shen Y.J. and Wei M. Alphabetical, which put her first, which he said was correct anyway, because the idea was hers.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the third week of October, she sent him a photograph.

The group dinner. Professor Huang had taken all eleven of his group to a hotpot restaurant to celebrate a paper, and someone had taken a picture of the long table, everyone red-faced and laughing over the steam. Yu Jie was in the middle, in a red jumper, laughing at something. Professor Huang was at the end, looking pleased with himself. And beside her, with his arm along the back of her chair, was a postdoc Miles didn’t know.

He was very handsome. He was tall and broad-shouldered and had perfect teeth and was laughing at whatever she was laughing at, leaning toward her.

Miles looked at the photograph for a long time.

He called her at eleven.

“Hi,” she said. “Did you get the picture? It was so good, Huang did a speech, he made a joke about corners, nobody laughed except me, I think he was really—”

“Who’s the man,” said Miles. “On your left. With his arm on your chair.”

There was a pause on the line.

“That’s Dr. Qiao,” said Yu Jie. “He’s a postdoc. He does tensor networks. Why?”

Miles sat at his one table in the staff flat and looked at the whiteboard on his kitchen wall, where Wednesday’s corners were still drawn in squeaking blue.

“I’d like to report,” he said carefully, “that I’m jealous.”

Silence on the line.

“I don’t think it’s rational,” said Miles. “I’ve thought about it. I have no evidence that anything is happening. You’re laughing at Huang, not at him. His arm is on your chair, not on you. You sent me the photograph yourself, which nobody does if they’re hiding something. All the data points the other way.” He took a breath. “I’m reporting it anyway. In the interests of transparency. Because I promised myself in September I’d be honest with you, and I think if I don’t say it, it’ll sit in my chest all night and I won’t be able to breathe around it.”

The silence on the line went on.

Then she started laughing.

Not at him. He could tell the difference now. She was laughing the way she had laughed at the cactus joke, with her head on the desk.

“Miles,” she said, when she could speak. “Dr. Qiao has been married for twelve years. He showed me forty photographs of his wife and their sailing boat at the dinner. The arm on the chair is because he's very drunk and the chair is holding him up.” A pause. “Also, he asked me last week whether my boyfriend was the Wei who wrote the paper on lensing in galaxy clusters, and when I said yes, he asked if I could get you to sign his copy.”

Miles put his hand over his eyes.

“Oh,” he said.

“Yes.”

“I’d like to withdraw my report.”

“You can’t,” said Yu Jie. “It’s on the record now. I’m keeping it. It’s the most romantic thing you’ve said to me since the dumplings.” Her voice changed. Softer. “Miles. Thank you. For telling me. Most people don’t. They just go quiet, and you find out three weeks later at dinner when they talk about the weather.”

“I don’t want to talk about the weather.”

“I know,” she said. “I love you. Go to bed. And bring a pen on Friday. For Dr. Qiao.”

He signed Dr. Qiao’s copy of his paper on lensing in galaxy clusters that Saturday, in a café near the institute, and Dr. Qiao, sober, turned out to be a shy, gentle man who talked about his wife and their boat for forty minutes and asked Miles three very good questions about gravitational time delay and nearly cried when Miles said one of them was the kind of question nobody asked.

On the train home, Wang asked, “Same girl?”

“Same girl,” said Miles. “I was jealous of a man with a boat.”

Wang thought about it.

“Happens to the best of us,” he said, and went on down the carriage.

✦ ✦ ✦

In December, there was a storm.

It came in off the sea on a Friday afternoon, the third Friday of the month, his weekend to go to her. By four o’clock, the wind was taking slates off the roofs on Bell Street. By five, the trains were cancelled. All of them. Every line out of the city, north and south, until the morning at least.

He stood on platform four at 17:55 and looked at the board. CANCELLED. CANCELLED. CANCELLED. All the way down.

The noodle woman looked at him from her stall with great sympathy and gave him his noodles for free.

He called her.

“I know,” she said, before he could speak. “I saw. It’s on the news. Are you all right? Are you at the station? Go home, Miles. Please. It’s dangerous.”

“I’m going to wait,” said Miles. “There might be one later.”

“There won’t be one later. They said on the news. Nothing until tomorrow morning. Go home.”

He stood on the platform. The wind was coming through the station roof in great howling gusts. A sign went past, flying.

It was the first weekend they had missed. Since September. Fourteen weekends, his and hers, every Friday since September, and not one missed.

He hadn’t known it would feel like this. He hadn’t known it would feel like being seventeen, standing in a library, watching something come apart that he couldn’t stop.

“Jie,” he said. His voice didn’t work properly.

“I know,” she said, very quietly. “I know. Me too.”

They didn’t say anything for a while. The wind howled through the phone.

“Go home,” she said again. “And call me when you get there. And then don’t hang up. I don’t care if it’s all night. Don’t hang up.”

He went home. Through the storm, on foot, because he wasn’t mad enough to ride a bicycle in it. It took forty minutes. He was soaked through. He called her from the doorway of the staff flat, dripping on the mat beside the cactus, and she answered on the first ring.

He didn’t hang up.

He had a hot bath with the phone on the edge of the bath, on speaker. She read to him from the paper she was refereeing, very seriously, in her most pompous voice, until he laughed so hard he got water in his ear. He made tea with the phone on the counter. He lay in the narrow bed with the phone on the pillow beside him, and the storm outside, and her voice coming out of it, small and tinny and five hours away, talking about nothing. About Tao Tao, who had a boyfriend now, a vet. About Lu Zhiyuan and Kai, who had moved to the capital in October, when Lu Zhiyuan was transferred to the Ministry, and who had her to dinner every other Sunday, and whose coffee was still terrible. About Professor Huang, who had started bringing her a croissant every morning because he had heard from Professor Gao that it was what was done.

At some point, around two, she stopped talking.

He listened. She was asleep. He could hear her breathing.

He lay in the dark with the storm outside and the phone on the pillow and listened to her breathe, five hours away.

In. Out. A small catch at the top of each breath, the one she didn’t know she made. He had heard it from the other side of a narrow bed for three months. He had never heard it from five hours away. The wind threw rain at the window like gravel. Somewhere across the sports ground a slate came off a roof and smashed. He put his hand flat on the pillow beside the phone, where her head would have been, and the cotton was cold, and he left it there anyway.

Then he whispered, very quietly, so as not to wake her:

“I love you.”

And from the phone, so faint it was almost nothing, half-asleep:

“For all n.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The pumps held on the nineteenth of January.

It was a Tuesday. He had been in the basement since six in the morning. He had a PhD student now, a quiet young man called Ouyang who had chosen to work for him over two other offers because, he said, Dr. Wei had once given him full marks for an answer that said I don’t know, but here’s how I would find out. He had one postdoc, funded at last. In September, the national science foundation had given him a grant. His own. Three years. The proposal he had written in March, after the foundation was dissolved. He had asked about the boundary conditions on page four, before anybody else could.

For five months they had been trying to make the horizon hold. The water flowed toward the narrow place in the middle of the tank, faster and faster, and the little waves they sent in from the far end slowed and slowed against it, and for a few seconds, a minute, they stopped. An edge past which nothing came back. And then the flow went unstable, and the water churned, and the horizon broke apart into foam.

On the nineteenth of January, at 8:52 in the evening, it held.

Ouyang saw it first. He was at the laptop on the broken chair from 1997, watching the camera feed, and he said, in a very small voice, “Dr. Wei. Dr. Wei. Look.”

Miles looked.

The water in the long clear tank was flowing steadily toward the middle. Smoothly. No foam. No churning. And the little waves Ouyang was sending in from the left, one after another, were slowing as they came, and slowing, and stopping. Stopping at exactly the same place every time. A line in the water, perfectly still. Holding.

One minute. Two. Five.

At ten minutes, Ouyang started to cry.

At fifteen, Miles took out his phone with shaking hands and called her on video.

It was Wednesday. 8:59 p.m. She was at her desk in the capital, with her notebook open and four pens in her hair, waiting for him to call from the kitchen whiteboard.

“You’re late,” she said. “You’re never late. Where are you? That’s not your kitchen.”

He didn’t say anything.

He turned the phone round. He held it up to the long clear tank, in the light of the bare bulb, with the water flowing toward the middle, and the little waves coming in from the left, slowing, slowing, stopping. All at the same line. Holding.

On the screen, five hours away, she went completely still.

“Miles,” she whispered. “Is that—”

“Fifteen minutes,” said Miles. His voice wasn’t working. “Sixteen now. It’s holding. It’s a horizon, Jie. It’s holding.”

She put both hands over her mouth.

He stood in the basement of the east wing in front of a four-metre tank full of water that had been bought with her grandmother’s money and kept with his, with a PhD student crying on a broken chair and the phone held up to it, so that the person who had given it to him could see.

A black hole. Made of water. On a table in front of you.

He had wanted one since he was nine.

“You did it,” she said, crying. “You did it. You made light bend in a water tank.”

“Not light yet. Waves. Light is next year.” He turned the phone back round to his own face. He was crying too. He hadn’t noticed. “It was you. It was your tank. You bought me time.”

“I bought you a lab,” said Yu Jie, through her tears, and laughed. “You can say it now. I don’t mind any more.”

He laughed.

Behind him, in the long clear tank, the horizon held. Twenty minutes. Twenty-five.

Ouyang, on the broken chair, wiped his face and wrote the time in the lab book in shaking letters. 19 January. 20:52. Stable.

And underneath, because he had seen his supervisor do it every day in a small notebook from his coat pocket, a single word on the right:

Her.

chapters.title: Her Mother Comes to Tea
chapters.desc: No warning, no appointment, pale grey silk on a basement ramp. Mrs. Shen inspects the physics lecturer, his tank, and his only clean mug. He explains entropy. She brings something she was supposed to have thrown away.
chapters.epigraph: “Messy is more likely than tidy, Mrs. Shen. There are more ways to be messy.” “And you think that’s a good thing.” “I think it’s a true one.”
chapters.content:
She came on a Tuesday in March, at 10:40 in the morning, without an appointment.

Ouyang saw her first. He was at the laptop by the tank, logging data, and he heard heels on the basement ramp. Heels were very unusual in the basement of the east wing. Nobody wore heels in the basement of the east wing. The floor was concrete and there were cables everywhere and once, in November, a postdoc had slipped on a puddle and broken her wrist.

He looked up.

A woman was coming down the ramp, very carefully, in pale grey silk and low grey heels, holding a handbag that probably cost more than his stipend. She was perhaps sixty. Her hair was perfect. Her face was perfect. She stopped at the bottom of the ramp and looked at the basement—the broken chairs from 1997, the cables, the laser bench, the long clear tank against the north wall with the water flowing toward the middle—with an expression of polite, total incomprehension, as if she had walked into the wrong room at a party.

Then she looked at Ouyang.

“I’m looking for Dr. Wei,” she said. Her voice was very pleasant. “The man at the front desk said he would be down here. Is he?”

Ouyang opened his mouth.

From under the tank, where he had been lying on his back with a spanner since nine, Miles said, “Ouyang, who is it?”

And then he slid out, and sat up, and saw who it was, and hit his head on the tank.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Mrs. Shen,” he said.

He stood up. He had grease on his hands and his cardigan and, he realised a moment too late, his face. His hair was standing up. He was wearing the old trousers he wore for the lab, with a hole in one knee. His glasses were on his head, not his nose, and he couldn’t find them, and then he found them, and put them on, and she came into focus, and she was still there.

“Dr. Wei,” said Shen Ruolan.

She looked at him. Up and down. At the grease. At the hole in his knee. At the spanner in his hand.

“I was told,” she said, “that you were a lecturer.”

“I am. I’m—this is my laboratory.” He put the spanner down on the laser bench. Then picked it up again. Then put it down. “Ouyang, this is Mrs. Shen. Yu Jie’s mother. Mrs. Shen, this is Ouyang. My PhD student.”

Ouyang stood up so fast he knocked over the broken chair.

“I’ll go and get—” he said. “Something. Coffee. Tea. I’ll—”

“Please,” said Shen Ruolan. “Don’t trouble yourself.”

Ouyang fled up the ramp.

They stood in the basement. Just the two of them. And the tank, humming, the water flowing toward the middle.

“Would you like some tea?” said Miles. “I have a kettle. Down here. And mugs.” He thought about it. “Mug.”

Shen Ruolan looked at him for a long moment.

“Yes,” she said. “Thank you. I would.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The kettle was on a shelf in the corner, beside the old sink, next to a box of jasmine tea and a packet of biscuits Ouyang kept for emergencies.

There was one clean mug.

It said WORLD’S OKAYEST SON.

He looked at it. He thought about washing one of the others, which were in the sink and had been there since Friday. He thought about how long it would take. He thought about her standing there, in pale grey silk, watching him wash mugs.

He made the tea in WORLD’S OKAYEST SON and gave it to her.

She looked at the mug in her hands. She read it. Her perfect face did not change at all.

“Your mother bought you this,” she said.

“My sister,” said Miles. “As a joke. When I was twenty-four. She said I didn’t call home enough to be the world’s best.”

“And do you? Call home?”

“Every Sunday now,” said Miles. “And Wednesdays, my sister calls me.” He paused. “Yu Jie made me. She said I had a mother who phoned the department secretary to ask if I was eating, and that I should be ashamed of myself.”

Something moved at the corner of Shen Ruolan’s mouth. Then it was gone.

She looked for somewhere to sit. There was nowhere, except the broken chairs. She looked at them with deep doubt.

Miles took off his cardigan and put it over the least broken one, the one Ouyang sat on, so that the grease and dust wouldn’t touch her silk.

She looked at the cardigan on the chair. Then at him. In his shirtsleeves, with grease on his face.

She sat down.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You know why I’m here,” she said.

“No,” said Miles honestly.

She held the mug in both hands. She didn’t drink from it.

“My daughter,” said Shen Ruolan, “has not spoken to me in a year. Not since the night at the dinner table, with the Lus. She sent me a ticket to her graduation, by post, and I didn’t go. She has not been to Sunday dinner. She has not been to New Year. She lives in the capital in a room in a residence with a single bed, and works for a man called Huang who brings her croissants, and every other weekend she gets on a train and comes back to this city, and does not come to see me.” Her voice was perfectly pleasant. “She comes to see you.”

Miles said nothing.

“My husband knows where she is,” said Shen Ruolan. “He knew before I did. He went to her graduation. Did you know that? He stood at the back. He told me in September. Three months later. He said, I clapped, Ruolan. I wanted you to know I clapped.” She looked down at the tea. “Thirty-seven years. He has never once kept anything from me. And then he kept that.”

“I didn’t know,” said Miles quietly. “About him telling you.”

“No. You wouldn’t.” She looked up at him. “I came to see what you are, Dr. Wei. What she chose. Instead of everything I made her for.” She looked round the basement. At the cables, the broken chairs, the laser bench, the long tank. At him, in his shirtsleeves, with grease on his face. “And I find a man in a cellar with a hole in his trousers, who serves me tea in a mug that says he is only okay.”

“Yes,” said Miles.

He didn’t argue. He didn’t defend himself. He stood in front of her by the laser bench with his hands at his sides and let her look at him.

“That’s what she chose,” he said. “I’m sorry it isn’t more.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Shen Ruolan looked at him.

Then she looked at the tank.

“What is it?” she said. “That. The water.”

He turned and looked at it too. The long clear tank. The water running the length of the tank, speeding up over the hump in the middle. The camera on its stand. The little waves Ouyang had been sending in from the left, which were still coming, every few seconds, slowing, slowing, stopping at the line.

“It’s a black hole,” said Miles. “Sort of. Made of water.”

She looked at him as if he had said it was a dragon.

“The water flows toward the middle,” he said. “Faster and faster. And if you put a little wave in, it tries to swim against the flow. Upstream. But the closer it gets to the middle, the faster the water is going, until at one point the water is going faster than the wave can swim. And the wave stops. It can’t get any further. It can’t come back.” He pointed. “There. That line. Where they all stop. That’s the horizon. The edge of a black hole. Past that, nothing gets out. Not even light. In a real one.”

She looked at the line in the water. The little waves coming in, slowing, stopping, all in the same place.

“And you made this,” she said. “To study black holes.”

“Yes. Because you can’t go to a real one. They’re very far away. And very dangerous. So you make one you can put on a table.” He looked at it. “I wanted to make one since I was nine.”

She was quiet for a long moment.

“My daughter’s money paid for this,” she said. “Her grandmother’s money.”

“The tank,” said Miles. “Only the tank. She took the rest back. The pumps I paid for from my own budget, and the rest from a grant I got myself.” He looked at her. “She told me it was my choice whether to keep it. I chose to.”

“Why?”

He thought about it. Properly.

“Because it’s the only thing anyone in her family ever gave anyone,” he said, “that wasn’t about what it looked like.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Shen Ruolan put down the tea.

She put it down on the laser bench very precisely, squared to the edge, the way she had put down a square of ivory silk a year ago at a dinner table.

“You think I’m a monster,” she said.

“No,” said Miles.

“You think I ruined her. You think I spent twenty-two years making her into something she wasn’t. A jewel. You think I kept her in a glass case.”

“I think,” said Miles slowly, “that you kept her very tidy.”

She looked at him.

He didn’t know why he said what he said next. He would think about it afterwards, many times. He would tell Yu Jie about it, much later, after the platform, and she would be quiet for a very long time.

He went to the old sink in the corner, where Ouyang’s emergency biscuits were. There was a roll of paper towel on the side. He tore off a sheet. And he came back, and took the pencil from behind his ear, and drew on it.

A box. With a wall down the middle. Dots on one side.

He held it out to her.

“This is entropy,” he said. “It’s the most important idea in physics. More important than black holes. It’s the reason time goes forward.” He tapped the drawing. “You have a box. You have a wall. All the dots on one side, very tidy. Then you take the wall away.” He drew it again, beside the first: the wall gone, the dots spread out through the whole box. “And the dots spread out. Always. They never go back to one side on their own. Do you know why?”

She looked at the paper towel in his hand.

“No,” said Shen Ruolan.

“Because there are more ways to be messy,” said Miles. “That’s all it is. Counting. There are only a few ways for all the dots to be on one side. There are millions and millions of ways for them to be spread out. So they spread out. Not because they want to. Because it’s more likely. Messy is more likely than tidy.” He looked at her. “You can keep the dots on one side. You can. It takes a wall. And it takes energy. All the time. Every single day. You have to keep pushing them back. And the moment you stop pushing—the moment you take the wall away—they go everywhere. Because that’s where they were always going to go.”

She was very still on the broken chair, in pale grey silk, on his cardigan.

“You kept her tidy for twenty-two years,” said Miles quietly. “It must have been very tiring.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Shen Ruolan did not say anything.

The tank hummed. The little waves came in from the left, every few seconds, and slowed, and stopped at the line.

She looked down at the paper towel. At the two boxes. The tidy one and the messy one.

“And you think the messy one is better,” she said finally. Her voice was not quite as pleasant as before. “You think it’s a good thing.”

“I don’t know if it’s good,” said Miles. “I think it’s true.” He paused. “I think she’s happier. I know she is. I can hear it on the phone. She’s in a room with a single bed and a man who brings her croissants and she’s happier than I’ve ever heard anyone be.” He looked at Shen Ruolan. “And I think she misses you. She doesn’t say it. But she does.”

The perfect face moved.

Just at one corner of the mouth. The way it had moved a year ago at the dinner table, when her daughter said I’m not afraid of you any more.

Shen Ruolan looked away.

She opened her handbag. She took out a small handkerchief, white, embroidered, and touched it very precisely to the corner of one eye, and put it back. Then she took out something else.

It was a box.

An old cardboard box, faded, about the size of a shoebox, with a picture on the lid that had once been bright and was now pale with age. A cartoon of a smiling scientist in a white coat, holding up a test tube that was bubbling over with green foam. Across the top, in big cheerful letters: MY FIRST CHEMISTRY SET. AGES 8+.

She held it in her lap.

“Her grandmother gave her this,” said Shen Ruolan. “For her eighth birthday. She set the curtains in the nursery on fire within a week.” Her voice was very level. “I told her I’d thrown it away. I told her it was dangerous, and unladylike, and that I’d thrown it in the rubbish. She cried for three days. And then her grandmother bought her another one and kept it at her house, and every Sunday, for six years, my daughter went to her grandmother’s kitchen and set things on fire, and came home smelling of smoke, and I said nothing, because her grandmother was the only person in that family I had never once won an argument with.”

She looked down at the box.

“I didn’t throw it away,” she said. “I put it in a cupboard in the storeroom. Behind the winter bedding. I don’t know why. I think I thought—” She stopped. “I don’t know what I thought. It’s been there for fifteen years. I found it again on Sunday.”

She held it out.

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles looked at the box. Then at her.

“I can’t take that,” he said. “It’s hers. It should come from you.”

“She won’t take anything from me.”

“She might,” said Miles. “If you asked.”

Shen Ruolan looked at him, with the box held out between them, in the basement of the east wing, by the long tank with the horizon holding.

“I don’t know how to ask her,” she said. “I don’t know how. I’ve never asked her anything. I’ve only ever told her.” Her voice cracked, very slightly, on the last word. She stopped. She drew a breath and put her perfect face back together. “You’re good at asking, she says. Lu Zhiyuan’s mother told me. She said my daughter told Zhiyuan that you are the only person who has ever asked her what she wanted.”

Miles didn’t say anything.

He took the box. Very carefully, in both hands, the way you would take something that might break.

“I’ll give it to her,” he said. “On Friday. She’s coming on the 18:15.” He looked at Shen Ruolan. “And I’ll tell her you kept it. Fifteen years. Behind the winter bedding. I’ll tell her exactly that.”

Shen Ruolan stood up from the broken chair. She brushed off her pale grey silk, though there was nothing on it, because his cardigan had been underneath.

She picked up his cardigan from the chair. She looked at it. At the grease on the elbow. At the hole in the left elbow.

She folded it. Very precisely. In thirds, the way you fold a shirt in an expensive shop. And handed it to him.

“You should have that mended,” she said.

“I will.”

“And your trousers.”

“Yes.”

“And get some more mugs.”

“Yes, Mrs. Shen.”

She went to the ramp. At the bottom, she stopped, and looked back at him, standing in his shirtsleeves with grease on his face and a faded chemistry set in his arms and his folded cardigan on top of it.

“Does she eat?” said Shen Ruolan. “In the capital. Does she eat properly?”

Miles looked at her.

He thought about his own mother, phoning the department secretary.

“Not always,” he said gently. “She forgets. When she’s working on something. She lives on White Rabbit sweets. Professor Huang brings her croissants, and on Sundays Lu Zhiyuan and Kai cook for her.” He paused. “I make her eat when she’s here. Every other weekend. I make eggs. I’m bad at them.”

Shen Ruolan stood at the bottom of the ramp.

“She likes them scrambled,” she said. “Very soft. With spring onions. She always did, when she was small. The cook used to make them for her on Sunday mornings, before her grandmother’s.” A pause. “Not in a pan. In a bowl over hot water. Slowly. That’s the only way she’ll eat them.”

Then she went up the ramp, in her low grey heels, very carefully, over the cables, and was gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ouyang came back down fourteen minutes later with two coffees and a packet of biscuits and an expression of terror, and found his supervisor sitting on the floor of the basement with his back against the laser bench and a faded cardboard box in his lap, looking at it.

“Dr. Wei?” said Ouyang. “Is she—did she—are you all right?”

“Ouyang,” said Miles. “Do you know how to scramble eggs in a bowl over hot water?”

Ouyang looked at him.

“…No?”

“Neither do I,” said Miles. He put the box down very carefully on the bench. “Find out. Please. I need to know by Friday.”

On Friday, at 23:18, on platform four, she got off the 18:15 and he was there, as always, and she ran, as always, and he caught her, as always, and in his arms she felt him holding something, and pulled back, and looked down.

A faded cardboard box. A smiling cartoon scientist. Green foam.

MY FIRST CHEMISTRY SET. AGES 8+.

She stopped breathing.

“Your mother came to the basement,” said Miles. “On Tuesday. She brought this. She said to tell you she didn’t throw it away. She put it in the storeroom, behind the winter bedding. For fifteen years.” He looked at her face. “And she said you like scrambled eggs very soft, with spring onions, in a bowl over hot water. So I learned. Ouyang and I practised all week. We used forty-one eggs.”

Shen Yu Jie stood on platform four with her first chemistry set in her hands, and cried, the way she had in the stairwell. Like something breaking open that had been shut for a very long time.

He held her while she did.

She cried with the box crushed between them, its old cardboard corners digging into both their ribs, because she would not let go of it and he would not let go of her. Her knees went, and he took her weight without a word and stood on platform four holding up a grown woman and a faded chemistry set while the last train to the coast was announced twice over their heads. She said she kept it into his coat. Then she said it again. Then she couldn’t say anything, and only shook, with her face pressed into the place below his collarbone where it fitted, and her fist knotted in his scarf, and the faint stale smell of old smoke rising off the box between them, fifteen years old, from her grandmother’s kitchen.

He didn’t tell her it was all right. He didn’t know if it was. He put his chin on top of her head and his hand on the back of her neck, under her hair, and held on, and let the platform empty around them.

On Sunday morning, in the staff flat, he made her eggs. Very soft. With spring onions. In a bowl over hot water. Slowly.

She ate them all.

He watched her do it, leaning against the kitchen counter, because he still owned only one chair, not touching his own. Every spoonful. As if he were taking readings.

“You’re staring,” she said, with her mouth full.

“They’re the right texture,” said Miles. “I wasn’t sure. Ouyang said the forty-first batch was the best, but Ouyang would say anything to stop eating eggs.”

She held the spoon out to him, with the last mouthful on it.

He ate it off the spoon. She watched his ears go red, which they still did, every time, even now.

Then she picked up her phone, and looked at it for a long time, and typed a message to a number she had not used in a year.

It said only:

Thank you for the eggs.

The reply came eleven minutes later. Three words.

You’re welcome. Darling.

chapters.title: Miles Meets His Own Past
chapters.desc: A flower shop in the Walled City on a Saturday in May. Elowen and Aurelia, together, at last on the same side, telling him he finally chose correctly. And a glass globe that has been quietly setting the roses on fire.
chapters.epigraph: “We fought over you in a library for a week.” “Eight days.” “He counted. Of course he counted.”
chapters.content:
The invitation came on a card with a pressed flower on it. A small blue one, five petals, with a yellow centre.

Saturday 8 May. 11 a.m. The shop. Bring her. — E.

P.S. Aurelia is coming. I’m sorry. I couldn’t stop her. Nobody can.

Miles looked at it for a long time at his one table.

He had not been to the Walled City since he was seventeen. He had never been to the shop. He had seen it once, in a photograph Aurelia had sent him after the gala, out of nowhere, with no message: a narrow green-painted shopfront in an alley, with buckets of flowers outside and a white-painted sign above the door that said Elowen’s.

“What’s the flower?” said Yu Jie, on the phone, that night.

“Blue. Five petals. Small. Yellow in the middle.” He turned the card over. “There’s nothing written about it.”

There was a pause on the line.

“Forget-me-not,” said Yu Jie. “It means true love. Remembrance. Don’t forget me.” Another pause. “Tao Tao’s grandmother grows them. Miles. Why is a woman you knew at sixteen sending you forget-me-nots?”

He thought about it, properly.

“I don’t know,” he said. “But I don’t think it means what you think.”

“What do I think?”

“I think,” said Miles carefully, “that you’re jealous.”

“I am not jealous. I’m merely curious about the botanical significance.”

“You said a woman you knew at sixteen in the voice you use for referees.”

A longer pause.

“…A bit,” said Yu Jie. “A small amount. Within experimental error.”

He sat at his one table with the card in his hand and smiled so hard his face hurt.

“Why do you sound pleased?” she said suspiciously.

“I’d like to report,” said Miles, “that I’m very pleased. I don’t think it’s rational. I’m reporting it anyway.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The Walled City was not a city and had not had a wall for sixty years.

It was a maze of narrow streets in the old part of town, by the river, where the buildings leaned together overhead and there were noodle shops and mah-jong parlours and tiny temples squeezed in between them, and washing hung from every window, and the shopkeepers knew everyone and everything, and outsiders got lost in ten minutes.

They got lost in four.

He had a map on his phone. It was no use at all. The streets weren’t on it, or were on it in the wrong places, or had names on the map that were not the names on the walls. After the third wrong turn, Yu Jie took the phone off him and put it in her pocket and asked an old woman selling tangerines from a basket.

“Elowen’s?” said the old woman. “The flower shop? Everybody knows Elowen’s.” She looked at Miles. At his height, and his glasses, and his grey cardigan, and his general air of a man who had been born in a library. Then she looked at Yu Jie. “Left, left, right, past the noodles, past the temple with the red door. Don’t go down the alley with the black cars at the end of it.”

“Why not?”

The old woman looked at her as if she were simple.

“Because that’s where he parks,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

They found it at 10:58.

It was smaller than the photograph. Narrow, green-painted, squeezed between a noodle shop and a shop that sold paper offerings for the dead. Outside, on the cobbles, there were buckets and buckets of flowers: peonies and roses and lilies and great armfuls of eucalyptus and something white and frothy that Yu Jie didn’t know the name of. The sign over the door said Elowen’s in white paint.

At the end of the alley, beyond it, there were three black cars, parked very neatly, with men in dark suits leaning on them. One of them, a large man with a shaved head and a tattoo on his neck, was eating noodles out of a carton, and looked at Miles as they came round the corner with an expression of calm, polite, enormous interest.

Miles looked back at him.

The large man lifted his chopsticks very slightly in greeting.

Miles, after a moment, raised his hand.

“Do you know him?” whispered Yu Jie.

“No,” whispered Miles. “I think he knows me.”

The bell over the door rang as they went in.

✦ ✦ ✦

Inside, the shop was full of flowers and light and the smell of earth and green stems, and something was burning.

Not much. A thin thread of smoke, rising from a bucket of red roses on the left-hand side of the long wooden counter. The petals on the top three were brown and curled at the edges, as if someone had held a lighter to them.

Behind the counter, with a fire extinguisher in one hand and an expression of black, silent fury, stood Zhao Zhendong.

He was in a black shirt with the sleeves rolled up. He was looking at the roses the way other men looked at people who owed them money. He had clearly been looking at them that way for some time.

He looked up when the bell rang.

He saw Miles.

Even holding a fire extinguisher over a bucket of smoking roses, he glared.

“Hello,” said Miles.

“Hello,” said Zhao.

The roses smoked.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Oh, thank God,” said a voice from the back of the shop, and Elowen came through the curtain from the workroom with her hair coming down and a pair of florist’s scissors in one hand and the look of a woman who has had the same argument every Saturday for a month and has made peace with losing it.

She looked at Miles. Then at Yu Jie. And smiled. The same quiet, warm, much-too-perceptive smile from the terrace.

“You came,” she said. “I wasn’t sure you would. Miles hasn’t been to the Walled City since he was seventeen.”

“How did you know that?”

“Because you told me, at seventeen, that you would never come back here,” said Elowen. “You said it smelled of fish and danger.” She came round the counter. “It does. Hello, Yu Jie. Thank you for bringing him.”

“Thank you for the forget-me-nots,” said Yu Jie.

Elowen looked at her with sudden interest.

“You know what they mean.”

“A friend’s grandmother grows them.”

“Then you know they don’t only mean love,” said Elowen. “They also mean I won’t forget you. Which is what you send to an old friend.” She looked at Miles. “I had to think very hard about what to send. I didn’t want to send you anything that would make your girlfriend want to hit me.”

Yu Jie laughed, startled.

“She already wants to hit me a little,” said Miles. “I think. From the gala. She’s too polite to say.”

“I’m not too polite,” said Yu Jie. “I’m a scientist. I’m reserving judgement until I have more data.”

Elowen looked at her for a moment. Then she started to laugh. Quietly. Then not quietly.

Behind the counter, the roses gave off another small, accusing thread of smoke.

“Zhendong,” said Elowen, without turning round, “it’s eleven o’clock.”

“I know it’s eleven o’clock,” said Zhao.

“It’s doing it again.”

“I know it’s doing it again.” He put the extinguisher down on the counter with great care. “I checked the wiring. I had the wiring replaced. I had the man who replaced the wiring checked.” A pause. “He is still very frightened.”

“It isn’t the wiring.”

“Then it is a person,” said Zhao, with great dignity. “And I will find them.”

And the bell over the door rang again, and Aurelia Chen came in.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came in like a storm front. In white silk trousers and a gold jacket and enormous sunglasses, with her husband behind her carrying four shopping bags and an expression of patient suffering, and she took one look at the shop—the flowers, the smoking roses, the arms dealer with a fire extinguisher, Elowen with her hair coming down, and Miles and Yu Jie by the door—and threw her arms in the air.

“Miles,” she said. “Miles Wei. In the Walled City. In Elowen’s shop. I’m having a medical event. Chen Si, I’m having a medical event, catch me.”

“I’m holding the shopping, my queen,” said Chen Si.

“Then put it down and catch me.”

He put it down. He did not catch her. She did not fall. She came across the shop and kissed Miles on both cheeks, and then turned, and looked at Yu Jie, and took off her enormous sunglasses.

“Hello, sweetheart,” she said. “I said I liked you. In the powder room. Do you remember?”

“Yes,” said Yu Jie. “I remember.”

“I saw the photograph. Page six. The steps of the Harbour Hotel. On your toes, in those trainers.” Aurelia put her hand on her heart. “I cut it out. It’s on my dressing table. Chen Si thinks it’s unhealthy.”

“I think it’s unusual,” said Chen Si, from beside the shopping.

“He thinks it’s unhealthy.” Aurelia turned back to Miles. Her face changed. The wicked brightness went out of it. Something else came in. “And Ruolan came to see you. In your basement. I heard. The whole city heard. Ruolan Shen, in a cellar, drinking tea out of a mug.”

“How did the whole city hear?”

“Because she told Lu Zhiyuan’s mother,” said Aurelia, “and Lu Zhiyuan’s mother told everyone, because she has been so happy since her son came out to her at a dinner table that she tells everyone everything.” She looked at Yu Jie. “Your mother is softening, sweetheart. Like butter. Slowly. In a cold kitchen. But softening.”

Yu Jie didn’t say anything. But her face went very still.

Then Aurelia sniffed the air, and turned round, and saw the roses.

“Oh, not again,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

It had been happening for four Saturdays.

Elowen explained it while Zhao glared at the roses. Every Saturday, at about eleven, something on the left-hand end of the counter got hot. Very hot. The first week it had been a bucket of tulips, which had wilted in twenty minutes. The second week, a paper order slip had gone brown and curled. The third week, a ribbon had started to smoke. This week, the roses.

Only on Saturdays. Only at eleven. Only that end of the counter. For about an hour, and then it stopped, all by itself, as if nothing had happened.

“He thinks it’s sabotage,” said Elowen. “A rival. An enemy. Someone with a grudge and a very strange way of showing it.”

“It is sabotage,” said Zhao.

“He’s had men watching the alley,” said Elowen. “For a month. On Saturdays. Bao has eaten so many noodles at the stall outside that the owner has named a dish after him.”

Miles wasn’t listening. He had been looking at the shop.

He had been looking for about ten minutes, the way he looked at the water in the tank. At the window at the front, facing the alley, where the sun came in. At the light on the floor. At the buckets. At the long wooden counter.

And at the thing on the windowsill.

It was a glass globe. Very large, perhaps forty centimetres across, perfectly round, old, slightly greenish, the kind of thing you might find in an antique shop or a sea captain’s house. It was filled to the brim with water, and in the water floated a single white lotus flower, turning slowly.

It was very beautiful.

The sun was coming through the window and straight through it.

“When did you get that?” said Miles.

Everybody looked at the globe.

“Five weeks ago,” said Elowen slowly. “It was our anniversary. He found it at an auction. It came from an old ship.” She looked at her husband. “He carried it up the alley himself, full of water, because he didn’t trust anyone else not to drop it.”

“Can I try something?” said Miles.

Zhao Zhendong looked at him. Glaring.

“You,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles went to the counter. To the left-hand end, where the roses were.

He took a sheet of white paper from the stack of order slips. He held it up, flat, just above the roses, facing the window. Then, very slowly, he moved it. Up. Down. Toward the window. Away.

And on the paper, as he moved it, a spot of light appeared.

Small. Blinding. Almost white. It sharpened as he moved the paper, shrank to the size of a coin, then a fingernail, then a grain of rice. It was so bright that Yu Jie had to look away.

The paper started to smoke.

He took it away quickly, before it caught. There was a small brown scorch mark in the middle, perfectly round.

The shop was silent.

“It’s a lens,” said Miles.

Nobody said anything.

“A sphere full of water bends light,” he said. “All the light that comes through it gets bent toward the middle, and it comes out the other side and meets in one place. A focus. Like a magnifying glass. People used to start fires with them, on ships.” He looked at the globe on the windowsill, the lotus turning in it. “On Saturdays at eleven, the sun comes down the alley at exactly the right angle. It goes through the globe, and the focus lands on that end of the counter. For about an hour. Then the sun moves on, and it stops.” He pushed his glasses up. “On weekdays it’s probably the same, but the shop’s open earlier and the buckets are somewhere else, so you don’t notice.”

He looked at Zhao.

“It isn’t sabotage,” he said. “It’s your anniversary present.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Nobody breathed.

Zhao Zhendong looked at the glass globe on the windowsill. The one he had carried up the alley himself, full of water, so nobody else would drop it.

He looked at the scorched paper in Miles’s hand.

He looked at the roses.

Then he looked at Miles, and glared at him harder than he had ever glared at anyone in his life.

“Four weeks,” he said. “I had men in the alley for four weeks.”

“I’m sorry,” said Miles.

“I had the wiring replaced.”

“I’m very sorry.”

“I had the electrician followed.”

“That,” said Miles, “seems excessive.”

“And you,” said Zhao, with deep and terrible feeling, “walk in, and look at it for ten minutes, and hold up a piece of paper.”

And Elowen, beside him, started laughing so hard she had to hold on to the counter, and Aurelia was laughing, and Chen Si put his hand over his eyes, and Yu Jie, by the door, was laughing and crying at the same time, watching the man she loved stand in a flower shop in the Walled City holding a scorched order slip and explaining focal points to the most frightening man in the city.

✦ ✦ ✦

They moved the globe.

Not out of the shop. Elowen wouldn’t hear of it. Into the corner, out of the direct sun, on a small table by the cooler. Miles checked it with the paper from every angle. Nothing. No focus. No smoke. Just a glass globe full of water with a lotus in it, and on the ceiling above it, now, a soft, shifting, rippling pattern of light, moving gently as the water moved.

“What’s that?” said Zhao, looking up.

“A caustic,” said Miles. “When light goes through water it bends, and where it bends, it gathers up, and you get those bright lines. They move because the water moves.” He swallowed. “I study that. Light bending. It’s my favourite thing.”

Zhao looked up at the ceiling for a long time. At the soft moving light above his wife’s flowers.

Elowen was looking at it too. Her face had gone very quiet.

“It’s beautiful,” she said.

Zhao looked at her face, turned up to the light.

Something happened to his own. Just for a moment. Then it was gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, with the roses replaced and the shop full of moving light, they sat in the workroom at the back of the shop. Elowen made tea. There were cakes from a bakery, very good ones; Miles recognised them. Su Mei’s. Elowen had ordered them. Of course she had.

Zhao stood by the door of the workroom with his arms folded, where he could see the ceiling.

“We fought over you,” said Aurelia, with a cake in one hand, to Miles. “In a library. In front of the whole school. Do you remember?”

“For eight days,” said Miles.

Aurelia stared at him.

“He counted,” said Elowen. “Of course he counted.”

“Eight days,” said Miles. “It started on a Monday. You took my physics notebook out of my bag and read the front page. No girlfriends until university. And read it out. And Elowen took it back off you. And you said I was yours. And she said I wasn’t anyone’s, I was a person. And then it went on for eight days, and there was the thing with the fire alarm, and the head teacher, and on the eighth day I walked out of the library and didn’t come back.”

He was quiet for a moment.

“I always thought,” he said slowly, “that you were both angry with me. For walking out. For choosing a textbook. That’s what everyone said. Wei chose physics over two girls.” He looked down at his tea. “That isn’t what happened. I didn’t choose physics. I was frightened. I was seventeen and I’d never had anyone want me, and then two people did, and it made the whole school go mad, and people got hurt, and it was because of me. Because I was the thing. So I stopped being a thing anyone could want. I thought that was safest.” He looked up. “I stopped for fourteen years.”

Nobody said anything.

“I wanted to tell you that,” said Miles. “Both of you. I never did. I’m sorry. You were both fifteen. It wasn’t your fault either.”

Under the little table, where nobody could see, Yu Jie’s hand found his knee, and then his hand, and held it. Hard. The way you hold on to someone on a platform.

He didn’t look at her. But his thumb moved, once, across her knuckles.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia had put her cake down.

She looked at him across the little workroom table. There was nothing wicked in her face at all.

“Miles,” she said. “We weren’t angry with you for walking out.” She glanced at Elowen. “We were angry with each other. We didn’t want you. Not really. Elowen wanted someone who didn’t want anything from her. I wanted someone who didn’t want me, because nobody ever didn’t. We were two very unhappy girls who wanted to win something.” She shrugged. “You were the prize. You were never the point.”

“I was asleep on my feet,” said Elowen quietly. “Every day. I sat at your table in the library because it was the only place nobody asked me for anything. You were kind to me. You were the only person in that school who was just kind and wanted nothing back.” She looked at him. “And when we tore it all apart over you, and you walked out, I didn’t blame you. I thought, Good. One of us got out.”

Miles looked at her.

“And now,” said Aurelia. She picked her cake back up. She turned, and pointed it, like a weapon, at Yu Jie, sitting beside him at the little table. “Now you’ve chosen. Properly. At last. Not a textbook. Not fear. Not a rule.” She said the word as if it were dirty. “Her.”

Yu Jie went pink.

“And she’s right,” said Aurelia. “She’s so right I can’t stand it. She stood up in a seminar and told a famous man his gap closes. She told Ruolan Shen to her face at her own table that she wasn’t a jewel. She gave away her grandmother’s money to buy you a bath and then took it back because you were an idiot about it.” She looked at Miles. “She’s worth ten of either of us at fifteen. You finally chose correctly, Miles Wei.” She took a bite of cake. “It only took you fourteen years.”

“Fifteen,” said Miles. “Nearly.”

Aurelia looked at him with her mouth full.

“I hate you,” she said fondly.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the door of the shop, when they were leaving, Elowen gave Yu Jie flowers.

Not forget-me-nots. A small, tight bunch of something Yu Jie had never seen before: white bell-shaped flowers, tiny, hanging from a single green stem, with a scent so sweet it filled the whole doorway.

“Lily of the valley,” said Elowen. “It means return of happiness.” She put them into Yu Jie’s hands. “It’s for both of you. But I wanted to give it to you. Because you’re the one who brought it back.”

Yu Jie looked down at the little white bells.

“Thank you,” she said. Her voice wasn’t quite steady.

Behind Elowen, in the doorway of the workroom, Zhao Zhendong unfolded his arms.

He came through the shop. Past the globe in the corner, with the light moving above it. Past the buckets of lilies. He stopped in front of Miles at the door.

He was very large. He was very close. Miles looked up at him and remembered the gala, the pillar, the flat dark eyes, Don’t be stupid about it.

“Physics boy,” said Zhao.

“Yes,” said Miles.

Zhao looked at him.

“Saturday,” he said. “Next Saturday. Eleven o’clock.”

Miles blinked.

“The light,” said Zhao. “On the ceiling. She likes it.” He paused. “You come. You show me how to make more. Different. Colours.” Another pause. “I will pay you.”

“You don’t have to pay me.”

“I pay everyone,” said Zhao.

Elowen made a small sound behind him.

Miles looked up at the most frightening man in the city, who was asking him, in his flat, expressionless voice, with his huge arms folded, for physics lessons, so that he could fill his wife’s flower shop with light.

“I’ll come,” he said. “When Yu Jie is here. Every other Saturday. I’ll bring a prism.”

Zhao looked at him.

“What is a prism.”

“It splits light into colours,” said Miles. “Rainbows. On the ceiling. On the walls. On the flowers. If you hang them in the window at the right angles, at eleven o’clock on a Saturday, the whole shop will be full of them.”

Zhao was silent for a long moment.

Then, very slowly, the corner of his mouth moved.

“Good,” he said.

He went back into the shop. He stood under the moving light on the ceiling, looking up at it, with his arms folded.

In the doorway, under the bell, Yu Jie laced her fingers through Miles’s, all the way.

“She’s worth ten of either of us,” she said, in a passable Aurelia.

“Aurelia exaggerates.”

“She said you finally chose correctly.”

“I didn’t choose,” said Miles. He looked down at her, with the lily of the valley in her other hand. “You knocked. I just didn’t want you to stop.” A pause. “Also, I’d like it noted that on the phone you were jealous of Elowen, and now she’s given you flowers, and I think you like her better than me.”

“Only a little,” said Yu Jie, and stood on her toes and kissed him, in the doorway of Elowen’s, in full view of three black cars.

And from the end of the alley, as Miles and Yu Jie came out onto the cobbles, the large man with the shaved head and the neck tattoo, who was still leaning on the black car, raised his carton of noodles at them, and said, cheerfully, to nobody in particular:

“Boss said he’d glare at him forever. Told you he wouldn’t last.”

chapters.title: The Apartment With Two Desks
chapters.desc: A one-line letter to the Head of Department. Two flights up on Bell Street. Two second-hand desks that face each other, and a cactus that moves house in a bicycle basket.
chapters.epigraph: “I have a personal interest in Dr.-to-be Shen. I have no academic authority over her. I would like this noted. I would also like it noted that I am very happy.”
chapters.content:
She came home on the last day of August, a year after she left.

Not for a weekend. For good. Or for four years, which was how long a doctorate took, which felt to both of them like the same thing.

It had taken a long time to arrange. Letters. Meetings. A phone call between Professor Gao and Professor Huang that lasted two hours and that Fang Hao, who was in Gao’s office at the time, described afterwards as two dragons negotiating over a pearl, except the pearl was a girl, except she isn’t a pearl, she told everyone very clearly at a dinner table. In the end, the dragons agreed. A doctorate at City University, in Professor Gao’s group, co-supervised by Professor Huang from the capital. Video calls every week. Three months a year in his lab. Corners.

Professor Huang had insisted on one condition. He had written it at the bottom of the agreement in his own hand.

She brings the croissant habit back with her. Gao’s group does not eat breakfast. It is barbaric.

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles wrote a letter.

It was his second letter to the Head of Department in eighteen months. The first had been one page and had taken eleven drafts and four hours. This one was three lines and took him nine minutes, at his desk in office 412, on the first Monday of August, with the door propped open with Principles of Quantum Mechanics.

To: Professor Zhou Lin, Head of Department From: Dr. Miles Wei Re: Declaration of personal relationship

Professor Zhou,

From 1 September, Shen Yu Jie will be a doctoral student in this department, in Professor Gao’s group. She and I are in a relationship, and from that date we will be living together. I have no academic authority over her. I am not her supervisor, I am not on her committee, and I will not examine any of her work. I would like this noted.

I would also like it noted that I am very happy.

Miles Wei

He put it under Professor Zhou’s door at 9:11.

At 9:40, his phone buzzed. An email. From Professor Zhou.

Noted. Both parts. — Z.

And then, a minute later, another one.

P.S. The second part especially.

✦ ✦ ✦

The apartment was on Bell Street, two doors down from Fang’s.

Su Mei had found it. Of course she had. The old woman who lived there had gone to live with her daughter in Hangzhou, and the daughter had asked around for someone quiet and respectable to rent it, and Su Mei had said, “I have a physicist and a physicist. They’re the quietest people I’ve ever met, except when they’re laughing, and they mostly laugh at things nobody else understands.”

It was on the second floor, above a shop that sold tea. Two rooms and a kitchen and a tiny bathroom with a window over the street. The floors were wooden and creaked. The ceilings were high. The windows were old and let in the draught and the light. From the kitchen window, if you leaned out, you could see the round porthole window of the attic above Fang’s, where she had lived for five months.

And in the main room, there was enough space, just, for two desks.

✦ ✦ ✦

They bought the desks on a Saturday, at a second-hand furniture market on the waste ground behind the old railway station, where the night market was.

She wanted old ones. Wooden. With drawers. She didn’t want anything new, she said; she’d had a whole life of new, and everything in it had been chosen by somebody else.

They walked up and down the rows for two hours. He looked at every desk as if it were an experiment. He measured them. He opened every drawer and closed it again to check it ran smoothly. He lay on his back underneath one to look at the joints, and a stallholder came over to ask whether he was all right.

“He’s a physicist,” said Yu Jie.

The stallholder looked at the long legs sticking out from under the desk.

“Ah,” he said, as if that explained a great deal.

In the end, she found them. Not him. Two desks, at the back of a stall run by an old man who had cleared out a school that was closing. Two wooden teacher’s desks, from the nineteen-sixties, heavy and square and scratched all over, with ink stains on the tops and three drawers each down one side. They were exactly the same. They had stood at the front of two classrooms side by side for fifty years.

She put her hand flat on the top of one. He put his on the other.

“These,” she said.

“These,” he agreed.

The old man sold them both for three hundred yuan and threw in a lamp. It took four men and a borrowed van from the tea shop downstairs to get them up to the second floor on Bell Street, and one of the men was Fang Hao, who said the whole way up that he was a theorist and theorists were not meant for this, and the whole way down again that he would not have missed it for anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

They put the desks facing each other.

Not side by side. Not against the wall. In the middle of the main room, under the high window, pushed together front to front, so that whoever sat at one could look straight across at whoever sat at the other.

It had been her idea.

“Like the glass room,” she said. “Like office 412. Like every Wednesday. You on one side, me on the other.” She looked at him across the two scratched wooden tops. “Except now there’s no three metres. Just two desks.”

He sat down at his. She sat down at hers.

They looked at each other across the desks, in the late afternoon light through the high window, with the creaking floor and the smell of tea coming up from the shop downstairs and the sound of Bell Street outside: a bicycle bell, someone calling to someone, Su Mei shouting at a delivery driver two doors down.

The desks were exactly the right width. Across them, he could reach her hand if he stretched.

He stretched.

She put her hand in his, on the scratched wood between them, over a fifty-year-old ink stain the shape of a cloud.

“It’s eighty centimetres,” said Miles. “The two desks together. I measured.”

“Of course you did.”

“Eighty centimetres,” he said, “is much better than three metres.”

She laughed, and squeezed his hand on the old wood, and didn’t let go.

✦ ✦ ✦

Schrödinger moved house in a bicycle basket.

He had to. There was no other way. Miles wouldn’t put him in the van with the desks, in case he got knocked over. He wouldn’t carry him in his hands down the hill, in case he tripped. So on the Sunday, the last thing, after the books and the kettle and the one table and one chair from the staff flat, which were going to Ouyang, who had nothing, Miles wrapped the cactus in a tea towel and put it very carefully in the basket of the old green bicycle, and wheeled the bicycle down the hill, walking, the whole way.

Twenty-two minutes, the straight way. He made it thirty-eight. He took the long way, along the old wall, because it was flatter.

She walked beside him. She didn’t say anything. She knew why.

Halfway along the wall, under the third lamp, where she had stopped one December night in a dress the colour of dawn and his jacket, he stopped too.

He looked at the lamp. At the wall. At the city below, the harbour and the ships and the Shen Building, lit up white across the water.

“You stopped here,” he said. “That night. You said I was the only person in that whole room who knew what you actually looked like.”

“I know.”

“And I said yellow. Biro. Four pens. A cardigan with sweet wrappers in the pocket. One shoelace undone.” He looked at her. At her feet, in her trainers. The left one. Undone. “Ink on your middle finger.”

She looked down at her hand. At the ink.

“You never wash it all off,” said Miles.

She stood under the third lamp on the old wall and looked at him, holding a bicycle with a cactus in the basket wrapped in a tea towel.

“Two years ago,” she said, “I would have given anything for you to touch me right here. Under this lamp. And you couldn’t.”

“I know.”

“You can now.”

He leaned the bicycle very carefully against the wall, with the cactus. He checked it wouldn’t fall. He checked again.

Then he put his hands on either side of her face, under the lamp, the way he had wanted to on a cold December night two years ago, three metres away, with his arms crossed against the cold.

And kissed her.

Schrödinger, in the basket, wrapped in a tea towel, declined to say whether he had seen.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first night, they didn’t unpack.

There were boxes everywhere. Books, mostly. His and hers. They had both underestimated how many books two physicists could own, and the boxes were stacked against every wall, and on the kitchen floor, and in the bathroom, and one, inexplicably, in the bath.

The bed was a mattress on the floor of the second room. The frame was coming on Tuesday.

The cactus was on the windowsill in the main room, between the two desks, where he could see both of them.

They lay on the mattress on the floor with the window open, and the sounds of Bell Street at night coming in: the noodle shop closing, a radio, someone laughing, the bakery two doors down already lit, Su Mei starting the dough for the morning.

She had her head on his chest. He had his arm round her. Neither of them had said anything for a long time.

“Miles,” she said, in the dark.

“Mm.”

“We live together.”

“Yes.”

“In a flat. On Bell Street. With two desks.”

“Yes.”

“I never lived anywhere I chose before.” Her voice was very quiet. “The house on the hill. The flat by the east gate. The room above Fang’s—I didn’t choose that either, you found it. And the room in the capital was the institute’s.” She was quiet for a moment. “This is the first place I’ve ever lived that I chose.”

He didn’t say anything. He tightened his arm.

“We chose it,” she said. “Both of us. And the desks. And the long way down the hill. And the—” She stopped. She lifted her head off his chest and looked at him in the dark. “Is this what it feels like? For other people? Choosing things?”

He thought about it, properly.

“I don’t know,” he said. “I don’t think I chose anything either. Not for fourteen years. I just did what was safest.” He was quiet. “I chose you. That was the first thing. Since I was seventeen. And then everything after it.”

She looked at him.

Then she put her head back down on his chest, and listened to his heart.

“By induction,” she said.

“By induction,” Miles agreed.

A long, contented silence.

“Miles.”

“Mm.”

“Why is there a box in the bath?”

“It’s the safest place,” said Miles, into the dark. “Low centre of gravity. Smooth sides. Nothing can fall on it.” A pause. “It’s the box with the mugs. Yours is on top.”

She lifted her head again.

“You put my mug in the bath so it would be safe.”

“And mine,” said Miles, with dignity. “Underneath. To support it.”

She laughed so hard she rolled off the mattress onto the floorboards, which creaked, and he reached out in the dark and pulled her back by the waist, and held on, and didn’t let her go again until it was light.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning, at 7:15, the first thing she did was get up, still in his grey jumper, and go into the main room, barefoot, over the creaking boards, and sit down at her desk.

He found her there at 7:20, when he came in with two cups of tea. The white mug, and WORLD’S OKAYEST SON.

She was sitting at the scratched wooden desk in the morning light from the high window, with her knees pulled up, opening the drawers. One. Two. Three. Looking into each one. Empty.

“What are you doing?” said Miles.

“Deciding what goes in them,” said Yu Jie. She looked up. “Nobody’s ever let me decide what goes in a drawer.”

He put her tea down on her desk. He went round, and sat down at his, opposite. Eighty centimetres.

And he watched her, over his tea, decide.

In the top drawer, she put her pens. All of them. Including the purple one with the cat on the end.

In the second drawer, her notebooks. Eleven from her undergraduate years. Two from the capital. The red envelope with twenty yuan from Tao Tao’s grandmother. A brown envelope with two hundred and twelve notes in red ink.

In the bottom drawer, very carefully, she put a faded cardboard box, with a smiling cartoon scientist and green foam on the lid.

MY FIRST CHEMISTRY SET. AGES 8+.

She closed the drawer.

Then she opened the top drawer of his desk, across from her, without asking, which made him laugh, and put something in it.

He leaned forward to look.

A plastic bag. Inside it, sticky notes. Yellow ones, every one in his small neat handwriting. Every joke he had stuck to the side of her tea, every note, from the third Wednesday of October to the last Wednesday before graduation. Thank you. Corners. (No joke today. Sorry.) Why did the photon take the train?

She put the bag in his drawer, beside the little stack of pink ones held together with a paper clip that he had been keeping there since October. Cu-Te. No chemistry. Acute one.

“You kept them,” he said. “Mine.”

“Of course I kept them. They were on my list. Twelve things.” She looked at the two piles side by side in his drawer, yellow and pink. “I counted, last night, while you were asleep. Yours and mine together. A hundred and twelve.” She closed his drawer. “They live there now. Together. Where the purple pen used to be.”

Across the eighty centimetres of two old teachers’ desks, in the morning light, on Bell Street, with the smell of bread coming in from two doors down, Miles Wei looked at the woman sitting opposite him in his grey jumper, with ink on her middle finger and one shoelace undone, though she wasn’t wearing shoes.

He had a ring in his coat pocket.

He had had it for three weeks. He had not decided yet how to give it to her. He had a plan. He was not going to tell her about the plan.

He drank his tea.

“What?” said Yu Jie. “You’re looking at me like you’re thinking about something.”

“I’m always thinking about something.”

“You’re thinking about something specific.”

“Yes,” said Miles.

She narrowed her eyes at him across the desks.

He smiled into WORLD’S OKAYEST SON, and said nothing at all.

chapters.title: A Ring Hidden in a Problem Set
chapters.desc: The second Wednesday of September, two years on, 3:47 p.m. Three problems on graph paper, a man who is a very bad liar, and a 113th sticky note.
chapters.epigraph: “I’ve got a problem I don’t know the answer to.” “You’re lying.” “How can you tell?” “Your ears.”
chapters.content:
On the second Wednesday of September, at 3:45 in the afternoon, Shen Yu Jie, doctoral student, first year, came up the stairs to the fourth floor of the Hall of Science.

She still came on Wednesdays.

She didn’t have to. She lived with him. She saw him every morning across eighty centimetres of two old teachers’ desks, and every evening, and every night. She could have talked to him about physics at breakfast, and often did, with her mouth full of scrambled egg, very soft, with spring onions, made in a bowl over hot water.

She still came on Wednesdays. At 3:45. To office 412. Because office hours were Tuesdays and Thursdays, and she had never once come on a Tuesday or a Thursday, and she wasn’t going to start now.

The door was propped open with Principles of Quantum Mechanics.

She knocked anyway.

“It’s open,” said his voice. “Unless you’re from facilities.”

“I’m not from facilities,” said Yu Jie.

“No,” said Miles. “I know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He was at his desk. Not at the chalkboard. At the desk, with his hands flat on it, sitting very straight, as if he had been sitting like that for some time.

On the desk in front of him, there was a white mug of jasmine tea, steaming. And beside it, a sheet of graph paper, folded once.

She stopped in the doorway.

She knew that posture. She had seen it on a terrace above a harbour, on a dark corner one block from a blue door, at the top of four flights of stairs at 4:01. She knew what his hands did when he was holding something inside them very carefully.

“What’s wrong?” she said.

“Nothing’s wrong.”

“You’re sitting like you’re about to tell me you’ve been offered a job in Antarctica.”

“I haven’t,” said Miles. “Nobody wants a theorist in Antarctica. There’s nothing to theorise about. It’s just ice.” He pushed his glasses up. “Sit down. Please. In the chair.”

She sat down in the Wednesday chair.

He pushed the tea across the desk toward her. Then the folded sheet of graph paper.

“I’ve got a problem,” he said. “I don’t know the answer to it. I wondered if you could help.”

She looked at him.

She looked at his ears.

“You’re lying,” said Yu Jie.

He went still.

“How can you tell?”

“Your ears,” said Yu Jie. “They go red when you lie. They went red in October, two years ago, when you said Bohr atoms were physically inaccurate and you didn’t care about my calendar. They went red at the gala when Aurelia asked if you’d missed her. They’re red now.” She narrowed her eyes. “You know the answer.”

“I might know the answer,” said Miles. His ears were the colour of a postbox. “But I want you to find it. Yourself. Without any help.” He paused. “I promise it’s a real problem. Three, actually. It’s a problem set. You can do it however you like. The long way or the short way.”

She looked at the folded graph paper. At his red ears. At his hands, flat on the desk, very still.

Something went through her. Very fast. She didn’t let it reach her face.

She unfolded the paper.

✦ ✦ ✦

PROBLEM SET 1 Due: whenever you like

Problem 1.

A particle is confined to a building of N floors. Its probability of being found on floor n is proportional to the number of times a certain student has climbed the stairs past floor n to reach the fourth floor on a Wednesday, minus the number of times she has stopped and cried on the landing between floors n and n + 1, plus the number of times she has run up all four flights at once in a graduation gown.

Using the data in Appendix A, find the floor on which the particle is least likely to be found, excluding the ground floor, which is where everyone starts.

She read it twice.

She looked up at him.

He was looking at the window. Very carefully. At Schrödinger’s replacement, a small round cactus Fang Hao had given him when Schrödinger moved to Bell Street, which Fang Hao had named Heisenberg, because, he said, you can never be sure where Miles has put it.

She turned the page over.

Appendix A.

It was a table. Every Wednesday since the second Wednesday of September, two years ago. Every one. With a column for the date, and a column for floors climbed, and a column for stopped on landing (Y/N), and a column for ran (Y/N). In his small neat handwriting. Two years of Wednesdays.

There was only one Y in the second column, and it wasn’t a Wednesday. He had added it in a row of its own, out of order, with a note: Monday. I know. It counts. Twenty-third of February. Landing between the third floor and the fourth.

There was only one Y in the third column. Twentieth of June. All four flights.

She sat in the Wednesday chair with the problem set on her knee, and couldn’t breathe for a moment.

Then she picked up a pen from her claw clip—the purple one, with the cat—and started to work.

✦ ✦ ✦

It wasn’t hard. It wasn’t meant to be hard. It took her six minutes, and she could have done it in two, but she wanted to take her time. She wanted to look at every row of the table. Every Wednesday. 1 Oct. 4 floors. N. N. 11 Feb. 3 floors. N. N. That was the glass room. 11 March. 0. N. N. 18 March. 0. N. N. The two weeks. Zeros. He had written them down. He had written down the Wednesdays she didn’t come.

The answer was the second floor.

Because the second floor was where Professor Gao’s lab was, and on most of the Wednesdays she had come up from the lab, so she never climbed the stairs past it from below. It was the floor she had passed least often. Except the ground floor, which was where everyone started.

She wrote 2 at the bottom of the page.

Then she looked at it for a while.

Second floor.

She thought about the flat on Bell Street. Two doors down from Fang’s. Above the tea shop.

On the second floor.

She looked up. He was still looking at Heisenberg, very hard.

She turned the page.

✦ ✦ ✦

Problem 2.

Two objects of identical construction, made of wood in approximately 1964, have stood at the front of two classrooms side by side for fifty years. They are now placed front to front, under a high window, so that two physicists sitting at them may see each other.

Each object has width w. When placed front to front, the total distance between the far edges is D.

The professional distance between the two physicists, in the period from the second Wednesday of September to 16:00 on the twentieth of June, was approximately three metres (constant).

Find D. Express your answer in centimetres. Compare it to three metres. Comment.

She put her hand over her mouth.

She didn’t need to work it out. She knew it. He had said it the first afternoon, his hand over hers on a fifty-year-old ink stain the shape of a cloud.

She wrote it anyway. Properly. Because he had asked her to do it properly, and because she wanted to see it written down in her own hand.

D = 80 cm.

Comparison: D / 3 m = 0.267. D is approximately one quarter of the professional distance.

Comment:

She stopped. She held the purple pen over the page.

Comment: Much better.

She turned the page. Her hands were not quite steady.

✦ ✦ ✦

Problem 3.

In the top drawer of the object described in Problem 2 (the one on the left, facing the window), there is a collection of N sticky notes.

The notes are of two colours. The yellow ones were written by a lecturer and stuck to the side of a cup of tea on Wednesday afternoons. The pink ones were written by a student and stuck to the door of office 412. Neither of them ever counted. One of them did, eventually, on the first night in a new flat, while the other was asleep.

Find N + 1.

Hint: you don’t need a hint.

And in the margin, very small, in the bottom corner, where once, two years ago, a girl in a yellow sundress had hidden the answer to a problem she had already solved:

You don’t need help. You never did. But I’d like to be there anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

She sat in the Wednesday chair.

She did not write the answer. She didn’t need to. She knew it. She had counted them herself, on her knees beside the mattress on the floor of the new flat, by the light from the street, while he slept with his arm flung out across the pillow where she had been.

A hundred and twelve.

N + 1.

A hundred and thirteen.

She looked up.

The chair across the desk was empty.

The door of office 412 was still propped open with Principles of Quantum Mechanics. The white mug of jasmine tea was still steaming on the desk. Heisenberg was on the windowsill.

He was gone.

She hadn’t heard him go. She had been reading. She had been reading every row of two years of Wednesdays and she had not heard the chair or the door or his footsteps in the corridor.

On the chalkboard behind the desk, where he had been sitting, there was writing. Fresh. She hadn’t seen it when she came in, because he had been sitting in front of it.

Problem set due: whenever you like.

I’ll be at my desk.

(The one on the left. Facing the window.)

✦ ✦ ✦

She ran.

She didn’t decide to. Her legs did it. She was out of the chair and through the door and down the corridor before she knew she was moving, past office 413, where Fang Hao’s door was wide open and Fang Hao was standing in it with a croissant halfway to his mouth and an expression of total, radiant, bursting knowledge, and he shouted after her “GO,” exactly as Su Mei had shouted it in the Great Hall, and she went.

Down the back stairs. Four flights. Past the landing with the narrow window. Past the third floor. Past the second. Through the fire door, through the lobby, past Mr. Pan at the porter’s desk, who did not look up from his martial arts novel but held out, without a word, as she went past, her trainers, which she hadn’t noticed she had kicked off under the Wednesday chair. Fang Hao must have sent them down in the lift. She didn’t stop to wonder how he’d beaten her. She took them and ran out of the main doors barefoot and down the steps.

Twenty-two minutes down the hill, the straight way, walking.

She did it in eleven.

✦ ✦ ✦

Bell Street. The tea shop. Two doors down from Fang’s. Su Mei on the step of the bakery with her arms folded, watching her come running down the street barefoot with her trainers in her hand and four pens falling out of her hair, and not saying anything at all, and not having to.

The narrow stairs. The second floor. The door, which was unlocked.

The main room. The high window. The afternoon light.

The two desks, front to front, eighty centimetres.

He was sitting at his. The one on the left. Facing the window.

He had got there first. On the bicycle, the straight way. He was still slightly out of breath. His glasses were crooked and his hair was standing up at the back and his ears were still the colour of a postbox.

The top drawer of his desk was closed.

She stood in the doorway, barefoot, with her trainers in her hand, breathing so hard she couldn’t speak.

He looked at her.

“You didn’t write the answer down,” he said. “To problem three.”

“I didn’t need to,” she said, when she could. “I knew it.”

“What is it?”

“A hundred and thirteen.”

He didn’t say anything.

She dropped her trainers. She crossed the room. She came round to his side of the desks, the left side, facing the window, and stood beside his chair.

And she opened the top drawer.

✦ ✦ ✦

Two piles of sticky notes. Yellow and pink. A paper clip on the pink. A plastic bag round the yellow.

A hundred and twelve.

And on top of both, a hundred and thirteenth.

Yellow. In his handwriting. Folded in half, and then in half again, into a small square, around something small and hard.

She picked it up.

She unfolded it. Very slowly. The way you would unfold something that might break.

Inside, on the yellow square, in his small neat writing, it said:

Why did the physicist propose with a problem set?

Because he knew she’d only say yes to something she’d solved herself.

And under that, smaller:

(This one isn’t a joke.)

And in the middle of the note, where he had folded it around, there was a ring.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was very simple.

A thin band of gold. A single small stone, clear and bright, set low so it wouldn’t catch on anything, because she worked with her hands and he had thought about that. It was not a jewel. It was not the kind of ring her mother would have chosen, or the Lus, or anyone in a ballroom. It would not have been noticed across a room.

She picked it up. She turned it in the light from the high window.

Inside the band, engraved, very small, there were two symbols.

∀n

For all n.

She stood beside his desk with the ring in one hand and the hundred and thirteenth sticky note in the other, in the afternoon light, on the second floor, on Bell Street, and couldn’t see either of them, because she was crying too hard.

He had stood up.

He was standing beside her. Not three metres away. Not eighty centimetres. Right there.

And then he wasn’t standing. He was on one knee, on the creaking wooden floor, between the two desks, in his grey cardigan with the elbow mended—Su Mei had done it, after Shen Ruolan told him to—looking up at her.

“I had a speech,” he said. “I had eleven drafts.”

“I know you did.”

“I can’t remember any of them.”

“I know,” said Yu Jie, crying and laughing at once. “You never can. That’s all right. Ask me.”

He looked up at her. At her wet face and her bare feet and the pens falling out of her hair. At the ink on her middle finger.
