“Shen Yu Jie,” said Miles Wei. “Will you marry me?”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t answer.

Not with words. She was a physicist. She was precise.

She turned round. She picked up the purple pen with the plastic cat on the end from where it had fallen onto his desk. She took the hundred and thirteenth sticky note. She put it flat on the scratched wooden top of his desk, beside the problem set, and under (This one isn’t a joke), in her small round quick handwriting, she wrote:

Yes.

And then, because she would not leave anything unproved:

(For all n.)

She held it out to him.

He read it, kneeling on the floor between the two desks.

He read it twice.

Then he took the ring from her hand, very carefully, and she held out her left hand, and it was shaking, and so was his, and it took him three tries to get it on, because neither of them could hold still, and on the third try she laughed and he laughed and it went on.

It fitted. Of course it fitted. He had measured. She would find out later how: he had borrowed a ring of hers from the drawer in the bathroom, one of Tao Tao’s grandmother’s cheap jade ones that she wore on Sundays, while she was asleep, and taken it to the jeweller in his pocket, and brought it back the same day, and she had never noticed.

He looked at the ring on her finger. The thin gold band. The small clear stone. Beside the ink stain.

“It isn’t a jewel,” he said. “I’m sorry. I thought about it. I didn’t want to give you a jewel. You told your mother you weren’t one.”

“It isn’t a jewel,” agreed Yu Jie, kneeling down on the creaking floor in front of him, so they were at the same height. “It’s a proof.”

And she kissed him, between the two desks, on the floor of the first place she had ever chosen to live.

✦ ✦ ✦

Two doors down, on the step of the bakery, Su Mei unfolded her arms.

She took her phone out of her apron pocket. She typed one message. To the croissant man, who was at that moment running down the hill from the Hall of Science with a paper bag in one hand and his phone in the other, having been unable to bear it any longer.

Window’s open. I heard her laugh. That means yes.

Fang Hao stopped dead in the middle of Bell Street, by the noodle shop, and read it, and put his face in the paper bag, and a passing cyclist had to swerve to avoid him.

And at the Hall of Science, in office 412, on the windowsill, Heisenberg the cactus sat beside a white mug of jasmine tea, still faintly warm, that nobody had drunk. Behind it, on the chalkboard, in the bottom right-hand corner, where once a girl in a yellow sundress had written a date, there was a new one, very small, in his handwriting, written at 3:30 that afternoon before she came:

Second Wednesday of September. 3:47 p.m.

Base case.

chapters.title: Quod Erat Demonstrandum
chapters.desc: Epilogue. Two red booklets in the morning. A garden behind the Hall of Science at 4:01 in the afternoon. A blackboard on an easel, a cake covered in Bohr atoms, and a proof that is finally finished.
chapters.epigraph: “Q.E.D. Which was to be demonstrated.”
chapters.content:
They got married twice on the twentieth of June.

The first time was at nine in the morning, at the Civil Affairs Bureau on Harbour Road, in a room with strip lights and a queue and a woman behind a desk who had married forty couples that week and stamped their forms with the efficiency of a machine. They sat on plastic chairs in front of a red backdrop and had their photograph taken for the certificate, side by side, shoulders touching, and the photographer said closer three times and then gave up and took it anyway. The woman stamped the forms. She handed them two small red booklets.

Miles opened his and looked at it for a long time.

Wei Miles. Shen Yu Jie. A photograph of the two of them against a red background. She was laughing. He was looking at her instead of the camera.

“That’s it?” he said.

“That’s it,” said the woman behind the desk. “You’re married. Next.”

They walked out onto Harbour Road into the June sunshine with two red booklets, married, and stood on the pavement, and looked at each other.

“That was very efficient,” said Miles.

“It was,” said Yu Jie.

“I thought it would feel different.”

“It will,” she said, and took his hand, the left one, with the thin gold band on it that matched hers. “At 4:01.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The second time was in the garden behind the Hall of Science.

It was not, strictly, a garden. It was a square of lawn between the back of the physics building and the back of the chemistry building, with a ginkgo tree in one corner, a stone sundial in the middle that had been put there in 1958 and had never told the right time, because whoever installed it had got the latitude wrong, and a bench where Professor Gao smoked when the balcony was too windy. Students crossed it to get to the canteen. Nobody had ever thought of it as anywhere.

Professor Zhou had given permission in October. In writing. In a one-line letter that said: Granted. I would like to be invited. He had been invited.

By three o’clock on the twentieth of June, it was full of chairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

Fang Hao was in charge of the chairs.

He was also in charge of the rings, the timing, the blackboard, the order of service, and keeping Miles from having a breakdown in office 412 between one and three. He was best man. He had accepted the role in October with tears in his eyes and a croissant in his hand and had been unbearable about it ever since.

“Sit,” he said, at 3:20, pushing Miles down into the Wednesday chair. “Breathe. Eat this.”

It was an egg sandwich. On proper bread. In triangles.

“I can’t eat,” said Miles.

“Eat or Mei will know. She always knows.” Fang Hao stood over him. “You’ve written a proof on that board downstairs. I’ve read it. It’s very good. The base case made me cry. Su Mei said it was the most romantic thing she’d ever read, and she once read a love letter her grandfather wrote in 1952 that was eleven pages and described her grandmother’s eyebrows.”

“Does it hold up?” said Miles. “The proof. Is it rigorous?”

“Miles,” said Fang Hao gently. “It’s a wedding.”

“I know. But is it rigorous?”

Fang Hao looked at him.

“Yes,” he said. “It’s rigorous.”

Miles ate the egg sandwich.

✦ ✦ ✦

They came at half past three.

His parents first. A small, quiet, grey-haired couple who had come up from the coast on the train on Thursday and had been staying in Su Mei’s attic room, which Su Mei had insisted on, under the sloping ceiling, beside the round window. His father in a brown suit he had bought for the occasion, with a pocket square that Wei Lan had made him wear. His mother in blue, carrying a bag of oranges, because she had heard about the oranges, and had decided it was the law. They had met Yu Jie for the first time in August, two years ago, in the small flat by the sea, and his mother had cooked eleven dishes, and Yu Jie had folded all the dumplings, and his father had sat with her at the kitchen table after dinner and talked about optics for three hours from the same library books he had borrowed for his son when Miles was nine. When she left, his mother had held her face in both hands and said, Thank you for making him laugh, and Yu Jie had cried on the train all the way home.

Wei Lan behind them, in green, already crying, which she said was professional and that she did it at every wedding.

Professor Gao, in her black jacket, sat in the front row on the left, where she could see the blackboard.

Professor Zhou, in a cardigan, with his reading glasses actually on his nose.

Tao Tao, in yellow, the maid of honour, with her vet, a cheerful enormous young man called Big Liu who had once delivered twin calves in a snowstorm and was terrified of Professor Gao.

Lu Zhiyuan and Kai, in matching grey, sitting together, openly, in the third row. Lu Zhiyuan’s mother beside them, in jade, holding her son’s hand. Not his father. Not yet. But his mother.

Elowen and Zhao, in the fourth row. Elowen in green silk. Zhao in black, holding a small glass prism up to the sunlight with great seriousness and turning it, very slightly, every time a rainbow appeared on the back of the chair in front, so that it landed on his wife’s hands. He had been practising for a year, every other Saturday, with his favourite physics teacher. They had come straight from the airport, from a month in Patagonia, and Elowen was still sunburnt. Aurelia and Chen Si beside them. Aurelia in gold, naturally. Chen Si in grey, with his hand on his wife’s knee, mildly prepared for anything.

Professor Huang, from the capital, with a box of croissants.

Bai Tianyu, now a final-year student, who had asked if he could come and been told yes and had been talking about it for months.

Ouyang, the PhD student, who had made the lab book entry. Dr. Qiao from the capital with his wife. Old Huang and Lin Ping. Mr. Pan, without his novel. Madam Kong, from the fortieth floor, who had come on her own and brought a box of biscuits from her desk drawer.

Dr. Ren Bo, who had been asked to help carry the cake, and had said yes.

And at the back, by the ginkgo tree, in a white apron over her good blouse, standing guard over a table with a cake on it the size of a small car, Su Mei.

The cake was seven tiers.

It was white. And on every tier, in purple icing, all the way round, there were tiny Bohr atoms. Hundreds of them. Physically inaccurate. Abandoned in 1925.

On the top tier, there was a single square of gold.

✦ ✦ ✦

The front row on the right was for the bride’s family.

It had three seats.

At a quarter to four, a tall, silver-haired man in a dark suit came round the side of the Hall of Science and stood at the edge of the lawn, looking at the chairs, as if he had never seen chairs before.

Shen Guoqiang.

He had come to the flat on Bell Street, in February, at seven in the morning, alone, without telling anyone, and climbed the two flights of narrow stairs and knocked, and when his daughter opened the door in her pyjamas he had stood on the landing with his expressionless face and said, I would like to walk you. If you’ll let me. I didn’t walk you anywhere when you were small. I would like to walk you to this. And she had cried, and said yes, and he had come in, and sat at Miles’s desk, facing hers, and drunk tea out of WORLD’S OKAYEST SON, and asked her, for the first time in his life, about corners.

He sat down in the first seat of the front row on the right.

Behind him, a few minutes later, his son. Shen Yu Ming. Thirty-six. In a perfect suit. On his phone. He sat down in the second seat, and looked at the lawn and the chairs and the sundial and the cake covered in atoms with polite, total indifference. Then he looked up at the blackboard on its easel at the front, where something was written that he couldn’t read, and something moved in his handsome cold face. He put his phone in his pocket.

The third seat was empty.

At 3:58, it was still empty.

At 3:59, there was the sound of heels on the path. Low ones. Careful.

Everyone turned round.

✦ ✦ ✦

Shen Ruolan came round the side of the Hall of Science alone.

She was not in grey. For the first time anyone at that wedding could remember, she was not in pale grey silk, or pale blue, or any of the cool pale colours she had worn to every gala for thirty-eight years.

She was in yellow.

Not bright. A soft, pale, butter yellow. A plain dress, well cut, very simple. No diamonds. One strand of pearls, small ones, very old, that Madam Kong recognised with a small gasp in the fifth row: they had belonged to the late Madam Shen Lihua, who had worn them every Sunday in her kitchen, while her granddaughter set things on fire.

She walked down the side of the chairs, past the ginkgo tree, past the cake covered in atoms, which she looked at, and past Professor Gao, who looked at her and did not smile, and she sat down in the third seat of the front row on the right, beside her husband.

Shen Guoqiang turned his head and looked at his wife.

She did not look at him. She looked straight ahead, at the blackboard on the easel.

He reached over, without a word, and put his hand over hers on her knee.

She let him.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 4:00, the music started. It was a string quartet of four second-years from the music department who had been bribed with a crate of Su Mei’s egg tarts.

At 4:00 and thirty seconds, Miles came out of the back door of the Hall of Science with Fang Hao and walked across the lawn and stood at the front, beside the blackboard on its easel, by the sundial that had never told the right time.

He was in the tuxedo. The one from the gala. The one his sister had made him buy and not rent. You’ll need it again.

It fitted. Su Mei had taken it in.

In his inside pocket, there was a purple pen with a plastic cat on the end. She had given it to him that morning, at breakfast, across the two desks. Something borrowed, she had said. Give it back after.

He stood at the front and looked at the back door of the Hall of Science and didn’t breathe.

At 4:01, it opened.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came out on her father’s arm.

Not in white. Not in silk. Not in anything her mother would have chosen, or the Lus, or a wedding magazine.

In yellow.

A long yellow dress, soft and plain and light, that moved when she walked. Tao Tao’s grandmother had made it. She had come in on the train from the village in March with a bolt of yellow cotton and her sewing machine and stayed in Tao Tao’s cousin’s flat for six weeks and made it by hand, and refused any payment except a red envelope with twenty yuan in it, the same twenty yuan, which Yu Jie had given back to her.

On her feet, under the dress, trainers. White ones. New. And on them, in biro, all over, in small round quick handwriting: equations. The harmonic oscillator. The Schrödinger equation. Her corners. And on the left toe, very small: P(1).

In her hair, the claw clip. Four pens.

No pearls. No diamonds. Nothing anyone in a ballroom would notice across a room.

She came across the lawn on her father’s arm. Past the cake. Past the ginkgo tree. Past the rows of chairs: past Su Mei and Madam Kong and Mr. Pan and Old Huang; past Bai Tianyu, who was crying; past Dr. Qiao, who was staring; past Elowen and Zhao, who held up his prism and threw a rainbow across the yellow dress as it went by, without the slightest change of expression; past Lu Zhiyuan and Kai and Lu Zhiyuan’s mother; past Tao Tao, who wasn’t even pretending not to cry; past Professor Huang, past Professor Zhou, past Professor Gao in the front row on the left.

Past her mother in the front row on the right, in yellow.

She saw. She stopped walking for a second. She looked at her mother, sitting in butter yellow, in her grandmother’s Sunday pearls.

Her mother looked back at her.

Neither of them said anything. Across two years. Across a dinner table and a single pearl on a silver stand and a chemistry set behind the winter bedding.

Then Shen Ruolan nodded. Once. Very small.

Yu Jie’s face crumpled. She held on to her father’s arm.

She walked the last five steps.

✦ ✦ ✦

Shen Guoqiang put his daughter’s hand into the physicist’s hand.

He held them both, for a moment, between his own. Then he looked at Miles. His expressionless face did not change at all.

“You explained entropy to my wife,” he said. “In a cellar. With a paper towel.”

“Yes,” said Miles.

“She told me about it. In the car. For forty minutes.” Shen Guoqiang paused. “Thirty-eight years. She has never once talked to me about anything for forty minutes.”

He let go of their hands.

He went and sat down beside his wife.

Miles was still holding her hand. A little too tightly, the way he had held it on the path to the Hall of Science two summers ago, as if someone might try to take it off him.

He bent his head, very slightly, toward her ear.

“You’re wearing yellow,” he said, under the string quartet.

“You noticed.”

“I always notice.” His voice was not steady. “You have the harmonic oscillator on your left shoe. You’ve got the sign wrong in the second term.”

“I know,” she whispered. “I did it on purpose. So you’d look.”

He looked down at her. Sixty people were watching, and he looked at her as if there were nobody in the garden at all, and she felt it all the way down to the biro on her toes.

✦ ✦ ✦

Professor Gao stood up.

There was no celebrant. There didn’t need to be; they were already married, by a woman with a stamp on Harbour Road. But there had to be somebody to stand at the front and say something, and they had both known for a year who it had to be, and Professor Gao had said, when they asked her in her office, Absolutely not, and then Fine, and then gone out onto the balcony and smoked three cigarettes one after another, and Fang Hao, who was there, swore she had been crying.

She stood beside the blackboard in her black jacket.

She did not smile.

“I have supervised forty-three final-year students in twenty-two years,” said Professor Gao. “Seven of them were brilliant. One of them is standing in front of me in a yellow dress with the Schrödinger equation on her shoes.” She looked at Miles. “And I sat on the panel that hired the man next to her, and watched him for five years, and told her once on a balcony that he was the loneliest man I had ever met.”

Miles looked at the grass.

“I was right,” said Professor Gao. “He was.” She paused. “He isn’t any more.”

She looked out at the chairs. At all of them.

“I don’t believe in speeches,” she said. “I believe in proofs. So I’ll be brief. These two people asked me to stand up here and say something true. Here is something true. In twenty-two years in this building, I have never seen two people work so hard to do the right thing, for so long, at such cost, when it would have been so easy to do the wrong one.” Her voice was very level. “They waited two hundred and sixty-six days. He wrote a letter. She gave back her grandmother’s money. Neither of them ever once asked the other to be less than they were.” She stopped. “That’s all. That’s all I have to say. Now they’re going to finish the proof, and then you can all have cake, and I’m going to go and stand behind the chemistry building and smoke.”

She sat down.

From the fifth row, Madam Kong said, “Hear, hear,” very quietly, and blew her nose.

✦ ✦ ✦

The blackboard on the easel had been carried out of room 301 that morning by Fang Hao and Dr. Ren Bo and Bai Tianyu, with Professor Zhou’s permission, which he had given in writing in one line: Granted. Bring it back.

On it, in white chalk, in his small neat handwriting, there was a proof.

They had written it together, over three Wednesdays, across eighty centimetres of two old teachers’ desks.

THEOREM. For all n ≥ 1: on day n, we choose each other.

PROOF (by induction).

Base case (n = 1). The second Wednesday of September. 3:47 p.m. A student came to an office on the wrong day with a problem she had already solved. The lecturer solved it the long way, to prove she didn’t need him. She left a pen. He kept it. They both went home and looked at the ceiling. P(1) holds.

Inductive step. Suppose that on some day k, we choose each other.

And then, beneath it, a list. In both their handwritings, alternating. His small and neat. Hers small and round and quick.

Day k: a cactus joke. Day k: the long way, because it was flatter for the shoes. Day k: oranges. Day k: two hundred and twelve notes. None of them an answer. Day k: a letter, at four in the morning. Day k: a stairwell. A finger’s width. Day k: “You bought me a lab.” “I bought you time.” Both true. Day k: still here. Day k: a suitcase with no wheel. Asking first. Day k: 4:01. Day k: a dumpling. The twelfth one. Day k: five hours on the train. Every other Friday. Day k: a horizon that holds. Day k: scrambled eggs, in a bowl over hot water. Day k: two desks. Eighty centimetres. Day k: a hundred and thirteen.

In every case, having chosen each other on day k, we chose each other again on day k + 1. There has not yet been a day when we didn’t. Therefore P(k) implies P(k + 1).

By the principle of mathematical induction, P(n) holds for all n.

And at the bottom, an empty space. Where the last line should go. The line that finishes every proof.

✦ ✦ ✦

Fang Hao held out two pieces of chalk.

Miles took one. Yu Jie took the other.

They stood side by side at the blackboard on the easel, in front of the sundial that had never told the right time, in a garden that wasn’t a garden, with sixty people on folding chairs behind them, and the ginkgo tree moving in the breeze, and an arms dealer in the fourth row throwing rainbows across the grass with a prism.

She looked at him.

He looked at her.

And together, in two handwritings, his small and neat, hers small and round and quick, they wrote the last line.

Q.E.D.

Quod erat demonstrandum.

Which was to be demonstrated.

And beneath it, they each drew half of a small square. The box that ends a proof. His half on the left. Hers on the right. They met in the middle. The corners didn’t quite match; her side was slightly crooked, the way her boxes always were.

Neither of them fixed it.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the front row on the left, Professor Gao, who did not believe in speeches, stood up and walked very fast round the back of the chemistry building, and did not come back for eleven minutes.

In the front row on the right, Shen Ruolan, in butter yellow and her mother-in-law’s Sunday pearls, looked at the crooked little box at the bottom of the blackboard for a long time, and took a white embroidered handkerchief out of her bag, and touched it very precisely to the corner of one eye, and did not put it away again.

In the fourth row, Zhao Zhendong tilted his prism, and threw a rainbow across the blackboard, right across the Q.E.D., exactly where he meant it to go. He had not stopped glaring at the physicist since the first note of the string quartet. He stopped now, and looked at the rainbow on the blackboard, and at his wife beside him, who was crying, and at Miles.

And the corner of his mouth moved.

“Good,” said Zhao, to nobody.

Beside him, Aurelia Chen put her head on her husband’s shoulder and sobbed with total abandon, and said, “He chose correctly,” to nobody, very loudly, and Chen Si said, “Yes, my queen,” and handed her his handkerchief, and then, after a moment, when he thought nobody was looking, used the corner of it himself.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, when the cake was cut—Su Mei did it with the bread knife, and Dr. Ren carried the slices round on a tray without dropping one, and was not, Miles noticed, entirely unhappy—and the string quartet had been paid in egg tarts, and the light was going gold across the lawn and the sundial was telling the wrong time with total confidence, and Professor Huang and Professor Gao were arguing by the ginkgo tree about corners, and Bai Tianyu was asking Miles’s father whether gravity was real and getting a very long answer—

Later, she found him at the blackboard.

He was standing in front of it on his own, with a glass of something sparkling he hadn’t asked for, looking at the proof.

She came and stood beside him. Close. No three metres. No eighty centimetres. Her shoulder against his arm.

“It’s finished,” he said.

“It’s finished,” she agreed.

“I’ve never finished one like this before.” He looked at the crooked box at the bottom. “Most proofs, when they’re finished, you put them away. You publish them. You move on to the next problem.” He was quiet. “I don’t want to put this one away.”

“You don’t have to.”

“No.” He looked down at her. At the yellow dress, and the pens in her hair, and the trainers with P(1) on the toe. “It’s by induction. It doesn’t end. It’s true for every day, and there’s always another day.” He thought about it, properly. “So it’s finished. And it’s never finished. Both.”

She smiled up at him.

“You’re a physicist,” said Shen Yu Jie. “You’re good at problems with two variables.”

He laughed.

Out loud. In the garden behind the Hall of Science, in front of everybody. Not the seminar laugh, or the terrace laugh, or the one against the chalkboard. A new one. Easy and warm and completely unafraid, as if he had been laughing his whole life and had never once stopped.

Across the lawn, in the front row on the right, his mother-in-law heard it, and turned her head, and watched him laugh, and watched her daughter laugh with him, in yellow, by a blackboard, with chalk on both their hands.

And for the first time anybody could remember, in thirty-eight years, Shen Ruolan smiled with her whole face.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, in the flat on Bell Street, on the second floor, above the tea shop, he couldn’t undo her dress.

It had forty-one buttons down the back. Tao Tao’s grandmother had sewn every one by hand, tiny cloth-covered ones, each with its own little loop, and she had told Yu Jie, very seriously, at the final fitting, that this was traditional, and that a husband should have to work for it.

Miles stood behind her in the main room, between the two desks, in his shirtsleeves with his bow tie hanging undone, and looked at the forty-one buttons.

“I see,” he said.

“Tao Tao’s grandmother says it’s traditional.”

“Tao Tao’s grandmother,” said Miles, “is a sadist.” He undid the first one. His fingers were not steady. “Forty-one.”

“You counted.”

“Of course I counted. I counted at the ceremony. I counted during Professor Gao’s speech.” He undid the second. Then bent his head and kissed the small square of skin it showed, at the top of her spine, and she shivered. “I’ve been thinking about them since four o’clock.”

He did not hurry. That was the cruellest part. He undid them one at a time, and after each one he kissed the new skin, slowly, working down her back, button by button, his breath warm, his hands spread on her waist over the yellow cotton to keep her still, and by the twelfth she had both hands flat on her own desk to hold herself up, and by the twentieth she was saying his name, and by the thirtieth she was begging him to just rip it.

“No,” said Miles, against her spine. “Tao Tao’s grandmother made it. It took her six weeks.”

“Miles.”

“Thirty-one,” he said, very calmly, and kissed the small of her back, and she made a sound that the tea-shop owner downstairs might have heard.

By forty-one, she had stopped being able to stand.

He caught her. He turned her round, and the yellow dress slid off her shoulders and down onto the creaking floor between the two desks, and he lifted her up and sat her on the edge of his own desk, on the scratched fifty-year-old wood, on the ink stain the shape of a cloud, and stood between her knees, and kissed her until neither of them knew what room they were in.

“Bed,” she said, eventually, against his mouth.

“In a minute.”

“Now.”

“I’m married to you,” said Miles, as if it had just occurred to him, and pulled back far enough to look at her, sitting on his desk in nothing but her trainers with P(1) written on the toe. His face did something she had never seen it do. “I’m married to you. For all n.”

She grabbed his undone bow tie in both fists and pulled him down.

They didn’t make it to the bed for a while. When they did, it was slow, and then it wasn’t, and then it was slow again, the long way and the short way and every way in between, with the window open and Bell Street going quiet below and the smell of bread starting two doors down at four in the morning, and he said I love you into her skin so many times that she stopped hearing the words and only heard him.

Afterwards, she lay across his chest and listened to his heart.

“Forty-one,” she said, into the dark.

“I know.”

“You did every single one.”

“It was a very important proof,” said Miles. “I didn’t want to skip any steps.”

She laughed so hard the bed shook.

Then, a little later, she got up, in his shirt, barefoot, and took a pencil and went to the wall beside the bedroom door.

The calendar was still there. They had brought it from the attic above Fang’s. Two hundred and sixty-six squares of graph paper, purple atoms in every one, a gold one at the end. And after it, the rows she had drawn in pencil, going off the paper and onto the plaster wall, square after square, row after row. Not a pearl. A dumpling. A train. A tank with a line in it. Two desks. A ring.

They went most of the way across the wall now.

He stood behind her, in his trousers and nothing else, with his bow tie still hanging round his neck, and his arms round her waist, and his chin on top of her head, and watched.

She found the square for the twentieth of June.

Two years ago, it had been gold. The end of everything. The last square on the calendar.

She drew in it.

Not an atom. A small box. A square, slightly crooked on the right-hand side, where two halves met in the middle and didn’t quite match.

Q.E.D.

And then she drew a line after it. And another square.

And another.

She didn’t know what would go in them.

She drew them anyway.

END

chapters.title: Who Hid Miles Wei’s Glasses (Again)
chapters.desc: A short investigation, conducted by Dr. Fang Hao, into the fourteenth disappearance of a pair of glasses on Bell Street. There is one obvious suspect. There is also a motive nobody expected.
chapters.epigraph: “Case file 14. The glasses were last seen on the subject’s face. The subject cannot see the case file.”
chapters.content:
CASE FILE 14 Investigating officer: Dr. Fang Hao (theorist, unpaid) Date: A Wednesday in November. The second autumn on Bell Street.

✦ ✦ ✦

The call came in at 7:52 in the morning.

Dr. Fang Hao was in the kitchen of the bakery two doors down, eating his third croissant of the day and reading a paper on string theory that he did not entirely believe, when his phone rang. It was Miles.

“Hao,” said Miles. “I can’t find my glasses.”

Fang Hao put down the croissant.

“Again?”

“Again.”

“That’s fourteen.”

“I know it’s fourteen. I’ve been counting.” A pause. “I have a lecture at nine. Second-year quantum. I can’t see the board. I can’t see the students. I can’t see my own notes. I tried to put the kettle on and I put it on the toaster.”

Fang Hao closed his paper.

“Where is your wife?”

There was a pause on the line.

“She’s at the lab,” said Miles. “She left at seven. She said she had an experiment. She kissed me goodbye.” Another pause. “She was smiling.”

Fang Hao picked up a notebook and a pen.

“I’m coming over,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The scene was the flat on Bell Street, second floor, above the tea shop.

The investigating officer arrived at 7:58, with a croissant for the subject, which the subject did not see until it was put directly into his hand.

The subject was standing in the middle of the main room in his pyjama trousers and grey jumper, with his hair standing up and an expression of profound, myopic suffering. He was holding a mug that said WORLD’S OKAYEST SON upside down.

“Your mug’s upside down,” said Fang Hao.

“I know,” said Miles. “There was no tea in it. I checked by feel.”

The investigating officer surveyed the scene.

Two desks, front to front, under the high window. Books everywhere. A cactus on the windowsill, in a blue pot, with a small handwritten label: Schrödinger. A whiteboard on the kitchen wall, covered in squeaking blue diagrams of something with corners. A graph-paper calendar beside the bedroom door, with rows of squares in pencil going most of the way across the plaster.

No glasses.

“Previous incidents,” said Fang Hao, opening his notebook. “Talk me through them.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Incidents 1–13. Summary.

1. March, first year on Bell Street. Glasses found in the fridge, beside the eggs. Subject believes he put them there himself, while reading. Plausible.

2. April. Glasses found inside a saucepan. Subject has no explanation.

3. April. Glasses found on top of Schrödinger. Subject: “I don’t know how that happened. It’s a cactus.”

4. May. Glasses found in the bakery, two doors down, on the pastry counter, beside a tub of peeled oranges. Su Mei claims no knowledge.

5–8. Assorted. Under the mattress. Inside a shoe. Inside the second drawer of the wife’s desk. In the pocket of the wife’s cardigan, while the wife was wearing it.

9. August. Glasses found on the subject’s own head. Subject: “That doesn’t count. That was my fault.”

10–13. Wednesdays. All four. The investigating officer notes this.

The investigating officer looked up from his notebook.

“Miles,” he said. “Eight of these were on Wednesdays.”

“Were they?”

“Nine, now. Today is Wednesday.”

Miles turned his face toward the window, where he could see a blurry light, and thought about it.

“Yes,” he said slowly. “I suppose they were.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The investigating officer conducted a search.

He looked in the fridge. Eggs, twelve. Spring onions. A carton of milk. No glasses.

He looked in the saucepans. Clean. No glasses.

He looked on top of Schrödinger. The cactus declined to confirm or deny.

He looked in the drawers of both desks. The subject’s desk: pens, papers, a plastic bag of yellow sticky notes and a paper-clipped stack of pink ones, a napkin with a drawing of a box on it, a purple pen with a plastic cat on the end. No glasses. The wife’s desk: pens, notebooks, a brown envelope, a faded chemistry set in the bottom drawer, and, in the top drawer, a small notebook he had not seen before, with a yellow cover.

He opened it.

It was a list.

Glasses, 1. Fridge. He came to find them and I was making breakfast. He had to stand right next to me to see whether they were behind the milk. He stood there for three minutes. He forgot about the glasses.

Glasses, 2. Saucepan. Didn’t mean to. He left them on the counter and I knocked them in. Doesn’t count.

Glasses, 3. Schrödinger. To see if he’d notice. He did. He apologised to the cactus.

Glasses, 4. Bakery. Su Mei helped. He came down in his pyjamas to ask if anyone had seen them, and stood at the counter with me for half an hour while I served customers, and ate four egg tarts, and didn’t go back upstairs until I finished my shift.

The investigating officer turned the page.

Glasses, 10. Wednesday. He works so late on Wednesdays now. Since the grant. He comes home at nine and goes straight to the kitchen whiteboard and doesn’t look up. So I hid them. He couldn’t see the whiteboard. He had to come and sit next to me on the sofa because I was the only thing in the room close enough to look at.

He said, “You’re within my focal range.”

He said it like it was the most romantic thing in the world.

It is.

The investigating officer closed the notebook.

He sat at the wife’s desk for a moment, in silence, with the yellow notebook in his hands.

Then he put it back in the drawer exactly where he had found it, and closed the drawer, and said nothing at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Well?” said Miles, from the middle of the room. “Have you found anything?”

“No,” said Fang Hao.

“Nothing at all?”

“Nothing relevant,” said Fang Hao, who was a theorist, and therefore very good at deciding what counted as relevant.

Miles sighed. He sat down at his desk. He felt for his tea, found the upside-down mug, turned it the right way up, discovered there was still no tea in it, and put it down again.

“I have a lecture in fifty minutes,” he said. “I’m going to have to teach the hydrogen atom from memory, to a room I can’t see, in a building I can’t see, and Bai Tianyu’s younger brother is in the second row, and he asks even more questions than Bai Tianyu did.”

“You’ll be fine. You could teach the hydrogen atom in your sleep.”

“I have taught it in my sleep,” said Miles. “She says I do it some nights. In detail.” He put his face in his hands. “She says I’m very clear about the angular momentum.”

The investigating officer looked at the subject for a long moment. At the subject’s hair, standing up. At his grey jumper. At his hands over his face.

“Miles,” he said. “Can I ask you something?”

“Yes.”

“The Wednesdays. When the glasses go missing. What do you do?”

Miles took his hands away from his face. He thought about it, properly.

“I look for them,” he said. “Everywhere. And I can’t find them. So I give up. And I can’t see the whiteboard, or my papers, or anything. So I go and sit on the sofa next to her.” He paused. “And she reads to me. From whatever she’s refereeing. In a very pompous voice. And I laugh.” He paused again. “And then usually we—it’s usually a very nice evening.”

“And then the glasses turn up.”

“The next morning,” said Miles. “Usually. Somewhere strange.”

There was a long silence in the flat on Bell Street.

Miles sat very still at his desk.

Slowly, a look came over his face. The look he got in front of a chalkboard when a problem that had been sitting there for weeks suddenly turned itself the right way up.

“Hao,” he said.

“Yes?”

“Did you look in her desk?”

“I looked in her desk.”

“Did you find anything?”

“Nothing relevant,” said Fang Hao again, very firmly.

Miles looked at him. At the blurry shape of him, by the window.

Then his ears went red. Slowly. All the way to the collar of his grey jumper.

“Oh,” said Miles Wei.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 8:40, the investigating officer escorted the subject to the Hall of Science.

On foot, because the subject could not be trusted on a bicycle. Up the hill, the straight way. The subject walked into one lamppost and apologised to it. The investigating officer steered him round the second. At the main door, Mr. Pan looked up from his martial arts novel and said, “Fourteen?”

“Fourteen,” said Fang Hao.

Mr. Pan reached under his desk.

He took out a spectacles case. Brown. Battered. He held it out.

“She left them at seven,” he said. “On her way to the lab. Said to give them to you at 8:45 and not a minute before.” He looked at the clock over the porter’s desk. “8:44. Close enough.”

Miles took the case. He opened it. He put his glasses on.

The world came into focus. The lobby. The stairs. Mr. Pan. Fang Hao, grinning so widely his face looked as if it might split.

And folded inside the case, where the glasses had been, a yellow sticky note.

Why did the physicist lose his glasses every Wednesday?

Because his wife wanted him within her focal range.

(Go and teach. Come home early. I’m making dumplings. You’re folding.)

Miles stood in the lobby of the Hall of Science and read it, now that he could, three times.

Then he put it in his pocket, very carefully, with the others, and went upstairs to teach the hydrogen atom to a hundred and forty second-years, and was, Bai Tianyu’s younger brother reported afterwards on the student forum, weirdly happy about angular momentum.

He came home at four. Not early. Very early.

She was at the kitchen counter in his grey jumper, flour to the elbows, with a stack of dumpling wrappers, and she looked round when the door opened and her face did something she didn’t quite manage to stop.

“You found them,” she said innocently. “Where were they?”

“Mr. Pan had them,” said Miles. “He doesn’t know how.”

“How strange.”

“Very strange.”

He washed his hands. He came and stood beside her at the counter. Not opposite. Beside. So close that his arm was against hers from shoulder to wrist, though there was the whole length of the counter to stand at, and his glasses were on his nose, and he could see perfectly well.

She looked up at him.

“You can see,” she said.

“Yes.”

“So you don’t need to stand this close.”

“No,” Miles agreed, and didn’t move, and picked up a wrapper, and folded the worst dumpling in the history of Bell Street, very slowly, with his arm against hers the whole time.

✦ ✦ ✦

CASE FILE 14. CLOSED.

Culprit: known.

Charges: none.

Investigating officer’s note: The subject has been informed of the motive and has asked that no action be taken. He has also asked the investigating officer not to tell the culprit that he knows. The investigating officer has agreed. The investigating officer would like it recorded that he has never in eleven years of marriage thought to hide his wife’s rolling pin in order to get her to sit next to him, and is now considering it.

Su Mei has been consulted on this point.

Su Mei has said that if he touches her rolling pin she will hit him with it.

Case closed.

chapters.title: The Night She Made Him Dance in the Empty Lab
chapters.desc: Midnight in the basement of the east wing. One pair of headphones, two people, a horizon holding in a tank of water, and a man who has never danced in his life.
chapters.epigraph: “I can’t dance.” “You can walk the long way for forty-one minutes. Dancing is just the long way, in a circle.”
chapters.content:
It was the night of the first paper.

Not the corners paper. That had been his and hers. This one was his: the water tank. Observation of a stable analogue horizon in a transcritical flow, Wei M., Ouyang J., and three others. Accepted that afternoon, at 4:12, by the best journal in the field, after eight months of reviewers and revisions and one referee who had asked so many questions about the boundary conditions that Miles had suspected, for a while, that it was Professor Zhou in disguise.

It wasn’t. Professor Zhou had said so. He had seemed slightly disappointed.

She came to the basement at eleven at night with a bottle of cheap sparkling wine from the shop at the bottom of the hill and two paper cups from the fourth-floor kitchen.

He was still there. Of course he was. Lying on his back under the tank with a torch in his mouth, checking a pump that did not need checking.

“Out,” she said.

He came out. He took the torch out of his mouth.

“It was accepted,” he said. As if she might not have heard. As if he hadn’t called her at 4:13 and said it four times in a row and then put the phone down and gone and stood in front of the tank for an hour.

“I know,” said Yu Jie. “I’m very proud of you. We’re celebrating.”

“I don’t really celebrate.”

“You do now,” she said, and opened the wine. It went off like a gunshot. The cork hit the ceiling, bounced off a pipe, and landed in the tank.

They both looked at it, bobbing on the surface of the flowing water, being carried slowly toward the middle.

Toward the horizon.

It slowed. It slowed. And then, at the line where the little waves always stopped, it stopped too. And sat there. Quite still. Unable to go back.

“Oh,” said Miles. “Oh, that’s wonderful.”

“It’s a cork.”

“It shouldn’t do that,” said Miles reverently. “The flow should carry it straight over the hump. It’s caught in the standing wave on the horizon. Look at it. It’s sitting right on the line. It can’t get back.” He was already reaching for his notebook. “I should write down—”

She took the notebook out of his hands.

“Miles,” she said. “It’s a cork. It’s midnight. We’re celebrating. Drink your wine.”

He drank his wine.

✦ ✦ ✦

The basement was dark except for the tank.

He had put lights under it, that spring. Long strips of white light along the bottom of the clear acrylic, so that the camera could see the waves better. At night, with the bare bulb off, they turned the whole tank into a long glowing bar of moving water, and the light came up through it and bent and threw shifting patterns across the low ceiling of the basement, over the pipes and the cables and the broken chairs from 1997.

Caustics. Like the ceiling of a flower shop in the Walled City.

They sat on the floor with their backs against the laser bench and the paper cups of cheap wine and looked at it.

“Do you know what I was thinking about,” she said, “at 4:13, when you called?”

“No.”

“The first time I came down here. To tell you about Huang’s letter. You were under the tank with a spanner, and the pumps were on, and you said, Come and look, I’ve got the flow steady.” She looked at the long glowing tank. “And I thought, this is the happiest I have ever seen anyone. A man under a tank with a spanner. And then I told you I was leaving.”

“You weren’t leaving,” said Miles. “You were going to the capital. That’s different.”

“It felt like leaving.”

“I know.” He was quiet. “It felt like that to me too. For about forty seconds. Then it felt like a problem with two variables.”

She laughed and put her head on his shoulder.

Above them, on the ceiling, the light from the tank moved and rippled and bent.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had headphones in her bag. She always had headphones in her bag. She listened to music in the lab, very loudly, while she worked; Professor Gao had complained about it twice and then, in the second year, started borrowing them.

She took them out now. She plugged them into her phone. She put one earbud in her own ear, and held the other out to him.

He looked at it.

“What is it?”

“A song,” said Yu Jie. “Put it in.”

He put it in.

It was something slow. Old. A woman singing in Cantonese, with a piano, very softly, about the moon. He didn’t know it. He listened to the first verse, sitting on the concrete floor of the basement with one earbud and her head on his shoulder.

“Tao Tao’s grandmother sings this,” she said. “When she’s folding dumplings. It was the song she was singing the first New Year I went to their flat. When I got the pleats right on the twelfth try.” She lifted her head. “It’s the first song I ever liked that nobody chose for me.”

He looked down at her in the light from the tank.

She stood up. She held out her hand.

“Dance with me,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I can’t dance,” said Miles.

He said it with total certainty. As if stating a law of physics.

“Everyone can dance.”

“I can’t. I’ve never danced. Not once. Not at school, not at university, not at a single department party, I never went to any of them, I went to the seminar and left before the wine.” He looked up at her from the floor. “At the gala, I stood by the food. Fang Hao told me to. Lu Zhiyuan danced with you and I held a plate.”

“I remember,” said Yu Jie. “Your knuckles were white.”

He went red.

She kept holding out her hand.

“You can walk the long way for forty-one minutes,” she said. “Along a wall, in December, three metres behind someone. You can stop under three lamps. You can turn left whenever she turns left.” She smiled. “Dancing is just the long way, Miles. In a circle.”

He looked at her hand for a long time.

Then he took it, and she pulled him up off the concrete floor, and he stood in front of her in the basement of the east wing in his grey cardigan, with one earbud in, in the light from a black hole made of water, and didn’t know what to do with his feet.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Put your hand here,” she said, and put it on her waist.

He put it there. Very lightly. As if she might break.

“And this one here,” she said, and took his other hand, and held it, out to the side, the way Lu Zhiyuan had held hers in a ballroom. Then she changed her mind, and brought it in, and held it against her chest instead, between them. “No. Not like that. That’s how they do it at galas. Like this.”

She stepped in. Close. No distance at all. Her cheek against his chest, under his chin. His hand on her waist. Their two hands held together between them, against her heart.

“Now what?” he whispered.

“Now nothing,” she said. “Now you just move. Very slowly. Any way you like. I’ll follow.”

He didn’t move.

He stood absolutely still, in the light from the tank, holding her, and she could feel his heart going very fast under her cheek.

“I don’t know which way,” he said.

“It doesn’t matter which way.”

“There must be a right way.”

“There isn’t,” said Yu Jie, into his cardigan. “That’s the whole point. There are more ways to be messy.”

He laughed. She felt it go through his chest.

And then, very slowly, he moved.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was bad at it.

He was very, very bad at it. He moved like a man working out a calculation in real time and getting the signs wrong. He stepped on her foot twice. He turned the wrong way and nearly walked them both into the laser bench. He kept looking down at their feet, as if he could solve them.

She didn’t care.

She stayed close, with her cheek against his chest, and followed him wherever he went. Round and round on the concrete floor. In a slow, uneven, lopsided circle, between the tank and the bench and the broken chairs.

After the second time round, he stopped looking at their feet.

After the third, he stopped stepping on hers.

After the fourth, she felt something change. His shoulders came down. His hand on her waist stopped being careful and became sure. He pulled her in, a little closer, and put his chin on top of her head, and closed his eyes, and stopped thinking about it at all.

And they just moved. Slowly. In the dark. In the light from the water.

The song ended. Another one started. Something else old and slow. Neither of them stopped.

On the ceiling above them, the caustics from the tank moved and bent across the pipes. In the tank, the cork sat on the horizon, quite still, where nothing could get back.

✦ ✦ ✦

She lifted her head, after a long time.

He was looking down at her. Without his glasses, she realised. He had taken them off at some point. She didn’t know when. They were on the laser bench, beside the paper cups.

“You can’t see,” she said.

“I can see you,” said Miles. “You’re within my focal range.”

She stood on her toes.

He kissed her. Slowly. In the middle of the basement, still moving, very slightly, to the song in one earbud each. Her hand came up out of his and went to the back of his neck, into his hair. His hand on her waist spread wide and held her against him. The earbud fell out of her ear. Neither of them noticed.

There was chalk dust on his cardigan, from the lecture that afternoon. She could taste it, faintly, on his collar when she turned her face into his neck. She breathed it in. Chalk and jasmine tea and him.

“Jie,” he said, very low, against her hair.

“Mm.”

“The basement door is locked.”

She went still.

“I locked it,” he said. “When you came in. Out of habit. Because of the equipment.” A pause. “I just wanted to mention it. In the interests of transparency.”

She pulled back and looked at him in the moving light. At his face, without his glasses. At the expression on it, which she had first seen on a narrow bed in a staff flat on the last night of August, and had been collecting ever since.

She started to laugh.

“Miles,” she said. “Are you suggesting—in the lab?”

“I’m not suggesting anything,” said Miles, going very red. “I’m stating a fact. About a door.”

“Next to your tank?”

“It’s a very stable tank.”

She laughed so hard she had to hold on to him. He held on to her, red to the collar, laughing too, helplessly, into her hair.

Then she stopped laughing.

She looked up at him. She reached past him to the laser bench and switched off the phone. The music stopped. The basement was silent except for the soft hum of the pumps, and the water flowing toward the middle, and both of them breathing.

“Do you have your coat?” she said.

He looked at her.

“On the chair,” he said. His voice had gone strange. “By the door.”

She took his hand. She led him across the basement in the light from the tank, past the broken chairs, to the old coat on the back of one of them, and spread it on the floor in the corner, in the shifting light, out of sight of the camera, which she switched off on the way past, because she was a physicist and thorough.

Then she turned round, and put both hands flat on his chest, and pushed.

Not hard. Just enough. He went down onto the coat, onto his back, on the concrete floor of his own laboratory, and looked up at her with an expression of total, delighted astonishment, and she knelt over him with one knee on either side of him and her hair falling down around both their faces like a curtain.

“You,” said Miles, “have done this before.”

“Never,” said Yu Jie. “I’ve thought about it. Since the first time you were under that tank with a spanner.” She bent down until her mouth was an inch from his. “Lie still. You always go first. You always ask. Tonight I’m asking.”

He lay still.

It nearly killed him. She could see it nearly killed him. She kissed him the way he usually kissed her, slowly, properly, from first principles: the corner of his mouth, the other corner, his jaw, the place under his ear that she had found on the last night of August, a year ago, and that made his breath stop every time, every single time, so that she could feel his whole body go rigid under her. She took his glasses off the bench and put them out of reach. She undid his cardigan button by button and asked at every one, May I?, in a perfect copy of his voice, until he was laughing so hard he couldn’t answer, and then she undid the rest without asking at all.

Above them, on the low ceiling, the light from the tank moved and rippled and bent. It fell across his bare chest in shifting bright lines, and across her arms, and her face, so that they were both covered in it, both moving in it, like two people at the bottom of a clear pool.

“Look,” she said, and held her hand up, and the caustics slid across her palm.

He looked. Not at the light. At her.

“I can’t see it properly,” he said. “You took my glasses.”

“You can see me.”

“You’re within my focal range,” said Miles, and his voice cracked in the middle, and she stopped teasing.

Then she bent down and put her mouth on the place under his ear, and he stopped being able to talk in sentences.

“Jie. Jie, that’s—your heart rate is—I can feel it, it’s at least—”

“Are you measuring my heart rate?”

“I can’t help it.” His hands were fisted in the coat beneath him, hard, as if he were holding on to the edge of something. “It’s one-forty. At least. And rising.” A ragged breath. “So is mine.”

“What else,” she whispered against his throat.

“What?”

“What else can you feel. Tell me. Like you’re taking notes.”

He told her.

In that low, careful lecture voice, flat on his back on the basement floor with her kneeling over him in the moving light, Dr. Miles Wei told her exactly what he could feel, in order, precisely, without leaving anything out, the way he would describe an experiment to a room of a hundred and forty people. Her weight. Her heat. The way her breath caught when his thumbs moved. What it did to him. What he wanted to do about it. Every word perfectly clear, perfectly calm, and devastatingly specific, and by the time he got to the third item on his list she had stopped breathing altogether and her face was burning and she had to put her hand over his mouth.

He kissed her palm.

“You asked,” he said, muffled.

“I know,” she said faintly. “I didn’t know you could talk like that.”

“Neither did I.” He took her hand away from his mouth. His eyes, without his glasses, were black. “I’ve been thinking it for a year. I just never said it out loud.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She let him sit up. She let his hands, which had been flat on the coat the whole time, gripping it, finally move, and they went straight to her, to her waist, under the hem of her jumper, warm on her skin, and she gasped at the heat of them and he pulled her down into his lap and kissed her so hard and so deep that the bright moving lines on the ceiling went out of focus for her too.

It was nothing like the first night in the staff flat. Nothing slow about it. Nothing careful. Her jumper went somewhere into the dark by the laser bench. His hands were in her hair and the claw clip came loose and the four pens went rattling across the concrete floor and rolled away under the tank. She heard herself laugh, breathless, and then not laugh, and then say his name, and his mouth was on her throat, her shoulder, the line of her collarbone, and the cold air of the basement was on her back and his hands were warm everywhere else and the contrast made her shiver so hard he stopped and held her and asked, against her skin, Cold?

No, she said. The opposite.

He laughed, low, into her shoulder.

And then he laid her down on his old coat, in the light from a black hole made of water, and they stopped talking.

✦ ✦ ✦

She would remember the sound of the pumps, steady under everything, like a heartbeat that wasn’t either of theirs.

She would remember the light. The whole time. Moving over them, bending, gathering into bright lines on his shoulders and his back and on her own arms where they were wrapped round him. The way it rippled every time the water moved, so that it seemed as if the room itself were breathing with them.

She would remember that he was not careful, this time, because she had told him not to be, and that she had never in her life felt so entirely wanted. Not looked at. Wanted. All of her. The mind and the hands and the chalk on her fingers and the voice that came out of her, low and unfamiliar, when he held her as if she were the only fixed point in a moving room.

She would remember that at the very end he said her name like something breaking, and held on to her so tightly she could feel every one of his ribs, and that she held on back, and that for a moment everything was perfectly still and perfectly bright, like the line in the tank where the waves stop and can’t come back.

And then the quiet. The pumps. His heart under her ear, slowing. His coat, which was very old, under her back, and his arm across her, and his breath in her hair.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Jie,” he said, after a long time.

“Mm.”

“I’ve worked in this basement for eighteen months.”

“I know.”

“I’m never going to be able to look at that laser bench again.”

She laughed into his chest, helplessly, until he was laughing too, the two of them lying on the floor of the east-wing basement on an old coat at one in the morning, covered in moving light.

“It’s a very stable bench,” she said.

He laughed so hard he got the hiccups.

They stayed until three. Then they got dressed in the dark, very badly—she put his cardigan on inside out and he couldn’t find his glasses for ten minutes, and she let him look, because it was funny—and walked home down the hill, the long way, along the old wall, holding hands, with chalk dust on both of them and four pens missing.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ouyang came in at seven in the morning to check the overnight data.

The basement door was unlocked. The bare bulb was on. The tank was humming, the water flowing steadily toward the middle. On the laser bench there were two paper cups, empty, and a bottle of cheap sparkling wine, also empty.

And in the tank, sitting exactly on the horizon, where it had been for eight hours without moving, a cork.

Ouyang looked at it.

He opened the lab book. He wrote the date and the time.

Then, under Notes, he wrote: Test particle (cork) introduced at approx. 23:00. Stable on horizon for >8 hrs. Origin of test particle: unknown.

He looked at the claw clip on the floor by the laser bench. At the empty cups. At a single purple pen with a plastic cat on the end, lying under the tank. At the old coat, folded very neatly on the back of a broken chair from 1997, with a little chalk dust on the collar.

He was a quiet young man. He had chosen to work for Dr. Wei because Dr. Wei had once given him full marks for an answer that said I don’t know, but here’s how I would find out.

He decided, on balance, that this was one of the things he did not need to find out.

He crossed out unknown.

He wrote: Celebratory.

chapters.title: Miles Calculates Before Holding Hands
chapters.desc: The second date. A cinema, a shared armrest, and a man with a napkin and a pencil in the dark, working out the optimal moment. She has already done the calculation. Hers is shorter.
chapters.epigraph: “Let θ be the angle of the armrest. Let t be the time elapsed since the lights went down. Let me be an idiot.”
chapters.content:
The second date was on the Tuesday.

He had not made a lesson plan. He had learned his lesson. The first one had gone into the window of a passing tram. He had, instead, made what he called a loose framework, which was one page long instead of four, and which he did not show her, and which consisted of three lines:

Cinema, 19:30. (She chose the film.) Noodles after. (Ask where.) Do not plan anything else.

And then, at the bottom, underlined twice:

Hold her hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

The problem was the cinema.

He had held her hand a great many times by then. Two days. In office 412, at 4:01, when she had taken his. On the Sunday at the chalkboard. At the night market, through the crowd. In the dark street by the broom shop. Walking back to Bell Street at midnight.

But every single time, she had taken his.

He had noticed this on Monday, lying awake in the staff flat. He had sat up in bed at two in the morning and turned on the light and said, out loud, to the cactus on the windowsill: “I’ve never once taken hers.”

The cactus had not responded.

He had lain back down and thought about it for an hour. Every time. Every single time. Her hand reaching for his. Never the other way. As if he were still on the far side of a rule, three metres away, with his arms crossed against the cold, waiting to be told it was allowed.

It was allowed now.

He was going to take her hand. At the cinema. On Tuesday. First.

✦ ✦ ✦

The film was a romantic comedy. She had chosen it because, she said, he had probably never seen one, and it was time.

He hadn’t. He had seen eleven films in the last five years, all of them documentaries about space, and three of them had had errors about white dwarfs.

They sat in row J, seats 14 and 15, in the small cinema on Harbour Road with the red velvet seats and the sticky floor. She had a bag of popcorn on her knee. He had a bottle of water and nothing else, because his hands were already sweating and he didn’t want to be holding anything when the moment came.

Between seats 14 and 15, there was an armrest.

One armrest. Shared.

He looked at it while the adverts played. It was red velvet over hard plastic, about six centimetres wide, worn shiny in the middle where twenty years of elbows had rested on it. At the moment, there was nobody’s elbow on it. Her arm was in her lap, with the popcorn. His was on his knee.

The armrest sat between them. Empty. Like a problem nobody had solved.

The lights went down.

✦ ✦ ✦

He took out the napkin.

He hadn’t meant to. He had told himself, on the way there, on the tram, that he would not do this. That he would just do it. Like a normal person. Reach over, in the dark, at some point, and take her hand.

But the lights went down, and the film started, and a woman on the screen dropped a cup of coffee on a man in a suit, and Yu Jie laughed, and he realised that he had absolutely no idea when some point was.

So he took the napkin out of his pocket. One from the night market, from the dumpling stall, slightly floury. And a pencil from his other pocket, because he always had a pencil.

He held it on his knee, in the dark, and wrote very small, by the light of the screen.

Let t = time since lights went down (min).

Let P(t) = probability that taking her hand at time t is welcome.

He thought about it.

At t = 0: P low. She is settling. Popcorn.

As t increases: P increases? Familiarity with film. Comfort. Darkness.

But: if t too large, she will wonder why I haven’t. P(wondering) increases with t. Possibly she will think I don’t want to.

Therefore: P(t) has a maximum. Find t.*

He looked at the screen. The woman and the man in the suit were arguing in a lift. Yu Jie was eating popcorn, watching, smiling.

He looked at the armrest.

Additional variables:

θ = angle of her arm. Currently in lap. Would need to move to armrest. Or I reach to lap? Lap seems presumptuous.

Popcorn: occupies her right hand. I am on her left. Her left hand is free. GOOD. But: butter? Salt? Do I mind? No. Does she mind if I mind? Unknown.

Emotional content of film: if I do it during a sad scene, it seems like comfort. During a romantic scene, it seems like a statement. During a funny scene, it seems random. Which do I want?

Statement.

He underlined it.

Therefore: wait for romantic scene. Estimate time to first romantic scene in a romantic comedy: ~25–35 min (genre conventions; Fang Hao says).

t ≈ 30 min.*

He looked at his watch. It was too dark to see it. He tilted it toward the screen. Eleven minutes.

Nineteen to go.

He put the pencil down.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nineteen minutes was a very long time.

He didn’t watch the film. He watched the armrest. He watched her left hand, resting on her knee, in the light from the screen. He thought about the angle. He thought about the butter. He thought about whether his own hand was too sweaty, and wiped it on his trousers, and then worried that she had seen him wipe it on his trousers, and that she would think it was strange.

At sixteen minutes, she shifted in her seat, and put her left elbow on the armrest.

He froze.

θ has changed, he wrote, very fast, on the napkin. Her arm is now on the armrest. Her hand hangs over the edge. Distance to my hand: ~15 cm. This was not in the model.

Is this a signal?

Or is she just comfortable?

If signal: I should act now. t = 16, not 30. Model is wrong.

If not signal: acting now is premature. P(16) < P(30).

Need more data.

He looked at her face, in the light from the screen. She was watching the film. Not him. She was smiling slightly at something the man in the suit had said.

He couldn’t tell.

He had spent nine months watching her face at a chalkboard. He could tell when she had found a mistake, when she was about to laugh, when she was hiding a wrong answer. He could tell the difference between her Sunday smile and her real one across four hundred people in a ballroom.

He could not, in row J of a cinema in the dark, tell whether her elbow on an armrest was an invitation.

He wrote: Insufficient data. And sat there.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty-two minutes, she spoke. Very quietly. Without turning her head.

“Miles.”

He jumped.

“Yes?”

“What are you writing?”

He looked down at the napkin on his knee. At the pencil. At Let P(t) = probability that taking her hand at time t is welcome. At θ has changed. At Insufficient data.

“Nothing,” he said.

She turned her head and looked at him in the light from the screen.

She looked at the napkin. She looked at the pencil. She looked at his face.

And something happened to her expression that he could read perfectly well, even in row J, even in the dark. It was the face she had made on the step outside Fang’s, reading Learning objective 3.

“Are you,” said Shen Yu Jie, very slowly, “doing maths about this?”

“No.”

“Your ears are red.”

“It’s dark. You can’t see my ears.”

“I can see them. They’re lit up by the screen. They’re glowing, Miles.” She held out her hand. Her left one, the one hanging off the armrest. Palm up. “Give me the napkin.”

He gave her the napkin.

✦ ✦ ✦

She read it in the light from the screen.

She read all of it. Let t. Let P(t). Lap seems presumptuous. Butter? Salt? Do I mind? No. Does she mind if I mind? Statement. t ≈ 30 min. θ has changed. Insufficient data.*

On the screen, the woman and the man in the suit had stopped arguing and were standing very close together in the rain. The music had gone soft. It was, he realised distantly, the first romantic scene. At twenty-three minutes. Fang Hao had been wrong about genre conventions.

She wasn’t watching it. She was reading his napkin.

She got to the bottom.

She didn’t laugh. He had thought she would laugh. She didn’t. She sat in seat 15, row J, in the dark, holding a floury napkin from a dumpling stall, and looked at it for a long time, and her face did something he hadn’t seen it do before.

“Miles,” she said, very quietly. “Why?”

“Why what?”

“Why are you calculating this? You’ve held my hand a hundred times since Saturday.”

He looked at the armrest.

“No,” he said. “You’ve held mine.”

She went still.

“Every time,” said Miles. “At 4:01. At the chalkboard. At the night market. By the broom shop. You reached for me. Every single time.” He kept looking at the armrest. “I never once reached for you. I worked it out on Monday night. I sat up in bed and said it out loud to the cactus. I’ve never once taken your hand first.” His voice was very low, under the music from the screen. “I spent nine months being the one who had to wait. Who wasn’t allowed. Three metres. I got so good at not reaching that I don’t know how to start.”

She didn’t say anything.

“So I thought I’d work it out,” said Miles. “Properly. The right time. So that when I did it, it would be—” He stopped. “So it would be right. So you’d know I meant it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the screen, the man and the woman were kissing in the rain. Somebody in row F sighed.

In row J, Shen Yu Jie looked at the napkin. Then she took the pencil out of his hand, without asking, which made him laugh in spite of himself, and wrote something at the bottom, under Insufficient data.

She gave the napkin back to him.

He tilted it toward the screen to read it.

Under his half a page of variables and probabilities and the angle of her arm, in her small round quick handwriting, she had written one line:

t = now. (I put my elbow on the armrest at t = 16 on purpose. I’ve been waiting six minutes.)*

He read it twice.

He looked up at her.

She was looking at him in the dark with her chin up and her eyes very bright. Her left arm was on the armrest. Her hand was hanging over the end of it. Fifteen centimetres from his.

Not reaching.

Waiting.

For him.

✦ ✦ ✦

He put the napkin in his pocket.

He looked at her hand. At the fifteen centimetres. At the worn shiny red velvet of the armrest, where twenty years of elbows had rested.

He thought about the second Wednesday of September. The harmonic oscillator, the long way. You need a different excuse. He thought about a chalkboard, and a flat line. A walk along a wall, three metres behind her. A dark corner one block from a blue door, both of them holding one sleeve of the same jacket. A stairwell. Two hands flat on a cold step, a finger’s width apart, neither of them closing the gap. A corridor outside room 301. Two hands raised, palm to palm, two metres apart.

Fifteen centimetres.

He reached across them.

He did it slowly. Not because he was calculating. Because he wanted to feel every centimetre of it. Because he had waited two hundred and sixty-six days to be allowed to do this, and then three more days to understand that he was, and he was not going to hurry it now.

His hand found hers on the armrest.

He turned it over. Palm up. He put his own on top of it. He laced his fingers through hers, all the way, the way she had done on the path to the Hall of Science.

He held on.

She let out a breath that was almost a laugh and almost something else, and turned her hand in his, and held on back.

They sat in row J, seats 14 and 15, holding hands on a shared armrest in the dark, and didn’t watch the rest of the film at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, at a noodle shop she chose, at a plastic table under a fluorescent light, he took the napkin out of his pocket and smoothed it flat on the table between them.

They looked at it together.

“You were wrong about t*,” she said. “You said thirty minutes. It was sixteen.”

“My model was wrong,” said Miles. “I assumed the variable was the film. It wasn’t. The variable was you.” He looked at the napkin. “You did the calculation faster. And you got the right answer. And then you waited six minutes for me to get there.”

“I’m very good at waiting,” said Yu Jie. “I did two hundred and sixty-six days.”

He looked at her across the plastic table, under the fluorescent light, with a bowl of beef noodles going cold in front of him.

Then he reached across the table. First. Without calculating. And took her hand.

She looked down at it. Then up at him. Her face was doing the thing again. The thing he had seen in the cinema, when she read Why?

“That one,” she said, “was much faster.”

“I’m learning,” said Miles.

He kept the napkin. Of course he did. It went in the drawer of his one table in the staff flat, and then in the drawer of his old teacher’s desk on Bell Street, with the pink sticky notes and the other napkin and the purple pen.

Years later, she found it there, looking for a pencil.

She sat at his desk and read it again. Let P(t). Lap seems presumptuous. θ has changed. Insufficient data. And at the bottom, in her own handwriting, younger: t = now.*

And under that, in his small neat writing, added at some point she hadn’t seen:

Corollary: t = now, for all subsequent t. Verified daily.*

chapters.title: The Sticky Note Archive
chapters.desc: For his thirty-fourth birthday, she gives him a binder. A hundred and twelve sticky notes, catalogued, dated, cross-referenced, and annotated. Some of them he doesn’t remember writing. One of them she never showed him.
chapters.epigraph: “Note 47. Yellow. 28 Jan. ‘Why can’t you trust an atom? They make up everything.’ (Second use. He forgot he’d already done it on 29 Oct. I didn’t tell him.)”
chapters.content:
It was a binder.

A plain blue ring binder, A4, the kind you could buy at any stationery shop for twelve yuan. She had bought it at the stationery shop at the bottom of the hill, with her own money, from the bakery, in September, the week they moved in.

He found it on his desk on the morning of his thirty-fourth birthday, on Bell Street, across eighty centimetres from hers. Wrapped in brown paper. Tied with string. With a yellow sticky note on top.

Happy birthday. Open it at your desk. Not at the kitchen whiteboard. Not in the basement. At your desk, with tea, with time.

(I’ll be at mine.)

She was. She was sitting at her old teacher’s desk, opposite, with her chin on her hand and her tea in the white mug, watching him.

He untied the string.

✦ ✦ ✦

The cover said, in her small round handwriting, on a white label:

THE STICKY NOTE ARCHIVE Office 412 / Glass Seminar Room / Various October – June Catalogued by S.Y.J. Total items: 112

He looked up at her.

She looked back, perfectly composed, with her chin on her hand.

He opened it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first page was an introduction.

INTRODUCTION

This archive contains every sticky note exchanged between Dr. Miles Wei (office 412) and Shen Yu Jie (final-year undergraduate, Physics) between the third Wednesday of October and the twentieth of June, inclusive.

Yellow notes (n = 61): written by M.W., attached to the side of a cup of jasmine tea, typically on Wednesdays at approx. 15:45.

Pink notes (n = 51): written by S.Y.J., attached to the door of office 412, typically on Wednesdays at approx. 17:30, on leaving.

Each note has been removed from its original location, flattened, placed in a clear plastic sleeve, and catalogued by date, colour, and content type. Content types are:

J = Joke (physics) J = Joke (physics, bad)* J = Joke (physics, so bad it’s good) N = Note (not a joke) R = Rule (or reference to) X = Other

Ratings are provided for jokes on a scale of 1–10, by the cataloguer. The cataloguer acknowledges that she is biased. The cataloguer does not care.

Annotations are by the cataloguer and represent her honest opinion at the time of cataloguing, which was September, two years later, in a new flat on Bell Street, at night, while the subject of the archive was asleep.

He read it twice.

Then he turned the page.

✦ ✦ ✦

NOTE 1. Yellow. 3rd Wed. Oct. Type: J.

“Why can’t you trust an atom? They make up everything.”

Rating: 4/10.

Annotation: The first one. I found it on the side of the tea when I came in. I didn’t know what it was at first. I thought it was a reminder. Then I read it and he was standing at the chalkboard with his back to me, pretending to look for chalk, and his ears were red, and I realised: he’s been thinking about this. He went home and he thought of a joke and he wrote it down and he stuck it on my tea and now he can’t look at me.

It’s a terrible joke. Everyone knows it. It’s on T-shirts.

I kept it in my notebook for nine months.

✦ ✦ ✦

NOTE 2. Pink. 1st Wed. Nov. Type: J.

“Why did the physics lecturer break up with the biology lecturer? There was no chemistry.”

Rating: 6/10.

Annotation: Mine. My first. Three weeks of yellow notes on my tea and I finally struck back. I wrote it in the corridor outside with the notebook against the wall. My hand was shaking. I stuck it on his door at six and walked away without looking back. Fang Hao saw me. He didn’t say anything. I found out later he started the score sheet that night.

✦ ✦ ✦

He turned the pages slowly.

NOTE 9. Yellow. 2nd Wed. Nov. Type: J.

“What did one ion say to the other? ‘I’ve got my ion you.’”

Rating: 9/10.

Annotation: So bad. SO bad. I laughed so hard I had to put my head on the desk. He looked so pleased with himself. It was the first time I saw him look pleased with himself. He looks about fourteen when he does it.

NOTE 14. Pink. 2nd Wed. Nov. Type: J.

“Cu-Te.”

Rating: 9/10.

Annotation: My best one. Copper and tellurium, periodic table. I drew the little boxes. He kept this one in his drawer. I didn’t know until two years later. He told me Professor Zhou said it was “quite good.”

NOTE 22. Pink. 4th Wed. Nov. Type: J.

“I would tell you a chemistry joke, but I know I wouldn’t get a reaction.”

Rating: 5/10.

Annotation: I wrote “(from you)” underneath and then crossed it out because it was too much. You can still see it through the crossing out if you hold it up to the light. He never held it up to the light. I checked.

He held it up to the light.

(from you)

He looked across the desks at her. She was looking very hard at her tea.

✦ ✦ ✦

NOTE 31. Yellow. 11th Wed. Type: N.

[No note.]

Annotation: The Wednesday he was sick. The door was locked. There was no tea and no note. This page is empty on purpose. I’m counting it because it was the first Wednesday I realised that if he wasn’t there, the shape of the week didn’t work.

NOTE 32. Yellow. 12th Wed. Type: N.

“Thank you.”

Annotation: Just that. No joke. The Wednesday after the soup. After the oranges. He didn’t say anything about it out loud. Neither did I. We did physics for two hours and never mentioned it. But this was on the tea.

Two words. I think it’s the best note in the whole archive.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was reading slowly now. Very slowly.

NOTE 38. Yellow. Jan. Type: N.

“Professor Gao says your thesis is on strained graphene. I’ve read three papers on it this week. I have questions. Real ones. Would you mind explaining it to me?”

“(No joke today. Sorry. The joke book is being replaced.)”

Annotation: This is the one. This is the one where I stopped hiding. I read it in office 412 with my mug in my hand and he was standing at the chalkboard with a clean piece of chalk held out toward me, and I thought: nobody has ever asked me to explain my work to them. Nobody. Not my mother, not my father, not my brother, not any man at any gala.

He asked if I would mind.

Professor Gao told him to. I found that out later too. I don’t care. He asked.

NOTE 44. Yellow. Jan. Type: N.

“Corners. Fixed. Not your way. Mine. (Better.)”

Annotation: Wait. This one’s mine. It’s yellow because I used his pad. It was on his desk and I took one. I’ve put it in the yellow section anyway, because it went on the side of HIS tea, for once. The only time.

He said, “Show me.” I showed him. He said, “That’s much better than mine.”

I’ve never been happier in my life. Not before that day. I’ve been happier since. But not before.

✦ ✦ ✦

He had to stop. He put the binder down on the desk and took his glasses off and pressed his hand over his eyes for a moment.

Across the desks, she didn’t say anything. She drank her tea.

He put his glasses back on. He picked up the binder.

NOTES 56–71. Type: N, J, J.*

Annotation: The glass seminar room. February to March. Fang Hao at the end of the table eating croissants. He kept making me tea in the white mug from the kitchen and putting notes on it, and Fang Hao kept pretending to mark. I have catalogued these as a group because I can’t look at them one by one. That was the bit where we had to be the most careful. Every note is about physics. Every single one. Look at them. “The second derivative here is wrong, I think.” “Have you tried hexagons?” “Squeaking marker pens are a crime against science.”
