They’re all about physics. And every one of them is a love letter. I don’t know how he did that. I couldn’t have.

✦ ✦ ✦

NOTE 72. Yellow. 11 March. Type: X.

[No note. Empty mug.]

NOTE 73. Yellow. 18 March. Type: X.

[No note. No mug.]

Annotation: The two weeks. I didn’t go. I’ve left these pages empty too. Fang Hao told me afterwards that the first week he made tea in my mug anyway, by accident, and poured it down the sink at six. The second week he didn’t make it, on purpose, and made his own.

I didn’t know any of that while it was happening. I was on the second floor, not eating, working fourteen hours a day, and walking past the glass room every morning without looking in.

Until I did.

NOTE 74. Whiteboard. 18 March. Type: N.

“Still here.”

Annotation: This isn’t a sticky note. It was on the whiteboard. I couldn’t take it. So I photographed it through the glass, at eight in the morning, on my phone. The photograph is in this sleeve. It’s a bit blurry. My hands were shaking.

He looked at the photograph in the sleeve. Blurry. Through glass. The bottom right-hand corner of a whiteboard. 20 June, 16:00. Still here.

✦ ✦ ✦

NOTE 75. Yellow. Via Old Huang. Type: N.

“You were right. I did the same thing. I’m sorry.”

“(Please don’t talk about the weather.)”

Annotation: Slightly damp. He wrote it eleven times. Tao Tao asked Fang Hao and Fang Hao told her. This is the eleventh. The rain got on it at the blue door.

I was still angry when I read it.

I kept it anyway.

NOTE 76. Yellow. Via Prof. Zhou. Type: N. (Written by S.Y.J.)

“I asked my father. Not you. I should have asked you in January. I’m asking now. The tank is yours. Keep it or don’t. Your choice. Still angry. Still peeling oranges.”

Annotation: Mine. Written in the lift going down the Shen Building. He kept it and gave it back to me for the archive. He said it belonged with the others.

✦ ✦ ✦

The last section had no heading. Just a date.

20 June.

NOTE 111. Pink. 20 June, approx. 11:00. Type: N.

“Today.”

Annotation: I stuck this on his door at eleven in the morning, before the ceremony. I went up to the fourth floor in my gown and stuck it on the door of office 412 and ran away before he could open it. One word.

He didn’t take it down. It was still there at 4:01.

He remembered. He had heard someone on the stairs at eleven. He had gone out into the corridor and found the pink square stuck to the outside of the open door. Today. He had stood in the doorway for a long time.

He turned the page.

NOTE 112. Yellow. 20 June, 16:02 approx. Type: N.

“Not constant.”

Annotation: This isn’t a sticky note either. It was written in chalk, on a board, and then on a wall. I couldn’t take that one. But Fang Hao took a photograph of it the next morning, when we were—when we weren’t looking, and gave it to me. I’ve counted it as yellow, because it was his.

It’s the last note of the archive. After that, there was no more three metres. No more tea on Wednesdays with something stuck to the side. No more pink squares on a door.

After that, we just talked.

✦ ✦ ✦

He closed the binder.

He sat at his desk on Bell Street, across from hers, with his hands flat on the blue cover, and didn’t say anything.

Then he looked up at her.

“That’s a hundred and twelve,” he said.

“Yes.”

“Sixty-one yellow and fifty-one pink.”

“Yes.”

“That doesn’t add up,” said Miles. “There are empty pages. There’s a whiteboard. There’s a chalk drawing on a wall. There’s one you wrote on my pad. You’ve—” He stopped. He looked at her. “You’ve adjusted the counting. You’ve made decisions about what counts. That’s not rigorous.”

“No,” said Yu Jie. “It isn’t.”

She was smiling.

“I wanted it to come out to a hundred and twelve,” she said. “Because that’s what I told you, on the first night in this flat. When you were asleep. I counted them on my knees on the floor by the light from the street and it came to a hundred and seven, and I thought, that’s wrong, there were more than that, and then I thought about the empty Wednesdays and the whiteboard and the wall.” She shrugged. “So I counted those. Because they were notes. They just weren’t on paper.”

He looked at her.

“That’s not science,” he said.

“No,” agreed Yu Jie. “It’s an archive. Archives are allowed to be biased.” She drank her tea. “Read the inside of the back cover.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He opened the binder again. At the back.

Taped inside the back cover, on its own, without a plastic sleeve, there was one more sticky note.

Pink.

Old. Slightly faded at the edges. The adhesive had gone, long ago; it was held on with clear tape.

He didn’t recognise it.

He read it.

Dear Dr. Wei,

I came to your office hours today on the wrong day with a problem I had already solved. You did it the long way to prove I didn’t need you. You were right. I didn’t.

I’m coming back next Wednesday anyway.

I think I might be in trouble.

— S.Y.J.

And at the top, very small, a date. The second Wednesday of September. Two years and a month ago.

He looked up.

“I wrote that one at 5:14,” said Yu Jie. “The first Wednesday. Sitting on the stairs, between the third floor and the fourth. On a pink pad I had in my bag. I was going to stick it on your door.” She looked at her tea. “I got as far as the corridor. And then I couldn’t. And I went home and lay on my bed and looked at the ceiling for three hours. And I put it in a notebook, and it stayed there.”

He was holding it very carefully.

“It’s note zero,” she said. “It doesn’t count. It’s not in the hundred and twelve. It came before the archive started.” She looked at him across eighty centimetres. “It’s the base case.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say anything.

He put the binder down very carefully on his desk, open at the back cover, with the pink note showing. He took off his glasses again. He put them on the desk.

Then he got up. He came round the desks. Not the short way. The long way, round the end, because the desks were pushed together and there was no other way, and it took him four steps, and she watched him take every one.

He knelt down beside her chair. He put his arms round her waist and his face in her lap, on the yellow sundress, and stayed there.

She put her hand in his hair.

“Happy birthday,” she said.

He said something into the sundress that she couldn’t hear.

“What?”

He lifted his head. His eyes were wet.

“I said,” said Miles, “I’m coming back next Wednesday anyway.”

She laughed. She bent down and kissed the top of his head.

“I know,” she said. “You always do.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The binder lives on the shelf above his desk now. Between Principles of Quantum Mechanics, retired from door-propping, and a framed photograph cut out of page six of the Harbour Daily.

The pink note on the inside of the back cover has been read so many times that the clear tape over it has gone cloudy.

Note zero.

The base case.

chapters.title: Zhao Zhendong Is Glaring at Me From Across the Room
chapters.desc: The Shen Foundation gala, from inside Miles’s head. A running log of one arms dealer’s stare, the reunion he has spent five years being embarrassed about, and the moment the glaring changed direction.
chapters.epigraph: “19:42. Still glaring. I have moved four metres to the left. The glare has moved four metres to the left.”
chapters.content:
From a notebook found in the inside pocket of a black tuxedo, size 40 long, the morning after the Shen Foundation Winter Gala. Handwriting: small, neat, increasingly unsteady.

✦ ✦ ✦

19:04. Arrived. Ballroom very large. Ice sculpture of a ship. Melting. Rate of melting approx. 2 cm/hour at the bow, judging by the drip into the tray. It will not survive the evening. I feel a certain kinship with it.

19:06. Located food. Picked up plate, per Rule 2 (Fang Hao). Plate empty. Holding it.

19:11. Have seen Professor Gao. Black dress. Looks like she would rather be on fire. Have seen Professor Zhou. He nodded at me. I think he is still thinking about the seminar.

19:14. Have not seen her yet.

19:20. The Shen family. Staircase. She is—

I don’t have a word. I’ve tried four. I’ve crossed them out. I’ll come back to this.

19:21. Her mother has a hand on her elbow. Like turning a vase.

19:22. I don’t like it.

19:22. That’s not a scientific observation. I’m recording it anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

19:31. Aurelia Song. Aurelia CHEN. Behind me. She has fixed my bow tie. In three movements. As at the reunion. Her husband says he has heard a great deal about me, “mostly unprintable.” I believe him.

19:33. Elowen.

19:33. And him.

✦ ✦ ✦

19:34. I need to record something for context. In case anyone finds this. In case I die.

Five years ago, at my old school’s sixtieth anniversary, I gave a speech about light. Gravitational lensing. I had slides. I dropped the clicker halfway through. That is not the embarrassing part.

The embarrassing part is that afterwards, I went out onto a balcony and found Elowen Lin on her own, in a red dress, looking at the city, and I asked her if she was happy. Which I still think was the right question. And then I went back inside, and there was a man by the wall. Very large. Black suit. The kind of stillness you see in a very heavy object that has decided not to move yet.

I went up to him. I don’t know why. I was out of breath from the speech. I said—I remember exactly—She doesn’t look like she wants to run.

He looked at me. He didn’t say anything. He just looked at me. For approximately four seconds.

I have thought about those four seconds roughly once a month for five years.

I found out later who he was. Zhao Zhendong. The newspapers have several words for what he does. Import and export is the politest. He married her. They were in the society pages. Fang Hao showed me the photograph and said, “Isn’t that the girl from your school?” and I said yes, and he said, “Isn’t that the man who sells guns?” and I said yes, and he said, “Miles, did you say something to the man who sells guns?” and I said yes, and he laughed for eleven minutes.

✦ ✦ ✦

19:35. He is by a pillar. Two metres behind Elowen and slightly to the left. Hands at sides. Same stillness.

He is looking at me.

19:35. No. Correction. He is glaring at me.

19:36. I said hello. He said “Yes.” That was all. Yes. Not hello. Yes. As in: Yes, I remember you. Yes, it was you on the balcony. Yes, I have been thinking about it for five years too.

19:36. Aurelia has whispered to her husband that he is “still jealous.” She appears delighted. Her husband appears to have expected this.

Jealous. Of me.

I am a physicist. I live in a staff flat. I have one egg. I would lose a fight to a coat stand.

19:37. The glare continues.

✦ ✦ ✦

19:42. Have moved four metres to the left, toward the dessert table, on the pretext of examining a tart. The glare has moved four metres to the left.

He hasn’t moved. Only his eyes. It’s like being tracked by a telescope.

19:44. Have moved back. The glare has moved back.

19:45. Tried an experiment. Smiled at him. Politely.

The glare intensified.

19:45. Experiment concluded. Will not repeat.

✦ ✦ ✦

19:52. Aurelia talking. A great deal. About the seminar video. Apparently somebody posted it online and she watched it six times. She says she never heard me laugh once in two years of school.

That’s true. I didn’t, much. Not after the library.

19:53. Elowen is quiet. She keeps glancing back at him. Every few seconds. As if checking he’s still there. He is always still there.

She has a green stain on her thumb. Stems. She cut flowers this morning and came straight here.

19:54. Aurelia has said, very loudly, that Elowen has three hundred white roses to do for a wedding tomorrow and that he is driving her to the flower market at half past three in the morning to carry the buckets. He has moved half a step closer to Elowen. A waiter came within two metres of her with champagne. The waiter has left. Quickly.

19:54. So that’s what the glare is for. Not me. Or not only me. Everything. Every waiter, every tray, every man within two metres. He has been standing by that pillar since she arrived, watching every single thing that comes near her, and I just happen to be the thing that has been near her longest.

19:55. That’s not jealousy. Or it is, but it’s not the kind Aurelia means.

It’s the kind that knows exactly how much it has to lose.

✦ ✦ ✦

19:58. Elowen told me he closed her shop for a week last month without telling her and took her to the mountains, because she hadn’t had a day off in ten years. He’d had someone learn the whole order book first. They’re going to Iceland in February, to see the northern lights. He has read eleven books about them.

She said he was the most frightening man in the city, and that he holds her coat like it’s made of glass.

I looked at him by the pillar. At the stillness. At the hands at his sides.

I think I understand the stillness now. It’s not a man deciding not to move. It’s a man holding himself very still because if he moves at all, he might not be able to stop.

I know that. I’ve been doing it since September. Three metres.

19:58. I don’t know why I’ve written that down. Fang Hao would say it’s because I’m projecting. Fang Hao would be right.

✦ ✦ ✦

20:03. She looked at me.

Across the ballroom. Between two men in tuxedos her mother is introducing. She stopped smiling. For one second.

I don’t have a word for this either. I’ve tried six. I’ll come back to it. I might not come back to it. Some things don’t have words. That’s why there’s mathematics.

20:03. Aurelia saw. Elowen saw. Chen Si saw.

20:04. He saw.

✦ ✦ ✦

20:04. Something has changed.

He has stopped glaring at me.

He is looking across the ballroom. At her. At the girl by the stage, with her mother’s hand on her elbow and the nine men. He looks for a long time. Then back at me.

The glare is gone. Something else has replaced it.

I’ve seen it before. On Professor Gao, in my office, in November, looking at the corner of my chalkboard. On Fang Hao, every Wednesday since October, through the cardboard wall.

It’s the face of someone who has just worked out the answer to a problem and is deciding whether to tell you.

20:05. He hasn’t told me.

20:05. He’s still looking at me.

20:05. I’d like to report that this is much worse than the glaring.

✦ ✦ ✦

20:30–22:45. [Several pages. Mostly about her. The terrace. Elowen. Are you happy? The diplomat. The waltz. Knuckles. A plate. Not reproduced here, at the request of the notebook’s owner, who says they are “not for anyone” and that his wife has already read them and “that’s enough.”]

✦ ✦ ✦

00:31. Still here. Rule 3. Don’t leave early.

Ballroom emptying. The ice ship has lost its bow entirely. It is now an ice raft.

00:38. Professor Gao went past. She said “Good.” Nothing else.

00:44. Aurelia kissed me on both cheeks and said Wednesdays in a terrible whisper. I don’t know how she knows about Wednesdays. I suspect Elowen. I suspect the terrace door was not as closed as I thought.

00:46. He’s coming this way.

00:46. With Elowen on his arm.

00:46. He has stopped in front of me.

✦ ✦ ✦

00:47. I need to record this exactly. I have a very good memory. I want to have it written down anyway.

He stopped. He looked down at me. He is approximately twenty centimetres taller than me, which I wouldn’t have thought possible, because I am tall, and I have never in my life been looked down at by anyone.

He said: She’s a good girl. The Shen one.

I said: Yes.

He looked at me for approximately four seconds. The same four seconds as five years ago. I counted.

Then he said: Don’t be stupid about it.

And walked on.

✦ ✦ ✦

00:48. I have been standing by the empty food table for one minute trying to work out whether I have been threatened or blessed.

00:49. Elowen looked back over her shoulder and smiled.

00:49. Blessed, then. Probably.

00:50. With that man, I think it might be the same thing.

✦ ✦ ✦

00:51. One more note, and then I’m going to go and find a taxi, and then I’m going to go home.

Five years ago, at a reunion, I told a man I had never met that the woman he was watching didn’t look like she wanted to run. I didn’t know who he was. I didn’t know what he did. I was out of breath and I said it because it was true and because I thought he should know.

I have been embarrassed about it for five years.

Tonight, he walked up to me in a ballroom and told me that the woman I was watching was a good girl. And not to be stupid about it.

He didn’t know I was in love with her. Nobody knows. I haven’t told anyone. I’ve barely told myself.

He worked it out from across a room, in one look, at 20:04.

00:51. I think he’s been waiting five years to return the favour.

00:52. I think I’m going to stop being embarrassed now.

00:52. Going outside. It’s cold. I hope she has a coat.

✦ ✦ ✦

[The last line of the notebook, added in different ink, much later, in the same small neat hand:]

She didn’t have a coat. I gave her my jacket. I walked her the long way. That is, as Zhao Zhendong would say, another story.

A year and five months later, he asked me to teach him how to fill a flower shop with rainbows. Every other Saturday. He pays me in tangerines. I didn’t ask for anything. He said he pays everyone.

He still glares at me. I’ve stopped minding.

I think it’s how he says thank you.

chapters.title: Miles Tries to Text With Emojis

chapters.epigraph: “Miles. Why did you just send me a picture of a test tube.” “It’s an emoji. Ouyang says people use them to express feelings.” “What feeling is a test tube.” “…Excitement?”
chapters.content:

chapters.title: Yu Jie Teaches First Years
chapters.desc: Doctoral student, first-year problem class, Thursday mornings, room 104. She is terrifying. They are terrified. By November, there is a queue outside the door on the wrong day.
chapters.epigraph: “There is no such thing as a stupid question in this room. There are only questions you haven’t asked yet, and those are the stupid ones.”
chapters.content:
Every doctoral student in the department had to teach.

It was in the contract. Four hours a week, in the first year: a problem class, where first-year undergraduates came in groups of twenty to work through the week’s homework with someone who was not a lecturer, and was therefore, in theory, less frightening.

Professor Gao gave Yu Jie first-year mechanics. Thursday mornings, nine until eleven, room 104.

“They’re eighteen,” said Professor Gao, on the balcony, smoking. “They’ve come from schools where they were the cleverest person in the room. Half of them have never been wrong in public in their lives. They will sit at the back and not ask anything and fail in January, and cry in my office, and I don’t have time.” She tapped ash over the railing. “Make them ask questions.”

“How?”

Professor Gao looked at her.

“You walked into a lecturer’s office on the wrong day with a problem you’d already solved,” she said, “because you’d watched him from the back of a lecture theatre for two weeks and he was the only person in the building who said I don’t know out loud.” She stubbed out the cigarette. “Be that.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the first Thursday, twenty first-years sat in room 104 in silence.

They sat in rows. Nobody sat in the front row. They had their homework out on the desks in front of them, and their pens, and their phones, face down, and they looked at the young woman at the front of the room with four pens in her hair and a yellow cardigan and biro on her trainers as if she were an exam.

She looked back at them.

She remembered being eighteen. She remembered sitting at the back of Lecture Theatre C in her first week, in a dress her mother had chosen, not asking anything, because if she asked something, someone might find out she didn’t know, and if someone found out she didn’t know, someone might tell her mother.

“Good morning,” she said. “My name is Shen Yu Jie. I’m a first-year doctoral student in condensed matter. I’m going to help you with mechanics on Thursdays.”

Silence.

“I’m going to tell you three rules,” she said. “Then we’ll start.”

She turned to the board. It was a whiteboard. She had asked facilities for a chalkboard. Facilities had said it was the twenty-first century.

She picked up a marker. It squeaked.

RULE 1. There is no such thing as a stupid question in this room.

She turned round.

“There are only questions you haven’t asked yet,” she said. “And those are the stupid ones.”

Twenty faces looked at her.

RULE 2. I will get things wrong. When I do, tell me. Out loud. In front of everyone.

“If you find a mistake I make,” she said, “and you tell me, and you’re right, you get a sweet.” She took a bag of White Rabbit sweets out of her bag and put it on the desk. “If you find a mistake I make and you don’t tell me, and I find out later, I will be very disappointed in you, and I will not be quiet about it.”

A girl in the third row, very small, with enormous glasses, put her hand over her mouth.

RULE 3.

She stopped. She held the marker against the board for a moment.

RULE 3. If you say “I don’t know,” you have to follow it with “but here’s how I’d find out.”

She put the marker down.

“That’s it,” she said. “Problem one. Who wants to start?”

Silence.

Nobody moved.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took four weeks.

The first Thursday, nobody asked a question. She did all the problems herself on the squeaking whiteboard and they copied them down in silence and left.

The second Thursday, nobody asked a question. She did problem three wrong on purpose, a sign error in the second line, and waited. Nobody said anything. She finished it, wrong, with the wrong answer at the bottom, and turned round and said, “Is that right?” and twenty people nodded.

She looked at them.

“No,” she said. “It isn’t. There’s a sign error in the second line. I put it there on purpose. Twenty of you saw this board and not one of you said anything.” She held up the bag of White Rabbit sweets. “Nobody gets one this week.”

The girl with the enormous glasses in the third row went bright red.

The third Thursday, she did it again. A different mistake, in problem two. A factor of two, missing. She finished it and turned round and said, “Is that right?”

The girl with the enormous glasses put her hand up.

Not very high. About as high as her ear. Shaking.

“Yes?” said Yu Jie.

“I think—” said the girl. Her voice was so quiet Yu Jie could barely hear it. “I think you’ve missed a factor of two. In the third line. I think—I’m sorry—I think it should be two m g, not m g. Because there are two masses. I’m sorry.”

The room went silent.

Yu Jie looked at the board. At the third line.

She looked at the girl in the third row, with her hand still up at the height of her ear, shaking.

“You’re right,” she said.

She picked up the bag of White Rabbit sweets. She walked down the room, between the desks, past the second row, to the third. She held out the bag.

“What’s your name?” she said.

“Li Xiaoqing,” whispered the girl.

“Li Xiaoqing,” said Yu Jie. “You’re right. I made a mistake and you found it. Take two. One for finding it. One for saying it out loud.” She held the bag out further. “And don’t ever say sorry for being right in this room again.”

Li Xiaoqing took two sweets.

She looked at them in her hand. Then up at Yu Jie. Her face was doing something that Yu Jie recognised, very suddenly, from the inside.

It was the face of someone who had been right in public for the first time in her life, and had not been punished for it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The fourth Thursday, there were nine questions.

The fifth Thursday, there were fourteen. A boy at the back called Huo, who wore a basketball shirt and had not said a word for a month, asked why you couldn’t just treat everything as a point, and it turned into a forty-minute argument about rigid bodies that the whole room joined, and they didn’t get to problem four.

The sixth Thursday, someone found a real mistake. Not one she’d put there. A real one. In problem five. She had copied a number wrong from the answer sheet. A boy in the second row said, “Er—isn’t that supposed to be 9.8, not 9.6?” and she looked, and it was, and she said “Yes,” so loudly and so delightedly that the whole room jumped, and she threw him the whole bag of sweets.

“That,” she said, “is the best thing that has happened in this room all term.”

The boy looked at the bag of sweets in his lap with an expression of total bewilderment.

“It was just a typo,” he said.

“It was a typo you noticed,” said Yu Jie. “And then you said it. Out loud. To a doctoral student. In front of nineteen people.” She pointed at him with the marker. “Do you know how many people in this building never do that? Do you know how many professors I’ve met who can’t say I think you’ve made a mistake to someone more senior than them? Do you know how many people I’ve watched talk for four minutes in an interview, pretending to know the answer to a question about boundary conditions, instead of just saying I don’t know?”

The boy shook his head.

“Lots,” said Yu Jie. “Lots and lots. Don’t be one of them.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By November, there was a queue.

Not on Thursday mornings. On Thursday afternoons. And on Tuesdays. And once, memorably, on a Wednesday at 3:45, outside the door of Professor Gao’s lab on the second floor, where Yu Jie had a desk: four first-years, with their homework, waiting.

Li Xiaoqing was at the front. She had her hand half up, at the height of her ear, even though nobody had asked her anything yet.

Yu Jie stopped in the corridor and looked at them.

“It’s Wednesday,” she said.

“We know,” said Li Xiaoqing. “Your problem class is Thursday. But we had a question. About the homework. We couldn’t wait.” She went red. “Is that—is that allowed?”

Yu Jie stood in the corridor outside Professor Gao’s lab, on a Wednesday, at 3:45, and looked at four eighteen-year-olds who had come on the wrong day with a question.

She thought about a door propped open with Principles of Quantum Mechanics. A sign with a green cat in a box. Other times: please email. I will reply. Eventually.

You need a different excuse for coming on a Wednesday.

“Come in,” she said. “Unless you’re from facilities.”

They looked at her in total confusion.

“Never mind,” said Yu Jie. “It’s a joke. You’ll get it in about three years. Come in.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She told him about it that night, across the two desks on Bell Street.

“They came on a Wednesday,” she said. “At 3:45. Four of them. With a question they could have waited a day for. Li Xiaoqing said they couldn’t wait.” She put her face in her hands. “Miles, I’m you. I’ve turned into you. I’m sitting in an office on the wrong day being found by people with questions.”

He was looking at her across the desks with an expression she couldn’t quite read.

“Were any of them boys?” he said.

She lowered her hands.

“Miles.”

“I’m asking for a friend.”

“You don’t have any friends except Fang Hao.”

“Fang Hao would also like to know. On my behalf.” He pushed his glasses up. “Someone came to my office on the wrong day once. I know exactly where it leads. I’d like it noted that I’m monitoring the situation.”

She stared at him across the eighty centimetres. Then she put her forehead down on her desk and laughed until it shook.

“Two of them were boys,” she said, muffled. “Huo is in love with a girl in chemistry. The other one cried when his top fell over.”

“Good,” said Miles. And then, recovering his dignity: “What was the question?”

“Why a spinning top doesn’t fall over.”

“That’s a very good question.”

“I know. It took two hours. We used a coin and a pencil and Professor Gao’s mug. She came in halfway through and saw us spinning her mug on the bench and didn’t say anything, and then she sat down at the back and listened to the rest of it.” Yu Jie took her face out of her hands. “And at the end, Li Xiaoqing said, I don’t know how gyroscopes work, but here’s how I’d find out, and then she told me. Properly. Step by step. Without saying sorry once.”

Miles didn’t say anything for a moment.

“Do you know what you’ve done?” he said.

“What?”

“You’ve made someone stop hiding,” said Miles.

She looked at him.

“Professor Gao said something to me once,” he said. “On the first day you came to her balcony and I didn’t know about it. She came to my office afterwards. She said, It isn’t flirting. It’s the first time in her life anyone has taken her mind seriously.” He looked down at his tea. “She told me to keep giving you the hard problems. She said that was my job.” He looked back up. “You’re doing it. For a girl with enormous glasses who says sorry for being right.”

Yu Jie was very still across the desks.

“I didn’t know she said that,” she said. “Gao. To you.”

“She also told me to get a better joke book.”

She laughed. It came out shaky.

“Did you?”

“No,” said Miles. “I’ve never got a better joke book. I’ve just been writing worse ones. For two years.” He reached across the eighty centimetres and took her hand. “Li Xiaoqing is very lucky.”

“Why?”

“Because,” said Miles, “she has someone who will tell her she’s right out loud, in front of nineteen people, and throw sweets at her for it. And then make her say why.” He held her hand on the old wood. “Most people don’t get that. I didn’t, until I was thirty-one. And then I got it from a student who came on the wrong day.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At the end of the year, the first-years filled in a feedback form about their problem classes.

Most of the forms were blank or said fine. That was normal. Fang Hao said his always said fine and once, memorably, he eats too many croissants.

Yu Jie’s were not blank.

Professor Gao brought them up to the fourth floor in a brown envelope and gave them to Miles, not to Yu Jie, because, she said, she wanted somebody to read them who would not immediately cry. Miles read them in office 412 with the door propped open, and immediately cried, and Fang Hao came in through the cardboard wall to see what was wrong and read them over his shoulder and also cried, and they had to close the door.

She is terrifying. In a good way. I asked my first question ever in a physics class in her room.

She threw sweets at me for finding a mistake. I have never been happier.

Rule 3 changed my life. I say it in every class now. My chemistry lecturer has started saying it back.

She made us spin Professor Gao’s mug. Professor Gao was there. Nothing bad happened.

She told me not to say sorry for being right. I didn’t know that was allowed.

And at the bottom of the pile, a form filled in very small, in careful handwriting, with a drawing in the corner of a girl with enormous glasses holding two White Rabbit sweets.

Before this class, I thought I wasn’t clever enough to be a physicist because I was scared of asking questions. Now I know that being scared and asking anyway is what makes you one. I don’t know how to say thank you properly. But here’s how I’d find out: I’m going to come back next year and be a mentor for the new first-years, and tell them the rules.

— L.X.Q.

Miles put the form down on his desk in office 412.

He looked at the bottom right-hand corner of the chalkboard, where, a long time ago, in small round handwriting, someone had written a date. It was still there. He had never wiped it off; he never would. Beside it, very small, in his own handwriting, there was a small square. Slightly crooked on the right-hand side.

He took a yellow sticky note. He wrote on it.

That evening, on Bell Street, she found it stuck to the side of her tea.

Why did the doctoral student make her first-years cry?

Because she taught them they were allowed to be right.

(That one isn’t a joke either. I’m very proud of you.)

chapters.title: The Department Christmas Party
chapters.desc: The first department party Miles Wei has attended in seven years. There is a quiz. He wins it. There is also karaoke, a dumpling race, a secret gift exchange and a dance-off with the Head of Department. She wins everything else.
chapters.epigraph: “Round Six: Physics. Dr. Wei, would you please stop answering before I’ve finished the question.”
chapters.content:
The Department of Physics Christmas party was held every year on the last Friday before the winter break, in the third-floor common room, with warm white wine in plastic cups, a buffet from the canteen, a quiz, and a great deal of determined, slightly desperate cheer.

Miles had not been to it in seven years.

He had gone once, in his first December. He had stood in a corner with a plastic cup for forty minutes while people talked about funding and their children and the new car park, and then a visiting professor had cornered him about dark matter for half an hour, and then he had left, quietly, through the fire door, and walked home, and never gone back.

“We’re going,” said Yu Jie, on the Monday.

“I don’t go.”

“You didn’t go. Past tense. Now you’re engaged to a doctoral student in the department and Professor Zhou has personally asked me to make sure you come, because, quote, it would be good for morale.”

“Whose morale?”

“Everyone’s,” said Yu Jie. “Fang Hao has started a pool on whether you’ll last an hour.”

Miles looked at her across the two desks.

“What are the odds?”

“Three to one against.”

He thought about it.

“Put fifty on me,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The common room had been decorated by the PhD students, which meant it had been decorated with enthusiasm rather than skill. There was tinsel on the whiteboard. Someone had made a Christmas tree out of a stack of old journals and a lot of fairy lights. There was a sign over the buffet that said MERRY CHRISTMAS AND A HAPPY NEW YEAR (APPROXIMATELY), and someone had added, in red marker, TO WITHIN EXPERIMENTAL ERROR.

Miles stood in the doorway at seven o’clock and looked at it all with the expression of a man entering a cave of unknown depth.

Yu Jie took his hand.

“Corner?” she said.

“Corner,” said Miles.

“No,” said Yu Jie. “Food. Rule two.”

They went to the food.

✦ ✦ ✦

The quiz was at eight.

It was run, every year, by Professor Zhou, who took it extremely seriously. He sat at a small table at the front of the room with a bell, a sheet of questions he had written himself, and a pair of reading glasses that he actually wore. There were eight rounds. Teams of four. The prize was a bottle of very good whisky that Professor Zhou bought himself and had never once, in twenty years, had to give to anyone outside the theory group.

Miles was on a team with Yu Jie, Fang Hao and Ouyang.

“I don’t know anything,” said Ouyang in terror. “I’m not good at quizzes. I only know about water.”

“There might be a water question,” said Yu Jie kindly.

There was not a water question.

✦ ✦ ✦

Round One: General Knowledge.

They came seventh out of nine. Miles knew the capital of Mongolia and nothing else. Fang Hao knew all the food questions. Yu Jie knew the answer to a question about opera because Tao Tao’s grandmother sang it, and to a question about the stock market, and then went very quiet, because she knew it from Sunday dinners at the museum.

Round Two: History. Sixth.

Round Three: Music. Ninth. Last. Miles thought a famous pop singer was a type of pasta.

Round Four: Sport. Ninth again. Nobody on the team had ever watched any sport. Ouyang said he had once watched a swimming race, for the fluid dynamics. Fang Hao said that was the saddest thing he had heard all year.

“We’re losing,” said Fang Hao, with despair, at the halfway point.

“We’re extremely losing,” agreed Yu Jie.

Miles was looking at the sheet. At the list of rounds.

Round Five: Film and TV.

Round Six: Physics.

Round Seven: Science (Other).

Round Eight: The Department.

“Wait,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Round Six: Physics.

Professor Zhou cleared his throat. He rang the bell.

“Question one,” he said. “What is the name given to the—”

“Chandrasekhar limit,” said Miles.

Professor Zhou looked at him over his reading glasses.

“I hadn’t finished the question, Dr. Wei.”

“You were going to say the maximum mass of a white dwarf star,” said Miles. “It’s the Chandrasekhar limit. About 1.4 solar masses.”

Professor Zhou looked at his sheet. He looked at Miles.

“…Yes,” he said. “Write it down. Question two. What—”

“Planck’s constant.”

“Dr. Wei.”

“Sorry.”

“Question two,” said Professor Zhou firmly. “What is the name of the constant that relates the energy of a photon to its frequency?”

“Planck’s constant,” said Miles.

“Thank you.”

“Question three—”

“Noether,” said Miles, and Yu Jie put her hand over his mouth.

✦ ✦ ✦

He got all ten.

He got all ten in Round Seven, too. Chemistry, biology, a question about plate tectonics that nobody else in the room knew and that he answered while eating a dumpling. A question about the speed of sound in water that Ouyang answered first, shouting it, overjoyed, and then sat down very red while the whole team cheered.

Round Eight was The Department.

“Question one,” said Professor Zhou. “In what year was the sundial in the garden installed?”

“1958,” said Miles. “The latitude’s wrong. It’s three degrees off. So it’s right at noon and gets worse all afternoon. Ten minutes out by five o’clock in summer.”

The room went quiet.

Professor Zhou took off his reading glasses.

“How do you know that?” he said.

“I checked it,” said Miles, surprised. “In my first year. I was bored. It was before—” He stopped. He went slightly red. “It was before I had Wednesdays.”

Somewhere in the room, someone said, “Awww.”

Professor Zhou put his reading glasses back on very slowly.

“Question two,” he said. “How many sticky notes were on the door of office 412 when it was photographed for the student forum in—”

“Professor Zhou,” said Yu Jie.

“Withdrawn,” said Professor Zhou. “Withdrawn. That was in poor taste. I wrote this in October. I apologise.” He crossed it out. “Question two. What is the correct answer to the question I ask every single candidate at every single thesis defence?”

The whole room, all sixty people, said it at once.

“Tell me about your boundary conditions.”

Professor Zhou looked out at his department.

He smiled. He did it more often these days. Fang Hao claimed to be keeping count.

✦ ✦ ✦

They won.

By one point. Over the theory group, who had won for nineteen years running and were very upset about it. Dr. Ren Bo, who was in the theory group, came over afterwards and shook Miles’s hand and said, stiffly, “The sundial. That was good. I didn’t know that,” and Miles said, “It’s three degrees,” and Ren said, “I heard,” and went away.

Professor Zhou handed over the whisky.

Miles held it. He had never won anything at a party in his life. He had never been at a party long enough to win anything.

“I’ve won a quiz,” he said, to Yu Jie, in wonder.

“You’ve won a quiz,” she agreed. “You got thirty-one out of thirty answers in the last three rounds.”

“There were only thirty questions.”

“You answered one of them before Professor Zhou finished asking it, and it turned out to be the answer to the next one.”

He looked at the whisky. He looked at her. He looked at Fang Hao, who was collecting money from three people at once for the pool, looking extremely smug.

“I’ve been here an hour and forty minutes,” said Miles.

“You have.”

“I haven’t left.”

“No,” said Yu Jie. “You haven’t.”

He looked round the common room. At the tinsel on the whiteboard and the Christmas tree made of journals. At Ouyang, who was being congratulated by two other PhD students about the speed of sound in water and looked as if he might faint with happiness. At Professor Gao, by the window, with a plastic cup of wine and an unlit cigarette, watching him.

“I don’t want to leave,” he said, surprised.

✦ ✦ ✦

After the quiz, there was karaoke.

There was always karaoke. Fang Hao had brought a machine from home that his wife had bought in 2009 and that had never been updated, so all the songs were at least fifteen years old. The PhD students sang first, very badly, in groups, for courage. Then the postdocs. Then, as always, Professor Gao, who sang one song every year, the same one, an old revolutionary anthem, in a fierce flat voice, without looking at the screen, and sat down to stunned applause, and refused to discuss it.

Then Fang Hao picked up the microphone and said, “And now, by special request—”

“No,” said Miles.

“—Dr. Miles Wei and Dr.-to-be Shen Yu Jie.”

“Absolutely not,” said Miles.

Yu Jie had already stood up.

She went to the front of the room. She took the microphone. She scrolled through the ancient machine’s list of songs, looking for something, while sixty physicists watched.

She found it.

The screen changed. An old song. A slow one. A woman singing in Cantonese, about the moon. The one from the basement.

Miles went completely still in his chair.

She held out her hand to him from the front of the room.

“You don’t have to sing,” she said, into the microphone. “I know you can’t. You just have to come up here and stand next to me.” She smiled. “Like a plate at a gala.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He went up.

He stood next to her at the front of the third-floor common room in front of sixty members of his department, holding nothing, with his hands at his sides, very straight, red to the ears.

She sang.

She had a good voice. Not trained. Not perfect. But true, and warm, and slightly husky on the low notes, and she sang the old song about the moon the way Tao Tao’s grandmother sang it when she was folding dumplings, not for an audience, just because it was the song.

He looked at her the whole time.

He didn’t look at the screen, or at the room, or at anybody. He looked at her, singing, with four pens in her hair and her eyes half-closed, in the light from a Christmas tree made of old journals.

Halfway through the second verse, she held the microphone out to him.

He looked at it.

The whole room held its breath.

He took it.

He didn’t sing. He couldn’t. He knew he couldn’t. He opened his mouth and nothing came out, and he stood there with the microphone and the words going past on the screen, and then he did the only thing he could think of.

He said them.

Not sung. Spoken. Quietly, into the microphone, in his lecture voice, over the music: the words of the song, one line after another, in Cantonese, which he did not speak, and had learned, he would tell her later, phonetically, from the recording on her phone, over three weeks, in the basement, when she thought he was checking the pumps.

He got every word right.

He gave the microphone back to her for the last line. She couldn’t sing it. She was crying. She laughed into the microphone instead, and the whole room laughed with her, and someone at the back started clapping, and then everyone was.

Professor Gao, by the window, put her unlit cigarette in her mouth and took it out again and put it back.

✦ ✦ ✦

And then, at the end of the night, there was the dance-off.

There was always a dance-off. It was a tradition nobody could remember starting. At eleven o’clock, the PhD students put on the oldest, worst song on Fang Hao’s ancient karaoke machine, very loudly, and the person who danced the longest without stopping won a small plastic trophy shaped like an electron, which had been passed down since 2004.

Miles did not dance.

He had been very clear about this. He had danced exactly once in his life, in a basement, in the dark, with one earbud, and it had been a private matter.

Yu Jie danced.

She danced for fourteen minutes. Against four PhD students, two postdocs, Fang Hao, who had to stop at minute six because of a croissant-related cramp, and Bai Tianyu’s younger brother, who had sneaked in.

At minute eleven, it was just her.

And Professor Zhou.

He had stood up at minute nine. Nobody had seen it coming. He had taken off his cardigan and folded it on his chair and walked out into the middle of the common room in his shirtsleeves and started to dance. Very gravely. With great precision. In a small, steady, rhythmic shuffle that he did not vary at all, and that had, it turned out, been winning the department dance-off every single year since 2004, because nobody had ever lasted long enough to beat him.

At minute twelve, they were face to face. The Head of Department and the doctoral student. In the middle of the floor. In front of everyone.

At minute thirteen, the whole department was chanting.

At minute fourteen, the song ended.

Professor Zhou stopped. He was breathing hard. He looked at the young woman in front of him, who was laughing and out of breath and still dancing, very slightly, on the balls of her feet, as if she could keep going all night.

He held out his hand.

She shook it.

“Dr.-to-be Shen,” said Professor Zhou, “that was the first time anyone has lasted to the end of the song in twenty years.” He went to his table and picked up the small plastic trophy shaped like an electron and held it out. “I believe this is yours.”

She took it.

“It’s physically inaccurate,” said Miles, from his chair, faintly.

“It’s an electron,” said Yu Jie, holding it up. “With orbits. It’s a Bohr model, Miles. It’s abandoned in 1925.”

“I know,” said Miles. “It’s perfect.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They walked home at one in the morning, down the hill, the long way, along the old wall, with a bottle of very good whisky, a plastic electron, and a box of leftover dumplings that Fang Hao had pressed on them at the door.

“I won a quiz,” said Miles, under the third lamp.

“You did.”

“You won the karaoke, the dumpling race, the secret gift exchange, and the dance-off.”

“I did.”

“And Professor Zhou.”

“I did not win Professor Zhou. Professor Zhou was undefeated for twenty years. I beat Professor Zhou. That’s different.” She held up the electron under the lamp. “He was very gracious about it. He said he’d been waiting for someone to do it since 2004. He said he was tired.”

Miles stopped under the third lamp.

He looked at her, with the electron and the dumplings and her hair coming down.

“Seven years,” he said. “I didn’t go to that party for seven years. I stood in the corner the first time and left through the fire door.”

“I know.”

“I stayed until one in the morning.”

“You did,” said Yu Jie. “You stayed until the end. Rule three.”

He looked at her for a long moment under the lamp.

“It wasn’t a rule,” he said. “I didn’t stay because of Fang Hao’s rule. I stayed because I didn’t want to leave.” He was quiet. “I didn’t know you could not want to leave a party. I didn’t know that was a thing that happened to people.”

She put the electron in her pocket. She put the dumplings on the wall.

She took his face in her hands.

“It happens,” she said. “When you’re with people you love.”

“I don’t love the whole department.”

“You love some of the department.”

He thought about it. Properly. Fang Hao. Ouyang, shouting about the speed of sound in water. Professor Gao, singing a revolutionary anthem in a flat fierce voice without looking at the screen. Professor Zhou, shuffling gravely in his shirtsleeves, undefeated for twenty years.

“Yes,” said Miles. “I suppose I do.”

“There,” said Yu Jie, and kissed him, under the third lamp, on the old wall, with a box of leftover dumplings beside them going cold.

✦ ✦ ✦

Footnote, added by Dr. Fang Hao to the department newsletter, January:

The Christmas party pool closed at 3:1 against Dr. Wei lasting one hour. Dr. Wei lasted six hours and two minutes. He also won the quiz, ending the theory group’s nineteen-year winning streak, and spoke the words of a Cantonese love song into a microphone in front of sixty colleagues, phonetically, without error. The theory group would like it noted that they are reviewing their preparation.

Professor Zhou has asked that it be noted that he has retired from the dance-off. He says he is “satisfied that the electron is in good hands.”

Dr. Wei collected one hundred and fifty yuan from the pool. He has donated it to the Department’s first-year problem-class fund, for White Rabbit sweets.

chapters.title: Physics Puns, Ranked
chapters.desc: A speech given at the first wedding anniversary dinner, in the back room of a dumpling stall at a night market, by the woman who has heard them all. Fifteen jokes. Ranked. With notes.
chapters.epigraph: “I have been asked to say a few words. I have chosen, instead, to rank his jokes. He has agreed to this. He says it is a fair test.”
chapters.content:
Transcribed by Tao Tao, maid of honour, on the back of a paper menu, at the dumpling stall at the far end of the night market, on the twentieth of June, one year after the garden. Present: twenty-two people on plastic stools. Also an old woman with a rolling pin, who refused to stop making dumplings for the speech.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Thank you all for coming.

“I want to thank Granny Wu, who is making dumplings behind me and has told me twice to hurry up because the water is boiling. I want to thank Su Mei for the cake, which has atoms on it again, and Fang Hao for being Fang Hao, and Tao Tao for writing this down, because Miles asked her to, because he says this is an important primary source.

“I was asked to say a few words tonight.

“I thought about it for a long time. What do you say, at a first anniversary? How do you sum up a year? Three, if you count from 4:01? Nearly four, if you count from the Wednesday?

“And then I realised. I don’t need to sum anything up. He’s already done it. He’s been doing it since the third Wednesday of October, three years ago, on the side of a cup of jasmine tea.

“So tonight, instead of a speech, I am going to rank his jokes.

“He has agreed to this. He says it’s a fair test.

“I have chosen fifteen. Out of, at last count, two hundred and seventy-four. I have rated each one out of ten. The ratings are final and not subject to appeal. Miles has already tried to appeal three of them in the taxi. All appeals were rejected.

“We will go from worst to best.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Fifteen.

“Why can’t you trust an atom? Because they make up everything.

“Rating: three out of ten.

“This was his first. Third Wednesday of October. I want to be very clear: it is a bad joke. It is on T-shirts. It is on mugs. A man at the night market sells it on a keyring. Bai Tianyu’s younger brother has it as his phone background.

“I kept it in my notebook for nine months.

“It’s still a three.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Fourteen.

“I would tell you a joke about sodium, but Na.

“Rating: three out of ten.

“He told this one to my mother. At tea. In our flat. In front of my father. It was the first time she’d come to the flat. She had just sat down at his desk, very carefully, as if it might be infectious. And he panicked, and he told her a joke about sodium.

“There was a long silence.

“Then my father laughed. Out loud. I have never in my life heard my father laugh out loud. My mother turned and looked at him as if he had grown a second head.

“So: the joke is a three. But it made my father laugh at my mother’s first tea. The joke stays a three. The moment is a ten.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Thirteen.

“What did the photon say when the bellboy asked if it needed help with its luggage? No thanks, I’m travelling light.

“Rating: four out of ten.

“This was his second note. The Wednesday after the atoms. And he has re-used it eleven times, including in his wedding speech, on the side of a train ticket, and in a grant application, which Professor Zhou made him take out.

“It loses six points for overuse.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Twelve.

“Schrödinger’s cat walks into a bar. And doesn’t.

“Rating: five out of ten.

“This one is objectively quite good. But he told it to Zhao Zhendong.

“At a banquet. The Zhaos’ seventh wedding anniversary. Zhao Zhendong had asked him to say something, because, he said, Miles was the one who filled the shop with rainbows. So Miles stood up in a private dining room in front of forty extremely dangerous people and told a joke about Schrödinger’s cat.

“Nobody laughed.

“Zhao Zhendong looked at him for four seconds.

“Then he said: Explain.

“And Miles explained quantum superposition to the most frightening man in the city for twenty minutes, with a napkin, while forty extremely dangerous people listened in total silence. And at the end, Zhao Zhendong said, So the cat is both, and Miles said Yes, and Zhao Zhendong said, Good, and sat down.

“Aurelia Chen tells this story at every party. She says it is the best thing she has ever seen.

“The joke is a five. The explanation is a nine.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Eleven.

“A neutron walks into a bar and asks how much for a drink. The bartender says, ‘For you? No charge.’

“Rating: five out of ten.

“Classic. Solid. Reliable. A neutron joke. It is the egg sandwich of physics jokes.

“He has told it every Wednesday that I have been ill. It is, I believe, his way of saying that he will look after me and not charge me for it. I believe this because he told me so, once, at three in the morning, with a fever of his own, and then forgot he’d said it.

“I didn’t forget.

“Still a five.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Ten.

“Why did the physicist break up with the biologist? There was no chemistry.

“Rating: six out of ten.

“Pink. Mine. November, year one. He has asked me to include it so that the list is fair. He says I should be held to the same standard.

“I would like it noted that Tao Tao, who is a biologist, has never forgiven me.”

“I haven’t,” Tao Tao has written here, in the margin of the menu.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Nine.

“What do you call an acid with an attitude? A-mean-o acid.

“Rating: six out of ten.

“This was the one on the Monday after our first real fight since the grant. Not the intercom one. The one in the kitchen, in our first winter on Bell Street, about whether I was working too much, which I was. It was a bad fight. I said things. He said things. He went to the basement and I went to the bakery and we didn’t speak for a whole evening, which is the longest we have ever not spoken since the two weeks in March.

“At two in the morning I went down to the basement to say sorry. He was asleep on the floor under the tank, on his old coat, with a spanner on his chest and his glasses still on, and his face was wet. I had never seen anyone cry in their sleep. I didn’t know people could. I stood on the ramp for a long time. I didn’t wake him. I took off my scarf and put it over him, and went home, and sat at my desk opposite his empty one until it got light, and that was the worst night I have had since the stairwell.

“On Monday morning, there was a sticky note on my tea.

“It said that. A-mean-o acid.

“And underneath: (You were right. I’m sorry. But you were also a bit mean. So was I. Can we both be acids together?)

“It’s a six. But it’s the only joke that has ever ended a fight.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Eight.

“Why did the lecturer catch a cold? Because he left his door open all autumn.

“Rating: seven out of ten.

“Wait. This was mine too. I wrote this on the tub of oranges, when he was ill. Close it at night. Open it on Wednesdays.

“He says he’s including it because it’s the one that started the eggs.

“I accept this. Seven.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Seven.

“Why did the physicist propose with a problem set? Because he knew she’d only say yes to something she’d solved herself.

“Rating: seven out of ten.

“This is the hundred and thirteenth note. It was wrapped around a ring.

“I want to be very honest. As a joke, it’s a four. It’s not really a joke. It’s barely a pun. It’s just a true statement with a question mark on it.

“But he also wrote (This one isn’t a joke) underneath it.

“And there’s a rule in this family, established on the twentieth of June three years ago at about 4:20 in the afternoon on the floor of office 412: if something isn’t a joke, you get extra points for saying so.

“Plus three. Seven.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Six.

“Cu-Te.

“Rating: nine out of ten.

“Mine. I know. But Professor Zhou said it was quite good, and Professor Zhou was undefeated at the department dance-off for twenty years until I beat him, so his word carries weight.

“Also, I’ve just remembered, it was me who made this list, so I can put whatever I want in it.

“Nine.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Five.

“What did one ion say to the other? I’ve got my ion you.

“Rating: nine out of ten.

“This is so bad. It is so bad. It is the worst joke in the whole archive. It is worse than the atoms.

“He told it to me on the second Wednesday of November, three years ago, and I laughed so hard I had to put my head down on his desk, and when I looked up he was standing at the chalkboard looking so pleased with himself that he looked about fourteen.

“I had never seen him look pleased with himself. I didn’t know he could.

“Every time I want to see that face again, I tell him this joke back. I’ve done it forty-one times. It works every time.

“Nine. Out of ten. For the face.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Four.

“Why did the photon take the train? Because it was travelling light, and it had five hours to think about someone.

“Rating: nine out of ten.

“He wrote this the night before I left for the capital. He didn’t sleep. He put it in my cardigan pocket. I found it at 7:41 on the train.

“It isn’t very funny. He said so himself. He wrote, It isn’t a very good joke. I didn’t sleep. I’ll do better in two weeks.

“He also wrote, at the bottom, I love you. For the first time. On a sticky note. Before he’d ever said it out loud.

“I held it in both hands all the way to the capital. Five hours.

“Nine.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Three.

“Why did the physicist lose his glasses every Wednesday? Because his wife wanted him within her focal range.

“Rating: nine out of ten.

“Wait.

“This was mine. This is the note I left in his glasses case with Mr. Pan. I didn’t—” [Here Tao Tao notes that the speaker turned round and looked at her husband, who was sitting on a plastic stool at the front, very red.] “—you put this in? You put this in? How did you even—you knew? You knew about the glasses?”

[Tao Tao notes that the husband nodded.]

“Since when?”

[The husband said: “Case file fourteen.”]

“Fang Hao.”

[Tao Tao notes that Dr. Fang Hao, at the back, put a croissant in front of his face.]

“Fine. Fine. Nine. It’s a nine. Moving on. We will discuss this at home.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Two.

“This isn’t a joke. It was never on a sticky note. It was on a whiteboard, in a glass room, on the eighteenth of March, three years ago, in the bottom right-hand corner, next to a date.

“Still here.

“Rating: ten out of ten.

“It is not funny at all. It is the least funny thing he has ever written.

“I walked past it every morning for two weeks without looking. And then one day, I looked. And I went to see my father the next morning. And everything since then—everything—the room above the bakery, the defence, 4:01, the train, the tank, the ring, this, all of you, these dumplings—everything came after that.

“Two words.

“Ten.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“One.

“The best joke.

“I thought about this for a very long time. I went through all two hundred and seventy-four. I read them all again, at our desks, on Bell Street, at night, while he was asleep.

“And the best joke isn’t on a sticky note at all.

“It’s something he said. Out loud. Once. On a cold night, on a terrace, above a harbour, to a woman he had known when he was sixteen, who asked him if he was happy.

“Elowen told me the line that same night, on the terrace. He told me the rest much later, in the flat on Bell Street. He said that Elowen asked him, and he didn’t know, and he had to think about it, properly, the way he thinks about everything.

“And then he said:

“Since September, I’ve been happy on Wednesdays.

“He said it wasn’t a joke.

“I think it’s the funniest thing anyone has ever said. Because it’s so precise. Because only he would ever give a time. Between 3:45 and about 5:30. On Wednesdays. Because he had been completely, desperately in love for three months and the most romantic thing he could think of to say about it was the timetable.

“It makes me laugh every time I think about it.

“And then it makes me cry. Every time.

“Ten out of ten.

“Miles. You’re happy on Wednesdays.

“Are you happy on the other days now?”

✦ ✦ ✦

[Tao Tao notes: at this point the speaker stopped, and looked at her husband, and waited.

The husband stood up. He was crying, very slightly. He didn’t seem to have noticed.

He said: “Yes.”

Then he thought about it, properly, while twenty-two people on plastic stools at a night market watched him think about it.

Then he said: “All of them. For all n.”

Granny Wu, behind the speaker, stopped making dumplings. She clapped. Once. Very loudly.

Then she said, in her northern dialect, something that the speaker translated afterwards as: “The water is boiling, the speech is over, eat.”

So we did.]

✦ ✦ ✦

Appended, in a small neat hand, on the back of the menu, under Tao Tao’s notes:

Appeal lodged by M.W. re: ranking of joke 15 (atoms). Grounds: the joke was the base case. Without it, there would be no jokes 1–14. A base case cannot be rated by the same standard as the inductive step.

Appeal reviewed by S.Y.J.

Appeal rejected. It’s still a three.

(But I kept it for nine months.)

(And I’ll keep it for all n.)

chapters.title: Miles at Sixteen
chapters.desc: The year before the library. A boy at the back of the advanced physics class who does impressions of the teacher, a tired girl at the end of his table, a girl who reads his notebook out loud, and eight days that taught him to stop wanting things. And the man who, fourteen years later, unlearned it.
chapters.epigraph: “No girlfriends until university.” — Wei Miles, aged sixteen, front page of a physics notebook
chapters.content:
At sixteen, Wei Miles was funny.

Nobody who met him later believed this. Not Fang Hao, not Professor Gao, not the hundred and forty second-years in Lecture Theatre C who posted online about the tragic quiet lecturer who compared himself to a particle. They knew a man who walked into chairs and apologised to them, who ate the same sandwich every day, who stood in the corner at parties and left through the fire door.

At sixteen, he did impressions.

Mostly of Teacher Hu, who taught advanced physics to the top twelve students in the school in a small room at the end of the science corridor with a radiator that clanked. Teacher Hu had a way of saying Obviously before every equation, in a long, rising, tragic voice, as if the universe were letting him down personally. Ob-vi-ous-ly, the force is equal to the mass times the acceleration. Miles could do it perfectly. He did it in the corridor before class, and the other eleven students in advanced physics laughed so hard that once, in October, a girl called Fan Ting had to go to the nurse.

He was the youngest in the class by a year. He was tall and thin and had a cowlick at the back of his head that would not lie down, and glasses that slid down his nose, and a father who taught maths at a different school on the coast and came home every evening and sat at the kitchen table with him working through library books on optics that neither of them fully understood.

He was happy. He didn’t think about it. He didn’t know you were supposed to. He had physics and a cowlick and a father at a kitchen table and eleven people who laughed at his impressions of Teacher Hu.

That was enough.

✦ ✦ ✦

He met Elowen Lin in the library, in the spring of his first year at the school.

She was fourteen. Two years below him. She was sitting at the end of the long table in the back corner, where he always sat, the one by the window that looked out over the sports field, with a pile of maths homework in front of her, asleep.

Not resting. Asleep. Her head on her arms. Her pen still in her hand.

He stood at the other end of the table with his physics notebook and didn’t know what to do.

He sat down. Quietly. At his end. He opened his notebook.

She slept for forty minutes. He worked for forty minutes. When the bell went, she woke with a jolt and stared at him down the length of the table, with a red crease on her cheek from her sleeve, and an expression he didn’t understand at all: like someone waking up in a place they didn’t expect to be safe.

“Sorry,” she said. “Is this your table?”

“It’s the library’s table,” said Miles. “You can sit at it.”

She looked at him for a moment longer.

Then she gathered up her maths and left.

She came back the next day. And the next. She sat at the far end and did her maths, or slept, and he sat at his end and did physics, and neither of them talked. Not for weeks. When they did, it was about nothing. Do you have a pencil. What’s the answer to number six. The radiator’s making that noise again.

He didn’t know, then, why she slept in the library. He didn’t know she came from the Walled City, from a house full of men with long boxes in the garage, and that she was holding up her whole family with her two thin arms, and that her mother had died when she was seven, and that the library was the only place in her life where nobody asked her for anything.

He only knew she was tired, and that she didn’t want anything from him, and that it was nice.

He never did his impressions for her. She never laughed. It didn’t matter. It was the most restful thing in either of their lives.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia Song came in the autumn, a year and a half later.

She was fifteen. She transferred from an expensive school in another city, for reasons nobody was told, and arrived on the first day in a uniform that had been altered by a tailor, with her hair perfect and a gold bracelet on her wrist that was against the rules and that no teacher ever made her take off. Every boy in the school looked at her. Every girl hated her. She liked it that way.

She noticed Miles in the second week.

He was in the corridor outside advanced physics, doing Teacher Hu. Ob-vi-ous-ly. The eleven others were laughing. Aurelia Song, passing on her way to somewhere else, stopped and watched.

Then she laughed too.

Not politely. Out loud. Head back. A great, wicked, delighted laugh that went all the way down the science corridor and made Teacher Hu himself come to the door to see what was happening.

Miles turned round and saw her. And went red to his collar.

“Do it again,” said Aurelia Song.

He did it again.

She laughed again.

That was the beginning.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t understand any of it.

That was the thing he would explain, fourteen years later, in a workroom at the back of a flower shop, to two married women with cake. He didn’t understand that Aurelia Song decided to want him the way she decided to want anything: because it was there, and because it hadn’t occurred to it to want her back. He didn’t understand that she started coming to the library, and sitting at the long table, in the middle, between his end and Elowen’s, and talking. He didn’t understand that Elowen, at the far end, went very still every time she did.

He didn’t understand why, in November, he looked up from his notebook one day and saw the two of them looking at each other down the length of the table with an expression that made the back of his neck go cold.

He was sixteen. He thought the world was made of physics, and physics was made of things that made sense.

He went home and wrote on the front page of his notebook, very neatly, under his name:

No girlfriends until university.

He underlined it twice. He thought it was a rule. He thought rules were things that kept you safe.

He was seventeen in December. His father gave him a book on general relativity. He read it in three days and understood about half of it and was so happy he couldn’t sleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

The eight days started on a Monday in March.

He would never be able to say afterwards exactly what started it. He had tried. At thirty-one, on a terrace above a harbour, he had tried to explain it to Elowen, and couldn’t. At thirty-three, in a flower shop, he had tried again and got as far as eight days before Aurelia cut in.

What he remembered was this:

He came into the library at lunchtime on the Monday and his notebook was not in his bag.

Aurelia had it.

She was standing in the middle of the long table, by the window, holding it open at the front page, with a crowd of people around her, reading it out loud. In her clear, carrying, delighted voice.

No girlfriends until university.

People laughed.

“Isn’t that sweet,” said Aurelia Song. “He’s made a rule. In his little notebook. Miles Wei has a rule.” She looked up and saw him in the doorway. She smiled. “But rules are made to be broken. Aren’t they, Miles? And I’ve decided. You’re mine.”

And at the end of the table, Elowen Lin stood up.

✦ ✦ ✦

He had never heard Elowen raise her voice. Not once in two years of the long table. She didn’t raise it now. She stood up from the end of the table and walked down the length of it, past Aurelia, and took the notebook out of her hands.

Just took it. Quite calmly.

“He isn’t anyone’s,” said Elowen Lin. Her voice was very quiet and very clear. “He’s a person. You can’t just decide.”

Aurelia looked at her.

Nobody in that school had ever taken anything out of Aurelia Song’s hands.

“Can’t I?” she said.

And that was the first day.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t remember most of the next seven clearly. They came back to him in pieces, for years, at three in the morning.

Aurelia waiting for him at the school gate every morning. Elowen walking past without looking at either of them. Aurelia sitting next to him at lunch. Elowen at the far end of the long table in the library, not sleeping any more, very straight, doing maths with a face like stone. The whispers in the corridors. People taking sides. People he didn’t know stopping him on the stairs to ask which one. Fan Ting from advanced physics, who had gone to the nurse laughing at his impression of Teacher Hu, telling him, quite seriously, that he had to choose.

He didn’t want to choose. He didn’t understand what he was choosing between. He liked Elowen because she was quiet and tired and didn’t want anything from him. He liked Aurelia because she laughed. He didn’t want either of them to be his. He didn’t want to be anyone’s.

He was seventeen. He wanted to read about general relativity.

On the fifth day, someone set off the fire alarm in the science corridor, and the whole school stood on the sports field in the rain for an hour, and in the crowd on the field Aurelia said something to Elowen that he didn’t hear, and Elowen said something back that he didn’t hear either, and Aurelia slapped her.

In front of the whole school.

Elowen didn’t slap her back. She just stood there, in the rain, with a red mark on her cheek, and looked at Aurelia with an expression that he would only understand years later: the expression of someone who had grown up in a house full of men who hit people, and had decided a long time ago that she would never be one of them.

The head teacher called all three of them in.

He sat in the head teacher’s office with Aurelia on one side and Elowen on the other, and the head teacher said, This is about you, Wei Miles. Two young women are fighting about you. What do you have to say?

And he understood, then, in that office, for the first time.

It was about him.

Not his fault, exactly. He hadn’t done anything. He had sat at a table and done impressions of Teacher Hu. But he was the thing. He was the reason. A girl had been slapped in the rain in front of four hundred people, and it was because of him.

Because someone had wanted him.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the eighth day, he walked into the library at lunchtime.

They were both there. Aurelia in the middle of the long table. Elowen at the far end. The room was full; people had come to watch, the way they had come every day for a week. There was a silence when he came in.

He looked at them both.

He went to his end of the table. He picked up his bag. He took his notebook out of it. He opened it to the front page, where it said, in his own handwriting, underlined twice, No girlfriends until university.

He looked at it for a long time.

Then he closed it, and put it back in his bag, and turned round, and walked out of the library.

He didn’t say anything. He didn’t look back. He walked down the corridor and out of the main door and across the sports field, where the fire alarm had been, and out of the school gate, and he didn’t stop walking until he was at the bus station, and he got on a bus to the coast, and went home, at two o’clock on a school day, and his father found him sitting at the kitchen table at five o’clock with the book on general relativity open in front of him, not reading it.

“Miles?” said his father. “What happened?”

He didn’t know how to explain. He had been sitting at the table for three hours. His school shirt was stuck to his back from the bus, and his hands, flat on the open book, would not stop shaking, and when he tried to speak his throat closed round the words like a fist. He was seventeen and too old to cry in front of his father, and he did anyway, without making any sound, the tears running off his chin onto general relativity, and his father didn’t say anything about it at all.

“I chose physics,” he said finally. Because that was what the school would say. That was what Fan Ting would say, and the whispers in the corridor, and the head teacher. Wei chose physics over two girls.

His father sat down across from him at the kitchen table.

He didn’t say anything.

Then he said, very gently, “That isn’t a choice, son. That’s a hiding place.”

Miles didn’t understand. He was seventeen.

He went back to school the next week. He sat at the long table in the library, at his end. Elowen came back and sat at hers, and didn’t speak, and neither did he, and it was quiet again. Aurelia didn’t come back to the library at all. In the corridor, she looked at him once, and then didn’t look at him again.

He never did another impression of Teacher Hu.

The eleven others in advanced physics asked, sometimes. Do Teacher Hu. Do the obviously. He said he’d forgotten how.

He hadn’t forgotten. He just knew, now, what happened when people liked you. When they laughed. When they wanted you. It made the world go mad, and people got hurt, and it was because of you.

So he stopped being someone people could want.

It was very easy. You just had to be quiet. You had to stand in corners. You had to not be funny, and not laugh, and make yourself very small, and very dull, and very far away, until nobody looked at you twice.

He was very good at it. He did it for fourteen years.

✦ ✦ ✦

Fourteen years later.

Office 412. The second Wednesday of September. 3:47 p.m.

A knock on the door.

“It’s open,” he said. “Unless you’re from facilities.”

The door opened.

A girl came in. Twenty-two. Yellow sundress, grey cardigan, trainers with biro all over them, a claw clip with four pens in it. She had a notebook held against her chest and a problem she had already solved, with the answer hidden in the margin.

She asked him about the harmonic oscillator.

He did it the long way. Twenty-five minutes. Hermite polynomials. To prove she didn’t need him.

And then he said, You need a different excuse for coming on a Wednesday.

He didn’t know why he said it. It was the first joke he had made out loud to another person in fourteen years. It came out of him before he could stop it, from somewhere very deep and very long unused, the same place that used to do Teacher Hu.

She looked at him.

She didn’t laugh. Not then. She just looked at him, from the chair, with her notebook and her pens and her answer in the margin, as if she had heard something under the joke. As if she had heard the boy who used to do impressions in a corridor, before the library, before the rain.

Then she left. And he sat at his desk for forty minutes and didn’t do any work, and kept looking at the door.

She had left a purple pen with a plastic cat on the end of it. With a question mark painted on its head.

He put it in his top drawer.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nearly three years after that. The garden behind the Hall of Science. A blackboard on an easel.

His father was sitting in the second row, in a brown suit with a pocket square his daughter had made him wear. He was sixty-eight. He had come up on the train from the coast. He had sat at a kitchen table with his son every evening for a year working through library books on optics that neither of them understood.

He watched his son stand at a blackboard in a tuxedo and write Q.E.D. beside a girl in a yellow dress.

He watched his son laugh.

Out loud. In front of everyone. Head back. The way he had laughed at sixteen, in a corridor, doing Teacher Hu.

Afterwards, by the ginkgo tree, he found him, and put a hand on his shoulder.

“Miles,” he said.

“Dad.”

His father looked at him. At the tuxedo. At the chalk on his hands. At his face.

“You came out,” said his father quietly. “Of the hiding place.”

Miles looked at him.

He thought about a kitchen table on the coast, at five o’clock on a school day, seventeen years ago. That isn’t a choice, son. That’s a hiding place.

He hadn’t understood, then. He had been seventeen.

He understood now.

“Yes,” he said. “It took a long time.”

“That’s all right,” said his father. He looked across the lawn, at his new daughter-in-law, who was showing Granny Wu from the night market how the sundial was three degrees wrong. “You had to wait for someone to come and knock.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That night. Bell Street. The second floor.

She was asleep. He was not.

He was at his desk, the old teacher’s desk on the left, facing the window, with the lamp on. He had a notebook open in front of him. Not a new one. An old one. Very old. A physics notebook from a school on the coast, with a cracked spine and a coffee ring on the cover. His mother had found it in a box in the flat by the sea and brought it up on the train, because, she said, she thought he might want it now.

He opened it to the front page.

Wei Miles. Advanced Physics.

And under it, in his own handwriting, aged sixteen, underlined twice:

No girlfriends until university.

He looked at it for a long time.

Then he picked up a pen. The purple one, with the plastic cat on the end, that she had lent him that morning as something borrowed and that he had forgotten to give back.

He drew a single neat line through No girlfriends until university.

And underneath it, in his small neat handwriting, aged thirty-four, he wrote:

Rule withdrawn. Counterexample found.

Second Wednesday of September. 3:47 p.m.

She knocked.

He closed the notebook. He put it in the top drawer of his desk, with a hundred and twelve sticky notes, two napkins, and a floury one from a cinema.

He put the purple pen on top of it. He would give it back in the morning.

Then he turned off the lamp, and went to bed, and lay down beside her in the dark, and she turned over in her sleep, the way she always did, and put her hand on his chest, flat, over his heart.

Not a finger’s width away.

Right there.
